His versatility extends beyond Hindustani music, as he has also accompanied Carnatic performers such as T. N. Krishnan, N. Ramani, U. Shrinivas, and Lalgudi Krishnan. Beyond the classical realm, Kalyanpur has worked with global artists, including touring with A.R. Rahman for the JAI HO World Tour and contributing to recordings with Keith Richards of The Rolling Stones on Katy Perry’s "Legendary Lovers" from her album *Prism*.

Kalyanpur’s contributions to music have been recognized with numerous accolades, including the "TOP" Grade Artist status from All India Radio, the 'Taal – Mani' award from Sur Singar Samiti, the Vidyasagar Award from ITC, and the Sangeet Visharad. He has also received the National Scholarship for Advanced Training from the Government of India and was awarded the prestigious Pandit Jasraj Competition by the Vedic Heritage Center in Long Island, New York.

His performances have taken him to prestigious international festivals, such as the Orient Arts Festival in Estonia, the Edinburgh Festival in Scotland (2003), the Earagal Arts Festival in Ireland, the Jazz Yatra in Mumbai, and the Great Lakes Folk Festival in Lansing, Michigan. Additionally, he has participated in the Saptak Festival, further showcasing his artistry on prominent stages.

Kalyanpur’s influence extends beyond live performances, as he is actively engaged in sharing his knowledge through platforms like the New England School of Music. His presence on social media, including an official website, MySpace, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and YouTube, reflects his commitment to connecting with a global audience. Through his dedication to the tabla and his collaborations across musical genres, Aditya Kalyanpur has established himself as a distinguished figure in the world of Indian classical and contemporary music.

title: Zewde Gebre-Sellassie
text:
Dejazmatch Zewde Gebre-Sellassie was an Ethiopian nobleman, historian, and former deputy prime minister of Ethiopia, born on 12 October 1926 in the village of Galdu, near Addis Ababa. His father, Dejazmatch Gebre Selassie Baria Gabr, was a governor, and his mother, Leult Wolete Israel Seyoum, came from a prominent family, including his grandfather, Ras Seyum Mengesha. His sister was Leult Ijigayehou Asfa Wossen, and he married Woizero Alem Tsehai Araya. Zewde received his early education under a tutor in Addis Ababa before attending schools in Jerusalem and Cairo during Ethiopia’s Fascist occupation. After Ethiopia’s liberation, he studied at Haile Selassie I Secondary School in Addis Ababa, then pursued English literature at the University of Exeter. He later completed legal training at St. Anthony’s College, Oxford, becoming a senior member from 1963 to 1971 and being called to the Bar at Lincoln’s Inn, London. After a period in public service, he returned to Oxford to earn a PhD in history, politics, and economics.

Throughout his career, Zewde held multiple high-ranking positions under Ethiopia’s imperial government. He began as an economic attaché and later headed the Press, Information, and Administration Division at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (1951–53). He then became Director-General of Maritime Affairs (1953–55) and Deputy Minister of Public Works, Transport, and Civil Aviation (1955–57). From 1957 to 1959, he served as Mayor and Governor of Addis Ababa, followed by a posting as Ambassador to Somalia (1959–60). He later became Minister of Justice (1961–63) and Ethiopia’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations (1972–74). In 1974, he briefly served as Minister of the Interior (March–May) and then as Minister of Foreign Affairs (May–November) before the Derg’s violent purge of government officials forced him into exile.

While in exile, Zewde became vice-president of the United Nations Economic and Social Council and later worked as an advisor to the UN Secretariat. He was recognized with national honors from at least seven countries, including the Federal Republic of Germany. In 1998, he joined other prominent Ethiopians in attempting to mediate between Ethiopia and Eritrea during their conflict.

Zewde was also a prolific writer, publishing several books on Ethiopian history and politics. His notable works include *Yohannes IV of Ethiopia: A Political Biography* (1975), *The Conflict of Ethiopia and Eritrea: Causes and Solutions* (2015), *The Blue Nile and its Basins: An Issue of International Concern* (2006), and *The Process of Re-unification of the Ethiopian Empire, 1868-1889* (1971). His academic and diplomatic contributions, along with his historical research, solidified his legacy in Ethiopian and African political and intellectual circles. He passed away on 15 December 2008.

title: Rebecca Romijn
text:
Rebecca Alie O’Connell, known professionally as Rebecca Romijn, is an American actress and former model born on November 6, 1972, in Berkeley, California. Her parents are Elizabeth Romijn, an English as a Second Language instructor, and Jaap Romijn, a custom furniture maker originally from the Netherlands. Romijn’s maternal grandfather was a Presbyterian minister. In her early teens, she struggled with insecurity and scoliosis, which caused her significant pain. Despite her height of 5 feet 11 inches, she played down rumors of being nicknamed the "Jolly Blonde Giant," later admitting she made up the story for humor. She studied music at the University of California, Santa Cruz, before transitioning into modeling, eventually moving to Paris for over three years.

Romijn’s modeling career began in 1991, and she quickly rose to prominence, appearing on the covers of numerous international editions of *Elle*, *Cosmopolitan*, *GQ*, *Esquire*, and *Sports Illustrated*. She worked with major fashion brands such as Escada, Christian Dior, Victoria’s Secret, and Tommy Hilfiger, and walked runways for designers like Giorgio Armani and Anna Molinari alongside supermodels like Naomi Campbell and Cindy Crawford. From 1998 to 2000, she hosted *MTV’s House of Style*, and she frequently appeared on lists of the world’s most beautiful women by publications like *Maxim*, *AskMen*, and *FHM*. She also had a guest role in the animated series *Space Ghost Coast to Coast*.

Her acting career took off in 2000 with her breakout role as Mystique in the *X-Men* film trilogy (2000–2006), a role that required extensive blue body paint and prosthetics. She later reprised the character in an uncredited cameo in *X-Men: First Class* (2011) and is set to return in *Avengers: Doomsday* (2026). She starred in *Femme Fatale* (2002) as dual characters, played Joan in *The Punisher* (2004), and appeared in films like *Rollerball* and *Godsend*. On television, she played Alexis Meade, a transgender character, in *Ugly Betty* (2007–2008) and starred in the short-lived series *Pepper Dennis* and *Eastwick*. She also had recurring roles in *Star Trek: Discovery* (2019) and *Star Trek: Strange New Worlds* (2022–present) as Una Chin-Riley. Additionally, she voiced Lois Lane in the DC Animated Movie Universe and starred as Eve Baird in *The Librarians* (2014–2018). She co-hosted the reality competition show *Skin Wars* and the dating series *The Real Love Boat* (2022–present) with her husband, Jerry O’Connell.

In her personal life, Romijn was married to actor John Stamos from 1998 to 2005, after they met at a Victoria’s Secret show. She later married Jerry O’Connell in 2007, and they have twin daughters born in 2008. Though she resumed using her maiden name, she revealed that she never legally changed it back from Romijn-Stamos. Beyond acting, she has dabbled in music, covering Prince’s "Darling Nikki" and appearing on RuPaul’s album *Realness*. Romijn’s career spans modeling, television, film, and reality TV, showcasing her versatility as an entertainer.

title: Daniel Bedingfield
text:
Daniel John Bedingfield, born on 3 December 1979 in Auckland, New Zealand, is a singer, songwriter, record producer, and actor of New Zealand-British descent. His musical career began in earnest in 2001 with the release of his debut single, "Gotta Get Thru This," which became a number-one hit in the UK. This success was followed by two more UK number-one singles, "If You're Not the One" and "Never Gonna Leave Your Side," all of which were featured on his debut album, *Gotta Get Thru This* (2002). The album, which he recorded at home using digital audio software, became a massive commercial success, selling over 1.6 million copies in the UK alone and more than 4 million worldwide. It reached number two on the UK Albums Chart, establishing Bedingfield as a prominent figure in early 2000s pop music.

In 2004, Bedingfield won a BRIT Award for Best British Male Artist. His second album, *Second First Impression*, was released the same year under Polydor Records, though it failed to match the success of his debut, peaking at number eight in the UK. Despite this, it included two UK Top 20 singles, "Nothing Hurts Like Love" (number three) and "Wrap My Words Around You" (number twelve). The album's third single, "The Way," did not chart as strongly, reaching only number 41. Following this, Bedingfield took an extended hiatus from solo releases but remained active in the music industry, co-writing songs for other artists. Notably, he worked with David Archuleta, Pixie Lott, and K-pop group Spica, co-producing their English-language single "I Did It." He also contributed to tracks by Tessanne Chin and The Raw Men Empire in Israel, as well as dancehall artist Busy Signal in Jamaica.

In 2012, Bedingfield returned to music with the single "Rocks Off," followed by the EP *Stop the Traffik – Secret Fear*. The EP featured experimental tracks and was supported by a controversial music video for the single "Secret Fear." That same year, he began judging on *The X Factor New Zealand*, mentoring the winning act, Jackie Thomas. He also appeared on *The X Factor Around the World* in 2013, performing his hits and collaborating with other judges. Beyond music, Bedingfield acted in the West End production of *The War of the Worlds* in 2016, playing The Artilleryman.

Bedingfield has also been involved in activism, particularly through his mother's organization, Global Angels, which focuses on humanitarian efforts. He helped launch the Stop the Traffik coalition, an anti-slavery campaign, and has used his platform to raise awareness about modern-day slavery. His personal life has included challenges, including a near-fatal car accident in 2004 that left him with severe injuries. He has also been open about being autistic.

As of 2024, Bedingfield announced a UK tour, reaffirming his enduring presence in the music industry. His career has spanned hit songs, songwriting collaborations, television appearances, and theatrical roles, making him a versatile figure in entertainment. His debut album remains a defining work of early 2000s pop, while his later projects showcase his continued creativity and adaptability.

title: Khalid Mahmood Mithu
text:
Khalid Mahmood Mithu (1960–2016) was a prominent Bangladeshi filmmaker and painter who made significant contributions to both the arts and cinema. Born in Dhaka in 1960, he came from a family deeply involved in the arts. His mother, Begum Momtaz Hossain Mithu, was a scriptwriter, and his uncle, Alamgir Kabir, was a well-known film director, which likely influenced his own career path. Mithu pursued higher education at the University of Dhaka, earning a Master of Fine Arts (MFA) in 1986 from the Faculty of Fine Arts.

His career in film began with the play *Dhusor Album*, which he directed in 1993. However, his most notable work in cinema came later with the 2010 film *Gohine Shobdo*, which earned him the prestigious Bangladesh National Film Award for Best Director. This recognition solidified his reputation in the Bangladeshi film industry. His next major project, *Jonakir Alo* (2014), was selected as Bangladesh’s official entry for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, though it did not receive a nomination. Despite this, the film marked another significant achievement in his career.

In addition to his work in film, Mithu was a talented painter. By 2004, he had held 11 solo exhibitions, showcasing his artistic talent and establishing himself as a respected figure in the visual arts. His ability to excel in both film and painting demonstrated his versatility and creativity.

Mithu was married to the painter Kanak Chanpa Chakma, and the couple had two children: a son, Arjo Srestha, and a daughter, Shiropa Purna. His personal life was as vibrant as his professional career, with his family and artistic endeavors playing significant roles.

Tragically, Mithu’s life was cut short on March 7, 2016, when a roadside tree collapsed onto the rickshaw he was traveling in, causing fatal injuries. The accident occurred in Dhanmondi Thana, Dhaka, and his sudden death was a great loss to both the Bangladeshi film and art communities.

Mithu’s legacy endures through his films, *Gohine Shobdo* and *Jonakir Alo*, as well as his contributions to painting. His work continues to be remembered and celebrated in Bangladesh, where he remains an influential figure in the arts. Despite his untimely death, his impact on cinema and visual arts remains significant, and his achievements continue to inspire future generations of artists and filmmakers.

title: Celâl Bayar
text:
Mahmut Celâlettin Bayar, better known as Celâl Bayar, was a prominent Turkish economist and politician who served as the third president of Turkey from 1950 to 1960 and previously as prime minister from 1937 to 1939. Born on May 16, 1883, in Umurbey, Bursa, he was the son of a religious leader and teacher who had emigrated from Ottoman Bulgaria. Bayar began his career working in banking and finance, eventually becoming a key figure in the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP), the political party that led the Young Turk Revolution. He played a significant role in organizing the CUP's branches in Izmir and Bursa and was involved in the 1913 Ottoman coup d'état. During the Turkish War of Independence, he supported the resistance against foreign occupation and participated in the Battle of Aydın. He was later elected to the Ottoman Parliament and served as a deputy for Saruhan (modern-day Manisa) and Izmir.

After the establishment of the Republic of Turkey, Bayar became a leading figure in the country's economic development. He founded İş Bankası, Turkey's first private bank, and played a crucial role in shaping the country's economic policies. As a member of the Republican People's Party (CHP), the sole legal party during the one-party period, he advocated for a blend of state intervention and private enterprise. In 1937, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk appointed him prime minister to implement liberal economic reforms, though his tenure was brief, ending in 1939 when he resigned due to disagreements with İsmet İnönü, Atatürk's successor.

In 1946, Bayar co-founded the Democrat Party (DP) with Adnan Menderes, Fuat Köprülü, and Refik Koraltan, marking the beginning of Turkey's multiparty system. The DP's platform emphasized political democratization, reduced bureaucracy, and economic liberalization while maintaining some elements of statism. The party's success in the 1950 elections led to a peaceful transfer of power, and Bayar was elected president. He was re-elected in 1954 and 1957, serving for a decade. During his presidency, Turkey aligned itself with the Western bloc, joining the Korean War in 1951 and NATO in 1952. Bayar also made the first official visit by a Turkish president to the United States in 1954.

Despite his moderate stance, Bayar's presidency saw significant social and economic changes. Inflationary policies encouraged private enterprise, and political participation expanded, particularly among Anatolians. However, the latter years of his presidency were marked by economic depression and increasing authoritarianism, culminating in the 1955 Istanbul Pogrom. His leadership was also characterized by a more partisan approach, as he publicly supported the DP during elections.

Bayar's presidency ended abruptly with the 1960 military coup. He was arrested and tried by the High Court of Justice on charges of treason and violating the constitution. Initially sentenced to death, his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. Despite two failed suicide attempts, he remained incarcerated until 1964, when he was released due to poor health. His release sparked protests, and he was briefly re-imprisoned before being freed permanently in November 1964. Bayar lived until the age of 103, passing away on August 22, 1986, after a brief illness. He remains one of the longest-lived former heads of state in history.

title: Rachel Weisz
text:
Rachel Weisz, an acclaimed English actress, was born on 7 March 1970 in Westminster, London, and grew up in Hampstead Garden Suburb. Her parents, George Weisz and Edith Ruth Teich, were immigrants to the UK from Hungary and Austria, respectively, fleeing the Nazis in 1938. Her mother converted to Judaism upon marriage, and Weisz’s maternal grandfather, Alexander Teich, was a Jewish activist. Weisz’s family valued the arts and encouraged independent thinking. She attended North London Collegiate School, Benenden School, and St Paul’s Girls School before studying English at Trinity Hall, Cambridge, where she graduated with upper second-class honours. While at university, she co-founded a drama group, Cambridge Talking Tongues, and won a Guardian Student Drama Award for an improvised play. She also trained under master clown Philippe Gaulier at École Philippe Gaulier.

Weisz’s acting career began in the early 1990s with television roles, including *Advocates II* and *Inspector Morse*. Her stage breakthrough came in 1994 with the revival of Noël Coward’s *Design for Living*, earning her a Critics’ Circle Theatre Award. Her film debut was in *Death Machine* (1994), followed by roles in *Chain Reaction* (1996) and *Stealing Beauty* (1996). She gained international recognition as Evelyn Carnahan in *The Mummy* (1999) and its sequel, *The Mummy Returns* (2001). During this period, she also appeared in *Suddenly Last Summer* (1999) at the Donmar Warehouse, earning critical praise.

In the 2000s, Weisz starred in several notable films, including *Enemy at the Gates* (2001), *About a Boy* (2002), and *Runaway Jury* (2003). Her performance as Tessa Quayle in *The Constant Gardener* (2005) earned her an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress, a Golden Globe, and a BAFTA Britannia Award. She also starred in *Constantine* (2005), *The Fountain* (2006), and *Agora* (2009), while winning a Laurence Olivier Award for her stage role in *A Streetcar Named Desire* (2009).

In the 2010s, Weisz continued to balance blockbusters and independent films, appearing in *The Bourne Legacy* (2012) and *Oz the Great and Powerful* (2013), as well as critically acclaimed works like *The Deep Blue Sea* (2011) and *The Favourite* (2018). For *The Favourite*, she won a BAFTA and received another Academy Award nomination. She also ventured into television with *Dead Ringers* (2023) and played Melina Vostokoff in *Black Widow* (2021).

Weisz’s personal life includes a past relationship with director Darren Aronofsky, with whom she has a son, and a marriage to actor Daniel Craig since 2011. They have a daughter together. She became a naturalised American citizen in 2011 and has been a brand ambassador for L’Oréal. Throughout her career, Weisz has been recognised for her versatility, earning multiple awards and critical acclaim across film, television, and theatre.

title: Michael Coulson (barrister)
text:
Michael Coulson was a British barrister, judge, and politician born on 23 November 1927 in the East Riding of Yorkshire, where his family had roots in Driffield. His father was a prosperous wool merchant, and Coulson attended the independent Fulneck School in Leeds before studying at Merton College, Oxford. He fulfilled his national service in the East Riding Yeomanry, part of Wenlock's Horse.

After completing his education, Coulson was called to the Bar by the Middle Temple in 1951 and joined the North Eastern Circuit, though he also practiced in London. He quickly gained a reputation for his exceptional memory, which he used effectively in his legal work. Around this time, he became involved in the Young Conservatives, helping to restructure the organization in northern England and even drafting their constitution. He also served in the Territorial Army, rising to the rank of Major in the Queen's Own Yorkshire Yeomanry.

In 1955, Coulson married Dilys Adair Jones, which brought him a 400-acre farm near Bolton Percy, North Yorkshire. Despite his enthusiasm for farming, he faced challenges, including a failed turkey farming venture during a harsh winter. The turkeys were eventually kept in the farmhouse airing cupboard for warmth, and the entire flock was later destroyed in a dispute with his father-in-law. Coulson also had a passion for horse riding and fox hunting, serving as secretary to meetings of the Bramham Moor and York and Ainsty Point to Point Races.

Coulson’s political career began with his election to Tadcaster Rural District Council, but he quickly aimed higher. In 1958, he was selected as the Conservative candidate for Kingston upon Hull North, a seat held by the Conservatives with a narrow majority. After an energetic campaign, he won the seat in the 1959 general election, increasing the majority to 702. His maiden speech in Parliament was noted for its wit and was reported in *Punch*. He supported Prime Ministers Harold Macmillan and Sir Alec Douglas-Home and was best known for successfully introducing a Private Member’s Bill to abolish the farthing as legal tender. In 1962, he became Parliamentary Private Secretary to the Solicitor General, Sir Peter Rawlinson, and was active in Commonwealth affairs as a member of the Conservative Commonwealth Council’s executive committee.

Coulson lost his parliamentary seat in the 1964 general election but soon advanced in his legal career. In 1965, he became an Assistant Recorder of Sheffield, and two years later, he was appointed Deputy Chairman of the Northern Agricultural Land Tribunal, a role he held for six years. From 1968, he also served as a Regional Chairman of Industrial Tribunals. His marriage to Dilys Adair Jones ended in strain, and in the 1970s, he relocated to the East Midlands to focus on chairing Industrial Tribunals full-time. He became a member of the Belvoir Hunt and, in 1977, married Barbara Chambers, a hunting acquaintance 20 years his junior.

In 1981, Coulson was appointed a Recorder of the Crown Court, and two years later, he became a Circuit Judge on the Midland and Oxford Circuit. Known in his home village of Wymondham, Leicestershire, as the "hunting Judge," he remained active in fox hunting and farming. In 1990, he received his final promotion as a Deputy Circuit Judge. One of his notable rulings came in 1994, when he awarded Trevor McAuley £5,900 in damages for unfair dismissal, including compensation for a campaign of mocking his Irish accent, setting a legal precedent. Coulson retired from the judiciary in 1998 at the age of 70 and died on 18 June 2002.

Throughout his career, Coulson combined his legal and judicial work with his interests in politics, farming, and hunting, leaving a mark in both the legal profession and his community.

title: Jashubhai Dhanabhai Barad
text:
Jashubhai Dhanabhai Barad was a prominent Indian politician from Gujarat, born on 15 September 1955 in the village of Badalpara near Veraval. Hailing from the Yadav (Ahir) community, he was widely respected and affectionately known as the "lion of Saurashtra" and the "lion of Sorath" (Sorath no savaj). His political career was marked by significant contributions to Gujarat's infrastructure and governance.

Barad's political journey began with his election to the Gujarat Legislative Assembly in 1990, representing the Somnath constituency. He was re-elected from the same constituency in 1995 and subsequently served as a Cabinet Minister for Water Resources and Irrigation, where he played a key role in the development of major projects like the Narmada and Ukai Dams. His work in this capacity highlighted his commitment to water resource management and infrastructure development, which were crucial for Gujarat's agricultural and industrial growth.

In 2004, Barad expanded his political influence by winning the Lok Sabha election from the Junagadh constituency, representing Gujarat in the 14th Lok Sabha. His tenure in the national legislature further solidified his reputation as a leader dedicated to regional development. After his Lok Sabha term, he returned to state politics and was elected to the Gujarat Legislative Assembly in 1998 and again in 2012, this time from the Talala Gir constituency. By the time of his death, he was serving his fourth term as a Member of the Legislative Assembly from Talala Gir, demonstrating his enduring connection with the electorate.

Barad's political career was tragically cut short when he passed away on 25 January 2016 at a hospital in Ahmedabad due to complications from a brain tumor. His death was mourned by many, and his legacy was carried forward by his brother, Bhagvanjibhai Barad, who won a subsequent election from the Talala Gir constituency with a substantial margin of 31,000 votes, defeating the BJP candidate Govindbhai Parmar. This family continuity in politics reflected the deep trust and support the Barad family enjoyed in the region.

Throughout his career, Jashubhai Barad was recognized for his leadership in water resource management and his contributions to regional infrastructure. His work earned him the titles "lion of Saurashtra" and "lion of Sorath," symbolizing his strength and dedication to the people of Gujarat. His legacy continues to influence local politics, and his memory remains an important part of the region's political history.

title: Diana Ivanova
text:
Diana Ivanova, a Bulgarian journalist, author, and documentary filmmaker, was born in Montana, Bulgaria, a town that was formerly known as Mihajlovgrad until 1993. She attended a local German school with ties to a school in Schmalkalden, Germany, and later pursued higher education at the University of Sofia, where she earned a Master’s in Journalism in 1991. Her early career included roles as a reporter and moderator at Bulgarian National Television and later as a radio journalist at Radio Free Europe in Prague from 1995 to 2003. In 2003, she completed training as a cultural manager at the International Centre for Culture and Management in Salzburg. She further expanded her expertise with a scholarship at the Institute of Human Sciences in 2005 and later became a group analyst, focusing on political traumas, particularly in Bulgaria and Germany.

Ivanova has been a freelance journalist since 2003, contributing to publications such as n-ost, Dnevnik, Capital (Bulgaria), Abitare, and Foreign Policy. She is also the manager of the New Culture Foundation and has researched the film archives of the Bulgarian secret services. Her journalistic approach, which she calls "slow journalism," prioritizes authenticity and deep engagement with subjects, often focusing on individual and collective traumas shaped by political circumstances. Influenced by social psychologists like Angela Kühner and Kai Erikson, she explores how historical events disrupt social bonds. Her work often revisits the past to understand present-day experiences and fosters cultural exchange through encounter groups and projects.

One of her notable projects is the annual Goatmilk Festival, held in the village of Gorna Bela Rechka in northwestern Bulgaria since 2004. This festival brings together elderly residents and international artists to share stories and memories, promoting intercultural understanding. In 2008, the festival helped replace a stolen village bell with a new one, funded by the Goethe-Institut and supported by European cultural programs. Another significant project, *I Lived Socialism* (2004–2006), collected 171 stories from Bulgarians about the lasting impact of socialism on their lives, later compiled into a book.

Ivanova also initiated *My Street*, a project that began in Bulgaria in 2005 during a waste crisis, encouraging participants to reflect on their relationship with their neighborhoods. This concept was later expanded to Cuba, where she collaborated with photographer Babak Salari to document residents’ stories and streets, culminating in two books. In 2008, she started *Traumas and Miracles*, a project documenting the lives of elderly inhabitants in Bulgaria’s poorest regions, which was exhibited in Vienna and Sofia.

Her filmography includes *Listen* (2014), a documentary about Radio Free Europe’s banned broadcasts in Bulgaria, which won the Best Director Award for its debut. She also contributed to other films, such as *The Town of Badante Women* (2009) and *Father* (2012). Since 2012, Ivanova has facilitated self-awareness groups in Bonn and Sofia, using group analysis to address political traumas. Her written works include *How to Make a Bell* (2010), *My Street: Cuban Stories* (2010), and *Trauma und Wunder* (2016), a collaboration with Babak Salari.

Ivanova has received numerous awards, including the HostwriterPrize in 2014, the Golden Rhyton Festival Award for *Listen*, the Robert Schumann Journalist Award in 2007, and the Writing for Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) prize in 2005. Her work reflects a deep commitment to cultural dialogue, historical reflection, and the healing of collective wounds through art, journalism, and psychology.

title: Cierre Wood
text:
Cierre Marcelle Wood, born on February 21, 1991, was an American former professional football player who played as a running back in the National Football League (NFL). His athletic career took a dramatic turn when he was later convicted of murder. Wood attended Santa Clara High School in Oxnard, California, where he excelled as a standout football player. During his senior year, he rushed for 1,632 yards and scored 20 touchdowns, while also catching eight passes for 182 yards and four additional touchdowns. His junior year was even more impressive, with 2,612 rushing yards and 34 touchdowns. His performance earned him recognition as a USA Today All-American in 2008, and he was selected to play in the 2009 U.S. Army All-American Bowl. Recruiting services like Rivals.com ranked him as a four-star prospect and the eighth-best running back in the nation. He ultimately chose to attend the University of Notre Dame, turning down offers from USC, UCLA, and California.

At Notre Dame, Wood redshirted in 2009 but became a key contributor the following year. After an injury to starter Armando Allen, Wood took over as the primary running back for the final six games of the 2010 season, rushing for 603 yards and three touchdowns while also catching 20 passes for 170 yards and two touchdowns. In his junior year, he fully took over the starting role, recording 1,102 rushing yards and nine touchdowns, along with 27 receptions for 187 yards. His senior season began with a two-game suspension for violating team rules, but he still finished the year with 742 rushing yards and four touchdowns in 11 games, sharing carries with teammate Theo Riddick. After his college career, Wood decided to forgo his final year of eligibility and entered the 2013 NFL draft.

Despite his college success, Wood went undrafted. He was signed by the Houston Texans as an undrafted free agent shortly after the draft but was released in October 2013 for unspecified team rule violations. He then bounced around the NFL, briefly joining the New England Patriots, Baltimore Ravens, and Seattle Seahawks, mostly on practice squads. In 2015, he signed with the Buffalo Bills and was promoted to the active roster before tearing his ACL in Week 5, ending his season. His NFL career fizzled out, and he later played in the Canadian Football League (CFL) with the Hamilton Tiger-Cats and Montreal Alouettes, though his time in Canada was also brief, as he was released in 2018.

Wood’s life took a dark turn in 2019 when he and his girlfriend, Amy Taylor, were arrested for the death of Taylor’s five-year-old daughter, La’Rayah Davis. The child was found with severe bruising and trauma, and authorities alleged that Wood had subjected her to extreme exercise as punishment for being overweight. Wood was charged with first-degree homicide and child abuse. In 2024, he was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 12 years and four months after entering an Alford plea, which acknowledges the evidence against him without a formal admission of guilt, to charges of second-degree murder and child abuse. His football career, once promising, ended in disgrace following this conviction.

title: Kerwin Bell
text:
Kerwin Douglas Bell, born on June 15, 1965, in Live Oak, Florida, is an American football coach and former player. He is currently the head coach of the Western Carolina Catamounts football team, a position he has held since 2021. Before entering coaching, Bell had a 14-season professional playing career as a quarterback in the Canadian Football League (CFL), World League of American Football (WLAF), and the National Football League (NFL).

Bell grew up in the small town of Mayo, Florida, where his parents worked as tobacco farmers. He attended Lafayette County High School, where he excelled in multiple sports, including football, basketball, and baseball. In 1981, he led the Lafayette Hornets to their first and only state football championship, earning the nickname "The Throwin' Mayoan." Despite his success, he received little attention from major college programs due to his high school’s small size and low division. Instead, he walked on to the University of Florida’s football team in 1983, where he was redshirted as a freshman.

In 1984, injuries to more experienced quarterbacks thrust Bell into the starting role for the Florida Gators. In his first game, he faced the defending national champion Miami Hurricanes on a nationally televised ESPN broadcast. He threw a game-winning touchdown pass with under a minute left, though Miami ultimately won. His performance solidified him as the team’s starting quarterback. That season, under head coach Charley Pell (who was later fired for NCAA violations), Bell led the Gators to a 9–1–1 record and was named SEC Player of the Year. Despite NCAA penalties that vacated the team’s SEC championship, Bell continued to excel, earning All-SEC and All-American honors in subsequent seasons. He finished his college career with 7,585 passing yards and 56 touchdowns.

After graduating in 1987 with a degree in psychology, Bell entered the NFL as a seventh-round draft pick of the Miami Dolphins. He never started an NFL game but did complete all five of his career passes for 75 yards and a touchdown, giving him the highest passer rating in NFL history (albeit in a small sample). His professional career primarily consisted of stints in the CFL and WLAF, where he played for teams like the Edmonton Eskimos, Toronto Argonauts, and Winnipeg Blue Bombers. His best season came in 1998 with the Argonauts, when he threw for 4,991 yards and 27 touchdowns, earning a CFL All-Star selection.

After retiring as a player, Bell transitioned into coaching. He started at Trinity High School in Ocala, Florida, leading the Celtics to a state championship in 2005. In 2007, he became the head coach at Jacksonville University, guiding the Dolphins to three conference championships in nine seasons. In 2016, he moved to Valdosta State University, where he led the Blazers to an undefeated 14–0 season and an NCAA Division II national championship in 2018. His tenure at Valdosta State earned him recognition for overseeing the highest-scoring offense in Division II that year.

In 2019, Bell joined the University of South Florida (USF) as offensive coordinator under head coach Charlie Strong, but he was dismissed along with the entire staff after the season. In 2021, he was hired as the head coach at Western Carolina, where he led the Catamounts to their first winning season in six years in 2022. Throughout his career, Bell has been known for his offensive coaching philosophy, influenced by his time under Steve Spurrier at Florida, where he learned the "Fun 'n' Gun" system. His ability to develop high-scoring offenses has been a defining feature of his coaching success.

title: Jacques Cousteau
text:
Jacques-Yves Cousteau (1910–1997) was a French naval officer, oceanographer, filmmaker, and author renowned for his pioneering work in underwater exploration and marine conservation. Born in Saint-André-de-Cubzac, France, Cousteau initially pursued a career in the French Navy, but an automobile accident in the 1930s forced him to shift his focus to underwater research. His early experiments with diving equipment, including the use of Fernez underwater goggles, laid the groundwork for his later innovations.

During World War II, Cousteau co-invented the Aqua-Lung, the first successful open-circuit self-contained underwater breathing apparatus (SCUBA), with Émile Gagnan. This invention revolutionized underwater exploration, enabling extended dives and the production of groundbreaking underwater documentaries. His 1953 book, *The Silent World: A Story of Undersea Discovery and Adventure*, correctly predicted the echolocation abilities of porpoises and was adapted into an acclaimed documentary film. Co-directed with Louis Malle, *The Silent World* won the 1956 Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival and the Academy Award for Best Documentary in 1957, making it the first—and for many years, the only—documentary to achieve both honors.

Cousteau’s career spanned decades of exploration and advocacy for ocean conservation. In 1946, he co-founded the GERS (Underwater Studies and Research Group) of the French Navy, advancing underwater research and archaeology. His expeditions aboard the research vessel *Calypso*—leased for a symbolic one franc a year—led to discoveries such as the wreck of the *Britannic* and the French ship *La Therese*. He also pioneered projects like *Precontinent* and *Conshelf*, which explored long-term underwater habitation, and developed the *Denise Diving Saucer*, an experimental submarine.

A prolific filmmaker, Cousteau hosted *The Undersea World of Jacques Cousteau* (1966–1976) and *The Cousteau Odyssey* (1977–1982), bringing the wonders of the ocean to millions. He authored numerous books, including *The Shark: Splendid Savage of the Sea* (1970), and co-founded the Cousteau Society in 1973 to promote ocean protection. His work earned him numerous accolades, including the UN’s International Pahlavi Environment Prize in 1977 and the U.S. Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1985. He was also elected to the Académie française in 1988.

Cousteau’s personal life was marked by both joy and tragedy. He married Simone Melchior in 1937, with whom he had two sons, Jean-Michel and Philippe. Philippe, who often joined his father on expeditions, died in a 1979 plane crash, deeply affecting Cousteau. After Simone’s death from cancer in 1990, Cousteau remarried in 1991 to Francine Triplet, with whom he had two more children. Cousteau remained a tireless advocate for the ocean until his death in 1997, leaving behind a legacy of scientific discovery, environmental activism, and a profound influence on global understanding of marine life.

title: André Le Nôtre
text:
André Le Nôtre (12 March 1613 – 15 September 1700) was a French landscape architect and the chief gardener to King Louis XIV, renowned for his revolutionary designs that epitomized the French formal garden style, known as *jardin à la française*. Born in Paris into a long line of royal gardeners, Le Nôtre’s grandfather, Pierre Le Nôtre, had overseen the Tuileries Garden, and his father, Jean Le Nôtre, served as head gardener under Louis XIII. This upbringing immersed Le Nôtre in horticulture from an early age, allowing him to develop both practical and theoretical expertise. He was educated in mathematics, painting, and architecture, studying under the painter Simon Vouet and architect François Mansart, where he forged a lifelong friendship with Charles Le Brun, a key collaborator in his future projects.

Le Nôtre’s career began in 1635 when he was appointed principal gardener to Gaston, Duke of Orléans. Two years later, he succeeded his father as head gardener of the Tuileries. His early work included modernizing the gardens of Fontainebleau (1645–1646) and designing parterres and terraces for Anne of Austria. By 1657, he had risen to Controller-General of the Royal Buildings, overseeing all royal gardens in France. His work was highly influential, yet he rarely documented his methods, instead conveying his vision through his gardens. Louis XIV, whom he advised closely, ennobled him in 1675. Le Nôtre’s reputation extended beyond France; he even accompanied the court during the Siege of Cambrai in 1677.

His first major design, the gardens of Vaux-le-Vicomte (1657–1661), was a collaboration with architect Louis Le Vau and painter Charles Le Brun. The project showcased Le Nôtre’s mastery of symmetry, perspective, and forced focal points, such as a hidden canal and an illusionary grotto. The gardens were completed in 1661, just before the arrest of their patron, Nicolas Fouquet, whose downfall allowed Le Nôtre’s team to transition into royal service.

Le Nôtre’s most celebrated work is the gardens of Versailles, where he transformed Louis XIV’s hunting lodge into a grand palace surrounded by meticulously designed landscapes. He introduced radiating avenues, including the expansive Avenue de Paris, and created a city plan that later inspired Washington, D.C.’s layout. His work at Versailles became the model for French formal gardens, characterized by geometric parterres, meticulously trimmed hedges, and water features.

Beyond Versailles, Le Nôtre designed gardens at Fontainebleau, Saint-Germain-en-Laye, Saint-Cloud, and Chantilly, often collaborating with his brother-in-law, Pierre Desgots. In Paris, he extended the Tuileries’ western vista, laying the groundwork for the Champs-Élysées. Abroad, his designs influenced gardens in England (Bicton Park, Greenwich Park), Italy (Racconigi, Venaria, Turin), and elsewhere. His later projects included the gardens of Château de Meudon and the Hôtel de Saint-Aignan in Paris.

Le Nôtre’s legacy endures as a pioneer of garden design, his work often contrasted with that of England’s Capability Brown. His innovations in symmetry, perspective, and grandeur redefined European landscape architecture. He died in 1700, leaving an indelible mark on the art of garden design. His life was dramatized in the 2014 film *A Little Chaos*, where he was portrayed by Matthias Schoenaerts.

title: Asafa Powell
text:
Asafa Powell, born on 23 November 1982 in Spanish Town, Jamaica, is a retired Jamaican sprinter who specialized in the 100 meters. He set the world record for the 100 meters twice, first with a time of 9.77 seconds in June 2005 and then with 9.74 seconds in September 2007. His personal best of 9.72 seconds ranks fourth on the all-time list, and as of September 2016, he had broken the 10-second barrier 97 times, more than any other athlete. Powell also holds the world record for the 100-yard dash, with a time of 9.09 seconds set in 2010. In 2016, he won an Olympic gold medal in the 4 × 100 meters relay.

Powell competed in the 100 meters at the 2004, 2008, and 2012 Olympics, finishing fifth in both 2004 and 2008. In 2012, he placed eighth after suffering a groin injury during the race. At the 2007 World Championships in Osaka, he won a bronze medal in the 100 meters and a silver in the 4 × 100 meters relay. He also achieved success at the Commonwealth Games, winning two gold medals and a silver. At the 2009 World Championships, he earned a bronze in the 100 meters and gold in the relay. Powell won the 100 meters at the IAAF World Athletics Final five times and was formerly the 100 meters world record holder.

In 2013, Powell and teammate Sherone Simpson tested positive for the stimulant oxilofrine. Both athletes withdrew from the 2013 World Athletics Championships, claiming they did not knowingly or willfully take a banned substance. They received an 18-month suspension in April 2014, but the Court of Arbitration for Sport lifted the ban in July 2014 after determining that the positive test resulted from an undisclosed ingredient in a supplement they had taken.

Powell, the youngest of six sons of two ministers, attended Ewarton Primary School and Charlemont High School in Jamaica. Initially planning to become a mechanic, he began running while studying in Kingston. His eldest brother, Donovan, was a 60 meters finalist at the 1999 World Indoor Championships. Powell joined the MVP Track & Field Club and was coached by Stephen Francis from 2001 onward.

Powell’s early career included competing at the ISSA High School Championships, where he finished fourth in the 200 meters and third in the 100 meters heats in 2000. After being coached by Stephen Francis, he won the Boys Under-20 100 meters at the JAAA National Championships in 2002 with a time of 10.50 seconds. At the 2002 Commonwealth Games, he finished fifth in the 100 meters semi-finals but won a silver medal in the 4 × 100 meters relay. In 2003, he was disqualified for a false start at the World Championships but later ran in the relay, where Jamaica failed to finish. He won his first national 100 meters title that year.

In 2004, Powell ran his first sub-10 second race (9.99 seconds) and set a national record of 9.87 seconds. He finished fifth in the Olympic 100 meters final but won both the 100 and 200 meters at the World Athletics Final. The following year, he broke the 100 meters world record with a time of 9.77 seconds in Athens, surpassing Tim Montgomery’s annulled record. He won the Jamaican National Championships but missed the World Championships due to a groin injury.

Powell’s 2006 season was his most successful, as he won gold in the 100 meters and the 4 × 100 meters relay at the Commonwealth Games. He equaled his world record twice and won all six Golden League events, earning $250,000. He was named IAAF World Athlete of the Year and received multiple awards. In 2007, despite injuries and a disappointing third-place finish in the World Championships 100 meters final, he broke the world record again with a 9.74-second run. He won silver in the relay and ended the year with another World Athletics Final victory.

In 2008, Powell faced injuries but still won an Olympic gold medal in the 4 × 100 meters relay, anchoring the team to a world record. At the 2009 World Championships, he won a bronze in the 100 meters and gold in the relay. His career was marked by consistent excellence, though plagued by injuries and a doping suspension. Powell retired as one of the greatest sprinters in history, known for his speed, record-breaking performances, and contributions to Jamaican track and field.

title: Carmelo Anthony
text:
Carmelo Anthony, born on May 29, 1984, in Brooklyn, New York, is a former professional basketball player who spent 19 seasons in the NBA. Widely regarded as one of the greatest scorers in NBA history, Anthony was a ten-time NBA All-Star, a six-time All-NBA Team member, and was named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team in 2021. He will be inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame twice in 2025—once as an individual player and again as part of the 2008 U.S. Olympic team.

Anthony had a challenging upbringing. His father, Carmelo Iriarte, of Puerto Rican and African descent, died when Anthony was two, and his mother, Mary Anthony, raised him and his siblings. The family moved to Baltimore when Anthony was eight. As a high school player at Towson Catholic, Anthony excelled, earning multiple player-of-the-year honors despite academic struggles. After transferring to Oak Hill Academy for his senior year, he led the team to a 32-1 record and was named a Parade First-Team All-American. He was also part of the 2002 McDonald’s All-American Game, where he won the dunk contest.

At Syracuse University, Anthony had an immediate impact as a freshman, averaging 22.2 points and 10.0 rebounds per game. He led the Orangemen to their first NCAA championship in 2003, earning the NCAA Tournament’s Most Outstanding Player award. His 33-point performance against Texas in the Final Four set an NCAA tournament record for most points by a freshman. After one dominant season, he declared for the 2003 NBA draft.

Selected third overall by the Denver Nuggets, Anthony quickly became a star. As a rookie, he averaged 21.0 points per game, setting multiple franchise and league records, including the youngest player to score 40 points in a game. He was named to the All-Rookie First Team and helped turn the Nuggets from a losing team to a playoff contender. Over his eight seasons in Denver, Anthony led the team to six straight playoff appearances, including a trip to the Western Conference Finals in 2009.

In 2011, Anthony was traded to the New York Knicks, where he became a franchise icon. On January 24, 2014, he set a Knicks single-game scoring record with 62 points against the Charlotte Bobcats, also breaking the Madison Square Garden scoring record. After a season with the Oklahoma City Thunder, a brief stint with the Houston Rockets, and two seasons with the Portland Trail Blazers, he finished his career with the Los Angeles Lakers.

Anthony was a dominant force for Team USA, winning four Olympic medals—including three golds (2008, 2012, 2016) and a bronze in 2004. He was the U.S. Olympic team’s all-time leading scorer and rebounder as of 2016. He ranks tenth on the NBA’s all-time scoring list.

Off the court, Anthony’s high school and college careers were marked by his talent, though he faced academic challenges before committing to Syracuse. His NBA career was defined by his scoring ability, leadership, and impact on multiple franchises. His legacy as a scorer and international basketball icon is cemented by his accolades, Hall of Fame induction, and enduring influence on the game.

title: Jorge Enríquez
text:
Jorge Enríquez García, born on 8 January 1991 in Mexicali, Baja California, was a Mexican professional footballer who played primarily as a defensive midfielder. He is best known for his contributions to the Mexican national team, particularly in youth and Olympic competitions, where he won a gold medal. Enríquez began his professional career with C.D. Guadalajara, making his debut on 5 February 2010 in a match against Pachuca CF during the Bicentenario tournament. He entered the game in the 86th minute as a substitute for Adolfo Bautista. His first goal for Chivas came in the quarter-finals of a tournament, scoring from outside the penalty area against Monarcas Morelia.

Enríquez’s club career included a loan spell with Club León in 2015, where he was sent for six months before returning to Guadalajara. Later, in June 2018, he was transferred to Omonia, marking a move outside of Mexico. During his time with Guadalajara, he won the Copa MX in the Apertura 2015 season, adding to his domestic accolades.

Internationally, Enríquez made his mark early in his career. He first represented Mexico at the 2011 CONCACAF U-20 Championship, where Mexico won the tournament and qualified for the 2011 Pan American Games. He was also part of the U-22 squad for the 2011 Copa América, though Mexico was eliminated in the group stage. At the 2011 FIFA U-20 World Cup, Mexico reached the semi-finals before losing to Brazil but secured third place by defeating France. Enríquez was recognized for his performance, earning the Bronze Ball as the tournament’s third-best player.

Enríquez continued to excel in youth competitions, helping Mexico win gold at the 2011 Pan American Games by defeating Argentina in the final. His most significant achievement came at the 2012 Summer Olympics, where he played a crucial role in Mexico’s gold medal-winning campaign. He contributed key passes and scored the first goal in the quarter-finals against Senegal, demonstrating his impact on the team’s success.

In addition to his Olympic gold, Enríquez won the CONCACAF U-20 Championship in 2011, the CONCACAF Olympic Qualifying Championship in 2012, and the Toulon Tournament in 2012. His individual honors also include the FIFA U-20 World Cup Bronze Ball in 2011. Enríquez’s career statistics reflect his contributions, though his last recorded international match was on 25 July 2013.

Enríquez’s legacy is defined by his success in youth and Olympic football, where he played a pivotal role in Mexico’s triumphs. His ability to perform at high levels in international competitions, combined with his technical skills and leadership as a midfielder, cemented his reputation as one of Mexico’s most accomplished young players of his era.

title: Rohit Sharma
text:
Rohit Sharma, born on 30 April 1987 in Bansod, Nagpur, is one of India’s most accomplished cricketers. A right-handed opener, he is known for his elegant strokeplay and has set numerous batting records. Sharma holds the record for the highest individual score in ODIs (264) and is the only player to score three double centuries in the format. He is also the leading run-scorer in T20 Internationals and holds the record for the most sixes in international cricket. Sharma has been a key figure in India’s limited-overs success, leading the team in ODIs and T20Is, and was the captain of the squad that won the 2024 T20 World Cup, after which he retired from the format. He was also part of India’s 2007 T20 World Cup-winning team and captained the side to victories in the 2013 and 2023 ICC Champions Trophies.

Sharma began his international career in 2007 and has since become one of the most decorated Indian cricketers. He made his ODI debut against Ireland and quickly established himself as a reliable middle-order batsman. His breakthrough came in the 2013 Champions Trophy, where he played a crucial role in India’s victory as an opener. He later shattered the ODI record with his 264-run innings against Sri Lanka in 2014. In the 2019 World Cup, he became the first batsman to score five centuries in a single edition and finished as the tournament’s top run-scorer, earning the Golden Bat.

In Test cricket, Sharma made his debut in 2013 against the West Indies, scoring a century on debut. He later became India’s Test captain in 2022 but announced his retirement from the format in 2025 after a disappointing run of form. Despite this, he scored 4,301 runs in 61 Tests at an average of 40.57, including a double century against South Africa in 2019.

Sharma’s leadership has been pivotal in Indian cricket. He led the Mumbai Indians to five IPL titles, the most by any captain in the tournament’s history. He also guided India to victories in the 2018 and 2023 Asia Cups and the 2018 Nidahas Trophy. Under his captaincy, India became the first team to win all ICC tournament finals, including the 2024 T20 World Cup.

In his personal life, Sharma married Ritika Sajdeh in 2015, and the couple has two children. He is a practitioner of the Sahaj Marg meditation technique and follows an eggetarian diet. Sharma has been recognized with the Arjuna Award (2015) and the Khel Ratna Award (2020), India’s highest sporting honors.

Throughout his career, Sharma has been a prolific run-scorer and a consistent match-winner. His ability to anchor innings and accelerate when needed has made him one of the greatest opening batsmen of all time. His records, leadership, and contributions to Indian cricket cement his legacy as one of the sport’s finest players.

title: Felix Newman
text:
Felix Newman, born in 1993, is a British rower who has achieved significant success in both academic and competitive rowing circles. He began his rowing career at Abingdon School, where he earned school colors and served as the captain of the Abingdon School Boat Club. After completing his education at Abingdon in 2012, he went on to attend Selwyn College, Cambridge. During his time at Selwyn, he was recognized for his achievements by winning a British Education Award in 2018.

Newman’s rowing career includes notable accomplishments in both university and international competitions. In 2014 and 2015, he was selected to row for the Goldie crew, a prestigious rowing team associated with St. Edmund’s College, Cambridge. His breakthrough came in 2016 when he was chosen for the bow seat of the Cambridge boat in the University Boat Race, a historic and highly competitive event between Oxford and Cambridge. Cambridge won the race that year, marking a significant victory for Newman and his team.

Beyond university-level competition, Newman has also excelled at the Henley Royal Regatta, one of the most prestigious rowing events in the world. He has been part of winning crews in this regatta on three separate occasions. Two of these victories came in the Princess Elizabeth Cup, a prestigious event for lightweight rowers, while the third victory was in the Thames Cup, another major competition. His success at Henley underscores his skill and consistency in elite rowing.

In addition to his university and regatta achievements, Newman has represented Great Britain on the international stage. In 2011, he was part of the men’s coxed four team at the World Rowing Junior Championships, which were held at Eton, England. This early international exposure highlights his talent and potential, which he has continued to develop throughout his career.

Newman’s career reflects a combination of academic achievement, leadership in school sports, and high-level competitive success. From his early days at Abingdon School to his victories in the Boat Race and Henley Royal Regatta, he has demonstrated excellence in rowing. His contributions to both university and national teams, along with his accolades such as the British Education Award, establish him as a notable figure in British rowing. His journey from school-level competition to international representation showcases his dedication and achievements in the sport.

title: Levi Roots
text:
Levi Roots, whose real name is Keith Valentine Graham, is a Jamaican-British businessman and celebrity chef best known for his Reggae Reggae Sauce. Born on 24 June 1958 in Clarendon, Jamaica, he was raised by his grandmother before moving to the UK at age 11 to join his parents. Initially raised as a Christian, he converted to the Rastafari faith at 18. According to the *Sunday Times Rich List*, his net worth is estimated at £30 million.

Roots initially gained fame as a musician, performing with artists like James Brown and Maxi Priest and even receiving a MOBO award nomination for Best Reggae Act in 1998. He was a close friend of Bob Marley when Marley lived in the UK and performed at a special event for Nelson Mandela in 1996. His transition into the food industry began with the creation of Reggae Reggae Sauce, a jerk barbecue sauce. In 2006, he sold 4,000 bottles at the Notting Hill Carnival, which helped launch his brand. His breakout moment came in 2007 when he appeared on *Dragons' Den*, seeking £50,000 for a 20% stake in his business. Despite mistakenly claiming a massive order (2.5 million litres instead of 2,500 kilograms), investors Peter Jones and Richard Farleigh offered him the money—for a 40% stake. Shortly after, Sainsbury’s began stocking the sauce in 600 stores. Roots initially claimed the recipe came from his grandmother, but later admitted it was a marketing ploy after disputes over its origins.

Beyond his sauce, Roots ventured into restaurants, opening the Papine Jerk Centre in Battersea from 2010 to 2012, where his children also worked. He provided lunchtime meals for Thames Christian College. In 2015, he opened a franchise restaurant in Westfield Stratford City, which closed in 2019. He has also written cookbooks, including *Levi Roots' Reggae Reggae Cookbook* (2008) and *Caribbean Food Made Easy* (2009), the latter accompanied by a BBC2 cooking show. His television appearances include *Ready Steady Cook*, *Celebrity Mastermind*, *Big Brother*, and a guest role in the 2011 film *Anuvahood*. In 2018, he appeared in *Death in Paradise* as Billy Springer. He joined the twenty-third series of *Celebrity Big Brother* in 2024 but was evicted after 11 days.

Roots’ personal life has been marked by challenges. He has eight children with seven different mothers and has faced legal troubles, including a six-month prison sentence at 15 for assaulting a police officer and a 1986 conviction for drug possession. He has been open about his difficult relationship with his father, whom he described as a "bit of a stranger." Despite these struggles, he has taken on prominent roles, such as becoming Chair of the St Pauls Carnival in Bristol in 2021 and Patron of RIFT Social Enterprise in 2024, which supports ex-offenders and the long-term unemployed. He has also received honorary doctorates from the University of the West of England and the University of Westminster.

title: Huang Xing
text:
Huang Xing (1874–1916) was a prominent Chinese revolutionary leader and politician who played a crucial role in the overthrow of the Qing Dynasty and the establishment of the Republic of China. Born in Gaotang, now part of Changsha in Hunan Province, Huang was a descendant of the famed Song Dynasty scholar and artist Huang Tingjian. He initially studied at the prestigious South Changsha Academy and later earned his Jinshi degree at the young age of 22. In 1898, he was selected to study at Wuchang Lianghu College, graduating in 1901. In 1902, he traveled to Japan to further his education at Tokyo's Kōbun Institute, where he developed a deep interest in military affairs and trained in modern warfare under a Japanese officer. His dedication to discipline was evident in his daily routine of practicing horsemanship and shooting.

Huang Xing's revolutionary career began in 1903 when he organized the Anti-Russia Volunteer Army in Japan to resist Russian expansionism in China. The group was quickly disbanded, but Huang remained committed to the revolutionary cause. Later that year, he returned to China and co-founded the Huaxinghui, a secret society dedicated to overthrowing the Qing Dynasty. He was elected its president and worked with other revolutionary factions to plan uprisings, including a failed 1905 attempt in Changsha. In Japan, he met Sun Yat-sen and became a key leader in the Tongmenghui, the revolutionary organization that sought to establish a republic in China. Over the next several years, Huang participated in multiple failed uprisings, including the Qinzhou, Fangcheng, and Zhen Nanguan uprisings, as well as the Huanghuagang Uprising in 1911, during which he lost two fingers in battle, earning him the nickname "Eight-Fingered General."

Despite these setbacks, Huang's efforts contributed to the eventual success of the Wuchang Uprising in October 1911, which marked the beginning of the Xinhai Revolution. Afterward, he commanded revolutionary forces in the Battle of Yangxia against Qing loyalists and became a leader of the Nanjing Interim Government. However, his relationship with Yuan Shikai, the provisional president of the Republic of China, soured after Yuan assassinated Huang's ally, Song Jiaoren, in 1913. Huang led resistance against Yuan during the Second Revolution but was forced to flee to Japan and later the United States. While in exile, he worked to raise funds to oppose Yuan's self-proclamation as emperor in 1915. After Yuan's death in 1916, Huang returned to China but died a few months later in Shanghai at the age of 42 due to cirrhosis. He was posthumously honored with a state funeral and buried on Yuelu Mountain in Changsha.

Huang Xing had several notable children, including Huang Yiou, a young revolutionary leader, and Huang Yihuan, known for his work with the blind community. His legacy is commemorated in various ways, including streets and parks named in his honor, a museum at his former residence, and a postage stamp issued in 1932. In modern times, he was portrayed by Jackie Chan in the 2011 film *1911*, released on the centennial of the Wuchang Uprising. Huang Xing's contributions as a revolutionary and military leader, alongside Sun Yat-sen, remain integral to the founding of modern China.

title: Jean-Claude Van Damme
text:
Jean-Claude Van Damme, born Jean-Claude Camille François Van Varenberg on 18 October 1960 in Berchem-Sainte-Agathe, Brussels, Belgium, is a Belgian martial artist and actor who achieved global fame as an action star. Raised in a bilingual family, he was introduced to Shotokan karate at age ten by his father and eventually earned a 2nd-dan black belt. His early competitive success included winning the European Professional Karate Association middleweight championship in 1979 and the Mr. Belgium bodybuilding title in 1978. Later, he trained in ballet, Taekwondo, and Muay Thai, citing ballet as particularly grueling physical preparation.

Van Damme moved to the United States in 1982, initially struggling financially while pursuing acting. His breakthrough came with *Bloodsport* (1988), a martial arts film based on the alleged true story of Frank Dux, which launched his career. The film’s success led to a string of action hits, including *Cyborg* (1989), *Kickboxer* (1989), *Double Impact* (1991), and *Universal Soldier* (1992). These films established him as a leading action star, known for his martial arts skills and charisma. He also achieved sex symbol status in the late 1980s and early 1990s, with films like *Lionheart* (1990) featuring his signature rear nudity.

Despite his early success, Van Damme’s popularity waned in the late 1990s and early 2000s. However, he made a critically acclaimed comeback with *JCVD* (2008), a meta-crime drama where he played a fictionalized version of himself. Later, he returned to action films, appearing as a villain in *The Expendables 2* (2012) and starring in projects like *Enemies Closer* (2013) and *Kickboxer: Retaliation* (2018). He also ventured into voice acting, contributing to *Minions: The Rise of Gru* (2022) and *Darkness of Man* (2024), while starring in the television series *Jean-Claude Van Johnson* (2016–2017).

Throughout his career, Van Damme’s films have grossed over $3.3 billion worldwide, cementing his status as an action cinema icon. Beyond acting, he has supported conservationist and animal rights causes. His journey from a struggling martial artist to a Hollywood star, marked by resilience and reinvention, reflects his enduring legacy in both film and combat sports.

title: Earl Garrison
text:
Earl Garrison was a notable political figure in Oklahoma, serving as a state senator from District 9 between 2004 and 2016. His district encompassed Muskogee and Wagoner counties, areas he represented with a focus on both education and rural interests. Garrison succeeded longtime State Senator "Bulldog" Ben Robinson, who was barred from seeking reelection due to term limits, marking a generational shift in the district's leadership. During his time in office, Garrison held several significant leadership roles, including Minority Whip from 2011 to 2014, where he played a key part in coordinating the Democratic caucus in the Republican-dominated state Senate. He also served as Assistant Minority Leader, further establishing his influence within the legislative body.

Beyond his political career, Garrison had a diverse professional background. He worked as an educator, reflecting his commitment to public service and community development. Additionally, he was a rancher, which aligned with his deep ties to rural Oklahoma and its economic needs. His military service was another defining aspect of his life; he served in the United States Air Force, demonstrating a lifelong dedication to civic duty and discipline. These experiences likely shaped his approach to legislation, particularly in areas related to veterans' affairs, education, and rural economic policies.

Garrison's legacy extended beyond his own career, as his daughter, Jessica Jean Garrison, entered the political arena. In November 2021, she announced her candidacy for Oklahoma's U.S. Senate seat held by James Lankford, though she later shifted her campaign to the open seat created by the retirement of Senator Jim Inhofe. This transition into state politics by a family member suggests a continuation of the Garrison name in Oklahoma politics, building on the foundation Earl Garrison established during his twelve years in the Senate.

Throughout his tenure, Garrison was involved in various legislative efforts, though the specifics of his legislative record are not detailed in the provided article. His roles as Minority Whip and Assistant Minority Leader indicate that he was a key strategist within the Democratic Party in Oklahoma, often navigating a challenging political landscape where Republicans held significant power. His career highlights the importance of perseverance and leadership in state politics, particularly for Democrats in a conservative-leaning state.

Garrison's professional and personal life were deeply intertwined with his service to Oklahoma. As an educator, he likely brought a focus on policy related to schools and higher education, while his ranching background would have informed his stance on agricultural and land-use issues. His military service further underscored his commitment to public service and may have influenced his positions on defense, veterans' benefits, and national security. Though the article does not delve into specific legislative achievements, his leadership roles suggest he was a respected figure in the Oklahoma Senate, contributing to the broader political discourse of the state.

In summary, Earl Garrison was a dedicated public servant who represented District 9 in the Oklahoma Senate for over a decade. His career was marked by leadership within the Democratic caucus, a commitment to education and rural communities, and a background that included military service, teaching, and ranching. His influence extended beyond his time in office, as his daughter entered politics, continuing the family's legacy of public service in Oklahoma. Garrison's story reflects the intersection of personal experience, professional expertise, and political leadership in shaping effective governance at the state level.

title: Jeffrey Viggiano
text:
Jeffrey Donald Viggiano, born on July 24, 1984, is a retired American-born Italian professional basketball player who concluded his career with Umana Reyer Venezia in Italy’s top-tier Lega Basket Serie A. His basketball journey began in high school at Suffield Academy in West Suffield, Connecticut, where he earned significant accolades. In 2000, he was named Gatorade Player of the Year in Connecticut and helped lead his team to the Connecticut State Championship, alongside teammate Dan Presser. Following high school, Viggiano attended the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he played four seasons for the UMass Minutemen.

After college, Viggiano began his professional career overseas. He first played in Sweden with the Norrköping Dolphins and later in Hungary with Soproni Sördögök KC. His breakout performance came in 2008 when he joined Nuova Pallacanestro Pavia in Italy’s second division, LegADue. That season, he averaged 14.1 points and 4.2 rebounds per game, catching the attention of top-tier Italian club Armani Jeans Milano. In August 2010, Viggiano was loaned to Angelico Biella for one year. His next move came in December 2011 when he signed with Benetton Treviso. In July 2012, he agreed to a one-year deal with Enel Brindisi, further establishing himself in Italian basketball.

In August 2013, Viggiano signed with Montepaschi Siena, a prominent team in the Lega Basket Serie A, for the 2013–14 season. The following summer, on July 1, 2014, he joined Umana Reyer Venezia, where he would spend the next several seasons. He re-signed with Venezia on July 16, 2015, for another year and again on July 1, 2016, indicating his stability and value to the club. His tenure with Reyer Venezia marked the latter part of his career before retirement.

Throughout his professional journey, Viggiano showcased versatility as a player, contributing both offensively and defensively in multiple leagues and teams. His career highlights include playing for elite Italian clubs and demonstrating consistency in performance, particularly during his time in the Lega Basket Serie A. His retirement concluded a career that spanned high school, college, and professional basketball across different countries, with a notable impact in Italian basketball.

title: Karl Eliasberg
text:
Karl Eliasberg (1907–1978) was a Soviet conductor whose most significant contribution to music and history came during the Siege of Leningrad, when he conducted a landmark performance of Dmitri Shostakovich’s Seventh Symphony. Born in Minsk on 10 June 1907, Eliasberg graduated from the Leningrad Conservatory as a violinist in 1929. He began his career as a conductor at the Leningrad Theatre of Musical Comedy, later moving to Leningrad Radio. By the time of the siege, he was the second conductor of the Leningrad Philharmonic and led the Leningrad Radio Orchestra.

The siege was a period of extreme hardship, with many musicians either starving or joining the military. When Shostakovich’s Seventh Symphony—dedicated to Leningrad—was scheduled for its local premiere in 1942, Eliasberg was tasked with assembling an orchestra. Only 15 members of the original Philharmonic remained, so he recruited players from the reserve orchestra and military bands. The concert, held on 9 August 1942, was a profound morale booster for the city’s beleaguered residents, who listened to the broadcast. Eliasberg’s efforts in organizing the performance also saved lives, as he ensured musicians received food ration cards by attending rehearsals and concerts.

For his role in the symphony’s premiere, Eliasberg was named a Meritorious Artist of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic in 1944. However, after the war, Yevgeny Mravinsky’s return to the Philharmonic effectively sidelined Eliasberg, forcing him into provincial work. He conducted in Leningrad only three more times between 1945 and 1975, each occasion featuring the Seventh Symphony. The most notable of these was in 1964, when he reunited with 22 surviving members of the original orchestra for a performance attended by Shostakovich. Eliasberg, moved by the occasion, dedicated it to those who had performed in 1942 but had since died. The audience gave a standing ovation, and Eliasberg later reflected on the weight of the moment, acknowledging the city’s peaceful present while urging remembrance of its wartime suffering.

Eliasberg’s later years were marked by obscurity, and after his death on 12 February 1978, his ashes were initially buried in an unremarkable plot at Piskaryovskoye Memorial Cemetery. Post-Soviet efforts, particularly by conductor Yuri Temirkanov and mayor Anatoly Sobchak, led to his ashes being reinterred in a more dignified location at Volkovo Cemetery’s Literatorskie Mostki.

Eliasberg left a small but significant recording legacy, including performances of Brahms’s *German Requiem*, Symphony No. 3, and Symphony No. 4 (the latter recorded live in 1960), as well as Mahler’s Symphony No. 4 and Shostakovich’s Seventh Symphony. His work was later recognized in popular culture, notably in Sarah Quigley’s 2011 novel *The Conductor* and in documentaries and films about the Siege of Leningrad and Shostakovich’s symphonies. Despite his later obscurity, Eliasberg’s bravery and artistic resilience during one of history’s darkest periods have ensured his enduring legacy.

title: Tacko Fall
text:
El Hadji Tacko Sereigne Diop Fall, born on 10 December 1995 in Dakar, Senegal, is a professional basketball player known for his extraordinary height of 7 feet 6 inches (2.29 meters). He played in the NBA for the Boston Celtics and Cleveland Cavaliers before moving to the Chinese Basketball Association (CBA) and later the Australian National Basketball League (NBL). Fall's height and physical measurements set records at the 2019 NBA Draft Combine, including the tallest height in shoes (7 ft 7 in), longest wingspan (8 ft 2.25 in), and highest standing reach (10 ft 2.5 in). His shoe size is a massive 22 (US), and his hands measure 10.5 inches in length and width.

Fall moved to the United States at 16 and began playing basketball in Houston, Texas, under the guidance of former NBA player Hakeem Olajuwon. As a high school player, he was one of the most highly scouted centers in the country, averaging 20 points, 15 rebounds, and 5.1 blocks per game as a senior. He committed to the University of Central Florida (UCF), where he played from 2015 to 2019. During his time at UCF, he was named American Athletic Conference Defensive Player of the Year in 2017 and led the Knights to their first NCAA tournament win in 2019. He faced fellow Senegalese giant Mamadou N'Diaye, also 7 ft 6 in, in college basketball's tallest-ever matchup.

After going undrafted in the 2019 NBA draft, Fall signed with the Boston Celtics on an Exhibit 10 contract. He impressed in the 2019 NBA Summer League, averaging 7.2 points, 4.0 rebounds, and 1.4 blocks while shooting 77% from the field. He signed a two-way contract and made his NBA debut in October 2019. Over two seasons with the Celtics, he became a fan favorite, leading the team in field goal percentage both years. In the G League with the Maine Red Claws, he averaged a double-double of 12.9 points and 11.1 rebounds while earning All-Defensive Team honors.

In 2021, Fall signed with the Cleveland Cavaliers but was waived in January 2022. He briefly played for the Cavaliers' G League affiliate, the Cleveland Charge, before joining the Xinjiang Flying Tigers of the CBA in 2022. In 2023, he signed with the Nanjing Monkey Kings, averaging 8.8 points, 6.1 rebounds, and 1.4 blocks per game. In 2024, he joined the New Zealand Breakers of the NBL but missed games due to injury. He returned to the Monkey Kings in 2025 before the Breakers parted ways with him in July of that year.

Off the court, Fall is a devout Muslim, choosing the number 99 in reference to the 99 names of Allah. He is academically gifted, maintaining a 4.0 GPA in high school, becoming fluent in English in eight months, and excelling in advanced math and science. He studied computer science at UCF with aspirations of working for tech companies like Siemens or Microsoft. His family includes two uncles standing 6 ft 8 in and a younger brother who was 5 ft 9 in at age seven, though none match his exceptional height. Fall's combination of size, skill, and intellectual prowess has made him a unique figure in basketball.

title: Santiago Vergini
text:
Santiago Vergini, born on 3 August 1988 in Máximo Paz, Santa Fe, Argentina, is a professional footballer who plays as a centre-back. He began his football career in the youth system of Vélez Sársfield, though he only played for the reserves in lower leagues. In June 2009, he moved to Paraguayan club Club Olimpia, where he made his professional debut on 13 September 2009 in a 0–2 loss against Club Libertad. Vergini scored his first professional goal on 7 November 2009 in a 2–1 victory over Sportivo Luqueño.
