She became the first sitting First Lady in the country’s history to hold a political position when her husband, President Mauricio Funes, appointed her as the Secretary of Social Inclusion in 2009. This role was later renewed by President Salvador Sánchez Cerén in 2014. Pignato’s tenure as Secretary of Social Inclusion focused on addressing human rights, family affairs, and gender equality, particularly through her initiatives to support women in El Salvador.

Before moving to El Salvador, Pignato was an activist in Brazil’s Workers' Party (PT) and an advisor to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president from 2003 to 2011. She documented human rights abuses during El Salvador’s civil war, which ended with the Chapultepec Peace Accords. In 1992, she relocated to El Salvador, where she represented the Workers' Party in Central America and became the Director of the Center for Brazilian Studies at the Brazilian Embassy in San Salvador. She later married Funes, a journalist and politician, with whom she had a son, Gabriel.

As First Lady and Secretary of Social Inclusion, Pignato launched Ciudad Mujer (Women’s City) in 2011, a flagship program aimed at aiding victims of gender-based violence and providing access to healthcare, financial advice, career training, and legal support. The initiative, which established five centers across El Salvador, offered services from 15 government agencies, including job training, reproductive healthcare, and legal aid for sexual assault victims. By November 2014, Ciudad Mujer had assisted an estimated 603,000 women. The program gained international recognition, with Brazil announcing plans to replicate it, while Guatemala, Colombia, and Mexico expressed interest in adopting similar initiatives.

Pignato faced opposition from politicians, evangelical groups, and the Catholic Church in implementing Ciudad Mujer. Despite this, the program became a model for women’s empowerment, with Pignato emphasizing the importance of making women visible in government policies. In 2012, President Funes delivered a speech declaring that “violence against women is violence against society,” marking a shift in national discourse on gender-based violence. Pignato also served as the President of the Salvadoran National Council for Youth and led the Salvadoran Institute for Women Development.

In 2011, El Salvador faced severe flooding that displaced 300,000 people and caused $840 million in damages. As both First Lady and Secretary, Pignato traveled to Washington, D.C., to lobby for U.S. humanitarian aid, meeting with officials, including U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and former President Bill Clinton. Her efforts earned her the Ellis Island Medal of Honor in 2012 for her work with the Salvadoran American community and women’s rights advocacy.

In 2014, Pignato and Funes publicly separated. In 2015, she announced a cancer diagnosis and took a temporary leave to undergo treatment. Legal troubles emerged in 2017 when it was revealed that Odebrecht, a Brazilian company, had financed Funes’ 2009 presidential campaign with illicit funds, allegedly at the behest of Lula da Silva. In 2018, an arrest warrant was issued for Pignato as part of an investigation into embezzlement, money laundering, and asset laundering involving Funes. Authorities considered her a flight risk, despite a request to allow her to post bail due to her health condition. The case remains ongoing.

title: Chris Woakes
text:
Christopher Roger Woakes, born on 2 March 1989 in Birmingham, is an English cricketer who represents England in all formats of the game and plays domestically for Warwickshire. He is a right-handed all-rounder, known for his fast-medium bowling and capable batting. Woakes has had a successful career, both domestically and internationally, and has been part of two World Cup-winning England teams—the 2019 ODI World Cup and the 2022 T20 World Cup.

Woakes began playing cricket at the age of seven, starting with Aston Manor Cricket Club before moving to Walmley Cricket Club. He progressed through Warwickshire’s youth system, playing for their under-15, under-17, academy, and Second XI teams between 2004 and 2007. He also played three matches for Herefordshire in the 2006 Minor Counties Trophy. Outside of cricket, Woakes was a trainee footballer with Walsall F.C. as a winger until the age of 14 and remains a supporter of Aston Villa F.C.

Woakes made his first-class debut for Warwickshire in 2006 during a tour by the West Indies, taking three wickets in his only match that season. He became a regular for Warwickshire’s First XI in 2008, taking 42 wickets in the County Championship at an average of 20.57, topping the team’s bowling averages. In 2009, he was called up to the England Lions squad, making his debut against the West Indies and taking a memorable 6/43 in the first innings. Later that season, he scored his maiden first-class century, a 131 not out against Hampshire, batting at number nine and sharing a 222-run partnership with Jonathan Trott. He reached 200 first-class wickets in July 2011 during Warwickshire’s victory over Sussex.

In the Indian Premier League (IPL), Woakes has played for Kolkata Knight Riders, Royal Challengers Bangalore, and Delhi Capitals. In 2017, he took 17 wickets in 13 matches for Kolkata, with best figures of 3/6. He was later bought by Royal Challengers Bangalore in 2018 but was released the following year. He was initially bought by Delhi Capitals for the 2020 IPL but withdrew to focus on England’s Test season. He later played for Delhi in the 2021 IPL, making his debut against Chennai Super Kings. In 2022, he joined Birmingham Phoenix for The Hundred.

Woakes made his international debut in 2011, playing in both a T20I and ODI against Australia. In his second ODI, he took 6/45, one of the best performances of his early career. He made his Test debut in the 2013 Ashes against Australia, taking 1/96 in the first innings. He became a key player in England’s limited-overs teams, particularly during the 2014 and 2015 series against Sri Lanka, India, and Pakistan. His standout performance came in 2016, when he took 11/102 in a Test match against Pakistan at Lord’s, earning a place on the honourable boards at the ground for both his batting and bowling achievements. He also scored an unbeaten 95 in an ODI against Sri Lanka the same year, a record for the highest score by a number eight or lower.

Woakes has been a consistent performer for England in all formats. He was part of the 2015 World Cup squad, though injury ruled him out of the final match. He played a crucial role in the 2019 World Cup, taking three wickets in the semi-final against Australia and another three in the final against New Zealand, helping England win their first World Cup since 1992. In 2021, he reached 150 ODI wickets, and in 2022, he was part of England’s T20 World Cup-winning team, playing in every match of the tournament. He is one of only six players to have played in both the 2019 and 2022 World Cup-winning squads.

In 2023, Woakes was recalled to the Ashes squad for the third Test at Headingley, where he took three wickets in each innings and scored the winning runs, finishing unbeaten on 32. His partnership of 59 runs with Harry Brook was England’s highest of the match. His strong performances throughout the series, including 19 wickets in six innings, earned him the title of England’s “player of the series.” Woakes has established himself as a reliable and impactful all-rounder, contributing significantly to England’s success in both Tests and limited-overs cricket.

title: Neil Googe
text:
Neil Googe is a British comics artist known for his work in both British and American comic book markets. His early career included contributions to *2000 AD*, where he worked on several *Judge Dredd* stories, such as "Trial of Strength," "War Games," and "Mind Ripper," alongside writers like John Wagner and Robbie Morrison. He also contributed to *Shotgun Mary: Blood Lore*, a four-issue mini-series published by Antarctic Press in 1997, and other *2000 AD* stories like "Dead of Winter" and "Coy's Big Score."

One of his most notable early projects was a graphic novel adaptation of the video game *Silent Hill*, which he completed in 1999. Despite being finished, advertised, and assigned an ISBN, the book was never published due to disputes between Konami and its European branch. Only four screenshots of the novel remain, and Googe himself lost the CD containing the full, completed work.

In 2000, Googe co-founded the British independent comic publisher *Com.x*, where he wrote and illustrated *Bazooka Jules*, a series that ran for three issues. Though the series was cut short, Googe expressed interest in continuing it, even planning a reboot under the title *Bazooka Jules: Tales from Caliber Bay* as a setting for role-playing games, supplemented by short comic stories. However, his focus shifted to the American market, where he gained prominence working with Wildstorm Comics.

At Wildstorm, Googe worked on *Majestic* with writers Dan Abnett and Andy Lanning, contributing to multiple issues and collected editions. He also collaborated with Gail Simone on *Welcome to Tranquility*, a critically acclaimed series that was collected into two volumes. Later, he worked with Christos Gage on *Wildcats: World's End*, a spin-off of the *Wildcats* series, and with Mike Costa on *World of Warcraft: Dark Riders*, a hardcover graphic novel published by DC Comics after the Wildstorm merger.

Since then, Googe has contributed to various one-shot issues for DC Comics, including *Rose and Thorn*, *Detective Comics Harley Quinn #1*, and a *Legends of the Dark Knight* issue featuring Harley Quinn, as well as *The Flash*. He also returned to *2000 AD* to work on *Survival Geeks* with writers Gordon Rennie and Emma Beeby.

Currently, Googe is involved in multiple projects, including *Welcome to the Hood*, a creator-owned work set to launch as a pen-and-paper role-playing game with an accompanying comic. He is also developing a *Pathfinder* supplement and other tabletop RPG products while continuing to work on regular comic assignments. His diverse career spans British and American comics, video game adaptations, and independent publishing, demonstrating his versatility as an artist and storyteller.

title: Cédric Bakambu
text:
Cédric Bakambu, born on 11 April 1991 in Vitry-sur-Seine, is a professional footballer who plays as a forward or winger for La Liga club Real Betis and the DR Congo national team. Beginning his career in France, he started at local club Ivry at age 10 before transferring to Sochaux four years later. Bakambu made his professional debut for Sochaux in 2010, appearing as a substitute in Ligue 1 and later scoring his first professional goal in a 2–2 draw against Lille. Over five seasons, he played 107 official games, scoring 21 goals, including a hat-trick in a cup match. Sochaux was relegated in 2014, the same season Bakambu was sent off in a match.

In 2014, Bakambu moved to Turkish club Bursaspor for €1.8 million, where he quickly became a key player. He scored 13 goals in 27 league games and was the top scorer in the Turkish Cup with eight goals, including back-to-back hat-tricks. Despite Bursaspor reaching the final, they lost to Galatasaray. The following year, he joined Spanish club Villarreal, making an immediate impact by scoring two goals on his La Liga debut. Over his time at Villarreal, Bakambu became a standout performer, scoring nine goals in the 2015–16 UEFA Europa League, earning a place in the competition’s Squad of the Season. In 2017, he was named La Liga Player of the Month after a hat-trick and further goals.

In January 2018, Bakambu transferred to Beijing Guoan for €40 million, overcoming a dispute over transfer taxes. He won the Chinese FA Cup in his first season and became the club’s all-time top scorer. After returning to Europe, he signed for Marseille in 2022, scoring on his debut, and later joined Olympiacos and Al-Nasr. In July 2023, he moved to Galatasaray, where he made his Champions League debut and scored a dramatic stoppage-time goal against Bayern Munich. In February 2024, he joined Real Betis.

Internationally, Bakambu represented France at youth levels, winning the 2010 UEFA European Under-19 Championship and finishing fourth in the 2011 FIFA U-20 World Cup. In 2015, he switched to the DR Congo national team, scoring his first goal in a 2–1 win over Angola. He was part of the squad for the 2017 Africa Cup of Nations and helped the team qualify for the 2019 tournament. After briefly retiring from international duty in 2022, he reversed his decision and assisted a goal at the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations.

Bakambu’s personal life reflects his dual heritage, having grown up with Congolese and French influences. He and teammate Dieumerci Mbokani narrowly escaped harm during the 2016 Brussels Airport terror attacks. Throughout his career, Bakambu has earned numerous accolades, including being named to the UEFA Europa League Squad of the Season and winning individual honors in China and Greece. His journey from France to multiple top clubs across Europe and Asia highlights his versatility and consistency as a forward.

title: Sada Thompson
text:
Sada Carolyn Thompson was an accomplished American stage, film, and television actress, born on September 27, 1927, in Des Moines, Iowa. Her parents, Hugh Woodruff Thompson and Corlyss Gibson, moved the family to Fanwood, New Jersey, when she was young. She graduated from Scotch Plains-Fanwood High School in 1945 and earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Theatre from the Carnegie Institute of Technology (now Carnegie Mellon University). She honed her craft at the Pittsburgh Playhouse, where she appeared in productions of classic plays like *The Seagull*, *Pygmalion*, *Our Town*, *Arms and the Man*, and *Blithe Spirit*.

Thompson began her professional career in regional theater before making her Off-Broadway debut in 1955 in *Under Milk Wood*. The following year, she appeared in a television production of *Goodyear Television Playhouse*. Her Broadway debut came in 1959 in the musical *Juno*, followed by roles in *The Effect of Gamma Rays on Man-in-the-Moon Marigolds*, *Tartuffe*, and *Twigs*. Her stage work earned her numerous accolades, including an Obie Award, a Tony Award for Best Actress in a Play for *Twigs* (1972), three Drama Desk Awards, and two Sarah Siddons Awards. In 2005, she was inducted into the American Theater Hall of Fame.

Thompson transitioned to television in the 1970s, initially being cast as Irene Lorenzo on *All in the Family* but was replaced after one episode due to creative differences. She found her most notable television role as Kate Lawrence in the drama series *Family* (1976–1980), a performance that earned her widespread acclaim. For her work on *Family*, she won the 1978 Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series and received three Golden Globe nominations. Over her career, she was nominated for the Emmy Award nine times, including for her role as Carla’s mother on *Cheers*.

In addition to *Family*, Thompson appeared in various television series, including *Owen Marshall: Counselor at Law*, *The Love Boat*, *Father Dowling Mysteries*, *Andre’s Mother*, *Indictment: The McMartin Trial*, *ER*, and *Law & Order*. Her film credits included *The Pursuit of Happiness*, *Desperate Characters*, and *Pollock*.

Personally, Thompson was married to Donald E. Stewart from December 18, 1949, until her death. The couple lived in Southbury, Connecticut, and had one daughter, Liza Stewart, who became a costume designer. Thompson passed away on May 4, 2011, in Danbury, Connecticut, at the age of 83, due to lung disease. Her contributions to theater and television cemented her legacy as a respected and versatile actress.

title: Vadhir Derbez
text:
Vadhir Alejandro González Torres, known professionally as Vadhir Derbez, is a Mexican actor and singer born on 18 February 1991 in Mexico City. He is the son of the well-known comic actor Eugenio Derbez. Derbez attended the prestigious military school Culver Academies in the United States for four years, where he developed an interest in equestrianism. He even participated in Barack Obama's 2008 Inaugural Parade in Washington, D.C., showcasing his horsemanship skills.

Derbez began his acting career at the age of six in 1997 with the program *Derbez en Cuando*, a television show featuring his father. He appeared in various sketches, including *Tatiana* and *En Familia con Chabelo* (2000), as well as *Diseñador de Ambos Sexos* (2001). His first major acting role came in 2002 with the telenovela *Cómplices Al Rescate*, followed by roles in *La Familia P. Luche* (2002), *De Pocas, Pocas Pulgas* (2003), *Par de Ases* (2004), and *Mujer, Casos de la Vida Real* (2004). In 2006, he gained recognition for his recurring role as Marco López Pérez in the popular series *Vecinos*, appearing in 36 episodes.

In 2010, Derbez competed in *Mira Quien Baila*, Univision’s first reality dance competition, and won the first season. He later starred in the series *Gossip Girl: Acapulco* (2013) as Maximiliano "Max" Zaga, one of the main characters. In 2016, he played César Suárez, the psychopathic son of a drug lord, in the telenovela *La Querida del Centauro*, a production aired in the U.S., Mexico, and South America. The same year, he starred in *Entre Correr y Vivir*, a series about the lives of race car drivers, where he portrayed Rodrigo Hernández. In 2019, he won the first season of *¿Quién es la Máscara?* as "Camaleón."

Internationally, Derbez appeared in the Netflix series *Sense8* (2016) alongside Miguel Ángel Silvestre and Alfonso Herrera. His theater career began in 2004 when he played Tom Sawyer in *Las Aventuras de Tom Sawyer*, an adaptation of Mark Twain’s novel. In 2013, he performed in the musical *Grease*, taking on multiple roles, and later starred in *Rock of Ages* (2014) as Jerry. He reprised his role in *Grease* in 2017 during a U.S. tour.

Derbez made his film debut in 2005, voicing the character Chuletas in the animated film *Imaginum*. His first live-action film role came in *Ladrones* (2015), followed by his leading role in *El Tamaño Sí Importa* (2016). He also appeared in *3 Idiotas* (2017), an adaptation of the Bollywood film *3 Idiots*, and made his Hollywood debut in *How to Be a Latin Lover* (2017), playing a younger version of his father’s character. In 2019, he starred in the comedy *Dulce Familia* as Beto.

Musically, Derbez released his first EP, *Vadhir Derbez*, on 2 September 2016, featuring the singles "Te Olvidé" and "Me Haces Sentir." The latter was re-released in 2017 with a live version. His song "Al Final" was included in the soundtrack of *3 Idiotas* (2017), and he later released singles like "Latin Lover" (2017), "Mala" (2019), and "Toda La Banda" (2019). His discography includes collaborations with artists such as Roxy, Ekin, Mario Bautista, and Ximena Sariñana, among others.

Throughout his career, Derbez has worked with major networks and production companies, including Televisa, Univision, Warner Brothers, Netflix, TV Azteca, and Telemundo. His versatility as an actor, singer, and performer has solidified his presence in both Mexican and international entertainment.

title: Michael L. MacDonald
text:
Michael L. MacDonald is a Canadian politician who has served as a Conservative member of the Senate since 2009. Born on May 4, 1955, in Louisbourg, Nova Scotia, he is the youngest of 10 children. He completed his education at the University of King’s College in Halifax, graduating in 1977 with an Honours degree in political science. His early political career began in 1978 when he worked as a researcher for the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada’s Research Office. Over the next several years, he held various political roles, including serving as an executive assistant to MLA Gerald Sheehy from 1980 to 1982, and then to Nova Scotia Premier John Buchanan from 1982 to 1984. He continued in this capacity, working for Thomas McMillan from 1984 to 1985 and Stewart McInnes from 1985 to 1987.

In addition to his political career, MacDonald has been the owner of the Fortress Inn in Louisbourg since 1988. He has also been an active candidate in multiple elections. In 1988, he ran for federal office in the riding of Cape Breton—East Richmond, finishing second with 7,173 votes. He later ran provincially in Nova Scotia for the Progressive Conservative Association in the Dartmouth-Cole Harbour riding in 1993, placing second with 2,905 votes, and again in 1998, where he finished third with 2,084 votes. In 2004, he contested the federal riding of Dartmouth—Cole Harbour, coming in third place with 8,739 votes.

MacDonald’s political career took a significant turn in 2009 when he was appointed to the Senate on the advice of then-Prime Minister Stephen Harper. His tenure, however, has not been without controversy. In February 2022, during the convoy protests in Ottawa, he was recorded in a video making derogatory remarks about Ottawa residents, criticizing their perceived entitlement and work ethic. He also expressed support for the protesters, stating he did not want them to leave, and jokingly referred to his wife as "a Karen" for wanting the protest to end. Following public backlash, he issued an apology in the Senate chamber for his comments.

Outside of politics, MacDonald resides in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, with his wife, Marilyn, and their two sons, Lauchlan and Liam. His career reflects a long-standing involvement in Canadian politics, both at the provincial and federal levels, alongside his role as a business owner. Despite his controversial remarks, he remains a sitting member of the Senate, continuing to represent the Conservative Party in Canada’s upper legislative chamber.

title: Thirayuth Boonmee
text:
Thirayuth Boonmee is a prominent Thai social scientist, public intellectual, and former student activist born on 10 January 1950. He is best known for his role in political activism during the 1970s and his later academic contributions to Thai intellectual life. As a student at Chulalongkorn University in 1973, Thirayuth emerged as a leader of the National Student Center of Thailand (NSCT), which organized protests against the military dictatorship of Thanom Kittikachorn and Praphas Charusathien. The NSCT led large-scale demonstrations, including a 10-day boycott of Japanese products in opposition to Japanese investments in Thailand. His activism reached a critical point in October 1973 when he and 12 other student activists were arrested for distributing leaflets demanding a new constitution. Rumors of their execution provoked massive anti-government protests, culminating in a gathering of around 400,000 people. The students were released later that month, and the king approved plans for a new constitution, marking a significant political shift. Thirayuth also played a role in exposing the Internal Security Operations Command’s involvement in the Ban Na Sai massacre, a brutal incident in which villagers in northeastern Thailand were killed.

The political landscape in Thailand took a violent turn on 6 October 1976, when a massacre of student protesters occurred at Thammasat University. Following this event, Thirayuth, like many other activists and intellectuals, fled to the jungles to join the Communist Party of Thailand (CPT). During this period, he became increasingly critical of the monarchy, making controversial statements in a 1977 broadcast where he described the monarchy as "obsolete and deteriorating" and suggested that its destruction would not harm the people. However, after the CPT dissolved in the early 1980s, Thirayuth returned to mainstream intellectual life, renouncing his socialist views and retracting his anti-monarchical statements.

After completing his studies in the Netherlands, where he earned a master’s equivalent degree in Philosophy, Sociology, and Anthropology from the International Institute of Social Studies in The Hague and the University of Nijmegen, Thirayuth returned to Thailand in 1985. He became a prominent academic, teaching in the Faculty of Sociology and Anthropology at Thammasat University. In 1997, he was recognized as one of Thailand’s ten most influential public intellectuals. His academic career continued to flourish, and in 2008, he was appointed director of the Sanya Dharmasakti Institute for Democracy at Thammasat University. In 2012, he was named a Professor of Anthropology, and in 2015, he moved to Thammasat University’s College of Interdisciplinary Studies. Throughout his academic career, Thirayuth has been an outspoken critic of political figures, most notably Thai Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra (2001–2006), for whom he coined the term "Thaksinocracy" to describe his authoritarian style of governance.

Thirayuth Boonmee’s life reflects a dynamic journey from radical student activism to academic prominence, marked by both political engagement and intellectual contributions. His early activism was pivotal in Thailand’s democratic struggles, while his later career as a scholar and public intellectual has cemented his influence in Thai society. His willingness to evolve his political views, from radical criticism to a more moderate stance, demonstrates a complex relationship with Thailand’s political and social landscape.

title: Bobby Fischer
text:
Below is a 500-word summary of the Wikipedia article on Bobby Fischer:

Robert James Fischer, born on March 9, 1943, in Chicago, Illinois, was an American chess grandmaster and the eleventh World Chess Champion. A prodigy, he won his first US Championship at 14, achieving a perfect 11–0 score in 1964—the only perfect score in the tournament's history. Fischer's path to the world title included sweeping matches against Mark Taimanov and Bent Larsen (both 6–0) and defeating Tigran Petrosian before winning the 1972 World Championship against Boris Spassky in Iceland. The match, framed as a Cold War clash between the U.S. and USSR, drew unprecedented global attention.

After refusing to defend his title in 1975 due to disputes with FIDE, the chess governing body, Fischer vanished from public view. He later resurfaced in 1992 to play an unofficial rematch against Spassky in Yugoslavia, which was under UN sanctions. This move led to U.S. legal action, forcing Fischer into exile. He was later arrested in Japan in 2004 for using a revoked U.S. passport and eventually granted Icelandic citizenship, where he lived until his death in 2008. Throughout his life, Fischer made antisemitic remarks, including Holocaust denial, despite his Jewish ancestry.

Fischer's contributions to chess include *My 60 Memorable Games* (1969), a foundational text, and the invention of the Fischer timing system, now standard in competitive play. He also created Fischer Random Chess (Chess960), a variant with randomized starting positions.

Born to Regina Wender Fischer, a single mother of Polish Jewish descent, and possibly fathered by Hungarian mathematician Paul Neményi, Fischer grew up in Brooklyn. His mother, a nurse and activist, struggled financially, and Fischer learned chess at six from a candy store set. By 1950, he was studying chess books and playing alone. His mother sought opponents for him, leading to his introduction to the Brooklyn Chess Club under Carmine Nigro, who mentored him. Fischer soon joined the Hawthorne Chess Club, run by master John Collins, where he honed his skills.

By 13, Fischer had won the U.S. Junior Championship and impressed experts with his game against Donald Byrne, dubbed "The Game of the Century." In 1957, at 14, he became the youngest U.S. Champion, earning the International Master title. His visit to the Soviet Union in 1958, where he played blitz against local masters, cemented his reputation. At 15, he qualified for the Candidates Tournament, becoming the youngest grandmaster at the time.

Fischer's early success was marked by relentless study and aggressive play. His matches in Yugoslavia and Cuba showcased his dominance, and his 1957 victory at the U.S. Championship secured his place in international competition. Despite his later controversies, Fischer's impact on chess remains profound, reshaping tournament rules and popularizing the game's strategic depths.

title: Jeffrey Satinover
text:
Jeffrey Burke Satinover, born on September 4, 1947, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American psychiatrist, psychoanalyst, and physicist. He has a diverse academic background, having earned degrees in various fields. He holds a Bachelor of Science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a Master of Education in Clinical Psychology and Public Practice from Harvard University, a medical degree from the University of Texas, and a Master of Science in physics from Yale University. Additionally, he obtained a diploma in analytical psychology from the C. G. Jung Institute in Zürich, becoming the youngest graduate there, and later received a PhD in physics from the University of Nice in France in 2009. Satinover has also trained as a Jungian analyst and is an accredited practitioner in the field.

Professionally, Satinover has held several notable positions. He was a distinguished visiting professor of math and science at King’s College in New York City, a Christian college affiliated with Campus Crusade for Christ, and has taught at the C. G. Jung Institute in Zürich. He is also a visiting scientist at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology. In the business world, he founded Quintium Analytics, LLC, a proprietary investment advisory company, in 2007, where he serves as managing director. Additionally, he is a member of the scientific advisory committee of the National Association for Research & Therapy of Homosexuality, an organization that promotes the idea that homosexuality can be changed through therapy.

Satinover is perhaps best known for his controversial views on homosexuality, same-sex marriage, and the ex-gay movement. His 1996 book, *Homosexuality and the Politics of Truth*, published by an evangelical Christian publisher, argues that homosexuality is not a true illness but may be a "spiritual sickness" and that gay activism distorts the truth, harming both society and homosexuals. The book debates the nature of homosexuality from psychological, religious, and scientific perspectives, suggesting that it involves compulsive impulses and that social and environmental factors play a significant role in sexual orientation. Satinover has testified in court cases and legislative hearings, including the 2003 Massachusetts Judicial Committee hearing, where he argued that homosexuality is not immutable and that children have a greater need for both a mother and a father in an adoption case in Florida.

Satinover has been involved in high-profile political discussions, including the 1991 confirmation hearings for U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas. During those hearings, he suggested to President Bush’s nephew that Anita Hill, who accused Thomas of sexual harassment, might be suffering from erotomania, a delusional disorder that could make her believe false accusations. He later presented this idea to Thomas’s Senate sponsor, John Danforth, and White House press secretary, Larry Thomas, though he did not testify in the hearings, as he had not examined Hill.

Beyond his work on homosexuality, Satinover has written on a range of topics in physics, neuroscience, and religion. His other notable works include *The Quantum Brain: The Search for Freedom and the Next Generation of Man* (2002), which explores the intersection of quantum physics and human consciousness, and *The Truth Behind the Bible Code* (1997), which examines claims about hidden messages in the Bible. He has also contributed to documentary films, such as *What the #$*! Do We (K)now!?* (2004) and its sequel, *What the Bleep!?: Down the Rabbit Hole* (2006).

Satinover identifies as Jewish but describes his worldview as eclectic. He has been married twice and is the father of three daughters. His career and writings reflect a blend of scientific, psychological, and religious perspectives, often engaging in debates on controversial topics.

title: Yehuda Lindell
text:
Yehuda Lindell is an Israeli professor of computer science at Bar-Ilan University, specializing in cryptography, particularly in the theory and practical applications of secure computation. Born on 24 February 1971, Lindell has made significant contributions to the field, earning recognition as an IACR Fellow in 2021. His academic journey began with a BSc and MSc in computer science from Bar-Ilan University, followed by a PhD from the Weizmann Institute of Science in 2002. After receiving a Raviv Fellowship, he spent two years at IBM’s T.J. Watson Research Center before returning to Israel in 2004 to join Bar-Ilan University as a faculty member. His work on secure computation has been supported by prestigious grants, including an ERC starting grant in 2009 and an ERC consolidators grant in 2014.

Beyond academia, Lindell has extensive industry experience. From 2004 to 2014, he served as a permanent cryptographic consultant for Safenet (formerly Aladdin). In 2014, he co-founded Unbound Security, where he initially served as Chief Scientist until 2018, then became CEO in early 2019, taking a leave from Bar-Ilan University. In January 2022, Unbound Security was acquired by Coinbase, where Lindell now leads the cryptography team.

Lindell’s research primarily focuses on secure multiparty computation, particularly in the areas of protocol composition, efficient two-party secure computation via the Yao garbled circuit construction, and multiparty computation using secret sharing. His most cited work, co-authored with Benny Pinkas, proposed using secure computation for privacy-preserving data mining, specifically the ID3 algorithm. He provided the first formal security proofs for the basic Yao protocol and the BGW protocol, and has contributed to designing two-party protocols resistant to active adversaries. His work has earned multiple awards, including the IBM Pat Goldberg Memorial Best Paper Award in 2006 for authenticated Byzantine agreement and the best paper award at ACM CCS 2016 for high-throughput multiparty computation protocols. In 2021, he published a review article on secure multiparty computation in the *Communications of the ACM*. Additionally, Lindell co-invented the AES-GCM-SIV mode of symmetric encryption, standardized by the IETF, and received the best paper award at ACM CCS 2017 for this research.

Lindell is also a prolific author, having co-written textbooks on cryptography with Jonathan Katz, including *Introduction to Modern Cryptography*, which is widely used as a standard reference in universities. His other notable books include *Composition of Secure Multi-Party Protocols* (2003), *Efficient Secure Two-Party Protocols* (2010, with Carmit Hazay), and several edited volumes, such as the *Proceedings of the 11th Theory of Cryptography Conference* (2014) and *Tutorials on the Foundations of Cryptography* (2017). The third edition of *Introduction to Modern Cryptography* was published in 2020. Lindell’s scholarly work is well-documented, with his publications indexed in the DBLP Bibliography Server and Google Scholar, reflecting his influence in the field.

title: Benjamin Lawrence Reid
text:
Benjamin Lawrence Reid was an American professor of English who had a distinguished academic and literary career spanning several decades, from the 1940s to the 1980s. Born on May 3, 1918, in Louisville, Kentucky, Reid spent part of his childhood in Texas. As a young man, he was an athlete, playing baseball in his youth and switching to basketball during his teenage years. He pursued higher education, earning a Bachelor of Arts from the University of Louisville in the 1940s, followed by a Master of Arts from Columbia University and a Doctor of Philosophy from the University of Virginia in the 1950s.

During World War II, Reid was a conscientious objector, which led him to work as a bridge constructor and a psychiatric hospital orderly. After the war, he began his teaching career as an English lecturer at Iowa State College from 1946 to 1948. He then moved to Smith College from 1948 to 1951 before joining Sweet Briar College in 1951, where he served as an instructor until 1956 and later as an assistant professor of English from 1956 to 1957. His longest academic tenure was at Mount Holyoke College, where he joined as an assistant professor in 1957. Over the years, he was promoted to associate professor in 1959, full professor in 1963, and finally became a distinguished English professor in 1970, remaining at Mount Holyoke until his retirement in 1983.

Beyond teaching, Reid was a prolific writer, publishing several books throughout his career. His early works, written in the late 1950s and early 1960s, stemmed from his university theses on Gertrude Stein and William Butler Yeats. He later shifted to biographies, including *The Man from New York: John Quinn and His Friends* (1968), a work that earned him the 1969 Pulitzer Prize for Biography or Autobiography. Another notable biography, *The Lives of Roger Casement* (1976), made him a finalist for the 1977 National Book Award in Biography and Autobiography. Between these two major works, he also published essays. In his later years, Reid wrote autobiographical works between 1988 and 1990.

Reid received several prestigious honors during his career. In 1963, he was awarded a Fulbright research grant to study at the University of London. In 1971, he received a fellowship from the National Endowment for the Humanities for his work on Bertrand Russell. His contributions to literature and academia were widely recognized, cementing his reputation as a distinguished scholar.

Benjamin Lawrence Reid passed away on November 30, 1990, in South Hadley, Massachusetts, following a heart attack and multiple strokes. His legacy endures through his academic work, his influential writings, and the awards he received for his contributions to biography and literary scholarship.

title: Jose Canseco
text:
José Canseco, born on July 2, 1964, in Havana, Cuba, is a former Major League Baseball (MLB) outfielder and designated hitter who played 17 seasons in the league. He rose to fame as a dominant power hitter with the Oakland Athletics, where he established himself as one of the game's top players. Canseco won the Rookie of the Year award in 1986 and the Most Valuable Player (MVP) award in 1988, the same year he became the first player in MLB history to hit 40 home runs and steal 40 bases in a single season. He was a six-time All-Star and a four-time Silver Slugger Award winner, earning the accolade three times as an outfielder and once as a designated hitter. Over his career, Canseco ranked fourth in Athletics history with 254 home runs and was one of only 14 players in MLB history to achieve 400 home runs and 200 stolen bases. His 462 career home runs place him 12th in American League history and second among players with fewer than 2,000 games played.

Canseco's early life was marked by his family's escape from Cuba following Fidel Castro's rise to power. His father, José Sr., lost his job and eventually relocated the family to Miami, where Canseco grew up. He played baseball at Miami Coral Park High School, where he earned MVP honors as a senior. The Oakland Athletics drafted him in the 15th round of the 1982 MLB draft, and he quickly rose through the minor leagues, earning the nickname "The Natural" for his prodigious power and potential. By 1985, he was called up to the majors and made an immediate impact, batting .302 with 5 home runs in 29 games. He won the 1986 Rookie of the Year award after hitting 33 home runs and driving in 117 runs, setting the stage for his breakout 1988 season.

In 1988, Canseco achieved his historic 40-40 season, becoming the first player to hit 40 home runs and steal 40 bases in a single year. He led the American League in home runs (42), RBIs (124), and extra-base hits (76) while batting .307. His performance earned him the AL MVP award unanimously, and he helped the Athletics win 104 games that season. Though Oakland lost the World Series to the Los Angeles Dodgers, Canseco's dominance was undeniable. The following year, he missed the first 88 games due to a broken wrist but still contributed to the Athletics' World Series victory over the San Francisco Giants.

Canseco's career was marked by both brilliance and injury. He battled back problems and other ailments that limited his time on the field, but he remained a feared hitter when healthy. In 1990, he signed a record $23.5 million contract, making him the highest-paid player in MLB at the time. He continued to produce, though injuries and declining performance eventually led to his departure from Oakland. He played for seven teams over his 17-year career, finishing with a .266 batting average, 462 home runs, and 1,207 RBIs. Despite his injuries, he averaged 40 home runs, 120 RBIs, and 102 runs scored per 162 games.

Controversy followed Canseco's career, particularly regarding performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs). In 2005, he admitted to using steroids and wrote a tell-all book, *Juiced: Wild Times, Rampant 'Roids, Smash Hits & How Baseball Got Big*, in which he claimed that the vast majority of MLB players used PEDs. After retiring from baseball, he briefly pursued a career in boxing and mixed martial arts. Canseco's legacy remains that of a trailblazing slugger whose talent was both awe-inspiring and marred by controversy. His 40-40 season and MVP award cement his place in baseball history, though his admissions about steroid use have cast a shadow over his achievements.

title: Kathleen A. McGrath
text:
Kathleen Anne McGrath, born on June 4, 1952, in Columbus, Ohio, was the first woman to command a United States Navy warship, breaking a significant barrier in military history. The daughter of Colonel James H. McGrath and Martha McGrath, she pursued an education that would later shape her distinguished career. In 1975, she earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science from California State University, Sacramento. She furthered her education by attending Officer Candidate School in Rhode Island and later obtained a Master of Arts degree in Educational Management from Stanford University in 1987.

Before joining the Navy, McGrath worked for the United States Forestry Service. In 1980, she transitioned to the U.S. Navy, where she would serve for over two decades. During her career, she was deployed to various regions, including the Western Pacific, the Persian Gulf, and the Mediterranean and Caribbean seas. Her leadership was first tested in 1993 and 1994 when she commanded the rescue and salvage ship USS *Recovery*. Though not a combatant vessel, the ship played a crucial role in naval operations. Lieutenant Commander Darlene Iskra had previously commanded a sister ship, USS *Opportune*, in 1990, but McGrath’s tenure marked a significant milestone.

In December 1998, Captain McGrath achieved a historic milestone when she became the commander of the frigate USS *Jarrett*, making her the first woman to lead a U.S. Navy combatant ship. This appointment was part of a broader effort by the Navy to integrate women into combat roles, following Congress’s 1994 decision to lift restrictions on women serving on combat aircraft and warships. McGrath was among a select group of five women, including Michelle J. Howard, Maureen Farren, Ann O’Connor, and Grace Mehl, chosen to pioneer this new era.

Her command of USS *Jarrett* included high-stakes missions. In March 2000, just six years after the ban on women in combat roles was lifted, McGrath led the ship from San Diego, California, to the Persian Gulf. The mission aimed to intercept boats suspected of smuggling Iraqi oil in violation of United Nations sanctions. Her leadership during this operation underscored the Navy’s growing acceptance of women in frontline roles. In May 2002, she was promoted to the rank of captain, further solidifying her legacy.

After her tour on USS *Jarrett*, McGrath served at the Joint Advanced Warfighting Unit in Alexandria, Virginia, contributing to strategic military planning. Her career was marked by numerous awards and decorations, including the Legion of Merit, the Meritorious Service Medal (with four awards), the Navy Commendation Medal (with two awards), the Navy Achievement Medal, and several campaign and service medals. These honors reflected her dedication and excellence in service.

McGrath’s personal life included her marriage to Gregory H. Brandon, with whom she had two children. Tragically, she passed away on September 26, 2002, at the age of 50, following a battle with lung cancer at the National Naval Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland. She was laid to rest in Arlington National Cemetery, a final tribute to her groundbreaking contributions to the U.S. Navy. Her death was mourned by the Navy, which recognized her as a pioneering figure in military history.

title: Djimon Hounsou
text:
Djimon Gaston Hounsou, born on April 24, 1964, in Cotonou, Benin, is a Beninese-American actor who has built a significant career in Hollywood. His journey began with a difficult childhood; at age 12, he immigrated to Lyon, France, with his brother, dropped out of school, and experienced homelessness. A chance encounter with a photographer introduced him to fashion designer Thierry Mugler, who encouraged him to pursue modeling. By 1987, Hounsou had established a successful modeling career in Paris. He moved to the United States in 1990, where his acting career began.

Hounsou’s early work included appearances in music videos for artists like Paula Abdul, Tina Turner, Janet Jackson, and Madonna, as well as a small role in the 1990 film *Without You I'm Nothing*. His breakthrough came in 1997 when he starred as Cinqué in Steven Spielberg’s *Amistad*, a performance that earned him a Golden Globe nomination. He later gained further recognition for his roles in *Gladiator* (2000) and *In America* (2002), the latter earning him an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor, making him the fourth African male actor to receive an Oscar nomination. In 2006, he was nominated again for *Blood Diamond*, which also won him the National Board of Review Award for Best Supporting Actor.

Throughout his career, Hounsou has taken on diverse roles in major franchises. In the Marvel Cinematic Universe, he played Korath the Pursuer in *Guardians of the Galaxy* (2014), *Captain Marvel* (2019), and the animated series *What If...?* (2021). In the DC Extended Universe, he voiced the Fisherman King in *Aquaman* (2018) and played the Wizard Shazam in *Shazam!* (2019), *Black Adam* (2022), and *Shazam! Fury of the Gods* (2023). His other notable film credits include *Stargate* (1994), *The Island* (2005), *Furious 7* (2015), *The Legend of Tarzan* (2016), *A Quiet Place Part II* (2021), and *Gran Turismo* (2023).

Beyond acting, Hounsou has ventured into directing with his documentary *In Search of Voodoo: Roots to Heaven* (2018), which explores the history and religious practices of West African Vodun. He has also been involved in activism, speaking at the United Nations Summit on Climate Change in 2009 and advocating for accountability from developed nations regarding environmental issues.

In his personal life, Hounsou dated model Kimora Lee Simmons, with whom he had a traditional commitment ceremony in Benin in 2008. They had a son in 2009 but separated in 2012. In 2025, Hounsou discussed the challenges he and other Black actors face in Hollywood, including typecasting and unfair compensation, attributing these struggles to systemic racism.

Hounsou’s career reflects both his resilience and his versatility, spanning film, television, documentary filmmaking, and activism. His contributions to cinema and his advocacy for social and environmental issues highlight his multifaceted influence in the entertainment industry.

title: Ahsee Tuala
text:
Ahsee Tuala is a professional rugby union player who was born in Samoa on 23 August 1989. When he was just two years old, his family moved to New Zealand, where he grew up in South Auckland. Tuala began his senior rugby career in New Zealand with the Counties Manukau Steelers, making his debut during the 2009 Air New Zealand Cup season at the age of 20. His versatility as a player allowed him to contribute in multiple backline positions, and he quickly became a key member of the Steelers, earning over 50 ITM Cup caps. Additionally, he was part of the Chiefs Development squads in 2010 and 2011, further honing his skills in New Zealand’s rugby system.

In 2015, Tuala made the move to English rugby, signing with Northampton Saints in the Aviva Premiership. Initially, his contract was set to last until the end of the 2014-15 season, but he soon secured a permanent deal, solidifying his place at the club. His breakthrough season came in 2016-17, where he established himself as a regular starter, particularly when George North was unavailable for international duty. Tuala’s performance that season was impressive, scoring five tries and helping Saints secure a spot in the European Rugby Champions Cup. His contributions earned him the Supporter’s Breakthrough Player of the Year award at the club’s end-of-season ceremony, beating out other newcomers like Nic Groom and Juan Pablo Estelles. One of his most memorable moments with Saints was scoring the match-winning try in a narrow victory over Stade Francais, which secured Northampton’s place in the top-tier European competition.

Internationally, Tuala’s early career was tied to New Zealand, where he was part of the wider squad for the New Zealand Under-20 team in 2009 and the New Zealand sevens training group in 2012. However, he chose to pursue international recognition with his home country, Samoa. In January 2012, he withdrew from the New Zealand sevens squad to focus on representing Samoa. His decision paid off when he was selected for the Samoan squad for the 2014 end-of-year tests, making his international debut on 14 November 2014 in a 23-13 win over Canada in Vannes, France. More recently, he was called up to the Samoan squad for the 2017 internationals, alongside fellow Saints teammate Ken Pisi. Throughout his career, Tuala has demonstrated versatility, adaptability, and a strong work ethic, making him a valuable asset both at club and international levels.

title: Vance Joy
text:
Vance Joy, born James Gabriel Keogh on 1 December 1987, is an Australian singer, songwriter, and musician who first gained fame with his 2013 hit "Riptide." His father worked in the computer trade, and his mother was a high school English teacher, with his paternal grandparents having immigrated from Ireland. Raised in Melbourne, Keogh attended St. Patrick's Primary School and later St. Kevin's College, where he graduated in 2005. He went on to earn a Bachelor of Arts and Bachelor of Laws from Monash University.

Before pursuing music, Keogh was a promising Australian rules footballer, playing for the Coburg Football Club in the Victorian Football League as a key defender from 2008 to 2009. He won the best first-year player award in 2008 but ultimately chose music over football, stating that he had reached his potential as a player and that his heart wasn't fully in the sport. His transition to music began while he was still playing football, as he wrote his first songs during that time.

Joy's musical career took off in 2013 when he signed a five-album deal with Atlantic Records. His debut EP, *God Loves You When You're Dancing*, was released in March 2013, featuring the breakthrough single "Riptide," which became a massive commercial success. The song topped the 2013 Triple J Hottest 100, peaked at number 6 on the ARIA Singles Chart, and was certified nine times platinum in Australia and five times platinum in the U.S. "Riptide" was inspired by a motel named Riptide that Joy visited as a child on family holidays. The song's success helped establish Joy as an artist, with its melody and storytelling resonating with audiences worldwide. He chose his stage name from a character in Peter Carey's novel *Bliss*, finding it both meaningful and catchy.

His debut studio album, *Dream Your Life Away*, was released in September 2014 and included hits like "Mess Is Mine," "First Time," and "Georgia." The latter was written in 2006 but refined over time. The album's deluxe edition featured live recordings and additional tracks. Joy supported the album with extensive touring, including opening for Taylor Swift on her *1989 World Tour*, which exposed him to a global audience. In 2015, he won Best Male Artist at the ARIA Music Awards and was named the Grand Prize winner of the International Songwriting Competition for "Riptide."

In 2018, Joy released his second album, *Nation of Two*, which debuted at number 1 in Australia and was certified gold. The album included singles like "Lay It on Me," "Like Gold," and "Saturday Sun," the latter inspired by California's Pacific Coast Highway. He also released a live album, *Live at Red Rocks Amphitheatre*, recorded during his *Nation of Two World Tour*. In 2019, he opened for P!nk on her *Beautiful Trauma World Tour*, further expanding his reach.

His third studio album, *In Our Own Sweet Time*, was released in June 2022. Leading up to its release, he collaborated with Benny Blanco and Marshmello on "You" (2021) and released "Missing Piece," which was featured on *Grey's Anatomy* and won an ARIA Award for Best Video. The song was inspired by his then-fiancée, Selen Us, whom he married in June 2023. They welcomed their daughter, Gigi, in early 2024.

Throughout his career, Joy has been recognized for his songwriting and performances, earning multiple ARIA Awards and other accolades. His music blends folk, indie, and pop influences, characterized by his distinctive voice and narrative-driven lyrics. Beyond his solo work, he has collaborated with artists like Noah Cyrus on the 2023 single "Everybody Needs Someone." His discography includes three studio albums, numerous EPs, and live recordings, cementing his status as one of Australia's most successful contemporary musicians.

title: Don DeLillo
text:
Donald Richard DeLillo, born on November 20, 1936, in New York City, is an acclaimed American novelist, short story writer, playwright, screenwriter, and essayist. His works explore a wide range of themes, including consumerism, nuclear war, language, technology, politics, and popular culture. DeLillo gained widespread recognition in 1985 with *White Noise*, which won the National Book Award for Fiction. He has since received numerous prestigious awards, including the PEN/Faulkner Award for *Mao II* (1991), the William Dean Howells Medal for *Underworld* (1997), the Jerusalem Prize (1999), the PEN/Saul Bellow Award (2010), and the Library of Congress Prize for American Fiction (2013).

DeLillo’s early life in the Bronx shaped his literary sensibilities. Growing up in an Italian-American Catholic family, he spent much of his childhood pretending to be a baseball announcer and was deeply influenced by jazz and postwar European cinema, particularly the works of Bergman, Antonioni, and Godard. He attended Fordham University, where he studied communication arts, and later worked in advertising before pursuing writing full-time. His parents’ support, especially as the eldest son, allowed him to follow his literary ambitions.

DeLillo’s first novel, *Americana* (1971), was followed by a prolific decade in the 1970s, during which he published six novels, including *End Zone* (1972), a dark comedy about football and nuclear war; *Great Jones Street* (1973), a rock-and-roll satire; and *Ratner’s Star* (1976), a science fiction novel praised for its intellectual depth. Though he initially wrote quickly, he later reflected that some of these early works could have been more carefully crafted. In 1978, he won a Guggenheim Fellowship, which funded travels to the Middle East and Greece, where he wrote *The Names* (1982), a thriller about a cult of assassins.

The 1980s marked a turning point in DeLillo’s career. *White Noise* (1985) brought him critical and commercial success, exploring themes of media, consumerism, and existential dread. His next novel, *Libra* (1988), a fictionalized account of Lee Harvey Oswald and the Kennedy assassination, sparked controversy but was also widely praised. DeLillo’s writing often opposes systems of power, corporations, and consumer culture, reflecting his belief that writers should challenge authority.

Influenced by modernist writers like James Joyce and William Faulkner, as well as jazz and film, DeLillo’s works are known for their dense prose and philosophical depth. His later novels, such as *Underworld* (1997), a sprawling epic spanning the Cold War to the digital age, further cemented his reputation as one of the most significant American novelists of his generation. Despite his success, DeLillo has remained a private figure, rarely engaging with media or public appearances. His writing continues to influence contemporary authors, and his exploration of modern anxieties and cultural shifts remains deeply relevant.

title: Susan Sarandon
text:
Susan Sarandon (née Tomalin) is an American actress with a career spanning over five decades, known for her extensive work in film, television, and theater. Born on October 4, 1946, in Jackson Heights, Queens, New York City, she is the eldest of nine children in a Roman Catholic family. Her father, Phillip Leslie Tomalin, was of English, Irish, and Welsh ancestry, while her mother, Lenora Marie Criscione, had Italian roots. The family moved to Edison, New Jersey, when Sarandon was young, where she attended Catholic schools and later Edison High School, graduating in 1964. She earned a Bachelor of Arts in drama from the Catholic University of America in Washington, D.C., studying under Gilbert V. Hartke.

Sarandon began her career in the late 1960s, making her film debut in *Joe* (1970) and appearing in the soap operas *A World Apart* (1970–1971) and *Search for Tomorrow* (1972). She gained prominence in *The Rocky Horror Picture Show* (1975) and worked with directors like Louis Malle in *Pretty Baby* (1978) and *Atlantic City* (1980), earning her first Academy Award nomination for the latter. Her role in *The Hunger* (1983) was notable for its controversial lesbian scene with Catherine Deneuve. She achieved widespread recognition in *Bull Durham* (1988), and her performance in *Dead Man Walking* (1995) won her the Academy Award for Best Actress. Other notable films include *Thelma & Louise* (1991), *Lorenzo’s Oil* (1992), *The Client* (1994), *Stepmom* (1998), and *Enchanted* (2007).

On stage, Sarandon made her Broadway debut in *An Evening with Richard Nixon* (1972) and later starred in the 2009 revival of *Exit the King*. She has also appeared in television, including guest roles in *Friends* (2001) and *Malcolm in the Middle* (2002), as well as starring in HBO’s *Bernard and Doris* (2008) and *You Don’t Know Jack* (2010). In 2017, she played Bette Davis in the FX miniseries *Feud*, earning a Golden Globe nomination.

Beyond acting, Sarandon is known for her political and humanitarian activism. She served as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador from 1999 and an FAO Goodwill Ambassador from 2010, focusing on social justice and humanitarian causes. She has been vocal in anti-war efforts, opposing the 2003 Iraq invasion, and has supported progressive political candidates, including Ralph Nader in 2000 and Bernie Sanders in 2016. She also advocates for civil rights, death penalty abolition, and LGBTQ+ issues.

Sarandon’s later work includes roles in *The Lovely Bones* (2009), *Cloud Atlas* (2012), and *Blue Beetle* (2023). In 2025, she will star in *Nonnas* alongside Vince Vaughn. Throughout her career, she has received numerous accolades, including an Academy Award, a BAFTA, and nine Golden Globe nominations. Her activism and artistic contributions have solidified her as a respected figure in Hollywood and beyond.

title: Jimmy Tompkins (priest)
text:
James John "Jimmy" Tompkins, born on 7 September 1870 in Margaree Forks, Nova Scotia, was a Roman Catholic priest whose progressive work in education and community development left a lasting impact on rural Nova Scotia. Throughout his life, he championed adult education, cooperatives, and economic empowerment, laying the foundation for the Antigonish Movement, which sought to improve the lives of fishing and mining communities in the region. The movement later evolved into the Extension Department of St. Francis Xavier University, now known as the Coady International Institute.

Tompkins’s early life reflected his dedication to education and self-reliance. From 1888 to 1895, he attended St. Francis Xavier University in alternating semesters while teaching Greek and Mathematics to fund his studies. After graduating, he pursued further education at the Urban College of the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide in Rome from 1897 to 1902. He was ordained a priest in the Lateran Basilica in Rome on 24 May 1902. Returning to Canada, he rejoined the faculty at St. Francis Xavier University, eventually rising to the position of vice-rector in 1907 and later serving as vice-president and prefect of studies.

During this period, Tompkins worked closely with the Carnegie Corporation to implement educational and institutional reforms. One of his most ambitious projects was an attempt to merge various sectarian and non-sectarian colleges in the Maritime Provinces into a single non-denominational university centered around Dalhousie University in Halifax. Despite support from the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Halifax, Edward McCarthy, the plan faced opposition from the Catholic Bishop of Antigonish, James Morrison, who not only blocked the merger but also exiled Tompkins to the remote fishing village of Canso, Nova Scotia, where he served as parish priest for Canso, Little Dover, and Queensport.

This relocation proved pivotal, as it exposed Tompkins to the severe economic struggles of the region’s fishing communities. Determined to help, he organized cooperative initiatives, including fisheries, stores, housing projects, and adult study groups, which became the core of the Antigonish Movement. The movement’s success led to its institutionalization as the Extension Department at St. Francis Xavier University, with Father Moses Coady, Tompkins’ double-cousin, at its helm. Key figures like Father Hugh MacPherson and A.B. MacDonald also contributed to the movement’s growth.

Tompkins’s career included several significant postings. In 1923, he became parish priest of the Star of the Sea Church in Canso. Later, in 1934, he was appointed chaplain at Bethany, the motherhouse of the Sisters of Saint Martha in Antigonish. From 1935 to 1948, he served as parish priest of St. Joseph’s Church in Reserve Mines, Cape Breton, where he established a cooperative housing association known as "Tompkinsville." He also founded the first regional library in Nova Scotia and the first credit union in the province. His motto, "It is not enough to have ideas, we have to put legs on them," encapsulated his belief in practical, actionable solutions to poverty and inequality.

In recognition of his contributions, Tompkins was awarded an honorary Doctor of Laws degree by Dalhousie University in 1919. He retired in 1948 due to declining health and spent his final years at St. Martha’s Convent in Margaree Forks. He died on 5 May 1953 at St. Martha’s Hospital and was buried in Reserve Mines.

Tompkins’s legacy endures through the Antigonish Movement and the institutions it inspired. His vision of education as a tool for empowerment and community-driven economic development continues to influence social and economic initiatives in Nova Scotia and beyond. His life has been documented in several biographies, including *Father Jimmy: Life and Times of Father Jimmy Tompkins* by Jim Lotz and Michael R. Welton (1997) and *Father Tompkins of Nova Scotia* by George Boyle (1953). The Tompkins Institute for Human Values and Technology at Cape Breton University also honors his contributions.

title: Ramli Sarip
text:
Ramli bin Sarip, widely known as "Papa Rock," is a prominent Singaporean musician, singer, songwriter, arranger, and record producer who played a pivotal role in shaping Singapore’s rock scene. Born on 15 October 1952, he gained fame as the lead vocalist and frontman of the influential Malay rock band Sweet Charity, which was formed in 1964 and remained active until he left in 1986. During his tenure with Sweet Charity, the band achieved significant success, contributing to what was dubbed a "rock explosion" in both Singapore and Malaysia, particularly during the 1970s and 1980s.

After parting ways with Sweet Charity, Ramli pursued a solo career, eventually signing with Warner Music. He made history as the first Malay rock singer to perform two solo concerts at the prestigious Istana Budaya in Kuala Lumpur. His contributions to music earned him the COMPASS Artistic Excellence Award in 1998. To support his solo work, he assembled a five-piece backing band called Sangkakala. In 1990, he hosted a Malaysian Hari Raya Puasa television special titled *Bersama Ramli Sarip*, which aired on the first day of the festive season. However, his long hair, which defied the broadcasting norms of the time, led to a seven-year ban from Radio Televisyen Malaysia (RTM) in 1993.

Throughout his career, Ramli has released 12 solo albums, showcasing his versatility and longevity in the music industry. Beyond music, he ventured into acting, appearing in the 2002 Singaporean satirical film *Talking Cock the Movie*. In 2011, he contributed his vocals to a remake of the song "Home," further cementing his influence in Singaporean music.

One of the most controversial moments in Ramli’s career came in 2019 when he performed a rock-inspired version of Singapore’s national anthem, "Majulah Singapura," at the National Day Parade. His rendition sparked intense criticism, including an open letter from Dr. Rohana Zubir, daughter of the original composer, Zubir Said. Dr. Zubir condemned the reinterpretation, arguing that it lacked the original anthem’s quality and integrity, and that the national anthem should remain unchanged to respect its historical significance. Despite the backlash, Ramli performed the anthem at the parade, marking a bold but divisive moment in his career.

In recognition of his contributions, Ramli was honored with the title of "Datuk" by the Yang di-Pertua Negeri of Malacca in 2013, a distinction reflecting his cultural impact. This title is part of the Companion Class II of the Exalted Order of Malacca (DPSM). Throughout his decades-long career, Ramli Sarip has been a defining figure in Singaporean and Malaysian rock music, leaving a lasting legacy as a pioneer and innovator.

title: Elizabeth Inglis
text:
Elizabeth Inglis, born Desiree Mary Lucy Hawkins on July 10, 1913, in Colchester, England, was an English actress best known for her role in *The Letter* (1940) and as the mother of American actress Sigourney Weaver. She was the daughter of Margaret Inglis (née Hunt) and Alan George Hawkins. Her acting career began in 1934 with the film *Borrowed Clothes*, marking her screen debut. The following year, she appeared in a small but notable role as Hilary Jordan in Alfred Hitchcock’s *The 39 Steps* (1935), a classic thriller that solidified her early presence in British cinema.

One of Inglis’s most notable stage performances was as the young maid Nancy in the original 1938 production of Patrick Hamilton’s play *Gas Light*, which premiered on December 5 and ran until June 10, 1939, after 141 performances. The entire cast, including Inglis, later recreated their roles for a live 1939 television adaptation broadcast on BBC Television, demonstrating her versatility across different media.

In 1940, Inglis moved to Hollywood and took on the role of Adele Ainsworth in William Wyler’s *The Letter*, a film adaptation of a 1927 play. By this time, she was using the stage name Elizabeth Earl, though she later reverted to her birth surname for her personal and later professional life. After this film, she largely stepped away from acting.

Her personal life took a significant turn when she married American television executive Pat Weaver in 1942, a marriage that lasted until his death in 2002. She retired from acting after their marriage to focus on family life. The couple had two children, including their daughter, actress Sigourney Weaver. In a unique connection to her daughter’s career, a photograph of Inglis was used in a deleted scene from *Aliens* (1986) to portray Amanda Ripley, the elderly daughter of Sigourney Weaver’s character Ellen Ripley.

Elizabeth Inglis passed away on August 25, 2007, in Santa Barbara, California, at the age of 94. Her career, though relatively short, included memorable roles in both British and American productions, and her legacy is further cemented through her connection to her famous daughter.

title: Michael Collins (astronaut)
text:
Michael Collins was an American astronaut best known for his role in the Apollo 11 mission, during which he orbited the Moon alone in the command module *Columbia* while Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the lunar surface. Born on October 31, 1930, in Rome, Italy, where his father, a U.S. Army officer, was stationed, Collins grew up in various locations due to his father’s military postings. He graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point in 1952, following in the footsteps of his father, brother, and uncle, all of whom had military careers. Collins chose the U.S. Air Force to avoid nepotism in the Army, where his family already had high-ranking positions.

After completing flight training, Collins became a fighter pilot, flying F-86 Sabre jets in France and participating in NATO exercises. In 1957, he married Patricia Finnegan, a social worker, after converting to Catholicism to accommodate her family’s faith. He later attended the U.S. Air Force Experimental Flight Test Pilot School at Edwards Air Force Base, where he trained alongside future astronauts like Frank Borman and Jim Irwin.

Collins was selected as part of NASA’s third group of astronauts in 1963. His first spaceflight was aboard Gemini 10 in 1966, alongside John Young. During this mission, they performed orbital rendezvous with two Agena Target Vehicles and conducted two spacewalks, making Collins the first person to complete more than one spacewalk. His expertise in pressure suits and extravehicular activities (EVAs) was critical to the mission’s success. Collins also became the fourth person and third American to perform a spacewalk.

On the historic Apollo 11 mission in 1969, Collins orbited the Moon alone while Armstrong and Aldrin landed, becoming one of only 24 people to ever travel to the Moon. He completed 30 orbits, ensuring communications and navigation support for the mission. His role was vital, as he had to remain in lunar orbit while his crewmates descended to the surface. After retiring from NASA in 1970, Collins worked in the Department of State as Assistant Secretary of Public Affairs and later became the director of the National Air and Space Museum, a position he held until 1978. He then served as undersecretary of the Smithsonian Institution and worked in the aerospace industry before starting his own consulting firm.

Collins was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1969 and the Congressional Gold Medal in 2011, alongside his Apollo 11 crewmates. He passed away on April 28, 2021. Throughout his career, Collins played a significant role in advancing space exploration, contributing to both military aviation and NASA’s early human spaceflight programs. His calm demeanor and technical expertise earned him respect in the astronaut corps, and his contributions to the Apollo program remain a key part of space history.

title: Francis Nicholson (painter)
text:
Francis Nicholson, born on 14 November 1753 in Pickering, North Yorkshire, was a prominent British artist known primarily for his landscape paintings in both watercolor and oil. He began his artistic journey by studying under a local artist in Scarborough before establishing himself in his hometown of Pickering, where he created sporting pictures and portraits for various Yorkshire patrons. By the mid-1780s, his focus shifted toward landscapes in watercolor, particularly depictions of country houses, which became a significant part of his work.

Nicholson gained recognition when he began contributing views of Yorkshire and Scotland to exhibitions at the Royal Academy starting in 1789. His work also appeared in the *Copper Plate Magazine*, where he provided topographical views. One of his notable collaborations was with engraver Francis Jukes, contributing "Views of England" to *The Beauties of England and Wales*, a multi-volume book published between 1801 and 1815. Although his clientele increasingly shifted toward London, Nicholson remained in Yorkshire for much of his career, living in Whitby, Knaresborough, and Ripon before finally relocating to London around 1803.

In 1804, he became a founding member of the Society of Painters in Watercolours, an organization for which he was a prolific contributor, regularly exhibiting his work. His influence extended beyond painting; in 1820, he authored *The practice of drawing and painting landscape from nature, in water colours*, a handbook that proved so popular it sold out and required a second edition in 1823. Nicholson’s contributions to the art world earned him admiration from contemporaries, including J.M.W. Turner, who regarded him highly.

Nicholson passed away in London on 6 March 1844 and was buried in Brompton Cemetery. His legacy endures through his art and his writings, which helped shape the development of watercolor painting. A self-portrait from around 1837 is held in the National Portrait Gallery, and in 2012, the Pickering and district Civic Society honored him with a Blue Plaque at 3 Hungate in Pickering. Beyond his artistic achievements, Nicholson’s daughter, Marianne Croker, was also an artist, poet, and author, further cementing the family’s place in cultural history. Nicholson is often referred to as the "Father of watercolor painting" and an early pioneer of lithography, leaving a lasting impact on British art.

title: Fifi Cooper
text:
Fifi Cooper, born Refilwe Boingotlo Moeketsi on 24 October 1991, is a South African recording artist known for her versatility in both R&B and rap music. She began her musical journey at the age of eight, participating in school performances and other extracurricular activities. Her formal education took place in Montshiwa, Mahikeng, where she developed her singing and dancing skills. She later attended Batswana High School and pursued higher education in media at Boston Media House.

Fifi Cooper’s professional music career started in 2008 with a guest appearance on Mo'Molemi’s album *Motzamai: Rebel With a Pause*. However, her breakthrough came in 2010 with the release of her rap single "Chechela Morago," which gained significant airplay and established her presence in the South African music industry. She also contributed vocals to several other artists’ works, including remixes of AKA’s "Baddest Remix," Mo'Molemi’s *Asia*, Khuli Chana’s *Lost in Time*, and Lection’s *Gentlemen’s Club*.

In 2015, Fifi Cooper signed with Ambitiouz Entertainment and released the single "Kisses," produced by AB Crazy and directed by Dino Benedetti. Her debut album, *20FIFI*, was released on 13 November 2015 and earned her three awards at the 15th Metro FM Music Awards. The album was also nominated in the "Best Newcomer of The Year" and "Best Female Artist of The Year" categories at the 2nd South African Music Awards.

However, in 2017, Fifi Cooper, along with A-Reece and the hip-hop duo B3nchMarQ, left Ambitiouz Entertainment. A legal battle ensued, with the label suing her for copyright infringement. The Johannesburg High Court ruled that she no longer owned the rights to the music she recorded under the label, ordering her to return or delete all copies. She was also required to pay damages and legal costs. The dispute arose because she had resigned without obtaining a clearance certificate. Julius Malema, leader of the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), intervened, viewing the case as a broader issue of injustice. The EFF negotiated an out-of-court settlement that restored her rights to perform her music.

After leaving Ambitiouz, Fifi Cooper founded her own record label, Mo Cooper Records, and released her second album, *Take Me Back*, in 2020. The 21-track album featured collaborations with artists such as Thabsie, Moozlie, Towdeemac, and Leon Lee. In November 2020, she released the single "Net So" from her upcoming 2021 album *Chapters*, with the music video directed by herself. On 11 March 2021, she released another single, "Motlogeleng."

Fifi Cooper is often referred to as the "Motswako first lady" due to her contributions to the Motswako and hip-hop genres. She describes her rap style as "unpredictable, punchy, and hearty." Beyond music, she is a single mother to a son named Resego. Her career highlights her resilience, creativity, and ability to navigate the challenges of the music industry while maintaining her artistic identity.

title: Maddy Crippen
text:
Madeleine Marie Crippen, also known as Madeleine Plankey after her marriage, is an American former competition swimmer who represented the United States at the 2000 Summer Olympics. Born on July 10, 1980, she had a distinguished career in swimming, earning multiple medals and accolades at both the national and international levels. Crippen’s early success included a silver medal as part of Team USA at the 1997 Pan Pacific Championships in Fukuoka, Japan. She continued to perform well in major competitions, placing fifth in the 400-meter individual medley and sixth in the 200-meter individual medley at the 1998 World Aquatics Championships in Perth, Australia. In 1999, she competed at the Pan Pacific Championships, finishing fourth in the 400-meter individual medley.

Crippen’s most significant achievement came when she secured a spot on the 2000 U.S. Olympic Team by placing second in the 400-meter individual medley at the Olympic Trials. At the 2000 Summer Olympics, she finished sixth in the event, showcasing her skill on the global stage. Her Olympic coaches included Hall of Fame coach Dick Shoulberg, who served as an advisory women's coach for the games that year. After the Olympics, Crippen continued competing at the 2002 Pan Pacific Championships and the 2003 World Championships in Barcelona, Spain. Throughout her career, she became a three-time U.S. national champion, winning two titles in the 400-meter individual medley and one in the 200-meter breaststroke.

During her time at Villanova University, Crippen swam for the Villanova Wildcats in NCAA and Big East Conference competitions. Her college career was marked by success, including an NCAA championship in the 400-yard individual medley and ten Big East championships. She was named Big East "Swimmer of the Year" in 1999 and 2001, as well as Villanova "Swimmer of the Year" in 1999, 2001, and 2002. In 2019, she was inducted into the Villanova Athletic Hall of Fame, further cementing her legacy in collegiate swimming.
