Counter’s business interests were extensive. He owned a foundry and a sawmill, invested in real estate, and was involved in the transportation sector. Notably, he was part of the Calvin Company, which proposed a ferry service to connect Kingston with the railway in Cape Vincent, USA, anticipating the future construction of the Grand Trunk Railway. He also held substantial waterfront rights and shares in the Penny Bridge, which later became the La Salle Causeway. Additionally, he proposed the construction of the Wolfe Island Canal, intended to facilitate quick water transportation to Cape Vincent, though this project was eventually abandoned. Counter played a key role in the incorporation of Kingston as a town in 1838, believing it would boost business and property values.

Politically, Counter sought a council seat in the town’s first election but was unsuccessful. However, he went on to serve multiple terms as the Mayor of Kingston, holding office in 1841-43, 1846, 1850, 1852-53, and 1855. During his tenure, he was instrumental in establishing the Board of Trade in 1839 and contributed to the construction of a new town hall, designed by architect George Browne. He secured a loan of £20,000 from England to finance the project. When Kingston became the temporary home of the Parliament of the Province of Canada in 1841, Counter organized accommodations for government officials, even giving up his own home to the vice-chancellor, R.S. Jameson, and renting out the Marine Railway offices to the government. He also donated the land for the Sydenham Street Church and laid its cornerstone in 1851, supporting the Wesleyan Methodists with generous contributions to their building fund.

Despite his influence, Counter faced financial difficulties due to heavy borrowing to support his business ventures and the development of the first subdivision in Kingston. In 1855, he resigned as mayor due to a conflict of interest involving his shares in the local gas company. Just months later, he was forced into bankruptcy after failing to meet a large mortgage payment. His residence at Plymouth Square, at the corner of Ontario and Johnson Streets, was eventually torn down in 1973.

A portrait of Counter, painted by American artist Alvah Bradish in 1842, remains a notable artifact. Bradish, known for his work in Rochester and Detroit, advertised his services in Kingston and was commissioned by the town council to paint Counter’s portrait. The painting, depicting the mayor in a simple Chain of Office and holding a scroll, was paid for by the councilors personally and not from public funds. The portrait was restored in the late 1970s and now hangs in the John Counter meeting room at Kingston City Hall, with copies held in various archival institutions.

title: Akbar Hossain
text:
Akbar Hossain, commonly known as Bir Protik Akbar Hossain, was a prominent Bangladeshi politician and military officer who played significant roles in both the independence of Bangladesh and its subsequent political landscape. He was born on 18 January 1941 in Kashari Patty, Comilla District, and began his military career by joining the Kakul Military Academy in Pakistan in May 1966. After his commission, he was posted to the 31 Baluch Regiment and later pursued a bachelor's degree from the University of Dhaka, which he completed in 1969.

During the Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971, Hossain actively participated in the struggle for independence, initially serving under Khaled Musharraf and later joining the Z Force led by Ziaur Rahman. His bravery during the war earned him the prestigious gallantry award, Bir Protik. After Bangladesh gained independence, he voluntarily retired from the Bangladesh Army in December 1973 at the rank of lieutenant colonel.

Following his military career, Hossain ventured into politics, becoming a key figure in the formation of the United People's Party (UPP) in January 1974, where he eventually became vice-president. In 1977, the UPP merged with the Jatiyatabadi Front, but Hossain left the alliance to join the Bangladesh National Party (BNP), contributing significantly to its establishment. Within the BNP, he held several important positions, including special secretary, joint secretary general, and vice-president, a role he maintained until his death.

Hossain's political career saw him hold multiple ministerial positions. In 1978, he was appointed Minister for Petroleum and Mineral Resources under President Ziaur Rahman. He first entered parliament in 1979, representing the Comilla 8th constituency, and was re-elected to the same seat four times. During the military rule of General Hossain Mohammad Ershad, Hossain was imprisoned on five separate occasions for his opposition to the regime.

After the end of the military dictatorship and the election of Khaleda Zia as Bangladesh's first female Prime Minister, Hossain returned to government as Minister for the Environment and Forests in October 1993. Later, in October 2001, following the BNP-led four-party alliance's victory in the 8th Jatiyo Sangshad elections, he was appointed Minister for Shipping. His political career was marked by his loyalty to the BNP and his commitment to democratic governance.

Akbar Hossain passed away on 25 June 2006 in Dhaka after suffering a massive heart attack. Throughout his life, he was recognized for his contributions to both the military and political sectors of Bangladesh, leaving a lasting impact on the nation's development.

title: Muhammad Alhamid
text:
Muhammad Alhamid, born on September 17, 1971, in Makassar, Indonesia, is a prominent academic, civil servant, and political figure. He comes from an Arab Indonesian family of the Ba 'Alawi sada clan, with his parents being Sayyid Alhamid and Syarifah Aisyah Sadiq Alaydrus. He is married to Lubena Umar Alahaddad, another Indonesian Arab, and they have five children: Fatimah Zahra, Jakfar Sodiq, Khadijah, Aisyah, and Umar Muchdar.

Alhamid completed his early education in Makassar, graduating from elementary school in 1984, junior high school in 1987, and high school in 1990. He then pursued higher education at Hasanuddin University, earning a Bachelor of Science in Government (SIP) in 1994 and a Master of Science (MSi) in 1999. He later obtained his doctoral degree from Airlangga University in 2007.

His academic career began as a lecturer at Hasanuddin University in 1997. He served as secretary of the Political Science Department from 2008 to 2010 and later became chairman of the department from 2010 to 2012. On February 28, 2015, he was inaugurated as a professor of Sociology at Hasanuddin University, delivering a speech on election accountability and system transformation. His professorship was conferred by the university chancellor, Professor Dwia Aries Tina Pulubuhu, in the presence of Vice President Jusuf Kalla and other notable figures. Additionally, he has taught at the University of West Sulawesi and the Makassar Institute of Public Administration.

Alhamid’s involvement in electoral oversight began in 2009 when he was elected chairman of the South Sulawesi Election Supervisory Committee (Panwaslu) for the 2009 elections. In 2012, he was selected by the People's Representative Council (DPR) as chairman of the Election Supervisory Board of the Republic of Indonesia (Bawaslu RI), serving until 2017. Following this, he was appointed as a member of the Election Organization Ethics Council of the Republic of Indonesia (DKPP RI) from 2017 to 2022, a position inaugurated by President Joko Widodo on June 12, 2017.

He has authored several publications, including books, journal articles, and academic theses. His notable works include *The Existence of the DKPP RI in Escorting Dignified Democracy and Elections* (2018), *Realizing Election Accountability* (2015), and *Judging Bawaslu Readiness in Dealing with 2014 Election Violations and Disputes* (2013). His doctoral dissertation, *Uwa and Social Change: Case Study of Uwa Leadership in the Process of Adopting Farmer Rabbise (Melon) Innovations in the Tolotang Community of South Sulawesi*, was completed in 2007.

For his contributions, Alhamid received the Satyalancana Karya Satya 10-year service award from President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono in 2012. In 2015, President Joko Widodo honored him with the 1st Class Star of the Defenders of Democracy, an award also given to Husni Kamil Manik, then-chairman of the General Elections Commission. The award was presented on the 70th anniversary of Indonesia’s independence, recognizing Alhamid’s role in upholding democratic values.

Throughout his career, Muhammad Alhamid has demonstrated a strong commitment to academia, electoral oversight, and public service, making significant contributions to Indonesia’s democratic institutions.

title: Coco Chanel
text:
Gabrielle Bonheur "Coco" Chanel (1883–1971) was a pioneering French fashion designer and businesswoman who revolutionized women's fashion in the early 20th century. Born into poverty in the charity hospital of Saumur, Chanel was the second child of Eugénie Jeanne Devolle and Albert Chanel, an itinerant street vendor. Her early life was marked by hardship; her mother died when she was 11, and her father sent her and her sisters to the convent of Aubazine, where she learned to sew. Later, she worked as a seamstress and performed in cabarets, earning the nickname "Coco," possibly derived from the song *Qui qu'a vu Coco* or the French term for a kept woman, *cocotte*.

Chanel’s career began in fashion when she opened a millinery shop in Paris in 1910, financed by her lover, Étienne Balsan. She later established boutiques in Deauville and Biarritz, selling sporty, casual clothing made from jersey fabric—a material traditionally used for men’s underwear. Her designs, such as the marinière (sailor blouse), were revolutionary, emphasizing comfort and simplicity. By 1919, she had registered as a couturière and opened her renowned maison de couture at 31 rue Cambon in Paris.

Beyond clothing, Chanel expanded into jewelry, handbags, and fragrances. Her most iconic creation, *Chanel No. 5*, launched in 1921, became a global sensation. She also designed the interlocked-CC monogram, which remains a symbol of the brand. However, her business dealings were contentious; she licensed her name to the Wertheimer brothers for *Chanel No. 5*, but later resented the financial arrangement, calling Pierre Wertheimer "the bandit who screwed me."

Chanel’s personal life was marked by relationships with influential figures. She had affairs with Balsan, Arthur "Boy" Capel (who funded her early ventures), and the Duke of Westminster. Capel’s death in 1919 deeply affected her, and she later collaborated with British aristocrats, including Winston Churchill. She also had a brief romantic relationship with composer Igor Stravinsky, whom she hosted in her home during his exile from Russia.

During World War II, Chanel remained in France under Nazi occupation. She had ties to the German intelligence service, the Sicherheitsdienst, and was involved in a failed peace overture to Churchill in 1943. After the war, she was interrogated but avoided charges due to Churchill’s intervention. She briefly relocated to Switzerland before returning to Paris in 1954 to revive her fashion house.

Chanel’s legacy is undeniable; she was the only fashion designer named in *Time* magazine’s 100 most influential people of the 20th century. Despite her controversial past, her innovations in fashion—such as the little black dress, tweed suits, and her emphasis on practical elegance—remain timeless. Her life was one of reinvention, from impoverished beginnings to becoming one of history’s most influential designers.

title: Roxana Miranda
text:
Roxana del Pilar Miranda Meneses was born on 24 April 1967 in Buin, Chile, to Francisco Miranda Araya, a municipal worker, and Orfilia de las Mercedes Meneses Roa, a seamstress. Her father passed away when she was six years old. She completed her secondary education at the Liceo Comercial de San Bernardo, where she also participated in student leadership as part of the school's student council. On 10 January 1994, she married Iván Luis Vargas García in San Bernardo, and the couple has four children.

Miranda has been actively involved in political and social activism. She served as the national leader of the Asociación de Deudores Habitacionales (ANDHA Chile), an organization representing home debtors, which later became known as "ANDHA Chile a Luchar Democrático." In 2009, she ran for a seat in the Chamber of Deputies representing District No. 30, but her campaign was unsuccessful, as she finished in seventh place with 4,332 votes, equating to 2.85% of the total. Prior to that, in 2008, she ran for mayor of San Bernardo as an independent candidate but received only 3,558 votes (4.24% of the total). She attempted to secure the same position again in the 2012 municipal election, but her support declined, as she garnered only 1,831 votes, or 2.77% of the total.

In her political career, Miranda became the president of the Partido Igualdad (Equality Party). On 20 January 2013, she was officially proclaimed as the party's candidate for the 2013 Chilean presidential election. By the end of May 2013, negotiations were reportedly underway between Miranda and another candidate, Marcel Claude, to consolidate their campaigns into a single candidacy. However, Miranda clarified that she had no intention of withdrawing from the race. On 29 May 2013, she submitted the required signatures to the Chilean Electoral Service to legalize the Partido Igualdad, thereby formalizing her candidacy.

Miranda presented her government program on 5 November 2013, the last of the presidential candidates to do so. The 125-page document outlined her vision for social reforms, which she described as a "plebeian program, of the people who wakes up and begins to organize itself to struggle for a better country." The program was structured around four main areas: "Superación del capitalismo" (Overcoming capitalism), "Que el pueblo mande" (Let the people rule), "Recuperación de nuestros derechos" (Recovering our rights), and "El buen vivir" (Good living). Despite her efforts, Miranda ultimately lost the election.

title: Wil Nieves
text:
Wil Nieves, born on September 25, 1977, is a former Puerto Rican professional baseball catcher and current minor league coach. He played in Major League Baseball (MLB) for multiple teams, including the San Diego Padres, New York Yankees, Washington Nationals, Milwaukee Brewers, Colorado Rockies, Arizona Diamondbacks, and Philadelphia Phillies. Nieves began his MLB career with the Padres in 2002, after being drafted in the 47th round in 1995. He appeared in 28 games for the Padres that season before being selected off waivers by the Anaheim Angels in December 2002.

In 2003, Nieves was traded to the New York Yankees in exchange for pitcher Bret Prinz. He earned a spot on the Yankees' 2007 roster after impressing during spring training, beating out Todd Pratt and Raul Chavez. While primarily serving as the backup catcher to Jorge Posada, Nieves was often regarded as Mike Mussina's "personal catcher." On July 8, 2007, he made his first non-catching appearance in the majors, playing first base in the ninth inning due to a shortage of position players. Nieves had a notable performance on July 21, 2007, going 2-for-3 against the Tampa Bay Devil Rays, but was later designated for assignment after the Yankees acquired José Molina. Despite his defensive strengths, Nieves batted only .164 during his time with the Yankees. He later played for Licey in the Dominican Winter League during the off-season.

In 2008, Nieves joined the Washington Nationals, starting with their Triple-A affiliate, the Columbus Clippers. On April 25, 2008, he hit his first major-league home run—a walk-off shot against the Chicago Cubs—as a member of the Nationals. Over the next few seasons, he served as the backup catcher to Jesus Flores in 2009 and Iván Rodríguez in 2010.

Nieves then signed with the Milwaukee Brewers in December 2010, playing for them for part of the 2011 season before being traded to the Atlanta Braves in July 2011 for a nominal fee of $1. However, he was soon demoted to Triple-A Gwinnett, making way for J.C. Boscan as the backup catcher.

In December 2011, Nieves signed a minor-league deal with the Colorado Rockies, earning a $414,000 salary. After a strong spring training (.409 batting average, 1 HR in 18 games), he was reassigned before the season began. He was later called up to the majors in May 2012, replacing Ramón Hernández, and provided mentorship to Wilin Rosario while also working with pitcher Jeremy Guthrie. Nieves suffered a turf toe injury in July 2012 and was placed on the disabled list, but was designated for assignment in August after hitting .298 with 1 HR and 5 RBI in 16 games.

On August 6, 2012, Nieves signed with the Arizona Diamondbacks, debuting with a two-run home run against the Pittsburgh Pirates on August 9. The following season, he joined the Philadelphia Phillies in December 2013. He made the Phillies' Opening Day roster in 2014 as the backup to Carlos Ruiz, but injured his leg in June, leading to his temporary replacement by Cameron Rupp. Nieves appeared in only 14 games that season.

In 2015, Nieves returned to the San Diego Padres on a minor-league contract, making the Opening Day roster after Tim Federowicz suffered a season-ending injury. He played in six games, hitting a grand slam against the San Francisco Giants on April 12, before being designated for assignment in May. The Braves later signed him to a minor-league deal, but he batted only .238 for Triple-A Gwinnett before being released in June 2015.

After retiring from playing, Nieves transitioned into coaching. In 2019, he joined the Boston Red Sox’s minor-league system as a coach for the Class A-Advanced Salem Red Sox. Throughout his career, Nieves was known for his defensive skills, mentorship, and occasional clutch hitting, including memorable moments like his walk-off home run for the Nationals and his grand slam for the Padres.

title: Jemima Goldsmith
text:
Jemima Marcelle Goldsmith, born on 30 January 1974 in London, is an English television and film producer, screenwriter, and former journalist. She is the founder of Instinct Productions, a London-based company specializing in television, documentaries, and film. Before becoming a producer, she worked as an associate editor for *The New Statesman* and as the European editor-at-large for *Vanity Fair*.

Goldsmith comes from a prominent family. Her mother, Lady Annabel Goldsmith, is the daughter of the 8th Marquess of Londonderry, while her father, Sir James Goldsmith, was a financier and former Conservative MP. Her paternal grandmother was French, and her father’s family has German Jewish roots. Goldsmith’s parents were initially married to other partners at the time of her birth but later married each other in 1978. She has two younger brothers, Zac and Ben Goldsmith, as well as several half-siblings, including Robin and India Jane Birley. She attended prestigious schools in London, including The Old Vicarage and Francis Holland Girls School, before enrolling at the University of Bristol to study English. She briefly dropped out in 1993 to marry Imran Khan but later returned to complete her degree in 2002. She also earned a master’s degree in Middle Eastern Studies from the University of London in 2003.

Goldsmith’s career in media and production has been notable. Through Instinct Productions, she has been an executive producer for several high-profile projects, including the Emmy-nominated *The Clinton Affair* and *The Case Against Adnan Syed*. She also produced the Golden Globe and Emmy-nominated series *Impeachment*, part of *American Crime Story*, which focused on the Clinton-Lewinsky scandal. In 2022, she wrote and produced the romantic comedy *What’s Love Got to Do with It?*, starring Lily James and Emma Thompson, which won multiple awards, including Best British Film. She has also worked on documentaries such as *We Steal Secrets: The Story of WikiLeaks*, *Unmanned: America’s Drone Wars*, and *Making A Killing: Guns, Greed and the NRA*. Additionally, she contributed to the fifth season of *The Crown* but requested her contributions be removed, believing the portrayal of Princess Diana would not be respectful. In 2024, she produced the popular podcast *A Muslim & A Jew Go There*, which addressed interfaith relations and was nominated for two British Podcast Awards.

Before her production career, Goldsmith was a journalist, contributing to publications like *The Independent*, *The Sunday Times*, and *The Observer*. She was also a feature writer for *British Vogue* and later became *Vanity Fair*’s European editor-at-large. In 2011, she guest-edited *The New Statesman*, which was widely praised for its focus on freedom of speech and included contributions from figures like Russell Brand, Julian Assange, and Hugh Grant.

Goldsmith has been involved in philanthropy and activism. In 1998, she launched a fashion label in Pakistan that employed women, with profits going to cancer hospitals. She has worked with UNICEF as an ambassador, supporting campaigns for children’s rights and disaster relief. She also founded the Jemima Khan Afghan Refugee Appeal and supported Palestinian refugee children through the HOPING foundation. Politically, she has campaigned against wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, advocated for press freedom, and supported Julian Assange before later criticizing him. In 2023, she participated in anti-hate vigils, speaking out against antisemitism and Islamophobia, and has faced threats due to her Jewish and Muslim heritage.

Goldsmith’s personal life has been well-documented. She married former Pakistani cricket captain and Prime Minister Imran Khan in 1995, converting to Islam and moving to Lahore. The couple had two sons, Sulaiman and Kasim, before divorcing in 2004. She later had relationships with actor Hugh Grant and comedian Russell Brand. In 2025, she accused the Pakistani government of targeting her sons over political vendettas against Imran Khan. Despite her background, she has expressed feeling caught between cultural identities, avoiding tribalism in her work and personal life.

title: Enamul Haque (engineer)
text:
Enamul Haque is a Bangladeshi politician and engineer who served as a member of the Jatiya Sangsad, representing the Rajshahi-4 constituency, from 2008 to 2024. Born on 21 October 1969, he pursued an undergraduate degree in engineering and also obtained an MBA. He entered politics as a member of the Bangladesh Awami League, winning his first election to the Jatiya Sangsad in 2008. He was re-elected on 5 January 2014, continuing his tenure as a representative of the Awami League.

Throughout his career, Haque faced several controversies. In September 2014, the Bangladesh Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) recommended charging him with corruption related to his company, Ena Enterprise. The allegations highlighted concerns about financial misconduct in his business dealings. Later, in January 2017, he publicly criticized Iqbal Sobhan Chowdhury, the editor of *The Daily Observer*, after the newspaper published a report linking him to the drug trade. Haque denied the accusations, but the incident drew significant attention to his political and personal conduct.

His relationship with the Awami League also became strained. In September 2017, local leaders from the party in Rajshahi accused him of creating divisions within the organization, accusing him of fostering factional disputes that weakened party cohesion. This internal strife further complicated his political standing.

In June 2020, Ayesha Akter Liza, a 35-36-year-old woman, accused Haque of deception and coercion, claiming he forced her to abort their unborn child. She asserted that they had married on 30 April 2013 and officially registered the marriage on 11 May 2018. However, Haque admitted to the marriage but claimed they had divorced on 23 April 2020, denying any wrongdoing in the matter. The allegations added to the growing list of controversies surrounding his public and private life.

Despite these issues, Haque remained in office until 2024. In September of that year, the ACC announced plans to investigate him for corruption, including allegations of money laundering, financial irregularities in government projects, and the illegal accumulation of wealth. The decision indicated a renewed focus on addressing corruption within political circles.

Haque’s career, marked by both political achievements and significant controversies, reflects the complexities of Bangladeshi politics. His engineering background and business ventures, combined with his political role, placed him at the center of public and legal scrutiny. The ongoing investigations into his financial dealings suggest that his legacy may be defined as much by the allegations against him as by his contributions to governance.

title: Abdelhamid Shabana
text:
Abdelhameed Shabana, born on 2 October 1985 in Egypt, is a professional footballer who is currently a free agent. He is a versatile attacking midfielder known for his electrifying playing style, though he can also perform effectively as a striker or a winger. Shabana gained significant recognition in Egyptian football for his impressive goals against some of the country's top clubs, including Zamalek, Al-Ahly, and Ismaily. His ability to perform at a high level against these prestigious teams cemented his reputation as a skilled and dynamic player.

Shabana’s international career includes representing Egypt at both the U20 and U23 levels. He participated in the African Games qualifiers, showcasing his talent on the continental stage. Additionally, he contributed to Egypt’s victory in the Qatar U23 Cup, further highlighting his capabilities in youth and senior international competitions.

Throughout his career, Shabana has played for several clubs, though his most notable achievements came with Al-Ahly and Churchill Brothers. While at Al-Ahly, he won the Egyptian Premier League in the 2010-2011 season, a major accomplishment in Egyptian football. His time with Churchill Brothers was also successful, as he helped the team secure the Federation Cup in 2014. These victories reflect his ability to perform in high-pressure environments and contribute to his team’s success.

As of 29 April 2014, Shabana’s club statistics were documented, though the article does not provide specific details on his performance metrics. His career trajectory suggests a player who has experienced both domestic and international success, though his current status as a free agent indicates he may be seeking new opportunities.

Shabana’s legacy in Egyptian football is marked by his ability to deliver crucial goals in high-stakes matches, his contributions to youth national teams, and his accolades with top-tier clubs. His versatility and attacking prowess have made him a memorable figure in the sport, particularly in his home country. Despite being a free agent at the time of the article’s writing, his past achievements continue to define his career.

title: Jefferson Thomas
text:
Jefferson Allison Thomas, born on September 19, 1942, in Little Rock, Arkansas, was the youngest of seven children and was named after Thomas Jefferson, the third U.S. president. He initially attended Horace Mann High School, a segregated all-black institution, where he participated in track athletics. In 1957, at the age of 15, Thomas volunteered to be part of the Little Rock Nine, a group of African-American students who sought to integrate the previously all-white Little Rock Central High School. On September 4, 1957, Thomas and the other eight students were prevented from entering the school by the Arkansas National Guard, acting under orders from Governor Orval Faubus, and a hostile crowd of around 400 people. A second attempt on September 23 was met with an even larger mob of approximately 1,000 people. The following day, President Dwight D. Eisenhower intervened, assuming control of the National Guard and deploying federal troops to escort the students into the school for the remainder of the academic year. Despite facing severe harassment, Thomas persisted and graduated from Central High School in May 1960.

After graduation, Thomas enrolled at Wayne State University in Detroit but soon moved to Los Angeles in mid-1961. There, he became actively involved in civil rights efforts, serving as Treasurer of the NAACP Youth Council and as State President of the Progressive Baptist Youth Convention. He also attended Los Angeles State College, where he earned a bachelor’s degree in Business Administration. During this time, he was elected President of the Associated Engineers and participated in student government. Thomas also served in the U.S. Army’s 9th Infantry Division during the Vietnam War as an infantryman.

In 1964, Thomas narrated *Nine from Little Rock*, a United States Information Agency film that showcased the progress of civil rights in America during the Cold War era. The film, which received an Academy Award, was distributed to 97 countries, demonstrating the U.S. government’s efforts to highlight racial advancements abroad. In the film, Thomas reflected on the significance of the Little Rock Nine’s experience, stating that it taught them resilience and growth.

Throughout his life, Thomas remained a prominent advocate for civil rights. He received numerous honors, including the Congressional Gold Medal, awarded by President Bill Clinton in 1999, and the NAACP’s Spingarn Award for bravery and heroism in 1999. In 2001, he was granted an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters degree from Ohio Dominican University for his contributions to human rights and equality. He also served as a mentor in the Village to Child Program and was a frequent speaker at educational institutions across the country.

Thomas spent over 27 years as a civil servant, retiring in 2004 from the Defense Finance and Accounting Service in Columbus, Ohio. In his later years, he served on the board of directors for the City of Refuge Learning Academy. He passed away on September 5, 2010, at the age of 67 due to pancreatic cancer, becoming the first member of the Little Rock Nine to die. After a funeral in Columbus, he was buried at Forest Lawn Memorial Park in Glendale, California.

Thomas’s legacy was further recognized in media, including the 1993 Disney Channel film *The Ernest Green Story*, in which actor Tico Wells portrayed him. His life and work continue to be remembered as a pivotal part of the civil rights movement, particularly for his role in the desegregation of Little Rock Central High School.

title: Abdullahi Mohammad Ahmad Hassan
text:
Abdullahi Mohammad Ahmad Hassan was a prominent Sudanese politician, educator, and diplomat who lived from January 1928 to June 22, 2022. Born in Barah, North Kurdufan, Sudan, he spent his early years in Al-Ubayyid, where he attended a Koranic school before transitioning to British colonial education. He studied at Hantoub Secondary School and later graduated from the University College of Khartoum’s Faculty of Arts in 1955. After graduating, he worked as a history teacher in Tonj and Khour Taqatt but resigned in 1958 to start a business in commercial advertisements and journalism in Khartoum. His political opposition to General Aboud’s military government, which seized power in 1958, led to intimidation and business difficulties, forcing him to relocate to Al-Ubayyid in 1959, where he established and ran an intermediate school. Later, he managed a girls' school in Omdurman before resigning in 1963 due to financial disputes and working briefly as a translator for the American Embassy.

Hassan’s political career began in his youth, when he joined the Islamic Liberation Movement in 1949, which sought Sudanese independence from British rule and the establishment of an Islamic state. As a student, he was a key recruiter for the movement, bringing in influential figures like Hassan Al-Turabi. After Sudan gained independence in 1956, he became a member of the Umma Party and was elected to parliament multiple times. He opposed military regimes, including Ibrahim Abboud’s coup in 1958 and Gaafar Nimeiry’s 1969 takeover, leading to his exile and later imprisonment. Upon his return in 1979, he served in various political roles, including overseeing Ansar affairs and becoming a government minister under Sadiq al-Mahdi’s coalition government in 1986. He held positions as Minister of Culture and Information, Minister of Foreign Trade, and advisor to the Prime Minister.

Following Omar Al-Bashir’s 1989 coup, Hassan was arrested and later appointed to diplomatic roles, including Ambassador to Italy, Spain, Greece, and San Marino. However, his disagreements with the government led to his recall in 1995. Afterward, he lived in the United Kingdom, where he worked as a political analyst, lecturer, and writer, while maintaining ties to Sudan. Hassan’s life reflected Sudan’s turbulent political history, from colonial resistance to post-independence struggles, and his career spanned education, journalism, diplomacy, and governance. He passed away in the UK at the age of 94.

title: Mattias Asper
text:
Nils Mattias Joacim Asper, born on 20 March 1974, is a former Swedish professional footballer and current football manager who specializes in coaching goalkeepers. He began his career with Mjällby AIF in the mid-1990s, establishing himself as the team’s first-choice goalkeeper before moving to AIK in 1998. At AIK, he initially struggled to secure a starting position, with Lee Baxter holding the role for the first seven games of the 1998 season. However, Asper made his debut on 8 June 1998 in a match against Östers IF, after which he replaced Baxter for the remainder of the season. His strong performances helped AIK turn their season around, as they went on to win the Allsvenskan title without losing a single game after his debut. The following year, AIK qualified for the UEFA Champions League and reached the group stage, while Asper set a new Allsvenskan record with a 797-minute clean sheet streak.

Asper’s impressive performances with AIK attracted attention from European clubs, leading to a move to Spanish side Real Sociedad ahead of the 2000-01 season. However, his time in Spain was less successful, and he later returned to Sweden on loan to Turkish club Beşiktaş J.K. before joining Malmö FF in 2002. With Malmö, he won the Swedish championship in 2004. After a long career, he announced his retirement from professional football on 26 November 2014.

On the international stage, Asper earned three caps for the Sweden national team between 1999 and 2002. He made his debut on 27 November 1999 in a friendly against South Africa, coming on as a halftime substitute for Magnus Kihlstedt. His second appearance came on 29 March 2000 in a friendly against Austria. He was named to Sweden’s UEFA Euro 2000 squad but served as the third-choice goalkeeper behind Magnus Hedman and Kihlstedt, with Sweden failing to advance past the group stage. His final international appearance was in a 2002 friendly against Russia.

Throughout his career, Asper was recognized for his excellence, winning the Swedish Goalkeeper of the Year award in both 1998 and 1999. He also collected several club honors, including an Allsvenskan title with AIK in 1998, the Svenska Cupen in 1998-99, and another Allsvenskan title with Malmö FF in 2004. After retiring, he transitioned into coaching, currently serving as the head coach of Kristianstad FC in Sweden’s Division 2. His career spanned multiple countries and leagues, showcasing his versatility and skill as both a player and later a manager.

title: G. Fowler Stewart
text:
George Fowler Stewart, commonly known as Fowler Stewart, was a prominent Scots-born businessman and public figure who made a significant impact in Adelaide, South Australia. Born in 1861, he was the youngest son of Charles Stewart, a well-known manufacturer from Kirkcaldy, Fifeshire, Scotland. Stewart received his education at a college in Edinburgh before beginning his career in 1879 at the London office of D. & J. Fowler, a firm founded by his uncles David, James, and later George Fowler. In 1881, he was sent to Adelaide to gain experience in the business, and by 1887, he had taken over the management of the company’s Fremantle, Western Australia branch. Over the following years, Stewart traveled extensively around the world before returning to Adelaide in 1889. In 1890, he married Laura Hill, the youngest daughter of William Hill, further solidifying his connections within the local community. When D. & J. Fowler became a public company, Stewart was appointed as a director in London, but he eventually returned to Adelaide in 1901. By 1914, he had retired from the company. His life came to an abrupt end on 3 January 1917 when he suffered a fatal heart attack at his home.

Beyond his business career, Stewart was deeply involved in various civic and political initiatives. He played a key role in the establishment of the Australian Dried Fruit Association, serving as its first secretary. Stewart was also an early advocate for the Federation of Australia, becoming one of the original members of the Federation League, which pushed for the unification of the Australian colonies. His political engagement extended to his role as chairman of the joint council of the Australasian National League and the Farmers' and Producers' Political Union, which later merged with the Liberal and Democratic Union to form the Liberal Union of South Australia. Stewart held multiple leadership positions within the Liberal Union, including serving as president of the Torrens electoral committee, president of the Glenelg branch, and a member of the State executive. His political activism was complemented by his cultural and community contributions. He was an active member of the South Australian Caledonian Society, even serving as its Chief in 1902, and later became involved in local governance, serving on the Glenelg Town Council in 1905. Additionally, he was a member of the South Australian Literary Societies' Union, becoming its president in 1906, and at one point acted as treasurer of the Union Parliament associated with that organization.

Stewart’s personal life was marked by his marriage to Laura Hill, whom he wed on 26 June 1890. Laura was a granddaughter of John Dunn of Mount Barker, and the couple had three children. Their eldest daughter, Helen Fowler Stewart, married Valentine Zerbini Alderman of Glenelg in 1917. Their second child, William Hill Dunn Stewart, was born in 1895, and their youngest son, Charles Gordon Stewart, was born in 1903. Charles later married Mary Frewin Hancock in 1936 and resided at Langkoop in Victoria. The family’s primary residence was named "Waldo," initially in Glenelg and later in Kensington Gardens. Stewart’s legacy endures through his business success, political activism, and community leadership, making him a notable figure in South Australian history.

title: Tom Buk-Swienty
text:
Tom Buk-Swienty is a Danish historian, journalist, and author, born on 19 July 1966 in Eutin, Germany, but raised in Sønderborg, Denmark. He earned degrees in history and American Studies from the University of Copenhagen and the University of California, respectively. Throughout his career, he has combined academic work with journalism and authorship, contributing significantly to historical research and public understanding of key events and figures.

From 1994 to 2005, Buk-Swienty served as the American correspondent for the Danish periodical *Weekendavisen*, providing insights into U.S. politics, culture, and society. Concurrently, he worked as a lecturer at the University of Southern Denmark in Odense until 2010. He later became an independent author and, since 2014, has held an adjunct professorship in history at the University of Southern Denmark. His professional journey reflects a deep engagement with both historical scholarship and contemporary storytelling.

Buk-Swienty’s writing career began during his time in the United States, where he produced works based on his extensive knowledge of American history and culture. Upon returning to Denmark, he shifted his focus to the Second Schleswig War (1864), a pivotal conflict in Danish history. His two-volume work on the war, *Slagtebænk Dybbøl* (2008) and *Dommedag Als* (2010), was critically acclaimed. The first volume, *Slagtebænk Dybbøl*, earned him the *Årets historiske bog* (Book of the Year in History) award in 2008, followed by the *Årets faglitterære pris* (Non-Fiction Book of the Year) in 2009 and the *Søren Gyldendal-prisen* in 2010. The success of the first volume led to the publication of the second, *Dommedag Als*, in 2010, further cementing his reputation as a leading authority on the war.

In addition to his work on 1864, Buk-Swienty has authored several other notable books. He published a two-volume biography of Wilhelm Dinesen, the father of renowned writer Karen Blixen. The first volume, *Kaptajn Dinesen - Ild og blod* (2013), and the second, *Kaptajn Dinesen - Til døden os skiller* (2014), explore the life of this complex and influential figure. His works have also been translated into English, including *The Other Half: The Life of Jacob Riis and the World of Immigrant America* (2008), a biography of the pioneering photographer and social reformer, and *1864: The Forgotten War that Shaped Modern Europe* (2014), which examines the broader historical significance of the Second Schleswig War.

Beyond his historical works, Buk-Swienty has contributed to other genres, including travel writing, reportage, and edited collections. His bibliography includes *Amerika Maxima* (2002), a travel narrative, and *Det sidste hus på prærien* (2006), a work of reportage. He also co-authored *Købmændenes historie* (2007) with Søren Mørch and edited *Ren kjærlighed kan jo aldrig dø* (2007), a collection of Jacob Riis’s diaries. His 2016 novel, *Det Ensomme Hjerte*, further demonstrates his versatility as a writer.

Buk-Swienty’s contributions to historical literature have been recognized with several prestigious awards. In addition to the aforementioned accolades, he received the *Læsernes Bogpris* (Readers’ Choice Award) in 2011. His works continue to be celebrated for their depth, clarity, and ability to engage both academic and general audiences. His official website and translations of his books, such as those published by Profile Books and W. W. Norton & Company, have further expanded his reach beyond Denmark. Through his writing, teaching, and public engagement, Buk-Swienty has made lasting contributions to the understanding of Danish and American history, leaving a significant mark on contemporary historiography.

title: Diego Godín
text:
Diego Godín, born on 16 February 1986 in Rosario, Uruguay, is widely regarded as one of the finest defenders of his generation. His professional career began at the age of 17 with Cerro, where his performances earned him a move to Nacional, Uruguay's top-flight side. After three seasons, he was transferred to Villarreal in Spain's La Liga in 2007. At Villarreal, he quickly established himself as a key player, contributing to the club's best-ever league finish (second place) in the 2007–08 season. He spent three seasons with Villarreal, becoming a consistent starter and forming a strong partnership with Argentine defender Gonzalo Rodríguez.

In 2010, Godín joined Atlético Madrid for a reported €8 million. His time at Atlético was his most successful period, during which he won eight major titles, including La Liga in the 2013–14 season. His defining moment in that campaign came in the final match against Barcelona, where his header secured a 1–1 draw, crucial to Atlético's title victory. He also played a key role in Atlético's 2012 and 2018 Europa League triumphs, as well as reaching the Champions League final in 2014 and 2016. Godín became Atlético's most-capped foreign player, earning recognition for his leadership, durability, and defensive excellence. He was nominated for the Ballon d'Or in 2016 and 2018, highlighting his status among the world's best defenders.

In 2019, Godín left Atlético on a free transfer to join Inter Milan, where he spent one season before moving to Cagliari. His time in Italy was less successful, though he scored crucial goals in both Serie A and the Europa League final. He later signed with Brazilian club Atlético Mineiro, winning the Supercopa do Brasil in 2022, before a brief stint with Argentine side Vélez Sarsfield, where he retired in July 2023. However, he briefly came out of retirement in 2024 to play for Uruguayan amateurs Porongos before retiring for good.

Godín was also a cornerstone of Uruguay's national team from 2005 to 2022, earning a record 157 caps. He represented his country at four World Cups (2010, 2014, 2018, 2022) and six Copa América tournaments, winning the 2011 edition. Known for his aerial ability, composure, and leadership, he captained Uruguay in numerous matches and was often praised for his defensive intelligence. Despite lacking pace, he compensated with exceptional positioning, timing, and physicality, making him one of the most reliable defenders in international football.

Beyond his playing career, Godín is known for his personal connections in football, including a close friendship with Atlético teammate Antoine Griezmann, whose respect for him was evident when Griezmann refrained from celebrating a goal against Uruguay in the 2018 World Cup. Godín’s influence extended beyond the pitch, as he was often cited as a role model for younger defenders.

Godín’s career was marked by consistency, longevity, and success at both club and international levels. His ability to adapt to different leagues and maintain high performance into his late thirties solidified his legacy as one of the greatest defenders of his era.

title: Trevor Noah
text:
Trevor Noah, born on February 20, 1984, in Johannesburg, South Africa, is a multi-talented entertainer known for his work as a comedian, writer, producer, political commentator, actor, and television host. He gained international fame as the host of *The Daily Show* on Comedy Central from 2015 to 2022, succeeding Jon Stewart. Noah has been recognized with multiple awards, including two Primetime Emmy Awards, and was named one of *Time* magazine's 100 most influential people in the world in 2018. He was also listed among "The 35 Most Powerful People in New York Media" by *The Hollywood Reporter* in 2017 and 2018.

Born to a Swiss-German father, Robert, and a Xhosa mother, Patricia Nombuyiselo Noah, Noah's parents' interracial relationship was illegal under South Africa's apartheid laws at the time of his birth. His mixed-race heritage—classified as "Coloured" under apartheid—shaped his upbringing in Soweto, a Black township in Johannesburg. Raised in a Christian household, Noah was also exposed to Jewish traditions after his mother converted to Judaism, including celebrating a bar mitzvah at age 13. He attended Maryvale College, a private Catholic school.

Noah's career began in South Africa, where he appeared in the soap opera *Isidingo* in 2002 and later hosted his own radio show, *Noah's Ark*, on YFM. His foray into comedy started after friends dared him to perform at a nightclub, leading to a successful stand-up career. He hosted various TV shows, including *Run the Adventure*, *The Real Goboza*, and *Siyadlala*, and competed in *Strictly Come Dancing* (South Africa) in 2008, finishing as runner-up. From 2010 to 2011, he hosted *Tonight with Trevor Noah*, a late-night talk show. He also performed stand-up comedy specials like *The Daywalker* (2009), *Crazy Normal* (2011), and *That's Racist* (2012).

In 2011, Noah moved to the United States, where he became the first South African comedian to appear on *The Tonight Show* and *Late Show with David Letterman*. In 2014, he joined *The Daily Show* as a correspondent before being announced as Jon Stewart’s successor in 2015. His tenure saw a decline in overall viewership but maintained strong appeal among millennials. Noah faced criticism for past jokes deemed offensive, including tweets and stand-up material about women, Jews, and other groups. Despite this, Comedy Central supported him, and his book *Born a Crime* (2016), a memoir about his childhood, became a *New York Times* bestseller and was adapted into a film starring Lupita Nyong’o.

Noah also hosted the Grammy Awards from 2021 to 2025 and the 2022 White House Correspondents' Dinner. He produced and starred in stand-up specials and appeared in films like *Black Panther* and *American Vandal*. In 2022, he announced his departure from *The Daily Show* to pursue other ventures, including podcasting (*What Now? with Trevor Noah*) and acting (*This Is Me... Now: A Love Story*). His comedy is influenced by Richard Pryor, Eddie Murphy, Chris Rock, and Dave Chappelle, while he has mentored comedians like Michelle Wolf and Hasan Minhaj.

Noah speaks multiple languages, including English, Zulu, Xhosa, and Afrikaans, and has ADHD. He has been a vocal commentator on global issues, including the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and racial disparities in media coverage. Despite controversies, Noah remains a prominent figure in comedy and political satire.

title: Lunay (singer)
text:
Jefnier Osorio Moreno, known professionally as Lunay, is a Puerto Rican singer and songwriter who gained prominence in the Latin urban music scene. Born on October 4, 2000, he developed an early passion for drums and soccer, which ultimately influenced his musical career. Soccer, in particular, played a significant role in shaping his musical direction, as he was inspired by the success of other Latin American urban artists. By the age of 12, he began recording freestyle raps, which he shared on Facebook. His improvised performances, often done in front of his soccer teammates, quickly went viral, attracting the attention of notable producers like Chris Jedi and Gaby Music.

Lunay’s professional journey began in 2017 when he started uploading music to SoundCloud under the name "Jefnier." His early track "Aparentas" gained traction, leading Chris Jedi and Gaby Music to offer him a record deal. After signing with them, he adopted the stage name "Lunay." His first releases under this new moniker included "Si Te Vas Conmigo" in May 2018 and "Dejame Saber" a month later. That same year, he collaborated on several tracks, including "A Solas" with Lyanno and "Como La Primera Vez" with Amarion. One of his most notable early collaborations was "Luz Apaga," featuring Ozuna, Rauw Alejandro, and Lyanno, which amassed millions of views on YouTube. Later in 2018, the remix of "A Solas" featuring Anuel AA, Brytiago, and Alex Rose also gained significant popularity, trending on YouTube.

In March 2019, Lunay released "Soltera," which became a major hit, surpassing five million views on YouTube in just five days. This track was later remixed with Daddy Yankee and Bad Bunny, further boosting his fame. Another notable collaboration came in August 2020 with American rapper Lil Mosey on the single "Top Gone," which appeared on the deluxe edition of Lil Mosey’s album *Certified Hitmaker*. Lunay’s growing success led to him being recognized as an artist "on the rise" at the 2019 Premios Juventud awards.

Lunay’s musical style differentiates itself from some of the more aggressive themes in urban music. In interviews, he has emphasized that his songs do not promote violence or disparage women, aligning with his personal values. He has stated that while he is part of the urban music genre, he does not believe in encouraging violence, as it goes against his spiritual beliefs.

On October 25, 2019, Lunay released his debut album, *Épico*, solidifying his place in the Latin urban scene. The album featured some of his most popular songs, including "Soltera," "No Te Quieren Conmigo," "La Cama," "A Solas," and "Aventura." These tracks highlighted his versatility as both a singer and songwriter, contributing to his growing fanbase. His ability to blend catchy melodies with relatable lyrics has made him a standout artist in contemporary Latin music.

Throughout his career, Lunay has maintained a strong connection with his audience, often engaging with them through social media and live performances. His rapid rise in the music industry is a testament to his talent and dedication, as well as the support of his collaborators and producers. With a commitment to positive messaging and a passion for music, Lunay continues to be a prominent figure in the Latin urban genre, with a promising future ahead.

title: Sérgio Moraes
text:
Sérgio Moraes, born on July 23, 1982, in Cohab, Brazil, is a former mixed martial artist who competed in the welterweight and middleweight divisions of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) and appeared on *The Ultimate Fighter: Brazil*. Nicknamed "O Orgulho da Cohab," or "The Pride of Cohab," Moraes is a highly accomplished Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu practitioner, having won the World Championship four times. His most famous Jiu-Jitsu moment came in 2008 when he defeated Kron Gracie. Affiliated with the Alliance Jiu-Jitsu Team, Moraes later became the head Jiu-Jitsu instructor at Evolução Thai in Curitiba, Brazil, and also taught at the Reza Martial Arts Center in Bahrain.

Moraes began his MMA career in 2006, compiling a 6-1 record in Brazil before making his U.S. debut in 2009 with Bellator, where he submitted Josh Martin in the first round. In 2012, he joined *The Ultimate Fighter: Brazil*, defeating Thiago Rela in the elimination round via heel hook and later submitting Delson Heleno with a rear naked choke in the quarterfinals. However, he lost to Daniel Sarafian in the semifinals via flying knee knockout.

Moraes made his UFC debut in 2012, replacing an injured Daniel Sarafian at UFC 147, but lost to Cezar Ferreira by unanimous decision. He quickly bounced back, submitting Renée Forte with a rear naked choke at UFC 153 and defeating Neil Magny with a first-round triangle choke at UFC 163, earning Submission of the Night. His career included notable wins over Omari Akhmedov (KO), Mickaël Lebout (decision), and Ben Saunders (submission), though he also faced tough losses, including a split draw against Kamaru Usman and a knockout loss to Warlley Alves. After a third-round KO loss to James Krause in 2019, he was released from the UFC.

Following his UFC stint, Moraes signed with Taura MMA in 2020 but lost his debut against Jared Revel by unanimous decision. Throughout his career, he earned recognition for his grappling skills, including a Submission of the Year nomination in 2013 and a Fight Matrix Comeback Fighter of the Year award in 2015. Moraes retired with a professional MMA record of 17 wins (7 by submission, 4 by KO/TKO) and 10 losses. Outside the cage, he remains an influential figure in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, continuing to teach and mentor athletes.

title: Adel Emam
text:
Adel Emam, born on 17 May 1940 in Cairo, is one of Egypt’s most celebrated actors, renowned for his extensive work in film, television, and theater. With a career spanning over 150 artistic projects, including more than 103 movies and 10 plays, he has become a cultural icon in Egypt and the broader Arab world. Emam is best known for his comedic roles but has also excelled in dramatic and socially conscious works, earning him widespread acclaim and a devoted fanbase. His versatility and ability to address political and social issues through his art have solidified his status as a cultural figure.

Emam’s early life was marked by modest beginnings. Born into a poor farming family in Cairo, he later moved with his family to various districts, including Helmiya, Omrania, and Mohandiseen. He studied at multiple schools before enrolling in Cairo University’s Faculty of Agriculture, where he developed an interest in theater. His artistic career began in university productions, most notably in the play *Ana Wa Howa Wa Heya* (1963). He graduated in 1962 and soon transitioned into professional acting, securing small roles in films like *My Wife, the Director General* (1966) and *My Wife’s Dignity* (1967). His breakthrough came with *My Wife’s Goblin* (1968), where he demonstrated his comedic talent alongside established stars like Salah Zulfikar and Shadia.

The 1970s marked Emam’s rise to prominence, with roles in films like *Virgo* (1970) and *Searching for the Scandal* (1973). His portrayal of Bahgat El Abasery in *Madraset El Moshaghbeen* (1973) became an iconic performance, showcasing his ability to blend humor with social commentary. By the 1980s, Emam had established himself as a leading actor, taking on diverse roles that ranged from comedy to crime dramas. *The Suspect* (1981) was a significant shift in his career, proving his ability to handle dramatic roles. He also collaborated with actress Soad Hosny in films like *Love in a Jail Cell* (1983), further enhancing his popularity.

The 1990s were the peak of Emam’s career, during which he became the highest-paid actor in Egypt and a dominant force in Arab cinema. His films during this period, such as *Playing with the Big Boys* (1991) and *The Terrorist* (1998), combined sharp social critique with humor, resonating deeply with audiences. He also starred in the critically acclaimed play *Al-Wad Sayed Al-Shaghal* (1985), which ran for eight years. His ability to address social and political issues through his work earned him a reputation as a cultural icon and a voice for change.

In his personal life, Emam has been married to Hala El-Shalaqani since the mid-1960s, a relationship that began against societal norms due to their differing backgrounds. They have three children: director Ramy Emam, actress Sarah Emam, and actor Mohamed Emam, who starred in *The Yacoubian Building*. Emam is known for his love of reading and gardening, reflecting his agricultural background. Despite his success, he remains modest, often crediting his wife and family for his achievements.

Beyond acting, Emam has been recognized for his humanitarian efforts, including his appointment as a UNHCR Goodwill Ambassador in 2000. His contributions to Egyptian and Arab cinema have earned him numerous accolades, including Lifetime Achievement Awards. With a reported net worth of millions, he is considered one of the wealthiest actors in Egypt. Emam’s legacy endures not only through his artistic achievements but also through his influence on societal discourse, making him a defining figure in modern Egyptian culture.

title: Samir Kochhar
text:
Samir Kochhar is an Indian actor and television presenter who has established himself as a versatile figure in both film and television. Born on 23 May 1980, he is best known for hosting the pre-match Indian Premier League show *Extraaa Innings T20* and for his role in Netflix India's acclaimed series *Sacred Games*. His career spans multiple mediums, including television, film, and sports entertainment.

Kochhar began his professional journey with Doordarshan, anchoring the AIDS awareness and travel show *Haath Se Haath Mila* alongside Sugandha Garg. His Bollywood debut came in 2003 with *Valentine Days*, a bilingual film directed by Sumeer Sabharwal. On television, he made his mark with *Dangerous*, a provocative talk show on sex that aired on Zoom. He later gained recognition for his role as Rajat Kapur in the popular soap opera *Bade Acche Lagte Hain*. In 2005, he appeared in *Zeher*, a romantic thriller directed by Mohit Suri, and later starred in the 2008 crime thriller *Jannat*, where he portrayed a police inspector.

His filmography includes critically acclaimed projects such as *Island City* (2015), directed by Ruchika Oberoi, which received praise at the Venice International Film Festival and the JIO MAMI Film Festival in Mumbai. He is also set to appear in *Mango Dreams*, a feature film directed by American filmmaker John Unchurch. In 2016, he featured in two major releases: *Housefull 3* alongside Akshay Kumar and *Mango Dreams*. Additionally, he is attached to *Hume Tumse Pyaar Kitna*, a film directed by Lalit Mohan, and *Jannat 3*, scheduled for release in 2025.

Beyond acting, Kochhar is an active participant in the *Celebrity Cricket League (CCL)*, representing the Mumbai Heroes team. His contributions to entertainment extend beyond the screen, showcasing his dynamic presence in sports as well.

In his personal life, Kochhar married his longtime girlfriend Radhika on 9 January 2010. The couple welcomed their first child, a son named Kabir, in April 2015, and a daughter named Sara in October 2017. His family life reflects a balance between his demanding career and personal fulfillment.

Kochhar’s diverse roles in film, television, and sports, coupled with his engaging persona as a host, have cemented his status as a notable figure in the Indian entertainment industry. His ability to navigate both mainstream and independent projects highlights his adaptability and dedication to his craft. With ongoing and upcoming projects, his career continues to evolve, demonstrating his enduring influence in entertainment.

title: Rosé (singer)
text:
Rosé, whose real name is Roseanne Park (born Park Chae-young) on February 11, 1997, is a New Zealand and South Korean singer and songwriter. Born in Auckland, New Zealand, to South Korean immigrant parents, she moved to Melbourne, Australia, at the age of seven. Growing up, she developed a love for music, learning to play the guitar and piano and performing in church choirs. She attended Kew East Primary School and Canterbury Girls' Secondary College in Melbourne before dropping out to pursue a career in K-pop.

In 2012, Rosé auditioned for YG Entertainment in Sydney and won first place out of 700 participants. She then moved to Seoul to train under the label. Before her official debut, she contributed vocals to G-Dragon’s song "Without You" from his 2012 EP *One of a Kind*, though her involvement was not publicly revealed until after she joined Blackpink. After four years of training, she was announced as the final member of the South Korean girl group Blackpink in June 2016, debuting with the group in August of the same year. Blackpink signed a global partnership with Interscope Records in 2018, expanding their international reach.

Rosé gained recognition beyond Blackpink through appearances on shows like *King of Masked Singer* and *Fantastic Duo*, where her vocal abilities were praised. In 2021, she released her debut solo single album, *R*, which set a record as the highest-selling first-week album by a Korean female soloist, with 448,089 copies sold. The lead single, "On the Ground," became a global sensation, topping the *Billboard* Global 200 and making her the first artist to achieve number-one status as both a soloist and a group member. The song also broke YouTube records for the most-viewed music video by a Korean soloist in 24 hours. "On the Ground" achieved significant chart success, including reaching number 70 on the *Billboard* Hot 100, making it the highest-charting song by a female K-pop soloist in the U.S. at the time.

In 2024, Rosé released "Apt." featuring Bruno Mars, which topped charts worldwide, including South Korea’s Circle Digital Chart and Australia’s ARIA Singles Chart. The song marked her as the first Korean female soloist to reach number one in Australia and enter the top three in the U.S. and UK. Her debut studio album, *Rosie*, followed in December 2024, debuting at number three on the *Billboard* 200, a record for a Korean female soloist. The album also peaked at number four in the UK and number two in Australia, further solidifying her global success.

Rosé has received numerous accolades, including six Guinness World Records, two MAMA Awards, and the Asia Artist Award for Song of the Year. She is also a prominent figure in fashion, serving as a global ambassador for luxury brands like Yves Saint Laurent and Tiffany & Co. Her distinctive vocal style, often described as an "electric" soprano, has earned her the nickname "the golden voice" among fans. In 2025, she was named one of *Time*’s 100 most influential people.

Beyond music, Rosé has been involved in various endorsements and collaborations, including campaigns with Perfect World Mobile, OIOI, Sulwhasoo, and the meditation app Calm. She has also made headlines for her fashion appearances, including attending the Met Gala and the Cannes Film Festival. Her influence extends to social media, where she is the second-most followed Korean individual on Instagram. Rosé’s career continues to break barriers, making her one of the most successful Korean female soloists in the global music industry.

title: Billy Conigliaro
text:
William Michael Conigliaro was an American baseball outfielder who played in Major League Baseball (MLB) for five seasons, from 1969 to 1973, with the Boston Red Sox, Milwaukee Brewers, and Oakland Athletics. Born on August 15, 1947, in Revere, Massachusetts, he was the younger brother of fellow MLB player Tony Conigliaro. Their father, Sal, worked at a tool and die shop and later became the plant manager, while their mother, Teresa, also encouraged their baseball careers. Conigliaro attended Swampscott High School, where he excelled as a three-sport athlete. In April 1964, he threw a no-hitter against Winthrop High School, just days after his brother Tony made his major league debut. That same year, he was drafted by the Boston Red Sox in the first round (fifth overall) of the inaugural MLB draft in 1965.

Conigliaro spent the next few seasons in the minor leagues before making his MLB debut on April 11, 1969, at age 21. In his first game, he entered as a pinch runner and stole a base in a 2–1 extra-innings win over the Cleveland Indians. Five days later, he made his first start and hit two home runs. Although he was briefly demoted to the minors in May, he returned to the Red Sox in September and finished his rookie season with a .288 batting average, four home runs, and seven RBIs in 32 games. His best season came in 1970, when he set career highs in hits (108), runs scored (59), home runs (18), RBIs (58), and games played (114). That year, the Red Sox shifted Carl Yastrzemski to first base to accommodate Conigliaro in the lineup. He also ranked fifth in the American League (AL) in assists as a left fielder with seven. However, he was deeply affected by his brother Tony being traded to the California Angels at the end of the season, and reportedly became "very emotional" over the move.

In 1971, Conigliaro batted .262 with 11 home runs and 33 RBIs, finishing eighth in the AL in doubles (26). Later that year, he was part of a major ten-player trade that sent him, along with George Scott, Jim Lonborg, Ken Brett, Joe Lahoud, and Don Pavletich, from the Red Sox to the Milwaukee Brewers in exchange for Tommy Harper, Marty Pattin, Lew Krausse, and minor-league outfielder Pat Skrable. Unhappy in Milwaukee, he announced his retirement in the middle of the 1972 season. He sought reinstatement in 1973, and the Brewers sold him to the Oakland Athletics. That season, he appeared in the American League Championship Series and the World Series, though he went hitless in seven at-bats. After undergoing knee surgery during the offseason, he was waived by Oakland in March 1974. He attempted a comeback with the Athletics in 1977 but declined a minor-league assignment, ending his career with a .256 batting average, 40 home runs, and 128 RBIs in 347 games.

Outside of baseball, Conigliaro was a student of Shotokan karate grandmaster Kazumi Tabata, who acknowledged him in a book. He married Keisha on October 19, 2002, and remained married to her until his death. Conigliaro died on February 10, 2021, at his home in Beverly, Massachusetts, from a heart attack. He was later honored in a 2014 first-pitch ceremony at Fenway Park in tribute to his brother Tony.

title: Arif Mohammad Khan
text:
Arif Mohammad Khan is an Indian politician born on 18 November 1951 in Bulandshahr. He has had a long and varied political career, currently serving as the Governor of Bihar since 2025. Before this, he was the Governor of Kerala from 2019 to 2024. A member of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), he previously held several Union ministerial positions, including roles in civil aviation and energy. His political journey has been marked by shifts in party affiliations, beginning with the Bharatiya Kranti Dal, followed by the Indian National Congress, Janata Dal, Bahujan Samaj Party, and finally the BJP.

Khan's political career began as a student leader, serving as the President of the Aligarh Muslim University Students' Union in 1972-73. He contested his first legislative assembly election in 1974 from Siyana constituency, though he lost. He later became a member of the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Assembly in 1977 at the age of 26. His entry into national politics came when he was elected to the Lok Sabha in 1980 from Kanpur and again in 1984 from Bahraich as a Congress member. However, he resigned from the Congress in 1986 over disagreements with Rajiv Gandhi’s government regarding the Muslim Personal Law Bill, which sought to allow Muslim men to avoid providing maintenance to divorced wives after the iddah period. This led him to join the Janata Dal, where he served as Union Minister of Civil Aviation. In 1998, he joined the Bahujan Samaj Party and was re-elected to the Lok Sabha from Bahraich. He later joined the BJP in 2004, though he lost his bid for re-election that year. His loyalty to the BJP was later rewarded with gubernatorial appointments in Kerala and Bihar.

Khan has been a vocal advocate for reform within Islam. He famously resigned from his ministerial position in 1986 in protest against the Congress government’s reversal of the Shah Bano case judgment, which had granted maintenance rights to a divorced Muslim woman. He supported the Supreme Court’s decision in that case and has consistently opposed practices like triple talaq, suggesting it should be punishable by imprisonment. He also criticized the enforcement of hijab as a conspiracy to restrict women’s rights and supported the Karnataka High Court’s decision against compulsory hijab-wearing. His views on madrasas and their teachings on blasphemy have also drawn attention, particularly after his remarks on the Udaipur murder of Kanhaiya Lal in 2022.

Khan has been involved in legal controversies, including the Jain Hawala case, where he was accused of receiving 7 crores of hawala money during his tenure as a Union Minister. However, he was later acquitted. He has also been an active writer, penning books and articles on Islam, Sufism, and socio-political issues. His 2010 book, *Text and Context: Quran and Contemporary Challenges*, was well-received. He has called for the abolition of the All India Muslim Personal Law Board and has been a strong supporter of the Supreme Court’s judgment in the Shah Bano case.

As Governor of Kerala, Khan faced political tensions, particularly over his opposition to the appointment of vice-chancellors from SFI/CPIM backgrounds to state universities. His tenure ended without a formal farewell from the Kerala government, including the Chief Minister. He was then appointed Governor of Bihar in 2024, assuming office in January 2025. Throughout his career, Khan has remained a controversial yet influential figure, known for his reformist stance on Muslim personal laws and his outspoken views on governance and social issues.

title: María José (singer)
text:
María José Loyola Anaya, known professionally as María José, is a versatile Mexican entertainer born on January 12, 1976. She is recognized as a singer, ballerina, flamenco dancer, athlete, and television personality. Her career began at age 15 in the 1990s when she joined the popular Mexican band Kabah as a vocalist. After leaving Kabah in 2006, she pursued a successful solo career, releasing six studio albums.

Before rising to fame, María José earned a B.A. in communications and gained early stage experience at age 14 as a dancer in the Spanish Dance Company led by Maria Elena Anaya, where she also performed flamenco. Her transition to music began in the mid-1990s with Kabah, establishing her as a prominent vocalist in the Mexican pop scene.

As a solo artist, María José gained significant attention in 2007 when she posed for the cover of *MAX* magazine and opened for Gwen Stefani’s *The Sweet Escape Tour* in Mexico. She also co-hosted and performed in the *Reventour* concert series. Her debut solo album, *María José*, was released in 2007, featuring the single "Quien Eres Tú" with Trey Songz, which blended dance and hip-hop influences. The album reached number 84 on Mexican charts, and subsequent singles like "Me Equiviqué" and "¿Dónde Está?" further promoted her career. She left Warner Music in 2008 to continue independently.

In 2009, she released her second album, *Amante de lo Ajeno*, a collection of 1980s pop hits, which included the popular single "No Soy una Señora." This was followed by *Amante de lo Bueno* in 2010, another 1980s covers album, featuring the hit "La Ocasión Para Amarnos." Her 2012 album, *De Noche*, marked her return to original material, with singles like "Tú Ya Sabes a Mí." In 2016, she released *Habla Ahora*, her third original album, featuring the single "Las Que Se Ponen Bien La Falda" with Ivy Queen.

In 2019, she celebrated her career with a live album, *Conexión*, recorded in Mexico City, featuring guest appearances from artists like Ha*Ash and Yuri. She also expanded into television, serving as a judge on *México Tiene Talento* and co-hosting *Esta Historia Me Suena*, where she also acted in some episodes. In 2020, she joined *La Voz* as a coach alongside Ricardo Montaner and Belinda, returning for a second season in 2021.

María José has cited Mariah Carey, Rocío Dúrcal, Mecano, Celine Dion, and Christina Aguilera among her major musical influences. Her career spans music, dance, and television, making her a prominent figure in Mexican entertainment.

title: Nikole Hannah-Jones
text:
Nikole Sheri Hannah-Jones, born on April 9, 1976, in Waterloo, Iowa, is an American investigative journalist renowned for her work on civil rights and systemic racism in the United States. The daughter of an African-American father and a white mother of Czech and English descent, Hannah-Jones grew up in a predominantly white environment due to a voluntary desegregation busing program. She attended Waterloo West High School, where she contributed to the school newspaper, and later earned a Bachelor of Arts in history and African-American studies from the University of Notre Dame in 1998. During her time at Notre Dame, she famously wrote a letter to the editor condemning racist language in a student publication, arguing that white historical violence far outweighed any claims of savagery against other cultures. She later obtained a master’s degree in journalism from the University of North Carolina Hussman School of Journalism and Media in 2003, where she was a Roy H. Park Fellow.

Hannah-Jones began her career in 2003 at the *Raleigh News & Observer*, covering education, particularly in Durham Public Schools. In 2006, she moved to *The Oregonian* in Portland, where she covered demographics, government, and census-related issues. She also wrote about the legacy of the 1965 Watts riots and, as a fellow with the Institute for Advanced Journalism Studies, researched Cuba’s healthcare and education systems under Raúl Castro. In 2011, she joined ProPublica, where she investigated housing discrimination, redlining, and the lack of enforcement of the Fair Housing Act, as well as the persistence of segregation in Alabama schools. Her work at ProPublica earned her numerous awards, including the Gannett Foundation Innovation in Watchdog Journalism Award in 2012.

In 2015, Hannah-Jones joined *The New York Times* as a staff reporter, focusing on racial segregation, education, and housing discrimination. Her reporting exposed systemic inequalities, including the conditions in the school district where Michael Brown was shot, highlighting how segregation contributed to educational and economic disparities. Her work has been widely influential, cited in discussions about racial justice and education reform. In 2017, she received a MacArthur Fellowship for her investigations into racial segregation, particularly in education, and was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 2021.

Hannah-Jones is best known for her leadership on *The 1619 Project*, launched in 2019 to mark the 400th anniversary of the arrival of enslaved Africans in Virginia. The project recontextualizes American history by centering the legacy of slavery and the contributions of Black Americans. The initiative included essays, poems, and a podcast, and won her the 2020 Pulitzer Prize for Commentary. However, the project faced criticism from historians like Gordon S. Wood and Leslie M. Harris, who disputed some of its claims, particularly the assertion that protecting slavery was a primary motive for the American Revolution. The *Times* later clarified that this was true for "some of the colonists."

In 2021, Hannah-Jones was offered a position at the University of North Carolina’s Hussman School of Journalism but was initially denied tenure, sparking controversy and protests. After the university’s trustees reversed their decision, she ultimately chose to accept a tenured position at Howard University as the inaugural Knight Chair in Race and Journalism, bringing $20 million in funding from the Knight, MacArthur, Ford, and an anonymous donor. At Howard, she also founded the Center for Journalism and Democracy.

Beyond her work at *The New York Times*, Hannah-Jones co-founded the Ida B. Wells Society for Investigative Reporting in 2016 to support investigative journalists of color. She has received numerous accolades, including the National Magazine Award for Public Interest in 2017, the NAACP Image Award in 2022, and a Primetime Emmy Award for *The 1619 Project* in 2023. She has authored several books, including *The 1619 Project: A New Origin Story* (2021) and *Born on the Water* (2021), a children’s adaptation of the project.

Hannah-Jones has been involved in some controversies, including her 2020 retweet of a conspiracy theory about government agents setting off fireworks during Black Lives Matter protests, which she later apologized for. She has also questioned the accuracy of a 2024 *Atlantic* essay about workplace discrimination at *The New York Times* over Chick-fil-A. Despite these incidents, her work continues to shape national conversations about race, education, and justice. She lives in Brooklyn with her husband, Faraji Hannah-Jones, and their daughter.

title: Robert Whittaker (fighter)
text:
Robert John Whittaker, born on 20 December 1990 in Ōtāhuhu, Auckland, New Zealand, is an Australian professional mixed martial artist who competes in the Middleweight division of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC). He is a former UFC Middleweight Champion and the first Australian to win a UFC championship. As of July 2025, he is ranked #7 in the UFC middleweight division.

Whittaker's martial arts journey began at the age of seven when his father enrolled him in a Goju-ryu karate school to develop self-discipline and self-defence.
