In his personal life, he married Elsie Darkoa on March 6, 2018, and the couple has a son, Nathan. Debrah also has another son, Samuel Amo-Ameyaw, who plays for Southampton FC.

Ameyaw Debrah’s work has solidified his reputation as a key figure in Ghanaian entertainment media, blending journalism, digital entrepreneurship, and artist management to promote African talent and cultural discourse.

title: Evgeny Shalunov
text:
Evgeny Vladimirovich Shalunov is a former professional road and track cyclist from Russia, born on 8 January 1992. He had a notable career in both disciplines, though his most significant achievements came in road racing. Shalunov began his professional career in mid-2011, signing a stagiaire (trial) contract with Team RadioShack in July of that year. Before joining RadioShack, he had already established himself as a promising talent, winning eight national events in 2011 while riding for the Lokomotiv–Urbycolan team.

The following year, in 2012, Shalunov moved to the Lokosphinx team and quickly made an impact. In March, he finished fourth in the La Roue Tourangelle, a race held in France, demonstrating his early-season form. Later that April, he secured his first major victory on the UCI Europe Tour by winning the Vuelta a La Rioja in Spain. His winning performance was marked by a solo attack around 30 kilometers from the finish, where he managed to hold off the competition to win by 28 seconds ahead of Euskaltel–Euskadi’s Pablo Urtasun and his teammate Mikhail Antonov. This victory was a breakthrough moment in his career, showcasing his ability to compete at an international level.

Shalunov’s success continued, and in 2017, he was selected to participate in the prestigious Giro d’Italia, one of cycling’s three Grand Tours. His inclusion in the start list for the race highlighted his standing as a competitive rider at the highest level of professional cycling. Although the article does not provide further details about his performance in the Giro, his selection alone underscores his capabilities and the confidence his team had in his abilities.

Throughout his career, Shalunov competed in both track and road events, though his most notable results came in road racing. His career spanned several years, during which he represented different teams and achieved a mix of national and international success. While his career may not have been as prolific as some of his contemporaries, his achievements—particularly his victory in the Vuelta a La Rioja and his Giro d’Italia selection—demonstrate his skill and dedication to the sport.

The article also notes external references to Shalunov’s profile, including his UCI (Union Cycliste Internationale) page, as well as listings on cycling databases such as Cycling Archives, ProCyclingStats, Cycling Quotient, and CycleBase. These references suggest that his career was well-documented and that he was recognized within the professional cycling community.

In summary, Evgeny Shalunov was a Russian cyclist who competed professionally from 2011 until his retirement. His career was highlighted by early national success, a major UCI Europe Tour victory, and a selection to the Giro d’Italia. Though the article does not provide further details about his later career or retirement, his achievements mark him as a respected figure in Russian and international cycling.

title: Charles Allen (jurist)
text:
Charles Allen, born on April 17, 1827, in Greenfield, Massachusetts, was a prominent American jurist who made significant contributions to the legal profession. His parents were Sylvester and Harriet (Ripley) Allen. Allen received his early education at Harvard University, graduating in 1847. He later pursued a legal career, studying law and being admitted to the bar in 1850. His dedication to legal scholarship was later recognized when Harvard awarded him an honorary LL.D. degree in 1892.

After being admitted to the bar, Allen practiced law in Greenfield for twelve years before transitioning to state-level legal roles. His most notable early appointment was as Massachusetts Attorney General, a position he held from 1867 to 1872. This role allowed him to shape state legal policies and establish himself as a respected legal authority. His tenure as Attorney General was followed by an even more influential career on the bench. From 1882 to 1898, Allen served as a justice on the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court. During these sixteen years, he gained a reputation as one of the most distinguished jurists of his time, known for his legal acumen and principled decisions.

Beyond his judicial and legal work, Allen was also a prolific writer. He authored several notable publications, including *Allen's Reports*, a 14-volume collection published between 1861 and 1867, which documented significant legal cases. In 1900, he published two other works: *Telegraph Cases*, which likely addressed legal issues related to the emerging telegraph industry, and *Notes on the Bacon-Shakespeare Question*, a scholarly examination of the controversial theory that Francis Bacon rather than William Shakespeare was the true author of Shakespeare’s works. This latter work reflected Allen’s intellectual curiosity beyond traditional legal matters.

Allen’s contributions to the legal field were well-documented in various biographical sources, including *The Twentieth Century Biographical Dictionary of Notable Americans* (1904) and *The Biographical Dictionary of America* (1906), both of which highlighted his career and achievements. His influence extended into legislative records, with mentions in the *Journal of the House of Representatives of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts* during the years of his service as Attorney General. Additionally, his death in 1913 was noted in *The Green Bag*, a legal magazine, further cementing his legacy in the legal community.

Allen passed away on January 13, 1913, at the age of 85, leaving behind a lasting impact on Massachusetts jurisprudence. His career spanned multiple roles—practicing attorney, state attorney general, and Supreme Judicial Court justice—each marked by a commitment to legal excellence. His writings further solidified his reputation as a scholar and jurist, ensuring his enduring legacy in American legal history.

title: Ruth Fischer
text:
Ruth Fischer, born Elfriede Eisler on 11 December 1895 in Leipzig, was an influential Austrian and German Communist who played a key role in early 20th-century communist movements. The daughter of a Jewish philosophy professor and a Lutheran mother, she was the elder sister of composer Hanns Eisler and communist activist Gerhart Eisler. She studied philosophy, economics, and politics at the University of Vienna before adopting her mother’s maiden name, Ruth Fischer, as her public identity. She married medical student Paul Friedländer in 1917, though they later separated, and she was briefly incarcerated for treason after a crowd proclaimed her editor of Vienna’s *Neue Freie Presse* in 1918.

Fischer co-founded the Austrian Communist Party (KPÖ) in 1918, claiming to be its first member. She opposed a failed communist uprising in Austria in 1919 and moved to Berlin, where she became a prominent figure in the Communist Party of Germany (KPD). Alongside her partner Arkadi Maslow, she led the KPD’s left wing, criticizing the party’s cautious leadership and advocating for aggressive revolutionary tactics, including the failed March Action of 1921. To secure German citizenship, she married fellow communist Gustav Golke, though he was later executed in Stalin’s Great Purge.

In 1923, Fischer and Maslow, along with Ernst Thälmann, gained control of the KPD after the failure of the Hamburg Uprising. They led the party through the 1924 elections, and Fischer was elected to the Reichstag and the Prussian House of Representatives. During this period, she publicly denounced Trotsky and even attacked the legacies of Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, comparing Luxemburg’s influence to a disease. However, her alignment with Soviet leader Grigory Zinoviev during the power struggle following Lenin’s death proved short-lived. By 1926, Stalin and other Comintern leaders deemed her unreliable, and she was expelled from the KPD after refusing to submit to the party line.

Exiled from the KPD, Fischer and Maslow formed an anti-Stalinist splinter group, arguing that Stalin’s rule represented a counter-revolution led by a bureaucratic class. She fled to Paris in 1933 after the Nazi takeover, and her German citizenship was revoked. In the 1940s, she emigrated to the United States, where she testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) against her brothers, contributing to Hanns Eisler’s deportation. During the Cold War, she worked as an informant for the CIA’s predecessor, the Pond, under the codename "Alice Miller," gathering intelligence on leftist movements in Europe, Africa, and China.

Fischer’s memoir, *Stalin and German Communism* (1948), was widely criticized for inaccuracies and biases. Scholars like J. P. Nettl and E. H. Carr dismissed it as unreliable, while Isaac Deutscher described her as a charismatic but inexperienced figure. She returned to Paris in 1955 and published additional works before her death in 1961 at age 65. Her only child, mathematician F.G. Friedlander, later became a Fellow of the Royal Society. Fischer’s papers are archived at the International Institute of Social History.

title: Jean Muir (actress)
text:
Jean Muir, born Jean Muir Fullarton on February 13, 1911, in Suffern, New York, was an American stage and film actress who became the first performer blacklisted after her name appeared in the anti-Communist pamphlet *Red Channels* in 1950. An only child, she grew up in a family where her father was a certified public accountant and her mother worked as a substitute teacher. Muir attended the Dwight School in Englewood, New Jersey, and later studied French at the Sorbonne University in Paris before pursuing an acting career.

Muir began her professional career as a model for the Walter Thornton Model Agency in New York City. At 19, she made her Broadway debut in *The Truth Game* (1930) under the stage name Jean Fullarton. She went on to act in several stage productions, including *Peter Ibbetson*, *Life Begins*, and *Saint Wench*. After the latter production closed quickly, a theatrical agent encouraged her to try Hollywood, leading to a screen test that caught the attention of Warner Bros. The studio signed her in 1933, and she worked steadily in supporting roles over the next three years, appearing in 14 films. She acted alongside notable stars such as Paul Muni, Richard Barthelmess, Franchot Tone, Joe E. Brown, and Warren William.

However, Muir’s independent nature and political activism soon put her at odds with Warner Bros. She refused to pose for publicity photos, wear makeup, or dress stylishly in public, which disappointed studio executives. Additionally, her financial support for striking lettuce workers in California and her early involvement with the Screen Actors Guild (SAG) drew disapproval. She marched in the union’s first Labor Day parade, organized meetings at her home, and made calls to secure picketers, actions that clashed with the studio’s expectations. Muir was also known for her inquisitiveness, questioning everyone from electricians to directors about their work, earning her the nickname "the studio pest." Her refusal to conform led to multiple suspensions, and in 1937, Warner Bros. terminated her contract. A *Billboard* news item at the time noted that she had "talked herself out of the picture industry."

Muir returned to New York to work in theater but briefly returned to Hollywood for a few more films, including *The Constant Nymph* (1943), where she acted alongside Joan Fontaine. She was also considered for the role of Melanie in *Gone with the Wind* (1939). After a hiatus from acting in 1943 to focus on raising her three children, she briefly returned to Broadway in 1947 with *Tenting Tonight* and later landed a role in the TV sitcom *The Aldrich Family* (1949), an adaptation of a popular radio program.

In 1950, Muir was listed as a Communist sympathizer in *Red Channels*, which led to her immediate dismissal from *The Aldrich Family*. NBC and the show’s sponsor, General Foods, cited public pressure as the reason for her removal, despite over 3,000 letters supporting her reinstatement. She became the first performer to lose work due to the *Red Channels* blacklist, a consequence of her past association with the Congress of American Women, a group federal authorities had labeled subversive.

In 1953, Muir testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee, denying she was a Communist but acknowledging her past support for organizations deemed subversive. She later regretted her testimony, particularly her decision to name names, which she had repressed from memory. The blacklist effectively ended her acting career for several years, though she returned to television in 1958 with guest appearances on shows like *NBC Matinee Theater*, *The Witness*, *Route 66*, and *Naked City*. By 1962, her acting career had concluded.

Muir then transitioned into teaching, working as a drama instructor at community centers in New York before moving to Missouri in 1968 to become the Master Acting Teacher at Stephens College. She also directed productions there and earned her own college degree from Stephens in 1977. After reaching the school’s mandatory retirement age, she briefly taught at the University of Missouri–Kansas City in 1981.

In her personal life, Muir married entertainment attorney and television producer Henry Jaffe on December 20, 1940, and they had three children. She reportedly struggled with alcoholism and cirrhosis of the liver in the mid-1950s. Muir died in a nursing home in Mesa, Arizona, on July 23, 1996, at the age of 85. She received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame at 6280 Hollywood Blvd.

title: Cris Cyborg
text:
Cristiane Justino Venâncio, better known as Cris Cyborg, is a Brazilian-American mixed martial artist and professional boxer widely regarded as one of the greatest female fighters in MMA history. Born on July 9, 1985, in Curitiba, Brazil, she began her athletic career in handball before transitioning to MMA at 19, making her professional debut in 2005. She holds the historic distinction of being the only fighter to become a quintuple champion, winning titles in five major promotions: Strikeforce, Invicta FC, the UFC, Bellator, and the PFL.

Cyborg’s career took off when she won the Strikeforce Women’s Featherweight Championship in 2009 by defeating Gina Carano in a groundbreaking main event, the first of its kind in major MMA promotions. She defended the title twice before moving to Invicta FC, where she became the inaugural featherweight champion in 2013. After a doping violation in 2012, which led to a suspension and a no-contest ruling in one of her fights, she returned to prominence in the UFC, winning the UFC Women’s Featherweight Championship in 2017. She defended the title twice before losing to Amanda Nunes in 2018, suffering her first knockout loss in MMA. After her UFC contract ended, she signed with Bellator, where she became the Women’s Featherweight Champion in 2020, defending the title multiple times before becoming a free agent in 2023. In 2024, she joined the PFL and won its inaugural Super Fights Women’s Featherweight Championship.

In addition to MMA, Cyborg has pursued boxing, making her professional debut in 2022. She has since compiled an undefeated record, earning multiple knockouts, including a first-round stoppage in her debut and subsequent victories in 2024 and 2025.

Cyborg’s personal life includes her marriage to fellow MMA fighter Evangelista "Cyborg" Santos, from whom she adopted her nickname, though they divorced in 2011. She became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2016 and later adopted her teenage niece, becoming the first mother to hold a UFC championship. She is engaged to her longtime boyfriend and trainer, Ray Elbe, and is involved in charitable work, including supporting Fight for the Forgotten, a nonprofit organization.

Throughout her career, Cyborg has faced and overcome numerous challenges, including weight-cutting issues, doping controversies, and high-profile rivalries. Her dominance in the featherweight division and her versatility as a striker and grappler have cemented her legacy as one of the most feared and respected fighters in MMA history.

title: Deyverson
text:
Deyverson Brum Silva, commonly known as Deyverson, is a Brazilian professional footballer born on 8 May 1991 in the Santa Margarida neighborhood of Rio de Janeiro. He began his senior career in 2011 with Grêmio Mangaratibense, a local club, where he quickly established himself as a key player. During his two-year stint, he scored 18 goals in 31 appearances, topping the team's scoring charts in the Campeonato Carioca Série C. His debut came on 10 March 2011, when he scored the opening goal in a 2–0 victory against Duquecaxiense.

In 2012, Deyverson joined Portuguese club Benfica after a successful trial period. He spent the 2012–13 season with Benfica's reserve team, making his debut on 19 September 2012 and scoring his first goal the following matchday in a 2–1 win over Oliveirense. Over the course of the season, he scored eight league goals in twelve starts, showcasing his scoring ability.

In August 2013, Deyverson moved to Belenenses, signing a four-year contract. He became the team's main striker in the 2014–15 season and scored the only goal in a 1–1 draw against Benfica at Alvalade. Later that year, he was loaned to German club 1. FC Köln, where he made his Bundesliga debut and scored his first goal against Eintracht Frankfurt on 8 March 2015.

In July 2015, Deyverson transferred to Spanish La Liga side Levante for a reported €2 million fee. He made his La Liga debut on 23 August 2015 in a 1–2 loss to Celta de Vigo and scored his first goal a month later, netting a last-minute equalizer against Eibar. His strong start continued with a brace in a 3–0 win over Sporting de Gijón, bringing his tally to four goals in ten matches. However, Levante was relegated, and in July 2016, Deyverson joined Deportivo Alavés on loan. He scored his first goal for Alavés in a 2–1 upset victory over Barcelona at Camp Nou.

In July 2017, Deyverson returned to Brazil, signing a five-year deal with Palmeiras. In his debut season, he scored seven goals, including a brace against Flamengo, as Palmeiras finished second in the league. The following season, he played a crucial role in Palmeiras' Campeonato Brasileiro Série A title win, scoring nine goals. However, his playing time decreased after the arrival of Luiz Adriano. In 2020, he briefly returned to Spain on loan with Getafe and later Alavés, but neither transfer became permanent.

Deyverson's most iconic moment came on 27 November 2021, when he scored the winning goal in the Copa Libertadores final in extra time, securing the trophy for Palmeiras and earning the Man of the Match award. He also played a key role in the 2022 Recopa Sudamericana and Campeonato Paulista victories.

In August 2022, Deyverson joined Cuiabá on a free transfer. He quickly became a vital player, scoring six goals in his first season, including a three-goal streak in consecutive matches. In 2023, he helped Cuiabá win the Campeonato Mato-Grossense and contributed with crucial goals, such as the winner against Internacional and a brace in a 3–0 victory over Flamengo.

In August 2024, Deyverson moved to Atlético Mineiro, where he continued his scoring form. He scored his first goal in a 3–0 win over Red Bull Bragantino and was named Man of the Match twice in the Copa Libertadores—first for a brace in a 2–0 win over Fluminense and later for a two-goal, one-assist performance against River Plate.

Most recently, in March 2025, Deyverson joined Fortaleza on a contract extending until December 2026, with an option for an additional year. Throughout his career, he has won numerous titles, including the Campeonato Brasileiro, Copa Libertadores, and domestic championships in Brazil. His ability to score decisive goals in high-pressure situations has defined his career, making him a respected forward in Brazilian and international football.

title: Joe McGinniss
text:
Joseph Ralph McGinniss Sr. (1942–2014) was an American writer known for his nonfiction and novels, with a career spanning over four decades. Born in Manhattan and raised in New York, he showed an early interest in writing, even choosing his middle name, Ralph, after the baseball player Ralph Kiner. He attended Archbishop Stepinac High School and the College of the Holy Cross, where he graduated in 1964. Rejected by Columbia University’s journalism program, he began his career as a reporter at the *Worcester Telegram* before moving to the *Philadelphia Bulletin* as a sportswriter and later the *Philadelphia Inquirer* as a columnist. In 1979, he became a writer-in-residence at the *Los Angeles Herald Examiner* and later taught creative writing at Bennington College, where he mentored future authors Donna Tartt and Bret Easton Ellis.

McGinniss gained national attention with his first book, *The Selling of the President 1968*, a bestselling account of Richard Nixon’s 1968 presidential campaign, which he stumbled upon after overhearing a fellow train commuter discussing campaign strategies. The book, published in 1969, spent 31 weeks on *The New York Times* bestseller list and was praised as a groundbreaking work on political marketing. It earned McGinniss widespread recognition, including appearances on major talk shows with Merv Griffin, David Frost, and Dick Cavett. After its success, he left journalism to focus on writing full-time, producing novels like *The Dream Team* (1972) and nonfiction works such as *Going to Extremes* (1980), a chronicle of his time in Alaska.

His most famous works were his true crime trilogy—*Fatal Vision* (1983), *Blind Faith* (1989), and *Cruel Doubt* (1991). *Fatal Vision*, which examined the Jeffrey MacDonald murder case, became a sensation and was adapted into a TV miniseries. MacDonald later sued McGinniss, alleging deception in his reporting, leading to a settlement. The case also inspired Janet Malcolm’s influential book *The Journalist and the Murderer*, which explored ethical dilemmas in journalism. McGinniss revisited the MacDonald case decades later in *Final Vision* (2012). His other true crime books, *Blind Faith* and *Cruel Doubt*, also received critical acclaim and were adapted for television.

McGinniss’s later work included *The Last Brother: The Rise and Fall of Teddy Kennedy* (1993), which was widely criticized for its lack of sourcing, speculative claims, and negative portrayal of the Kennedy family. The book was panned by reviewers, with some calling it "awful" and "prurient." He retaliated by suggesting the Kennedys had orchestrated a smear campaign against him. In 2011, he published *The Rogue: Searching for the Real Sarah Palin*, an unauthorized biography of the former Alaska governor and 2008 vice-presidential nominee. The book, based on his research in Alaska, included unflattering claims about Palin, though it was criticized for its reliance on unnamed sources and its tone.

Throughout his career, McGinniss faced controversies, including a $1 million advance for a book on the O.J. Simpson trial, which he ultimately returned after deciding the case was a "farce." His later years were marked by personal struggles, including alcoholism and depression. In 2012, he revealed he had terminal prostate cancer and died in 2014 at the age of 71. Despite the controversies, his work left a lasting impact, with tributes from figures like Roger Ailes and Gene Weingarten. His legacy endures as a writer who pushed boundaries in journalism and true crime, often sparking debate about ethics and accuracy.

title: Yuyan
text:
Yuyan, born on 17 May 1918 in Wangfujing, Beijing, was a Manchu calligrapher and a member of the Aisin Gioro clan, the imperial family of the Qing dynasty. As the second son of Pucheng and Jinggui of the Fuca clan, he was a distant cousin of Puyi, the last Emperor of China. His grandfather, Zailian, was a descendant of the Daoguang Emperor, solidifying his ties to the Qing imperial lineage. In 1936, Yuyan was summoned by Puyi, who had been installed as the puppet ruler of Manchukuo by Japan in 1934, to join his court in Changchun. Puyi affectionately nicknamed him "Xiaoruizi" (Little Rui), reflecting their close relationship.

After the collapse of Manchukuo in 1945, Yuyan was arrested by Soviet forces and imprisoned alongside Puyi in the Far East Region of the Soviet Union until 1950. He was then transferred to China and held at the Fushun War Criminals Management Centre in Liaoning from 1950 to 1957. Throughout his life, Yuyan claimed that Puyi had appointed him as heir to the Chinese throne during their imprisonment, though Puyi’s autobiography only mentioned considering him as a potential heir. According to Qing succession laws established in 1937, Puyi’s younger brother, Pujie, was the rightful heir.

Following his release from Fushun, Yuyan worked as a language teacher and later in a haberdashery factory. His life was marked by further hardship; he was arrested in 1959 and sent for hard labor in a Beijing detention center, and again in 1966 during the Cultural Revolution, when he was sent to Shanxi. He was not released until 1979, after which he returned to Beijing and worked as a road sweeper.

Despite these struggles, Yuyan was a skilled calligrapher and poet. In 1987, he was appointed as a state consultant for the restoration of the Prince Gong Mansion in Beijing. His claim to the throne drew significant attention, particularly after British journalist Tony Scotland featured him in *The Empty Throne: The Quest for an Imperial Heir in the People's Republic of China* (1993), a book documenting Scotland’s search for a potential heir to the Chinese imperial throne.

Yuyan married twice: first to Magiya Jinglan, a Manchu, in 1943, and later to Zhang Yunfang after Jinglan’s death in 1948. He had three sons: Hengzhen (1944–2023), Hengkai (b. 1945), and Hengjun (b. 1966), each with their own families, including grandchildren like Hengxing, Jin Yinghui, and Jin Qitong. Yuyan died on 18 January 1999, leaving behind a legacy as a controversial figure in the history of the Qing dynasty’s remnants and a symbol of the tumultuous political changes in 20th-century China.

title: Bobby Thomson
text:
Bobby Thomson was a Scottish-born American baseball player, nicknamed "the Staten Island Scot," who played as an outfielder and right-handed batter in Major League Baseball (MLB) from 1946 to 1960. He spent most of his career with the New York Giants, where he gained lasting fame for hitting the "Shot Heard 'Round the World," a walk-off home run that won the 1951 National League pennant for the Giants. Born in Glasgow, Scotland, in 1923, Thomson moved to New York City as a child and signed with the Giants in 1942. He served in the U.S. Army Air Forces during World War II, playing semiprofessional baseball in 1945 while awaiting discharge.

Thomson's rookie season in 1947 was impressive, as he batted .283 with 29 home runs and 82 RBIs. Over his career, he achieved eight 20-home-run seasons and was selected as an All-Star three times (1948, 1949, and 1952). In 1949, he had his best season statistically, batting .309 with 109 RBIs. His 1951 season, however, was the most memorable. After the Giants overcame a 13½-game deficit to tie the Brooklyn Dodgers on the final day of the regular season, a three-game playoff was held. Thomson's dramatic home run off Ralph Branca in the final game of the playoff, with the Giants down 4–2 in the ninth inning, secured the pennant. The moment was immortalized by broadcaster Russ Hodges's excited call, "The Giants win the pennant!" The Giants went on to lose the World Series to the New York Yankees, but Thomson's home run remained one of the most famous moments in baseball history.

Years later, it was confirmed that the Giants had engaged in sign stealing during the 1951 season, using a telescope and a buzzer system to relay the opposing catchers' signals. While Thomson always denied knowing the pitches in advance, some teammates admitted to relaying stolen signs. The controversy did little to diminish the legend of the home run, and Branca himself acknowledged that even if Thomson knew the pitch, he still had to hit it.

After leaving the Giants, Thomson played for the Milwaukee Braves, Chicago Cubs, Boston Red Sox, and Baltimore Orioles before ending his MLB career in 1960. He also spent one season playing in Japan for the Yomiuri Giants in 1963. Over his career, he batted .270 with 264 home runs and 1,026 RBIs. Following his playing days, he worked as a sales executive in New York and later moved to Savannah, Georgia, where he lived until his death in 2010.

Thomson received numerous honors, including induction into the Scottish Sports Hall of Fame, the Staten Island Sports Hall of Fame, and the renaming of his high school's field in his honor. The Edinburgh Diamond Devils, a Scottish baseball team, also named their home stadium Bobby Thomson Field. His legacy endures as one of baseball's most iconic figures, forever linked to the "Shot Heard 'Round the World."

title: Hoshiar Singh Dahiya
text:
Colonel Hoshiar Singh Dahiya, a distinguished Indian military officer, was born on 5 May 1936 in Sisana village, Sonipat district, Haryana, into a Jat family of the Dahiya clan. His father, Choudhary Hira Singh, raised him in a rural setting. After completing his schooling and a year of study at Jat College in Rohtak, Dahiya joined the Indian Army, where he was commissioned into The Grenadiers Regiment on 30 June 1963. He was promoted to lieutenant on 30 June 1965 and served in various roles, including his first posting in NEFA (North-East Frontier Agency). During the 1965 Indo-Pakistani War, he fought in the Rajasthan sector and was mentioned in despatches for his actions. His career progressed steadily, and he was promoted to captain on 30 June 1969.

Dahiya's most notable achievements came during the 1971 Indo-Pakistani War, for which he was awarded the Param Vir Chakra, India’s highest military honor. On 15 December 1971, his battalion was tasked with establishing a bridgehead across the Basantar River in the Shakargarh Sector. As the commander of the left forward company, he was ordered to capture the heavily fortified enemy locality of Jarpal. Despite facing intense shelling and sustained machine-gun fire, Dahiya led a fierce assault, ultimately capturing the objective in a brutal hand-to-hand fight. Over the next two days, the enemy launched multiple counterattacks, including two supported by armored vehicles. Despite heavy shelling and tank fire, Dahiya moved from trench to trench, inspiring his troops to hold their ground. On 17 December 1971, after being seriously wounded, he manned a medium machine gun himself, inflicting heavy casualties on the enemy until the attack was repelled. The enemy retreated, leaving behind 85 dead, including their commanding officer and three other officers. Despite his severe injuries, Dahiya refused evacuation until the ceasefire was declared.

For his extraordinary bravery, leadership, and indomitable spirit, Dahiya was posthumously awarded the Param Vir Chakra. The citation highlights his selflessness, determination, and refusal to abandon his men despite his injuries.

After the war, Dahiya continued his military career, being promoted to substantive major on 30 June 1976. He served as an instructor at the Officers Training School in Madras (now Chennai) and later at the Indian Military Academy in Dehradun. He was promoted to lieutenant-colonel on 8 April 1983 and eventually commanded his battalion. Upon reaching the retirement age for his rank, he retired on 31 May 1988 with the honorary rank of colonel. He settled in Jaipur but frequently visited his village, where he encouraged many young men to join the armed forces. He passed away on 6 December 1998 at the age of 61 due to a cardiac arrest and was cremated with full military honors. He is survived by his wife, Dhano Devi, and three sons, two of whom followed in his footsteps by becoming commissioned officers in The Grenadiers, with one joining the 3rd Grenadiers.

Dahiya’s legacy extends beyond his military service. In 2017, the Indian Army’s official website published his Param Vir Chakra citation, and his character was portrayed by actor Mohanlal in the Malayalam film *1971: Beyond Borders*. His story remains a testament to courage, leadership, and dedication in the face of overwhelming odds.

title: Eric Winter
text:
Eric Barrett Winter, born on July 17, 1976, in La Mirada, California, is an American actor known for his work in television and film. Raised in the nearby city of La Puente, Winter graduated from Los Altos High School and later attended UCLA, where he earned a degree in psychology. His initial foray into acting was motivated by the need to support his college education, as he began modeling and auditioning for small roles in soap operas. Before becoming a full-time actor, Winter had a successful modeling career, appearing in high-profile campaigns, including a print ad for Tommy Hilfiger. He also starred in a television commercial for Britney Spears' fragrance, *Curious*, alongside the pop star.

Winter's acting career began with a prominent role in the NBC soap opera *Days of Our Lives*, where he portrayed Rex Brady from 2002 to 2005. After leaving the show, he took on smaller roles in various television series, including *CSI*, *Love, Inc.*, *Charmed*, and *Just Legal*. He also appeared in *ABC Family's* *Wildfire* as R.J. Blake, a bull rider whose character was killed off in a 2007 episode. Other early television appearances included guest roles in *The Parkers* and *The Ex-List*, as well as a recurring part in the ABC drama *Brothers & Sisters*, where he played Jason McCallister, the brother of Senator Robert McCallister (Rob Lowe) and a love interest for Kevin Walker (Matthew Rhys). Winter also starred in the short-lived CBS series *Viva Laughlin* and *Moonlight*, both of which were canceled after brief runs.

His film career includes supporting roles in *Harold & Kumar Escape from Guantanamo Bay* (2008) and *The Ugly Truth* (2009), as well as the medical drama *The Good Doctor*. In 2010, he starred in the Lifetime television movie *Sundays at Tiffany's* as Michael Friend, the imaginary friend of the lead character, played by Alyssa Milano. From 2010 to 2012, Winter gained recognition for his role as FBI Agent Craig O'Laughlin in the CBS crime drama *The Mentalist*, where he played the boyfriend and later fiancé of Grace Van Pelt (Amanda Righetti). He also had a recurring role in the ABC comedy-drama *GCB* in 2012 and appeared in the video game *Beyond: Two Souls*. Between 2013 and 2014, he starred in the Lifetime fantasy-drama series *Witches of East End* as Dash Gardiner, but the show was canceled after two seasons.

Since 2018, Winter has starred in the ABC drama *The Rookie* as Sergeant Tim Bradford. The show, which follows a middle-aged man entering the LAPD as a rookie officer, has been a long-running success for the network.

In his personal life, Winter was married to actress Allison Ford from 2001 to 2005. He later dated actress Roselyn Sanchez, whom he met in 2005, and the couple became engaged during a holiday trip to Puerto Rico in 2007. They married on November 29, 2008, at a historic fort in San Juan. The couple has two children—a daughter born in January 2012 and a son born in November 2017.

title: Maxime Masson
text:
Maxime Masson was a Roman Catholic priest born on October 15, 1867, in Saint-Justin, Quebec, the son of farmer Amable Masson and Zoe Paquin. He pursued his education in classics at Séminaire Saint-Joseph de Trois-Rivières and theology at the Grand Séminaire de Trois-Rivières, where he was ordained on July 8, 1894, by Bishop L.F. Lafleche. His early career as a priest included serving as a vicar in several parishes: Saint-Justin (1894–1899), Saint-Léon-le-Grand (1902), and Saint-Timothée of Hérouxville (1902–1903). In February 1903, he was appointed as the pastor of Sainte-Thècle, a position he held for an impressive 52 years until July 1955.

During his tenure in Sainte-Thècle, Masson played a pivotal role in the construction and development of key religious and educational institutions. He oversaw the building of the parish church from 1903 to 1905, as well as the construction of the rectory and other buildings associated with the Fabrique de Sainte-Thècle. In 1912, he facilitated the establishment of the monastery for the Daughters of Jesus, and in 1939, he was instrumental in the creation of the first college in Sainte-Thècle, operated by the Brothers of St. Gabriel. His contributions extended beyond architecture; he was also involved in education, serving as the first president of the village’s school board from 1915 to 1947.

Masson was not only an administrator but also a skilled craftsman. He designed and built several notable works in Sainte-Thècle, including the parish cemetery’s stone calvary (1935), a cement lion (1939) placed outside the church, and the intricate paintings on the ceiling of the sacristy. He carved the Stations of the Cross from stone imported from France and created various decorative elements such as cement flowerpots, balls, steps, and a fountain near the church and rectory. Additionally, he crafted a wooden clock with a base resembling the church towers and the high altar.

Throughout his career, Masson recorded 2,497 baptisms in the parish registers between 1903 and 1955, reflecting his deep involvement in the spiritual life of Sainte-Thècle’s community. He was also an early adopter of modern technology, owning one of the first automobiles in the town—a 1911 Ford Model T.

One of the most significant challenges Masson faced was the 1938 hurricane, which caused the collapse of the two towers of the church on August 3. Beyond his religious and architectural contributions, he was recognized for his leadership in the Catholic Action movement and other pious associations.

In recognition of his lifelong dedication to Sainte-Thècle, two local landmarks were named in his honor: École Masson (the old boys' school) and Masson Street, which connects the lower village to the church. After retiring in 1955, Masson lived his final years in Sainte-Thècle and passed away on October 2, 1960. He was buried in the parish cemetery, leaving behind a lasting legacy as a builder, educator, and spiritual leader.

title: James Tyrrell
text:
Sir James Tyrrell (c. 1455 – 6 May 1502) was an English knight who served as a loyal officer under Richard III. His most infamous association is with the murder of the Princes in the Tower—Edward V and his younger brother, Richard of Shrewsbury, Duke of York—though the veracity of these claims remains disputed. Tyrrell was born into a prominent family, the eldest son of William Tyrrell of Gipping, Suffolk, and Margaret Darcy. His father was executed in 1462 following an alleged plot against Edward IV, though no evidence survives to confirm his involvement. Tyrrell’s early career was marked by his service to the Yorkist cause. He fought at the Battle of Tewkesbury in 1471 and was knighted by Edward IV. Shortly after, he entered the service of Richard, Duke of Gloucester, who later became Richard III.

Under Richard III, Tyrrell was appointed High Sheriff of Cornwall in 1484. However, his role in Richard’s court ended with the Yorkist defeat at the Battle of Bosworth in 1485, where he was absent, having been in France at the time. After Henry VII ascended the throne, Tyrrell was pardoned twice in 1486 and reinstated as governor of Guînes, a strategically important English-held town near Calais. His loyalty to the Yorkist cause resurfaced in 1501 when he supported Edmund de la Pole, the leading Yorkist claimant to the throne. In response, Henry VII sent Thomas Lovell to arrest Tyrrell, leading to his trial and execution for treason in 1502. He was buried at the church of the Austin Friars in London, and his attainder was later reversed in 1507.

The most controversial aspect of Tyrrell’s life is his alleged confession to the murder of the Princes in the Tower. According to Sir Thomas More’s *History of King Richard III*, written decades after the events, Tyrrell admitted to organizing the boys’ deaths under Richard III’s orders, implicating John Dighton as an accomplice. However, no original confession document exists, and contemporary chroniclers like Polydore Vergil made no mention of such an admission. Scholars argue that More’s account may have been influenced by Tudor propaganda or derived from statements made under torture. Later Elizabethan chronicles expanded the narrative, claiming Tyrrell buried the princes under a heap of stones before moving their bodies at Richard’s command. Some modern researchers, such as Professor Tim Thornton, have pointed to a chain mentioned in the will of Margaret Capel, Tyrrell’s sister-in-law, as potential evidence of his involvement, though this remains speculative.

Tyrrell married Anne Arundel in 1469, and they had three sons and a daughter. His eldest son, Sir Thomas Tyrrell, continued the family line, while his other children married into notable families, including the Wentworths and the Willoughbys. Shakespeare’s 1593 play *Richard III* cemented Tyrrell’s infamy by portraying him as the orchestrator of the princes’ murders, a depiction that has persisted in popular culture. Despite the enduring mystery surrounding the princes’ fate, Tyrrell’s role remains a subject of historical debate, with no definitive proof of his guilt. His life was marked by shifting allegiances, military service, and a controversial association with one of England’s most enduring historical mysteries.

title: Imbolo Mbue
text:
Imbolo Mbue is a Cameroonian-American novelist and short story writer who has gained recognition for her thought-provoking works exploring immigration, the American Dream, and social inequality. Born in 1981 in Limbé, Cameroon, in the country’s English-speaking region, she spent her early years there before moving to the United States for higher education. Her family sponsored her studies abroad, and in 1998, she arrived in the U.S. to pursue a degree in business management at Rutgers University, graduating in 2002. She later earned an M.A. from Columbia University in 2006.

After completing her education, Mbue began working in the corporate sector in New York City, but the Great Recession led to her job loss, an experience that deeply influenced her writing. During this time, she observed stark class disparities in the city, particularly noting how many Black cab drivers served wealthy executives—a contrast that inspired her debut novel, *Behold the Dreamers* (2016). The book examines the complexities of immigration, financial struggle, and the elusive nature of the American Dream through the lives of its characters, many of whom grapple with hardship, disillusionment, and identity. Mbue has emphasized that her writing is deeply personal, drawing from her own experiences as an immigrant, including financial instability and the emotional toll of rebuilding one’s life in a new country. She believes literature should foster empathy, particularly in discussions about immigration, which she argues often lack compassion in policy and public discourse.

*Behold the Dreamers* received widespread critical acclaim, praised for its nuanced portrayal of America as both a land of opportunity and systemic exclusion. The novel’s release in 2016 coincided with the presidential election, drawing attention to the country’s contentious immigration debates. The *Washington Post* noted how the book highlighted the bureaucratic barriers that prevent many from achieving the American Dream, while NPR commended its depiction of a nation simultaneously blessed and vulnerable. In 2017, Oprah Winfrey selected the novel for her book club, further cementing its cultural impact. The book has since been translated into French and German.

Mbue became a U.S. citizen in 2014 and currently resides in New York City with her husband and children. In 2014, she secured a substantial publishing deal with Random House, signaling early recognition of her talent. Her second novel, *How Beautiful We Were* (2021), shifts focus to environmental devastation in Africa, driven by corporate exploitation. The book critiques the long-term consequences of unchecked greed, particularly in the oil industry, and has been discussed in literary circles for its bold themes. Like her debut, this work has been translated into multiple languages, including French and German.

Beyond her novels, Mbue has contributed to anthologies, such as *New Daughters of Africa* (2019), edited by Margaret Busby. Her writings reflect a commitment to storytelling that challenges societal norms and gives voice to marginalized perspectives. Through her work, Mbue continues to explore the intersections of identity, migration, and global inequality, using fiction as a tool for provoking thought and fostering empathy in a divided world.

title: Gopi Sundar
text:
Gopi Sundar C. S., born on 30 May 1977 in Kochi, Kerala, is a versatile Indian music director, programmer, playback singer, songwriter, actor, and performer who has made significant contributions to the Malayalam, Telugu, and Tamil film industries. His early exposure to music came from his father’s recording studio and his mother’s radio programs, which sparked his passion for music. Despite dropping out of school after failing his SSLC exams, his parents supported his musical aspirations, allowing him to pursue a career in the field. He initially studied at the Government Music College in Chennai but discontinued his course due to disillusionment.

Sundar began his career by composing jingles for television commercials, eventually creating nearly 5,000 jingles. He also worked as a keyboardist and programmer, collaborating with prominent music directors like the Bollywood duo Vishal–Shekhar on songs such as "Ek Main Aur Ek Tu Hai" and "Aankhon Mein Teri." His breakthrough in film music came with *Notebook* (2005), followed by *Flash* (2007), which marked his first official soundtrack composition. His work in *Big B* (2007) earned him recognition for his background score, which enhanced the film’s technical finesse. This collaboration with director Amal Neerad marked the beginning of a long-term partnership.

In 2008, Sundar made his Tamil film debut with *Poi Solla Porom*, and his first major award came for *Anwar* (2010), where he received the Filmfare Award for Best Music Director. His work in *Ustad Hotel* (2012) was highly acclaimed, with the song "Appangalembadum" becoming a massive hit. The film’s soundtrack earned him multiple awards, including another Filmfare Award and a Pearl Award for Best Background Score.

In 2013, Sundar sang "Titli" for the Bollywood blockbuster *Chennai Express*, further expanding his reach. His compositions for *1983* (2014) earned him the National Film Award for Best Background Score, while *Bangalore Days* (2014) fetched him another Filmfare Award. He also made his acting debut in *Salalah Mobiles* (2014) with a cameo as a qawwali singer. His work in *Ennu Ninte Moideen* (2015) and *Charlie* (2015) further solidified his reputation, earning him additional accolades.

Sundar ventured into the Telugu film industry with *Malli Malli Idi Rani Roju* (2015) and *Bhale Bhale Magadivoy* (2015), both of which received positive reviews. His compositions for *Pulimurugan* (2016) were selected for the 90th Academy Awards nominations, and the film became the highest-grossing Malayalam movie. He also worked on *Oopiri* (2016) and *Devi* (2016), further expanding his presence in Tamil and Telugu cinema.

In addition to his film work, Sundar launched his own recording label, *Gopi Sundar Music Company*, in 2014 to support aspiring musicians and facilitate low-budget productions. He also formed a live performance band, *Band Big G*, in 2016, which has performed in Dubai and other international venues. His recording studio, *Sunsa Digital Workstation*, is a state-of-the-art facility in Chennai where he records his compositions.

Sundar has frequently collaborated with directors Rosshan Andrews, Amal Neerad, and Arun Kumar Aravind, as well as lyricists Rafeeq Ahamed, Santhosh Varma, and B.K. Harinarayanan. His contributions to Indian cinema have earned him prestigious awards, including a National Film Award, a Kerala State Film Award, and two Filmfare Awards South. His ability to blend traditional and contemporary sounds has made him one of the most sought-after music directors in the Indian film industry.

title: Aert van der Neer
text:
Aert van der Neer was a Dutch landscape painter active during the Dutch Golden Age, best known for his small-scale night scenes illuminated by moonlight and fires, as well as his snowy winter landscapes, often depicting canals or rivers. Born around 1603 in Gorinchem, he lived and died in relative obscurity, unlike some of his contemporaries, such as Aelbert Cuyp and Meindert Hobbema. According to the historian Arnold Houbraken, van der Neer initially worked as a steward for the lords of Arkel, which may explain why no paintings from his early years survive. He later became an amateur painter, possibly influenced by the Amsterdam painters Rafael and Joachim Govertsz Camphuysen, whose sister, Lysbeth, he married in 1629. The couple had six children, all but one baptized in the Nieuwe Kerk in Amsterdam, where they lived on Kalverstraat.

Van der Neer struggled financially throughout his life, barely supporting his family through his art, which was not highly valued. In 1659, he opened a wine tavern to supplement his income, but by 1661, he had gone bankrupt. He died in abject poverty in 1677, and his remaining paintings were reportedly valued at only five shillings each. His son Eglon van der Neer later became a noted portrait painter.

His earliest dated works, from 1639 and 1642, are now in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam and a private collection in Kiel, respectively, but these are considered immature and of lesser quality. His later works, such as *Winter Landscape* (1643) and *Moonlight Scene* (1644), show greater skill. He witnessed the 1652 fire that destroyed Amsterdam’s old town hall and painted multiple versions of the event, now held in galleries in Berlin and Copenhagen.

Though Amsterdam was his primary residence, his paintings suggest familiarity with the canals and forests near Haarlem and Leiden, as well as the rivers Meuse and Rhine. He also depicted Dordrecht, the hometown of Aelbert Cuyp, and there is evidence of a close friendship between the two artists. They occasionally collaborated on the same canvases, with Cuyp adding figures and cattle to van der Neer’s landscapes. Some works in the collections of the dukes of Bedford and Westminster feature both artists’ contributions, with Cuyp painting figures against van der Neer’s backgrounds. Examples of their joint works can be found in the Louvre, the National Gallery in London, and the Städel Institute in Frankfurt.

Van der Neer’s preferred subjects were Dutch rivers and waterways, often depicted at sunset or in the dark. He excelled at capturing the translucent effects of moonlight, using warm browns and steel grays to reveal distant objects in shadow. He also frequently painted frozen landscapes with skaters, sleighs, and fishermen, always avoiding a harsh, frosty appearance. His compositions were not rare, but they were less commercially valuable than those of Cuyp or Hobbema. Nevertheless, his works were highly sought after by collectors, with around 150 known examples in public collections. The Hermitage in Saint Petersburg holds the finest selection, while other notable works are in the National Gallery and Wallace Collection in England. Van der Neer’s legacy endures through his atmospheric, evocative landscapes, which remain distinctive within the Dutch Golden Age tradition.

title: Karl Urban
text:
Karl Urban, born Karl-Heinz Urban on 7 June 1972 in Wellington, New Zealand, is an accomplished actor with a career spanning film, television, and video games. His early exposure to cinema came through his mother, who worked for Film Facilities in Wellington, sparking his interest in acting. Urban began performing at a young age, appearing in a single line on the New Zealand TV series *Pioneer Woman* when he was eight. He continued acting in school productions but did not pursue it professionally until after high school. After attending Wellington College and briefly enrolling in Victoria University of Wellington, he moved to Auckland, where he secured guest roles in TV shows, including *Shark in the Park*, where he played a heroin addict. He later moved to Bondi Beach, Sydney, in 1995 before returning to New Zealand.

Urban’s breakthrough into Hollywood came with the 2002 horror film *Ghost Ship*. He gained further recognition as Éomer in *The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers* (2002) and *The Return of the King* (2003). His diverse filmography includes roles in *The Bourne Supremacy* (2004) as Kirill, *Doom* (2005) as John "Reaper" Grimm, and *The Chronicles of Ridddick* (2004) and *Riddick* (2013) as Vaako. He also starred in *Judge Dredd* (2012), a role he described as high-octane and action-packed, though the film underperformed commercially. A lifelong *Star Trek* fan, Urban played Dr. Leonard "Bones" McCoy in the reboot film series, earning praise for his portrayal. He reprised the role in *Star Trek Into Darkness* (2013) and *Star Trek Beyond* (2016).

On television, Urban starred in *Almost Human* (2013–2014), a sci-fi series about a detective paired with an android. In 2019, he gained widespread acclaim for his role as Billy Butcher in *The Boys*, an Amazon Prime Video series based on the comic book by Garth Ennis. His other notable works include *Pete’s Dragon* (2016), where he played Gavin Magary, and *Thor: Ragnarok* (2017), in which he portrayed Skurge. He also had a cameo as a stormtrooper in *Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker* (2019) and voiced the lead role in the animated film *The Sea Beast* (2022).

Urban’s personal life includes a marriage to makeup artist Natalie Wihongi, with whom he has two sons, Hunter and Indiana (named after his favorite film series, *Indiana Jones*). The couple separated in 2014. From 2014 to 2018, he dated actress Katee Sackhoff. Urban is also known for his philanthropic work, serving as a celebrity ambassador for KidsCan, a New Zealand charity supporting disadvantaged children. In 2022, he became an official ambassador for UNICEF Aotearoa New Zealand, advocating for children’s rights. He participated in the 2020 *Reunited Apart* YouTube series, reuniting *Lord of the Rings* cast members to promote charity donations.

Urban’s career reflects his versatility across genres, from action and sci-fi to drama and superhero roles, solidifying his status as a respected actor in both New Zealand and Hollywood.

title: Blanca Errázuriz
text:
Blanca Elena Errázuriz Vergara, born on 9 April 1894 in Viña del Mar, Chile, was a prominent socialite and the former wife of American businessman and football player John de Saulles. She was the eldest daughter of Guillermo Errázuriz Urmeneta, a mining magnate, and Blanca Vergara Alvarez, known as the "Star of Santiago," making her part of the influential Errázuriz family of Basque descent. When Blanca was just two years old, her father died, and she was later educated at the Sacred Heart Convent in London. In 1911, at the age of 16, she met John de Saulles, an American businessman 15 years her senior, while he was in Chile negotiating a railway contract. Despite initial family objections due to their age and religious differences (Blanca was Roman Catholic), they married in December 1911 at an English Catholic chapel in Paris. Before marrying Blanca, de Saulles had been engaged to two other heiresses, Mary Elsie Moore and Eleanor Granville Brown, and he briefly served as U.S. Minister to Uruguay in 1914, though he never took up the post.

The couple settled in New York City and had one son, John Longer "Jack" de Saulles, born on Christmas Day 1912, with steel magnate Charles H. Schwab as his godfather. However, their marriage quickly deteriorated due to de Saulles' infidelities, and Blanca filed for divorce in 1916. Around this time, she befriended Rudolph Valentino, then a struggling dancer, who later testified in her divorce proceedings to support her claims of her husband's infidelity. De Saulles, angered by the divorce and Valentino's testimony, used his political connections to have Valentino and a madam named Mrs. Thyme arrested on flimsy charges. After a brief imprisonment, Valentino was released, but the scandal ruined his reputation temporarily. Blanca, however, severed all contact with him after the trial.

On 3 August 1917, shortly after her divorce was finalized, Blanca drove to her ex-husband's home in Meadowbrook Colony, near Westbury, New York, to demand custody of their son, as per a court order de Saulles had ignored. A heated argument ensued, and when he attempted to disarm her, she shot him five times. He was rushed to the hospital but died shortly after. Blanca remained at the scene and surrendered to the police, who charged her with first-degree murder. Her trial became highly publicized, with suffragettes rallying behind her as a symbol of women fighting against patriarchal oppression. Her defense was led by noted criminalist Henry Uterhart, and her French maid, Suzanne Monteau, provided crucial testimony supporting her version of events. On 1 December 1917, after months of proceedings, Blanca was unanimously acquitted in what was described as a "popular" verdict.

Following her acquittal, Blanca moved to San Francisco, where she secured full custody of her son. They later traveled to Japan before returning to Chile, where she settled. In 1921, she remarried to engineer Fernando Santa Cruz Wilson in Santiago, though the marriage ended in divorce. By the late 1930s, Blanca's health had declined, and she became estranged from her son, who moved back to the United States. On 20 March 1940, she died by suicide at her home in Viña del Mar, taking an overdose of barbiturates.

Blanca's case inspired the 1918 silent film *The Woman and the Law*, directed by Raoul Walsh, which loosely adapted her story. The film featured the name "de Saulles" changed to "La Salle," though the credits acknowledged its basis in her real-life events. Tragically, Blanca's brother, diplomat Guillermo Errázuriz, also took his own life in 1922 after being rejected by actress Peggy Hopkins Joyce, who had starred in the film.

title: Andreas Ivanschitz
text:
Andreas Ivanschitz, born Andrej Ivančić on 15 October 1983 in Eisenstadt, was a retired Austrian footballer who played primarily as an attacking midfielder. His 18-year professional career included stints with several clubs across Europe and the United States, beginning with Rapid Wien, where he spent his youth career after joining from local side ASK Baumgarten at age 15. Ivanschitz made his professional debut for Rapid Wien in October 1999 at just 16 years old, appearing in an Austrian Cup match. He later made his league debut in 2000 and went on to play 177 games for the club, scoring 27 goals. During his time at Rapid Wien, he won the Austrian Championship in the 2004–05 season and was named Austrian Footballer of the Year in 2003.

In January 2006, Ivanschitz moved to Red Bull Salzburg before being loaned to Greek club Panathinaikos in August 2006. The loan deal eventually became permanent in June 2008. After three years in Greece, he joined German club Mainz 05 on a two-year loan in July 2009, with an option for a permanent transfer. Mainz exercised this option early, signing him permanently in January 2011. Ivanschitz spent nearly four years at Mainz before moving to Spanish side Levante in June 2013. During his first season in La Liga, he scored three goals in 29 appearances, including the winner against Rayo Vallecano and a goal in a 2–0 victory over Valencia.

In August 2015, Ivanschitz transferred to Major League Soccer (MLS), joining Seattle Sounders FC. Due to an injury, his debut was delayed until September 2015, when he assisted a late equalizer against the San Jose Earthquakes. In 2016, he played a key role in Seattle’s MLS Cup victory, converting a penalty in the shootout that secured the club’s first championship.

On the international stage, Ivanschitz represented Austria from 2003 to 2016, earning 69 caps and scoring 12 goals. He was part of Austria’s squad at UEFA Euro 2008. Outside of football, Ivanschitz comes from a musical family and plays multiple instruments. He is also part of the Burgenland Croat community. His son, Ilia Ivanschitz, is a footballer who currently plays for Red Bull Salzburg.

Throughout his career, Ivanschitz won the Austrian Bundesliga with Rapid Wien and the MLS Cup with Seattle Sounders. His individual accolades include being named Austrian Footballer of the Year in 2003. His contributions to both club and country solidified his reputation as one of Austria’s most skilled midfielders of his generation.

title: Hayden Panettiere
text:
Hayden Panettiere, born on August 21, 1989, is an American actress and singer known for her roles in television, film, and video games. She began her career as an infant, appearing in a commercial at eleven months old. Her formal acting debut came in 1994 when she joined the cast of the ABC soap opera *One Life to Live*, playing the role of Sarah Roberts until 1997. During this time, she also took on the role of Lizzie Spaulding in the CBS soap opera *Guiding Light* (1996–2000). For her portrayal of a leukemia-stricken character in *Guiding Light*, Panettiere received recognition from the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society for raising awareness about the disease.

Panettiere’s early film work includes a voice role in *A Bug’s Life* (1998), for which she earned a Grammy nomination, making her the fifth youngest nominee in the award’s history. She also appeared in films like *Remember the Titans* (2000), *Raising Helen* (2004), and *Ice Princess* (2005). In television, she gained widespread recognition for her role as Claire Bennet, a cheerleader with healing abilities, in the NBC series *Heroes* (2006–2010). Her performance led to invitations to science fiction conventions worldwide.

In 2012, Panettiere starred as Juliette Barnes in the ABC/CMT musical drama *Nashville* (2012–2018), earning two Golden Globe nominations for Best Supporting Actress. She also appeared in the *Scream* horror franchise, playing Kirby Reed in *Scream 4* (2011) and returning for *Scream VI* (2023). Her other film credits include *Amanda Knox: Murder on Trial in Italy* (2011) and *Custody* (2016).

In video games, Panettiere provided the voice for characters in the *Kingdom Hearts* series (2002–2017) and starred as Samantha "Sam" Giddings in *Until Dawn* (2015) and its remake. She also pursued a music career, releasing singles like "Wake Up Call" (2008) and contributing to soundtracks for *Nashville* and Disney projects.

Beyond acting, Panettiere has been involved in activism, supporting causes such as animal rights, anti-whaling campaigns, and the D.C. statehood movement. She has also been an ambassador for organizations like the Ronald McDonald House Charities and the Candie’s Foundation, which addresses teen pregnancy.

Panettiere’s personal life has included relationships with *Heroes* co-star Milo Ventimiglia and boxer Wladimir Klitschko. She publicly advocated for domestic abuse awareness in 2020. Tragically, her younger brother, actor Jansen Panettiere, died in 2023 at age 28. Panettiere has maintained a varied career in acting, music, and activism while navigating both personal and professional challenges.

title: Deitrick Haddon
text:
Deitrick Vaughn Haddon, born on May 17, 1973, is a multifaceted American gospel artist known for his contributions as a singer, songwriter, pianist, arranger, record producer, and pastor. His music primarily falls within the progressive and contemporary gospel genres, earning him widespread recognition in the Christian music industry. Haddon gained further public attention as a cast member on the Oxygen reality television series *Preachers of L.A.*, which documented the lives of six Los Angeles-based pastors, including himself.

Haddon’s solo career began in 2002 with the release of *Lost & Found*, his debut album under Tyscot/Verity Records. The album achieved significant success, reaching the top of *Billboard*’s Top Gospel Charts and earning critical acclaim. The lead single, "Sinner’s Prayer," became a hit, receiving extensive airplay on both gospel and mainstream R&B radio stations. His follow-up album, *Crossroads* (2004), featured a retro 1970s sound and the upbeat single "God is Good." Haddon notably performed these tracks on *Soul Train*, a rare move for a gospel artist, signaling his willingness to crossover into mainstream audiences. In 2006, he released *7 Days*, a contemporary gospel album with a traditional-leaning lead single, "Heaven Knows," which he produced himself. Additionally, Haddon contributed to the comeback album *Brand New Day* for veteran gospel singer Vanessa Bell Armstrong, collaborating with his brother Gerald on its production.

His work with the Voices of Unity ensemble earned him accolades, including the Gospel Music Workshop of America’s "New Artist of the Year—Urban Contemporary" and "Album of the Year—Urban Contemporary" for their album *Live the Life*. In 2008, Haddon released *Revealed*, which included the popular single "Love Him Like I Do," featuring Mary Mary and Ruben Studdard. He expanded into film with his acting debut in the 2010 DVD release *Blessed and Cursed*. His fifth studio album, *Church on the Moon* (2012), debuted at No. 1 on *Billboard*’s Top Gospel chart and No. 65 on the *Billboard* 200, solidifying his prominence in gospel music. Haddon continued to diversify his career, starring as Clarence Burnett in the 2019 TV One movie *Sins of the Father*.

Haddon’s personal life has been marked by both family and ministry. He married Damita Chandler in 1996, and the couple pastored Kingdom Culture Church in Detroit, founded by Haddon’s father, for two and a half years beginning in 2009. After 15 years of marriage, they divorced in 2011. He later married Dominique Haddon (née McTyer), and together they have two daughters, Destin and Denver, and a son, Deitrick II. Currently, they serve as the Founders and Senior Pastors of Hill City Church in Los Angeles, where Haddon is the senior pastor and Dominique is the executive pastor. His career and personal life reflect a blend of artistic innovation, spiritual leadership, and a commitment to gospel music’s evolution.

title: Clancy Brown
text:
Clancy Brown, born Clarence James Brown III on January 5, 1959, in Urbana, Ohio, is an accomplished American actor with a prolific career spanning film, television, and voice acting. Known for his authoritative and often villainous roles, Brown has become a recognizable figure in Hollywood. His father, Clarence J. "Bud" Brown Jr., was a newspaper publisher and congressman, while his mother, Joyce Helen Eldridge, was a conductor and pianist. Brown attended St. Albans School in Washington, D.C., and later graduated from Northwestern University.

Brown's film career began in the 1980s, with notable roles such as Rawhide in *The Adventures of Buckaroo Banzai Across the 8th Dimension* (1984), Frankenstein's monster in *The Bride* (1985), and the iconic villain Kurgan in *Highlander* (1986). He also played the tyrannical Captain Byron Hadley in *The Shawshank Redemption* (1994), Sheriff Gus Gilbert in *Pet Sematary Two* (1992), and Sergeant Zim in *Starship Troopers* (1997). His more recent film roles include Stanley Thomas in *Promising Young Woman* (2020) and the Harbinger in *John Wick: Chapter 4* (2023).

On television, Brown has appeared in a variety of roles, including Brother Justin Crowe in the cult-favorite series *Carnivàle* (2003–2005), Waylon "Jock" Jeffcoat in *Billions* (2018–2019, 2023), and Kurt Caldwell in *Dexter: New Blood* (2021–2022). He has also made guest appearances in popular shows like *ER*, *Lost*, *The Flash*, and *Daredevil*.

Brown is also a prolific voice actor, most famously voicing Mr. Krabs in *SpongeBob SquarePants* since 1999. His extensive voice work includes Lex Luthor in multiple DC Comics animated series and films, Long Feng in *Avatar: The Last Airbender*, Savage Opress in *Star Wars: The Clone Wars*, and Surtur in *Thor: Ragnarok*. He has also lent his voice to video games, including *Crash Bandicoot*, *Detroit: Become Human*, and *World of Warcraft*.

In his personal life, Brown has been married to Jeanne Johnson since 1993, and the couple has two children. His versatility as an actor, combined with his commanding presence, has made him a fixture in both live-action and animated media.

title: Tarik Elyounoussi
text:
Tarik Elyounoussi is a former professional footballer born on 23 February 1988 in Al Hoceima, Morocco. He moved to Norway with his family at the age of 11 and began his football career in local clubs, including Nylende and Trosvik. Recognized as one of Fredrikstad’s most talented players in decades, he won the Norwegian Young Player of the Year award in 2006 and 2007, also contributing to Fredrikstad’s Norwegian Cup victory in 2006. His performances attracted attention from top clubs, and in 2008, he was transferred to SC Heerenveen in the Dutch Eredivisie for a fee of €3.5 million. He made an immediate impact, scoring in his debut match and contributing in European competitions, including a crucial goal in the UEFA Cup.

After two seasons at Heerenveen, Elyounoussi was loaned to Lillestrøm SK in 2010 and later returned to Fredrikstad in 2011. In 2012, he joined Rosenborg, one of Norway’s most successful clubs, where he played until 2013. That year, he moved to 1899 Hoffenheim in Germany before transferring to Olympiacos in Greece in 2016. During his time at Olympiacos, he played a key role in securing the Greek Super League title in the 2016–17 season. In 2017, he had a short loan spell with Azerbaijani club Qarabağ but made little impact.

In 2018, Elyounoussi signed for AIK in Sweden, where he won the Allsvenskan title. He later moved to Japan’s Shonan Bellmare in 2020, spending three seasons there before retiring at the end of the 2023 season. Throughout his career, he was known for his versatility, playing as both a forward and a winger.

On the international stage, Elyounoussi represented Norway, scoring on his debut against Uruguay in 2008—a feat that remains one of the fastest debut goals in the team’s history. He later scored against Denmark in 2012 and captained Norway in friendlies against South Africa and Zambia in 2013, netting the winning goal in the latter match. His cousin, Mohamed Elyounoussi, is also a Norwegian international footballer.

Elyounoussi’s career was marked by success at both club and international levels, earning domestic league titles in Greece and Sweden, as well as a Dutch Cup title with Heerenveen. He concluded his professional career after a distinguished journey across multiple leagues and countries.

title: Roman Pavlyuchenko
text:
Roman Anatolyevich Pavlyuchenko, born on 15 December 1981 in the village of Mostovskoy, Krasnodar Krai, is a former Russian footballer who played as a striker and is now a football coach, currently serving as a forwards coach with Rodina-2 Moscow. His professional career began in the lower divisions of Russian football, starting at Dynamo Stavropol in 1999, where he made 31 appearances and scored 11 goals in his debut season, though the club was relegated. Despite this setback, Pavlyuchenko was recognized as one of the top young talents by *Sport Express*. He then moved to Rotor Volgograd in 2000, where his early matches were marked by a red card in his debut, but he gradually established himself as a reliable forward over three seasons, scoring a total of 14 goals.

In 2003, Pavlyuchenko joined Spartak Moscow, becoming a key player and eventually their most prolific goalscorer. Over five seasons, he scored 69 goals in 141 appearances, earning the league's top scorer title twice (2006 and 2007) and leading Spartak to the UEFA Champions League. His standout performances included a hat-trick against Kuban Krasnodar and crucial goals in Champions League qualifiers, notably against Slovan Liberec and Inter Milan. His loyalty and goalscoring prowess earned him deep respect from Spartak’s fanbase.

In 2008, Pavlyuchenko transferred to Tottenham Hotspur in the English Premier League for £13.7 million. His time at Spurs was mixed; while he showed flashes of brilliance, including scoring in multiple domestic cup competitions and memorable goals against Inter Milan in the Champions League, he often struggled for consistent playing time. A controversial moment came in May 2009 when he stormed off the pitch after being substituted, though he later apologized. His most productive spell at Spurs came in the 2010–11 season, where he scored crucial goals, including a brace on the final day to secure fifth place and European qualification. Despite his contributions, he left in 2012 to rejoin Lokomotiv Moscow, where he spent three seasons but saw reduced playing time.

After stints with Kuban Krasnodar (2015) and Ural Yekaterinburg (2016), Pavlyuchenko played in lower-tier Russian leagues, including Ararat Moscow and Znamya Noginsk, where he famously scored four goals in a single game at age 38. His career ended in 2022 after being banned for violent conduct.

Internationally, Pavlyuchenko earned 51 caps for Russia, scoring 21 goals. He was a standout at Euro 2008, where he scored crucial goals against England, Sweden, and the Netherlands, earning a spot in the tournament’s Team of the Tournament. He also scored a hat-trick in a 2012 European qualifier against Armenia. His international career spanned nearly a decade, though he missed the 2010 World Cup due to injury.

Pavlyuchenko’s career was marked by highs, including domestic and international success, and challenges, such as inconsistent playing time in England. His technical ability, work ethic, and resilience, even in the lower leagues, solidified his legacy as one of Russia’s most reliable strikers.

title: Melvin Van Peebles
text:
Melvin Van Peebles (1932–2021) was a pioneering American filmmaker, actor, writer, and composer known for his groundbreaking contributions to cinema, particularly the blaxploitation genre. Born in Chicago, Illinois, as Melvin Peebles, he graduated from Ohio Wesleyan University in 1953 before serving in the U.S. Air Force. He later added "Van" to his surname during his time in the Netherlands in his late 20s. His early career included working as a cable car gripman in San Francisco, which inspired his first book, *The Big Heart*, a collection of writings and photographs.

Van Peebles began his filmmaking journey with short films in the late 1950s, including *Pickup Men for Herrick* (1957). Unable to secure work in Hollywood, he moved to France, where he gained recognition for his short film *Les Cinq Cent Balles* (1961). His feature film debut, *The Story of a Three-Day Pass* (1967), based on his novel *La Permission*, won an award at the San Francisco International Film Festival, attracting Hollywood’s attention. His first American film, *Watermelon Man* (1970), starring Godfrey Cambridge, explored themes of racial identity and alienation.

In 1971, Van Peebles released *Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song*, a self-funded film that became a landmark in African American cinema. The film’s success helped establish the blaxploitation genre, though critic Roger Ebert argued it was not merely an exploitation film. Van Peebles wrote, directed, edited, and composed the score, demonstrating his versatility. The film’s success earned him a $15 million gross and praise from the Black Panthers for its political themes. His son, Mario Van Peebles, later portrayed his father in the 2003 biographical film *Baadasssss!*

Van Peebles continued to work across multiple mediums. He wrote and directed the musical *Don’t Play Us Cheap* (1973), based on his earlier stage play, and contributed to Broadway productions like *Ain’t Supposed to Die a Natural Death* (1971–72), which earned Tony and Grammy nominations. He also co-wrote *Greased Lightning* (1977) and worked on other musicals, including *Reggae* (1980) and *Waltz of the Stork* (1982). In the 1980s, he briefly pursued a career as an options trader while remaining active in film and theater.

Throughout the 2000s, Van Peebles continued to create, directing films like *Confessionsofa Ex-Doofus-ItchyFooted Mutha* (2008) and appearing in documentaries such as *How to Eat Your Watermelon in White Company (and Enjoy It)* (2005). He also released music, including the 2012 album *Nahh... Nahh Mofo*, and collaborated with bands like Burnt Sugar. In 2019, he participated in a Brooklyn screening of *Sweetback* with a live reinterpretation of the soundtrack.

Van Peebles was married to German actress Maria Marx, and they had three children, including actor and director Mario Van Peebles. He received numerous honors, including a 2001 Commander of the Legion of Honour from France and induction into the Black Filmmakers Hall of Fame in 1976. He passed away on September 21, 2021, in Manhattan, New York, at the age of 89. His legacy endures as a trailblazer in independent cinema and a multifaceted artist who defied conventions throughout his career.

title: Carrie Ann Inaba
text:
Carrie Ann Inaba, born on January 5, 1968, in Honolulu, Hawaii, is a multi-talented American television personality, dancer, choreographer, actress, and singer. She is best known for her role as a judge on *Dancing with the Stars*, a position she has held since 2005. Additionally, she co-hosted and moderated the CBS Daytime talk show *The Talk* from 2019 to 2021. Before gaining fame in the U.S., she began her career as a pop singer in Japan, where she released three singles and hosted radio and television shows from 1986 to 1988. However, she later shifted her focus to dancing, which became her most recognized talent.

Inaba’s early life was marked by a deep connection to dance. She began dancing at age three and later attended the University of California, Los Angeles, where she earned a bachelor’s degree in world arts and cultures. Her breakthrough in America came when she joined the cast of *In Living Color* as one of the original "Fly Girls," a group of dancers on the Fox sketch comedy series from 1990 to 1992. She later performed as a featured solo dancer in Madonna’s 1993 *Girlie Show World Tour*, a role that required her to shave her head, which she ultimately considered worthwhile.

Throughout her career, Inaba has made numerous film and television appearances. She played Fook Yu in *Austin Powers in Goldmember* (2002), alongside Diane Mizota, who portrayed her fictional twin sister. Though the roles were initially fun, Inaba later expressed regret over the negative stereotypes the characters represented.
