title: Mike Adenuga
text:
Mike Adenuga, a Nigerian billionaire businessman, is widely recognized as one of Africa’s wealthiest individuals. As of May 2024, Forbes estimated his net worth at $6.7 billion, ranking him as the fifth-richest person on the continent. His primary business ventures include Globacom, Nigeria’s second-largest telecommunications company, which also operates in Ghana and Benin. In addition to telecoms, Adenuga holds significant stakes in Equitorial Trust Bank and Conoil, an oil exploration firm. His diverse business portfolio has solidified his reputation as a leading entrepreneur in Nigeria and beyond.

Born on 29 April 1953, Adenuga hails from a family with strong academic and business backgrounds. His father, Oloye Michael Agbolade Adenuga Sr., was a schoolteacher, while his mother, Omoba Juliana Oyindamola Adenuga, was a businesswoman of royal Ijebu descent. Adenuga is of Yoruba ethnicity. He completed his secondary education at Ibadan Grammar School in Ibadan, Oyo State, and Comprehensive High School in Aiyetoro, where he earned his Higher School Certificate. To support his university education, he worked as a taxi driver. He later graduated from Northwestern Oklahoma State University and Pace University in New York with degrees in Business Administration.

Adenuga’s entrepreneurial journey began early, and by 1979, at the age of 26, he had already amassed his first million naira through the sale of lace materials and the distribution of soft drinks. His foray into the oil industry came in 1990 when he secured a drilling license. Just a year later, his company, Consolidated Oil (now Conoil), struck oil in the shallow waters of Ondo State, making him the first indigenous Nigerian company to achieve commercial oil production. This milestone marked a significant turning point in his career, establishing him as a key player in the Nigerian oil sector.

In the telecommunications industry, Adenuga faced challenges but ultimately succeeded. In 1999, he was granted a conditional GSM license, which was later revoked. However, he secured a second license in 2003 during a government auction, which led to the establishment of Globacom. His success in telecommunications was further recognized in 2007 when he was named African Entrepreneur of the Year at the inaugural African Telecoms Awards. In 2015, he made a bold move by attempting to acquire Comium Côte d’Ivoire, an Ivorian mobile telecom operator, for $600 million, though the outcome of this bid is not detailed in the article.

Adenuga’s contributions to business and society have earned him numerous honors. In 2012, the Nigerian government bestowed upon him the prestigious Grand Commander of the Order of the Niger, one of the highest national awards. He also holds a Yoruba chieftaincy title, "Otunba Apesin," from the Ijebu clan, reflecting his cultural significance. In 2018, he was awarded the insignia of a Commander of the Legion of Honour by French President Emmanuel Macron, further cementing his international recognition. Additionally, in 2019, New African magazine listed him among the Top 100 most influential Africans, highlighting his impact on the continent.

Adenuga’s career is a testament to resilience, innovation, and strategic business acumen. From humble beginnings as a taxi driver to becoming a billionaire industrialist, his journey has inspired many. His ventures in oil, banking, and telecommunications have not only contributed to Nigeria’s economic growth but have also positioned him as a key figure in African business. His accolades and titles further underscore his influence, both within Nigeria and on the global stage.

title: Danny Almonte
text:
Danny Almonte Rojas, born on April 7, 1987, in Moca, Dominican Republic, is a former baseball player who gained fame as a Little League pitcher in the early 2000s. He moved to The Bronx, New York, in 2000, where he began playing Little League Baseball. His father, Felipe Almonte, had previously established a youth baseball league in Moca that still bears his name. Almonte quickly became a standout player, throwing fastballs up to 79 miles per hour and earning the nickname "Little Unit" in reference to major-league pitcher Randy Johnson. In 2001, he led his Bronx team, nicknamed the "Baby Bombers," to the Little League World Series, where he threw a no-hitter in the regional finals and a perfect game in the tournament, striking out 62 batters in three starts. His team finished in third place, and the players were celebrated with honors, including a key to the city from Mayor Rudy Giuliani.

However, suspicions arose about Almonte's age. His physical maturity and pitching velocity led to rumors that he was older than the age limit of 12 for Little League. Investigations by opposing teams failed to find conclusive evidence, and Little League officials initially backed Almonte’s claimed birth year of 1989. But in September 2001, *Sports Illustrated* discovered a 1994 birth registration in the Dominican Republic listing Almonte as born in 1987, making him 14 during the 2001 tournament. Dominican officials later confirmed this, revealing that Almonte’s parents had presented conflicting documents—his mother claiming a 1989 birth and his father initially registering a 1987 birth. Felipe Almonte was accused of falsifying records, and prosecutors filed criminal charges against him. Almonte was declared ineligible, and the Baby Bombers forfeited their wins. Felipe and the league president, Rolando Paulino, were banned from Little League for life.

Further complications arose when New York City officials discovered Almonte had not been enrolled in school during the 2000–01 school year, violating state law. Dominican officials later confirmed he had attended school in the Dominican Republic until June 15, 2001, which would have made him ineligible for the Little League World Series even if he had been 12. After the scandal, Almonte remained in New York under Paulino’s guardianship. He played high school baseball in the Bronx and attended tryouts for Major League Baseball, though he was not drafted. He went on to play for New Mexico Junior College and the Southern Illinois Miners of the Frontier League, though his professional career was unremarkable. By 2010, he had returned to the Bronx, working as a volunteer assistant coach at his high school alma mater, Cardinal Hayes High School, where he later became an official assistant coach. In 2005, at age 18, Almonte married Rosy Perdomo, who was 30 at the time.

The scandal surrounding Almonte’s age remains one of the most infamous incidents in Little League history, highlighting issues of age fraud and the pressures faced by young athletes. Despite the controversy, Almonte was ultimately cleared of wrongdoing, and his father was the primary figure held accountable. Almonte’s talent and the controversy surrounding his career have left a lasting impact on discussions about youth sports ethics.

title: James Franco
text:
James Edward Franco, born on April 19, 1978, in Palo Alto, California, is an American actor and filmmaker with a diverse career spanning film, television, and theater. His parents, Betsy Lou Verne (a children's book author) and Douglas Eugene Franco (a Silicon Valley businessman), had mixed European ancestry, including Portuguese, Swedish, and Jewish heritage. Franco grew up in an academic, liberal, and largely secular household with two younger brothers, Tom and Dave, both of whom also became actors. As a teenager, Franco excelled in academics and even interned at Lockheed Martin, but he also faced legal troubles, including arrests for underage drinking, graffiti, and theft. These incidents led to him briefly becoming a ward of the state, though he eventually turned his life around.

Franco initially attended UCLA as an English major but dropped out after his first year to pursue acting, taking lessons at the Playhouse West. To support himself, he worked at McDonald's, where he practiced accents on customers. His first prominent role came in 1999 when he starred as Daniel Desario in the short-lived but critically acclaimed NBC series *Freaks and Geeks*, which later gained a cult following. He made his film debut in *Never Been Kissed* (1999) and played a jock in *Whatever It Takes* (2000). His breakthrough role was in the 2001 biographical film *James Dean*, for which he won a Golden Globe and received nominations for an Emmy and a Screen Actors Guild Award. To prepare, he smoked two packs of cigarettes a day, bleached his hair, and immersed himself in James Dean’s life.

Franco gained international fame as Harry Osborn in Sam Raimi’s *Spider-Man* trilogy (2002–2007), though he was initially considered for the lead role of Peter Parker. He continued to take on challenging roles, including a homeless drug addict in *City by the Sea* (2002) and a troubled veteran in *Sonny* (2002), for which he conducted extensive research. In 2004, he reprised his role in *Spider-Man 2*, which was a critical and commercial success. Over the next few years, he appeared in films like *The Great Raid* (2005), *Annapolis* (2006), and *Tristan & Isolde* (2006), often undergoing rigorous training for his roles, such as boxing and sword fighting.

In 2008, Franco starred in the stoner comedy *Pineapple Express* alongside Seth Rogen, a collaboration that continued in *This Is the End* (2013), *Sausage Party* (2016), and *The Disaster Artist* (2017). His role in *The Disaster Artist* earned him a Golden Globe for Best Actor. That same year, he played Scott Smith in *Milk* (2008), for which he won an Independent Spirit Award. In 2009, he joined the cast of the daytime soap opera *General Hospital* as an artist obsessed with a character, a role he described as performance art.

Franco had a standout year in 2010 with roles in *Date Night*, *Eat Pray Love*, and *Howl*, where he portrayed poet Allen Ginsberg. His performance in *127 Hours* (2010), as Aron Ralston, a climber who amputated his own arm to survive, earned him widespread acclaim and an Academy Award nomination. To prepare, he spent weeks isolated on set, studying academic texts. The film was both a critical and commercial success.

In the following years, Franco starred in *Rise of the Planet of the Apes* (2011), *Spring Breakers* (2012), and *Oz the Great and Powerful* (2013). He also hosted *Saturday Night Live* twice (2008 and 2009) and appeared in the HBO series *The Deuce* (2017–2019). However, his career has been marred by controversy. In 2014, a 17-year-old alleged that Franco, then 35, tried to meet her in a hotel room. In 2018, five women accused him of inappropriate or exploitative behavior while he was their acting teacher or mentor. A lawsuit filed by former students resulted in a $2.2 million settlement in 2021.

Franco’s early life was marked by academic achievement and legal troubles, but his determination led him to a successful acting career. He has tackled a wide range of roles, from blockbuster franchises to independent films, and has won multiple awards. Despite his professional achievements, his reputation has been tarnished by allegations of misconduct.

title: Andy Middleton
text:
Andy Middleton is an American jazz saxophonist, known for his work as both a tenor and soprano saxophonist. Born on May 22, 1962, in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, he grew up in a musical family and began playing the alto saxophone at the age of nine. He pursued his education at the University of Rochester from 1980 to 1982 and later attended the University of Miami from 1982 to 1987. During his time at the Banff Centre in Alberta, Canada, in 1985 and 1986, he formed connections with prominent jazz musicians such as Dave Holland, Kenny Wheeler, Steve Coleman, John Abercrombie, Richie Beirach, and David Liebman.

In 1987, Middleton moved to the New York City area, where he became an active member of the jazz scene. He performed with notable ensembles, including the Bob Mintzer Big Band, the Lionel Hampton Big Band (which recorded his composition "Two Brothers," written with his brother Rob Middleton, on the album *Cookin' in the Kitchen*), and the Maria Schneider Jazz Orchestra. He also formed his own long-running quartet, which featured a rotating lineup of musicians such as guitarist Ben Monder, drummers John Hollenbeck and Owen Howard, bassist Scott Colley, and pianists Henry Hey, Andy Ezrin, and David Berkman.

Middleton's recording career began in 1991 with *Acid Rain*, released on the French label Owl Records and featuring pianist Joey Calderazzo. His second album, *Terra Infirma* (1995), was produced by David Liebman and released by EMI France, showcasing a quartet with pianist Renee Rosnes, bassist Paul Imm, and drummer Alan Jones, along with a horn section. In 1992, he co-founded the group The Fensters, a sax-driven quartet with Alan Jones, François Theberge, and bassist Paul Imm, which released two albums: *Jazz Music, Vol. 1* (1992) on Arta Records and *Jazz Music, Vol. X* (1996) on Challenge Records. In 1999, he recorded *Nomad's Notebook* with ECM Records guitarist Ralph Towner, bassist Dave Holland, drummer Alan Jones, trombonist Noah Bless, and percussionist Jamey Haddad. His subsequent album, *Reinventing the World* (2003), featured trumpeter Kenny Wheeler and trombonist Nils Wogram.

In 2006, Middleton relocated to Vienna, Austria, where he began teaching at the Music and Arts University of the City of Vienna. Over his career, he has received numerous accolades, including the Outstanding Jazz Soloist award from *DownBeat* magazine in 1987, first prize for Best Soloist and Best Arranger at the 13th Europ' Jazz Contest in Belgium in 1991, a National Endowment for the Arts Performance Grant in 1996, and multiple grants from organizations such as the Brooklyn Arts Council, the Fund for U.S. Artists at International Festivals, the New York Foundation for the Arts, and Chamber Music America. He was also awarded a film composition grant from the Austrian government in 2014.

Middleton's discography as a leader includes *Jazz Music Vol. 1* (1992), *Jazz Music Vol. X* (1996), *Acid Rain* (1991), *Terra Infirma* (1995), *Nomad's Notebook* (1999), *Reinventing the World* (2003), *The Muir Woods Suite* (2006), *The European Quartet Live* (2007), *Between Worlds* (2010), and *Three Hearts, Three Minds* (2010). As a sideman, he has appeared on recordings by artists such as Lionel Hampton, Owen Howard, Maria Schneider, and Piotr Wojtasik. His contributions to jazz have been recognized both as a performer and a composer, cementing his reputation as a versatile and influential figure in the genre.

title: Anderson Silva
text:
Anderson Silva, born on 14 April 1975 in São Paulo, Brazil, is widely regarded as one of the greatest mixed martial artists of all time. He is a former UFC Middleweight Champion and holds the record for the longest title reign in UFC history, spanning 2,457 days from 2006 to 2013. During this period, he achieved 16 consecutive victories, including a remarkable streak of nine wins in a row at UFC. Silva left the UFC in November 2020 and transitioned to professional boxing. In 2023, he was inducted into the UFC Hall of Fame.

Silva's martial arts journey began in childhood, training in jiu-jitsu with neighborhood kids. As a teenager, he expanded his skills to taekwondo, capoeira, and muay Thai. His professional MMA career started in 1997, initially competing in the welterweight division in Brazil. After an early loss in 2000, he embarked on a nine-fight winning streak, culminating in a victory over undefeated Shooto champion Hayato Sakurai in 2001, becoming the first to defeat him.

From 2002 to 2006, Silva fought for PRIDE Fighting Championships and Cage Rage. His PRIDE debut was against Alex Stiebling, whom he defeated due to a cut from a high kick. He then outpointed Alexander Otsuka and knocked out Carlos Newton with a flying knee. However, he suffered a surprising loss to Daiju Takase via triangle choke, leading to a temporary demotivation. After relocating to Brazilian Top Team, he rebounded with wins over Jeremy Horn, Lee Murray, and Curtis Stout, defending his Cage Rage title. A controversial loss to Ryo Chonan in PRIDE, where Chonan submitted him with a rare flying scissor heel hook, marked the end of his PRIDE tenure.

Silva joined the UFC in 2006, making his debut with a first-round knockout of Chris Leben, earning Knockout of the Night. He quickly challenged and defeated Rich Franklin for the UFC Middleweight Championship, knocking him out in the first round. This victory earned him another Knockout of the Night and the 2006 Knockout of the Year.

Silva's title reign was characterized by dominant performances, including submissions of Travis Lutter and Dan Henderson, and knockouts of Nate Marquardt, Rich Franklin (in a rematch), and Forrest Griffin. However, his reign also included controversies, such as his fight with Patrick Côté, where he was criticized for seemingly avoiding contact, and his non-aggressive decision win over Demian Maia, which drew widespread criticism from UFC president Dana White. His fight against Chael Sonnen in 2010 was another highlight, as Silva survived Sonnen’s relentless ground control to secure a fifth-round submission, marking his first major adversity in the UFC.

Despite occasional criticism for his fighting style, Silva’s legacy as one of the most skilled and dominant fighters in UFC history remains unmatched. His striking precision, versatility, and ability to adapt to opponents made him a legend in the sport. After his UFC career, he transitioned to boxing, continuing his career in combat sports.

title: Edgar Bennett
text:
Edgar Bennett III, born on February 15, 1969, is a former NFL player and current coach, serving as the wide receivers coach for the Jacksonville Jaguars. His football career began at Robert E. Lee High School in Jacksonville, Florida, where he earned varsity letters in football, basketball, and track. Under the guidance of coach Corky Rogers, Bennett became a Class 4A All-State running back and was recognized as a SuperPrep All-Dixie selection.

Bennett attended Florida State University, where he played for the Seminoles. Primarily a fullback, he was part of a backfield that included notable players like Amp Lee, Marquette Smith, and William Floyd. When Lee was suspended for the Cotton Bowl, Bennett started at halfback. Known for his versatility, he amassed over 2,300 all-purpose yards on 389 touches and scored 20 touchdowns. He was also a standout receiver, catching 93 passes for more than 1,000 yards, and demonstrated speed with a 4.5-second 40-yard dash.

After college, Bennett was drafted by the Green Bay Packers in the fourth round of the 1992 NFL Draft (103rd overall). Starting his career as a fullback, he transitioned to starting running back in 1995, rushing for 1,067 yards. He was a key receiver for the Packers, leading the team in receptions. While he remained the starting running back in 1996, Dorsey Levens gained more playing time later in the season. Bennett was part of the Packers' Super Bowl XXXI-winning team. His career with the Packers ended prematurely when he ruptured his Achilles tendon in the 1997 preseason, forcing him to sit out the entire season. In 2005, he was inducted into the Green Bay Packers Hall of Fame.

Following his playing career, Bennett joined the Packers organization in 2001 as director of player development. He later became the team’s running backs coach for six seasons before being promoted to wide receivers coach in 2011. In 2015, head coach Mike McCarthy elevated him to offensive coordinator.

In 2018, Bennett left the Packers to become the wide receivers coach for the Oakland Raiders under Jon Gruden. He remained with the team, now known as the Las Vegas Raiders, under new head coach Josh McDaniels until February 2025, when he was dismissed. Just days later, the Jacksonville Jaguars hired him as their wide receivers coach.

Outside of football, Bennett is a devoted family man. His daughter, Elyse Bennett, was the seventh overall pick in the 2022 NWSL Draft, joining the KC Current. Bennett’s career reflects a seamless transition from a versatile player to a respected coach, leaving a lasting impact on the teams he has worked with.

title: Phillip Gillespie
text:
Phillip J. Gillespie, born on 23 October 1975 in Frankston, a suburb of Melbourne, Victoria, is an Australian cricket umpire and former cricketer. After a playing career cut short by injuries, he transitioned into umpiring, becoming a respected figure in domestic and international cricket. His journey began in 2009 when, following injuries to his Achilles tendon, jaw, and knee while playing for the Rowville Cricket Club, he decided to stay involved in the sport by becoming an umpire in the Victorian Premier Cricket competition.

Gillespie’s umpiring career progressed rapidly. He made his List A debut in February 2013 during a match between the England Lions and Victoria. He went on to officiate in eight matches of the Matador BBQs One-Day Cup, demonstrating his growing competence at the elite level. His involvement in women’s cricket was also significant, as he umpired two Women’s National Cricket League matches, including the 2015 semi-final between New South Wales and Victoria. His experience in women’s cricket continued with assignments in the Women’s Big Bash League, including the 2016–17 season’s second semi-final, where the Sydney Sixers defeated the Hobart Hurricanes.

His first-class debut came on 15 February 2015 during a Sheffield Shield match between New South Wales and Victoria, a game notable for Doug Bollinger’s hat-trick. By March 2017, he had officiated in ten first-class matches, including the clash between Tasmania and Queensland at Bellerive Oval. In international cricket, Gillespie made his debut in 2014 during the West Indies women’s tour of Australia, umpiring all four Women’s One Day International (WODI) matches. He continued to officiate in WODIs, including the final two matches of South Africa’s 2016 series in Australia. Additionally, he umpired three matches in the 2016–17 ICC World Cricket League East Asia–Pacific Region Qualifiers, involving teams like Fiji, the Philippines, and Vanuatu.

Gillespie’s professional development was further strengthened when he was accepted into the 2015 intake of the Australian Sports Commission National Officiating Scholarship program, a prestigious initiative designed to train officiants for elite-level competition. In May 2015, he replaced Damien Mealey on the National Umpire Panel, a testament to his rising status in Australian cricket. His career reached another milestone on 7 October 2022 when he stood in his first Twenty20 International (T20I) match, between Australia and the West Indies.

Outside of cricket, Gillespie is a supporter of the Richmond Tigers in the Australian Football League and works as a police officer in the Victorian Police Force. His diverse background and dedication to officiating have established him as a key figure in both domestic and international cricket. As of March 2017, his umpiring record included six WODIs, ten first-class matches, nine List A matches, ten Twenty20 matches, and nine Women’s T20 matches, showcasing his versatility and expertise across different formats of the game.

title: Balázs Bekő
text:

Born on 15 December 1971, Bekő has built a career in football management, primarily in Hungary’s top-tier league, the Nemzeti Bajnokság I (NB I). His managerial journey began in June 2013 when he was appointed as the head coach of Kecskeméti TE, a club competing in the NB I. During his tenure at Kecskeméti TE, Bekő took charge of a team in one of Hungary’s most competitive football leagues, responsible for tactical decisions, team selection, and overall performance. In the summer of 2015, Bekő moved to another prominent NB I club, Diósgyőri VTK (Diósgyőr). title: Mike Melvill
text:
Michael Winston Melvill, born on November 30, 1940, in Johannesburg, South Africa, is a distinguished pilot and test pilot whose career is marked by groundbreaking achievements in aviation and spaceflight. He gained international recognition as one of the test pilots for SpaceShipOne, the experimental spaceplane developed by Scaled Composites, a company founded by aerospace designer Burt Rutan. Melvill’s most notable accomplishment came on June 21, 2004, when he piloted SpaceShipOne on its historic flight 15P, reaching the edge of space. This made him the first commercial astronaut and the 435th person to enter space. His second significant flight, 16P, marked the first competitive flight in the Ansari X Prize competition, further solidifying his legacy in the field of private space exploration.

Melvill’s career in aviation began in earnest in 1978 when he met Burt Rutan in California. At the time, Melvill flew there to showcase a VariViggen aircraft he had built at home. Impressed by his skills, Rutan hired him on the spot. By 1982, Melvill had risen to the position of lead test pilot for Rutan, a role that allowed him to contribute to numerous innovative aircraft projects. In 1997, he and Dick Rutan, Burt’s brother, undertook an ambitious global flight known as the "Spirit of EAA Friendship World Tour." Flying two Long-Eze aircraft they had built, Melvill and Dick Rutan circumnavigated the world, completing some legs of the journey in flights lasting over 14 hours. This remarkable feat demonstrated their endurance and skill in long-distance aviation.

Melvill’s most celebrated achievement, however, came in 2004 with his flights aboard SpaceShipOne. The success of these missions earned him and the entire Scaled Composites team the $10 million Ansari X Prize, a competition designed to promote private spaceflight. His pioneering work in this area helped catalyze the modern private space race, inspiring further developments in commercial space travel. Later in his career, Melvill held the position of Vice President and General Manager at Scaled Composites, where he continued to influence the direction of aerospace innovation.

Beyond his historic spaceflights, Melvill holds an impressive array of aviation certifications, including FAA Commercial certificates for single-engine and multi-engine land aircraft, helicopters, gliders, and instruments. He also holds the distinction of being the 435th person to reach space, a milestone that underscores his significance in the annals of human spaceflight. As of 2020, he was the sole or joint holder of ten FAI aviation world records across various categories, further cementing his reputation as an aviation pioneer. Additionally, in 1999, he received the Iven C. Kincheloe Award for his high-altitude developmental flight testing of the model 281 Proteus aircraft.

Melvill’s career exemplifies the intersection of innovation, daring, and technical expertise. From his early collaborations with Burt Rutan to his historic spaceflights and record-breaking achievements, he has played a crucial role in advancing both aviation and private space exploration. His contributions have left an indelible mark on the industry, inspiring future generations of pilots and aerospace engineers.

title: Lucas Boyé
text:
Lucas Ariel Boyé is an Argentine professional footballer who plays as a striker for Granada in Spain's Segunda División. Born on 28 February 1996, Boyé began his career with River Plate, where he quickly progressed through the ranks. His unofficial debut for the first team came in January 2014 during a friendly match against San Lorenzo, entering the game as a substitute in a 3–1 loss. He later played in another preseason friendly against San Luis, which River Plate won 3–1, and made his official debut in the 2013–14 Copa Argentina, helping his team win 6–5 on penalties against Ferro. Boyé made his Argentine Primera División debut in August 2014 in a 1–1 draw against Gimnasia y Esgrima, and just four days later, he scored his first league goal in a 3–1 victory over San Lorenzo, assisted by Tomás Martínez.

In February 2016, Boyé signed a four-year contract with Italian club Torino, though he did not immediately join the team, with the move set to take effect in July 2016. Before fully settling in Italy, however, he was loaned out to several clubs. In January 2018, he joined Spanish side Celta on loan, followed by a season-long stint with Greek club AEK in 2018–19. During his time at AEK, he scored his first goal for the club in a 4–0 win over Aris Thessaloniki and later netted his first career brace in a 2–1 victory against Apollon Smyrnis.

Boyé then moved to England in 2019, joining Championship club Reading on a season-long loan. He scored his first goal for Reading in an EFL Cup match against Wolverhampton Wanderers, though he also missed a penalty in the resulting shootout, which Reading ultimately lost. In September 2020, Boyé joined newly promoted La Liga side Elche on loan with an option to buy. The following May, Elche exercised that option, signing him permanently. After nearly three years at Elche, he transferred to Granada in August 2023 for a reported €7 million, plus additional incentives, signing a four-year contract.

Nicknamed "El Tanque" (The Tank) or "El Toro" (The Bull), Boyé is known for his physical presence, agility, and technical ability as a center forward. He is praised for his work rate and selfless contributions to his team, drawing comparisons to former forward Abel Balbo. During his time at River Plate, he won multiple titles, including the Copa Libertadores, Copa Sudamericana, Recopa Sudamericana, Suruga Bank Championship, and Copa Euroamericana, all in 2014 and 2015.

As of May 2024, Boyé has represented Argentina at the international level, though his most recent recorded match was in March 2022. His playing style, combined with his impressive early career achievements, has established him as a notable figure in South American and European football.

title: Rosaline Elbay
text:
Rosaline Elbay is an Egyptian actress, producer, and writer known for her work in both stage and screen. Born and raised in Egypt, she attended a British school in Cairo, growing up fluent in English, Arabic, and French. As a child, she performed in a production of *The Sound of Music* at age 11 and was inspired by *The Mummy* to pursue archaeology. She studied Classics and Archaeology at Oxford University before earning a master’s in Political Science and Colonial History. Later, she trained at the Actors Studio in New York City with Elizabeth Kemp and completed an MFA in Acting at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art (LAMDA).

Elbay began her career in UK theater, specializing in Shakespeare before transitioning to film. In 2018, she made her Egyptian film debut in *Diamond Dust*, an adaptation of Ahmed Mourad’s novel, and starred in *Fork & Knife*, which premiered at the El Gouna Film Festival. That same year, she appeared in the music video for “Fakra” by Massar Egbari, a band from the 2011 Egyptian Revolution. The Cairo International Film Festival named her its first face for young filmmakers, a role she repeated in 2019.

Her television career took off in 2019 when she starred as Amani in *Ramy*, a Golden Globe and Peabody Award-winning series. She also gained critical acclaim for her role as Sara in *Qabeel*, earning two Al-Wafd Critics’ Choice Awards for Best Supporting Actress and Best New Face. That year, she co-hosted the El Gouna Film Festival and had her screenplay, *Garlic*, selected for the festival’s TV Development Workshop.

In 2020, Elbay left the MBC Masr series *Forgetfulness* due to health concerns during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2021, she joined the Netflix series *Kaleidoscope* as Judy Goodwin, the crew’s demolitions specialist, which debuted in 2023 and became Netflix’s most-watched show. Off-Broadway, she played Diana, Princess of Wales in *Dodi & Diana* alongside Peter Mark Kendall. In 2023, she appeared in *Let Liv* (premiering at Tribeca), *Jagged Mind* (Hulu), and voiced a character in *Seventh-Year Itch*.

In 2024, Elbay joined the second season of *The Diplomat* as Nora Koriem, Chief of Staff to Vice President Grace Penn. She also starred in *Do No Harm* (2025) and was cast in *A Better Place* (2025) alongside Theo Rossi and Billy Campbell. Additionally, she is executive producing an unnamed animated project.

Beyond acting, Elbay is an advocate for women’s rights and refugee support. In 2019, she wore a dress made of recycled plastic by refugee women at the El Gouna Film Festival, advocating for the UNHCR. She has spoken out against gender violence, including contributing to the cancellation of a concert by a singer accused of assault. In 2020, she wrote an op-ed for *Mada Masr* about her experience with domestic violence. She also supports diversity in film and backed the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike. During the pandemic, she left *Forgetfulness* due to a preexisting heart condition.

Elbay resides in New York, where she also paints and remains involved in archaeology. In 2024, she co-produced *The Olive Tape*, a fundraising album benefiting Anera, featuring artists like Nick Hakim and Narcy. Her career continues to span film, television, and activism, making her a prominent figure in both Egyptian and international entertainment.

title: Jackson Martínez
text:
Jackson Arley Martínez Valencia, born on 3 October 1986 in Quibdó, Chocó, was a Colombian professional footballer who played as a striker. He began his career with Independiente Medellín in 2004, making his debut on his 18th birthday in a 2–2 draw against Junior. Martínez quickly established himself as a key player, scoring his first professional goal later that season and helping Medellín qualify for the playoffs. His breakthrough season came in 2008 under manager Santiago Escobar, where he scored 11 goals and helped the team finish as runners-up in the league. In 2009, he was the league's top scorer with 18 goals, leading Medellín to their fifth league title, including braces in multiple matches and a hat-trick in the Copa Libertadores. Despite early career struggles, he became a prolific scorer, attracting interest from international clubs.

In January 2010, Martínez joined Mexican club Chiapas, where he scored nine goals in his first season, finishing fourth in the top scorer's table. Injuries disrupted his subsequent seasons, but he remained a key player, including in the Copa Libertadores, where he scored crucial goals against Junior. His performances caught the attention of European clubs, and in 2012, he signed for Porto for €8.8 million. At Porto, Martínez had an immediate impact, winning the Portuguese Supercup and becoming the league's top scorer in his first season with 26 goals. He continued his prolific form in the 2013–14 and 2014–15 seasons, winning the top scorer award for three consecutive years. Notably, he scored twice in the 89th and 90th minutes against Shakhtar Donetsk in the Champions League, completing a remarkable comeback.

In July 2015, Martínez joined Atlético Madrid for €35 million, but his time in Spain was less successful. After scoring only once in his first seven games, he suffered an ankle injury that limited his playing time. In February 2016, he moved to Guangzhou Evergrande Taobao for a then-record €42 million, but a severe ankle injury in October 2016 sidelined him for nearly two years, leading to the termination of his contract in 2018.

Martínez returned to Portugal with Portimonense in 2018, signing a permanent deal in 2019. He contributed with goals, including a brace and an 88th-minute winner, and was named captain in his final match in July 2020. For Colombia, he earned 40 caps between 2009 and 2015, scoring nine goals. He represented his country at the 2011 and 2015 Copa América and the 2014 FIFA World Cup, where he scored twice against Japan. His career was ultimately cut short by injuries, but he left a lasting impact in both South American and European football.

title: Margaret Rose Vendryes
text:
Margaret Rose Vendryes (March 16, 1955 – March 29, 2022) was a prominent visual artist, curator, and art historian who spent much of her career in New York. Born in Kingston, Jamaica, she initially studied costume design before shifting her focus to fine art. She earned a Bachelor's degree from Amherst College in 1984, followed by an MA in Art History from Tulane University in 1992 and a PhD from Princeton University in 1997. At Princeton, she became the first Black woman to earn a PhD in art history, specializing in African American art history.

Vendryes held several academic and curatorial positions throughout her career. From 2000 to 2001, she was a visiting lecturer in Art & Archaeology and African American Studies at Princeton University. She later served as associate professor of Modern American and Contemporary Art at the City University of New York from 2002 to 2007. Additionally, she worked as a lecturer in African Art at Boston University in 2009 and at Wellesley College from 2011 to 2013. She also chaired the Department of Performing and Fine Arts and directed the Fine Arts Gallery at York College in New York, a role she held from 2000 until her death. At the time of her passing, she was set to become the Dean of the School of the Museum of Fine Arts at Tufts University in Boston.

Throughout her career, Vendryes was an advocate for nuanced interpretations of art, cautioning against overly race-centered approaches that might limit the understanding of an artist's work. In 2008, she authored *Barthé, A Life in Sculpture*, focusing on the work of Richmond Barthé, an African American sculptor. She also curated exhibitions, including *Richmond Barthé: The Seeker* at the Ohr-O’Keefe Museum of Art in 2010 and *Beyond the Blues* at the New Orleans Museum of Art. In 2015, she delivered the opening lecture for *The Visual Blues*, an exhibition featuring works from the Harlem Renaissance.

Her own artistic work was notable for its exploration of power, race, gender, and beauty. In 2005, she began *The African Diva Project*, a series of multi-media pieces combining oil and cold wax on canvas with embedded African masks. The series juxtaposed portraits of Black American women icons—such as Donna Summer, Aretha Franklin, Grace Jones, and Whitney Houston—with traditional African masks, which are typically worn by men. This juxtaposition allowed her to examine the intersections of identity and representation. In 2014, the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture commissioned her to create *My spirit is too ancient to understand the separation of soul & gender - Guro Ntozake* for an exhibition celebrating the 40th anniversary of Ntozake Shange’s *for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf*. The exhibition traveled to several venues, including the African American Museum in Philadelphia and the City Without Walls gallery in Newark, New Jersey.

Vendryes was a longtime board member of the Leslie Lohman Museum and contributed to numerous publications, including *The Visual Blues* (2014), *In Search of Missing Masters* (2008), and *Factory Work: Warhol, Wyeth and Basquiat* (2006). She also co-authored *The Artist Portrait Series: Images of Contemporary African American Artist* (2001) and wrote her dissertation, *Expression and Repression of Identity: Race, Religion, and Sexuality in the Art of American Sculptor Richmond Barthé* (1997).

Margaret Rose Vendryes passed away on March 29, 2022, due to respiratory failure. The Southeast Queens Artists' Alliance announced her death, and the Childs Gallery in Boston hosted a memorial exhibition in her honor from November 2022 to January 2023. Her work as an artist, curator, and scholar left a lasting impact on the fields of African American art history and contemporary visual culture.

title: Abraham Ancer
text:
Abraham Ancer is a Mexican-American professional golfer born on 27 February 1991 in McAllen, Texas, with dual American and Mexican citizenship. He was raised in both Texas and Reynosa, Mexico, and attended Sharyland High School in Mission, Texas. Ancer played college golf at Odessa College and the University of Oklahoma, where he earned a degree in General Studies in 2013. During his amateur career, he was a first-team All-American at Odessa College and finished tied for second in the Junior College National Golf Championship. At Oklahoma, he won twice in his first year, achieving the sixth-lowest scoring average in school history (72.03) and finishing second in all-time scoring average by the end of his career.

Ancer turned professional in 2013. His early professional career included a strong performance on the Web.com Tour, where he won the Nova Scotia Open in 2015 and finished 11th in the regular season money list, earning a PGA Tour card for 2016. However, his rookie season on the PGA Tour was inconsistent, and he lost his card after finishing 190th in FedEx Cup points. He returned to the Web.com Tour in 2017, securing another PGA Tour card by finishing third on the money list after recording five top-5 finishes, including three runner-up finishes.

In his 2018 PGA Tour season, Ancer had several strong finishes, including a 9th-place result at the OHL Classic at Mayakoba, an 8th-place finish at the Houston Open, and a 4th-place finish at the Quicken Loans National. His high finish at the Quicken Loans National earned him a spot in the 2018 Open Championship, his first major, though he missed the cut. He earned $1.7 million and finished 60th in the FedEx Cup that year. In 2018–19, he had top-5 finishes in the CIMB Classic and the Shriners Hospitals for Children Open, entering the world top-100 for the first time. He then won the 2018 Australian Open by five strokes, securing a spot in the 2019 Open Championship. In 2019, he finished second in the Northern Trust and tied for 21st at the Tour Championship, earning $478,000 in FedEx Cup bonus money.

Ancer was selected for the 2019 Presidents Cup International team, where he went 3–1–1, with his only loss coming in a highly anticipated singles match against Tiger Woods. In 2020, he finished runner-up at the RBC Heritage, leading the field in driving accuracy (82.1%) and greens in regulation (90.3%). He also competed in the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, finishing tied for 14th. His breakthrough PGA Tour win came in August 2021 at the WGC-FedEx St. Jude Invitational, where he defeated Hideki Matsuyama and Sam Burns in a sudden-death playoff. This made him the fourth Mexican player to win on the PGA Tour and the first to win on the European Tour.

In June 2022, Ancer joined LIV Golf, leading to his suspension from the PGA Tour. He won his first LIV Golf individual event at the 2024 LIV Golf Hong Kong and also claimed a team victory in Bangkok. Additionally, in February 2023, he won the PIF Saudi International on the Asian Tour, securing a wire-to-wire victory. Ancer has six professional wins to his name, including one on the PGA Tour, one on the European Tour, one on the Asian Tour, one on the PGA Tour of Australasia, one on the Web.com Tour, and one on LIV Golf. His major championship record includes two missed cuts before 2019 and a best finish of tied for 52nd at the 2021 PGA Championship. He has represented Mexico in the 2018 World Cup and the International team in the 2019 Presidents Cup.

title: Pablo Zabaleta
text:
Pablo Javier Zabaleta Girod, born on 16 January 1985 in Buenos Aires, is a former Argentine professional footballer who primarily played as a right-back but was also capable of operating on both flanks. Known for his tenacious and determined playing style, Zabaleta earned a reputation as a reliable and passionate defender throughout his career. He began his football journey at San Lorenzo, joining their youth academy at the age of 12 after being signed from local club Obras Sanitarias. Initially playing as a defensive midfielder, he later transitioned to a right-sided position.

In 2005, Zabaleta moved to Spanish club Espanyol for a fee of €3 million, having previously captained Argentina’s under-20 team to victory in the 2005 FIFA World Youth Championship. During his time at Espanyol, he played a crucial role in their 2005–06 Copa del Rey triumph, featuring in the final where they defeated Real Zaragoza 4–1. He also represented the club in the 2006–07 UEFA Cup final, though Espanyol ultimately lost to Sevilla on penalties.

In 2008, Zabaleta joined Manchester City, rejecting offers from Juventus to pursue his ambition of playing in the Premier League. He quickly became a fan favorite and a key player, making 333 appearances over nine seasons. During his tenure at Manchester City, Zabaleta contributed to the club’s success in winning the FA Cup (2011), two Premier League titles (2012 and 2014), two League Cups (2014 and 2016), and the Community Shield (2012). His leadership and work ethic earned him the admiration of the club’s supporters, and he was often named as a stand-in captain. In 2013, he was awarded Manchester City’s Player of the Year after a standout season, and the following year, he helped the team complete a full set of major English honors by winning the League Cup. Despite a controversial red card in the 2013 FA Cup final, Zabaleta remained a consistent performer and was praised by manager Pep Guardiola as a "legend" upon his departure in 2017.

After leaving Manchester City, Zabaleta signed for West Ham United in 2017, where he spent three seasons, making 80 appearances and scoring one goal. He became the first Argentine and only the third South American to reach 300 Premier League appearances in 2020. His international career was equally distinguished, having represented Argentina at various youth levels, including winning the 2005 U-20 World Cup and the 2008 Olympic gold medal. He also played in the 2014 World Cup, finishing as runners-up, and the 2015 Copa América, where he provided an assist in a crucial group-stage victory over Uruguay.

Following his retirement in 2020, Zabaleta transitioned into coaching and media roles. He briefly worked as a pundit for the BBC during the 2018 and 2022 World Cups and later joined ESPN for their La Liga coverage. In January 2023, he was appointed as an assistant coach for the Albania national team under head coach Sylvinho. Zabaleta, of Spanish Basque descent, is also known for his personal dedication to his family, including a tattoo bearing his mother’s name on his chest.

Throughout his career, Zabaleta accumulated numerous accolades, including being named to the PFA Team of the Year in 2012–13, earning Manchester City’s Player of the Month awards on multiple occasions, and being selected for the FIFPro World XI fifth team in 2013 and 2014. His contributions to both club and country solidified his legacy as one of the most respected and hardworking defenders of his generation.

title: Kaoru Kuroki
text:
Kaoru Kuroki, born on 21 January 1965, was a Japanese former adult video (AV) performer and multimedia personality known for her outspoken views on sex and society, which earned her comparisons to figures like Cicciolina, Dr. Ruth, and Linda Lovelace. Born into a conservative, middle-class family as the daughter of an engineer, Kuroki demonstrated artistic talent from a young age. She left public school at 15 to attend art college and later studied Renaissance art history at Yokohama National University. While still a student, she began appearing in adult videos, initially viewing them as a form of performance art. However, she soon recognized the genre’s raw, primitive nature, comparing it to satisfying a basic appetite rather than a refined artistic pursuit. She admired directors like Nagisa Oshima and Bernardo Bertolucci but distinguished AVs from traditional film, emphasizing their documentary-like quality and immediate gratification.

Kuroki’s AV debut came in October 1986 with *SM Poi no suki*, directed by Toru Muranishi, a pioneer of documentary-style Japanese AVs. Her videos often featured improvised monologues on topics like sexual liberation, followed by S&M-themed performances. Her approach was intentionally confrontational, blending submission with self-assertion, which some viewers found unsettling. She argued that her work challenged societal norms, forcing men to confront their own repressed desires. Her collaboration with Muranishi continued when he founded Diamond Visual, and her videos typically included segments where she addressed the camera before transitioning into more explicit content.

Kuroki’s mainstream breakthrough occurred in 1988 when she stopped shaving her underarm hair as a protest against Japan’s censorship of pubic hair in media. This act drew media attention, and she became a sought-after guest on talk shows, where she discussed sex and feminism with unapologetic frankness. Her appeal extended beyond AV audiences to women, who appreciated her feminist perspectives. She also appeared in the TV drama *Shigotonin, Kyōto e Iku Yamiuchinin no Nazo no Shuryō* and collaborated with fellow AV star Kimiko Matsuzaka in instructional videos and films. In 1988, she met Cicciolina, whom she regarded as a mentor, though they differed on S&M, which Kuroki saw as a form of empowerment rather than submission.

Kuroki retired from public life in 1994, later alleging physical abuse by Muranishi before her departure. In 2002 and 2004, magazines published unauthorized stories about her private life, leading to a successful lawsuit against Shogakukan for invasion of privacy, with a judgment awarding her 1.7 million yen. At her peak, her AVs sold an average of 17,000 copies each, a remarkable figure in the industry. Critics noted that she redefined the AV actress’s image, presenting herself as an informed choice rather than a desperate one. Her outspokenness and mainstream crossover helped legitimize the AV industry in Japan, and she is often cited as the first high-profile AV actress. Her life was later dramatized in Netflix’s *The Naked Director*, where she was portrayed by Misato Morita.

title: G. Venugopal
text:
G. Venugopal, born Gopinathan Nair Venugopal on 10 December 1960, is a well-known Indian playback singer, primarily recognized for his contributions to Malayalam cinema. His singing career began in 1984 with the film *Odaruthammava Aalariyam*, and since then, he has lent his voice to over 400 films, in addition to recording more than 500 private albums. Born in Thattathumala, near Kilimanoor, Venugopal comes from a musically inclined family. His father, Gopinathan Nair, hails from Thattathumala, while his mother, Sarojini, was the head of the music department at the Government College for Women in Thiruvananthapuram. His maternal aunts, K. Sharadamani and K. Radhamani, were popularly known as the Parur sisters, adding to the family's musical legacy. His cousins, Sujatha Mohan and Radhika Thilak, are also singers, and his niece, Shweta Mohan, follows the family tradition in the music industry.

Venugopal married Reshmi on 8 April 1990, and the couple has two children, Arvind and Anupallavi. Arvind has also pursued a career in playback singing, continuing the family’s musical heritage. Apart from his professional achievements, Venugopal has been recognized for his cultural contributions, including receiving the Janmashtami Award in 2022 from Balagokulam for his contributions to the art and culture of Kerala. Notably, he was the youngest recipient of this prestigious honor.

Venugopal has been a prominent figure in Malayalam music, earning several awards for his outstanding performances. In 1988, he received the Kerala State Film Award for Best Male Playback Singer for the song *Unarumee Gaanam* from the film *Moonnam Pakkam*. He won the same award in 1990 for *Thaane Poovitta Moham* from *Sasneham* and again in 2004 for *Aadadi Aadaadadi* from *Ullam*. Additionally, the Kerala Film Critics Association recognized his talent with awards in 1987 for *Onnam Ragam Paadi* from *Thoovanathumbikal* and in 1989 for *Mainaka Ponmudiyil* from *Mazhavilkavadi*. His versatility and skill were further acknowledged at the Asianet Film Awards in 2006, where he won Best Playback Singer (Male) for the song *Kainiraye* from *Baba Kalyani*.

Beyond his work in films, Venugopal has also ventured into television, serving as a judge on the show *Shyamambaram*, which aired on Zee Keralam in 2023. His influence extends beyond commercial music, as he has also contributed to devotional albums, as evidenced by his latest Devi devotional releases. His career reflects a deep commitment to Malayalam music, earning him respect as one of the industry’s most accomplished playback singers. With a career spanning several decades, Venugopal’s work continues to be celebrated for its emotional depth and technical brilliance.

title: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva
text:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known mononymously as Lula, is a Brazilian politician, trade unionist, and former metalworker who has served as the 39th president of Brazil since 2023. Born on 27 October 1945 in Pernambuco, Lula had a difficult childhood, leaving school after second grade to work as a street vendor, shoeshiner, and later a metalworker. Inspired by his brother, a Communist Party member, he became a trade unionist, rising to lead the Steel Workers' Union in the 1970s. During Brazil’s military dictatorship, he organized workers' strikes, leading to his brief imprisonment in 1980. That same year, he co-founded the left-wing Workers' Party (PT).

Lula first ran for president in 1989 but lost to Fernando Collor de Mello. He ran again in 1994 and 1998, both times losing to Fernando Henrique Cardoso. In 2002, he moderated his platform, abandoning his earlier stance on debt audits, and won the presidency in a runoff. His first two terms (2003–2011) saw economic growth, reduced inflation, and a significant reduction in poverty, thanks in part to social programs like *Bolsa Família*. Despite his popularity—leaving office with an 80% approval rating—his presidency was also marked by the *Mensalão* corruption scandal, in which PT officials bribed legislators for votes.

After leaving office, Lula remained politically active, supporting his successor, Dilma Rousseff, until her impeachment in 2016. In 2017, he was convicted of money laundering and corruption in the *Operation Car Wash* investigation, serving 580 days in prison. His 2018 presidential bid was barred under Brazil’s *Ficha Limpa* law, and his PT candidate, Fernando Haddad, lost to Jair Bolsonaro. In 2021, Brazil’s Supreme Court annulled his convictions, citing bias, allowing him to run again in 2022. He defeated Bolsonaro in a runoff, becoming the first Brazilian to defeat an incumbent president and the oldest person to assume the presidency at 77.

Lula’s personal life has included three marriages, two of which ended in widowhood. He has five children, including one from a relationship outside marriage. A devout Catholic, he added "Lula" to his legal name in 1982. His political career has been defined by his rise from poverty to the presidency, his role in Brazil’s redemocratization, and his advocacy for workers' rights and social welfare. However, his legacy is also tarnished by corruption scandals, legal battles, and polarizing political divisions.

title: Lionel Messi
text:
Lionel Messi, born on 24 June 1987 in Rosario, Argentina, is widely regarded as one of the greatest footballers in history. A prolific forward and captain of both Inter Miami in Major League Soccer and the Argentina national team, Messi has set numerous records, including eight Ballon d’Or awards, six European Golden Shoes, and 45 career trophies. His achievements include the most goals in a calendar year (91), the most goals for a single club (672 for Barcelona), and the most goal contributions in both the FIFA World Cup (21) and Copa América (32). With over 870 career goals and 380 assists, Messi’s impact on the game is unparalleled.

Messi’s professional career with Barcelona began at age 17 when he made his competitive debut in October 2004. Under manager Frank Rijkaard, he gradually became a key player, winning his first La Liga title in 2005. His breakthrough season came in 2008–09 under Pep Guardiola, when he helped Barcelona achieve the first treble in Spanish football (winning La Liga, Copa del Rey, and the Champions League). This success earned him his first Ballon d’Or in 2009. Messi continued to dominate, setting the European record for most goals in a season in 2011–12 and becoming Barcelona’s all-time top scorer. In 2014–15, he led Barcelona to a second treble, securing his fifth Ballon d’Or. As captain from 2018, he won a record sixth Ballon d’Or in 2019. During his 21-year tenure at Barcelona, Messi won 34 trophies, including 10 La Liga titles and 4 Champions League victories.

In 2021, financial difficulties at Barcelona led Messi to join Paris Saint-Germain (PSG), where he won back-to-back Ligue 1 titles before moving to Inter Miami in 2023.

For Argentina, Messi is the national team’s all-time leading goalscorer and most-capped player. After winning a gold medal at the 2008 Olympics, he became captain in 2011, leading Argentina to three consecutive finals in the 2014 World Cup, 2015 Copa América, and 2016 Copa América Centenario—all of which they lost. After briefly retiring in 2016, he returned to help Argentina qualify for the 2018 World Cup. In 2021, he ended Argentina’s 28-year trophy drought by winning the Copa América, earning his seventh Ballon d’Or. The following year, he led Argentina to victory in the 2022 World Cup, their first in 36 years, and won his eighth Ballon d’Or in 2023. He added another major title with the 2024 Copa América.

Beyond football, Messi has been a global icon. Endorsed by Adidas since 2006, he was the highest-paid footballer for several years and the world’s highest-paid athlete in 2019 and 2022. Named to Time’s 100 Most Influential People in 2011, 2012, and 2023, he also won the Laureus World Sportsman of the Year in 2020 and 2023. In 2020, he became the second team-sport athlete to surpass $1 billion in career earnings. After joining Inter Miami, he was named Time’s Athlete of the Year in 2023 and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2025.

Messi’s early life was marked by a growth hormone deficiency, which threatened his career until Barcelona signed him in 2001. His youth career at Newell’s Old Boys and Barcelona’s La Masia academy showcased his extraordinary talent, setting the stage for his legendary career. His influence extends beyond statistics, cementing his legacy as one of football’s greatest players.

title: Terrence Romeo
text:
Terrence Bill Vitanzos Romeo, born on March 16, 1992, is a Filipino professional basketball player who concluded his PBA career with the Terrafirma Dyip. Primarily playing as a point guard or shooting guard, Romeo began his collegiate career at Far Eastern University (FEU) after being scouted from Letran High School. As a junior, he set the UAAP Juniors record for most points in a game with 83, surpassing Paolo Mendoza’s previous mark. His performance earned him the 2009 UAAP Juniors Most Valuable Player (MVP) award, averaging 37.1 points, 4.1 assists, and 4.0 steals per game.

His transition to the FEU seniors team was initially challenging, but he grew into a key player, earning UAAP Rookie of the Year in 2010. Over the next three seasons, he improved steadily, becoming the team’s primary scorer. In his senior year (UAAP Season 76), he led the league in points (22.2 per game) and steals while finishing third in assists, securing the UAAP MVP award. This made him only the third guard in UAAP history to win the honor, following RR Garcia and Johnny Abarrientos. During college, he also played for the Big Chill Super Chargers in the PBA D-League before declaring for the 2013 PBA draft, where he was selected fifth overall by GlobalPort.

Romeo’s PBA career started strongly, scoring 34 points in his second game and impressing fans with his scoring ability. As a rookie, he was compared to veteran Mark Caguioa, whom he admired. His sophomore season saw him lose weight to improve his agility, and he led the league in local scoring with 21.4 points per game. He also won the 2015 PBA All-Star Game MVP and Three-Point Shootout championship. By his third season, he and Stanley Pringle formed the "Slash Brothers" duo, leading GlobalPort to its first-ever PBA Semifinals. That year, he was named to the PBA Mythical First Team after averaging 24.1 points per game.

In 2018, Romeo was traded to TNT KaTropa due to a disagreement with his coach. Later that year, he was traded again, this time to the San Miguel Beermen, where he played until 2024. His time with San Miguel included a standout performance in the 2019 Commissioner’s Cup Finals, where he scored 29 points in a double-overtime victory. He re-signed with the team in 2023 but was traded to Terrafirma in 2024, marking what he described as one of the saddest moments of his career.

Internationally, Romeo represented the Philippines in 3x3 basketball, winning the 2014 FIBA 3x3 World Tour Manila Masters with Manila West. He was recognized as the top 3x3 player outside Europe, the Americas, and Qatar. He also competed in the 2015 FIBA 3x3 World Tour and was part of Gilas Pilipinas 3.0, participating in tournaments like the William Jones Cup and the FIBA Asia Championship.

In 2025, Romeo transitioned to coaching, making his debut as head coach of the PSP Gymers in the Women’s Maharlika Pilipinas Basketball League (WMPBL), working alongside assistants Vic Manuel, CJ Perez, and Arvin Tolentino. Throughout his career, Romeo was known for his explosive scoring, flashy dribbling, and versatility as both a guard and leader.

title: Henry VII of England
text:
Henry VII, born on 28 January 1457 at Pembroke Castle, was the first monarch of the House of Tudor, ruling England and Ireland from 1485 until his death in 1509. His claim to the throne was bolstered by his maternal lineage: his mother, Margaret Beaufort, was a great-granddaughter of John of Gaunt, a key figure in the Lancastrian branch of the Plantagenet dynasty. His father, Edmund Tudor, died before his birth, leaving Henry to be raised by his uncle Jasper Tudor and later by William Herbert, a Yorkist supporter. The Wars of the Roses between the Lancastrians and Yorkists shaped Henry’s early life, forcing him into exile in Brittany for 14 years after the Yorkist victory in 1471.

Henry’s path to the throne was secured through a combination of military triumph and strategic marriage. In 1483, he pledged to marry Elizabeth of York, the eldest daughter of Edward IV, uniting the warring Lancastrian and Yorkist factions. With French and Scottish support, he invaded England in 1485 and defeated Richard III at the Battle of Bosworth Field, becoming the last English king to seize the crown by force. To legitimize his rule, he retroactively declared himself king from the day before Bosworth, ensuring that Richard’s supporters were deemed traitors. His marriage to Elizabeth of York, formalized in 1486, symbolized the end of the Wars of the Roses, though Henry remained wary of potential rivals.

Henry’s reign was marked by efforts to stabilize the monarchy and economy after decades of civil war. He introduced new taxes, including the controversial "Morton’s Fork," a method devised by his chancellor, Archbishop John Morton, to ensure nobles paid higher taxes regardless of their spending habits. He also confiscated lands through resumptions and tightly controlled expenditure, rebuilding the royal treasury. His financial policies, while effective, were criticized for their harshness, and abuses in tax collection were revealed after his death.

Despite his fiscal prudence, Henry faced multiple rebellions. The most notable were the 1487 rebellion of Lambert Simnel, who claimed to be Edward, Earl of Warwick, and the 1490s schemes of Perkin Warbeck, who pretended to be Richard of Shrewsbury, one of the Princes in the Tower. Henry crushed these uprisings, often showing surprising clemency to defeated rebels, though he executed the Earl of Warwick and later William Stanley, his own chamberlain, when they were suspected of treason.

Henry’s Welsh ancestry played a role in his rise, as he emphasized his ties to the legendary Cadwaladr and used the red dragon as a symbol. His careful management of the nobility, including laws against livery and maintenance, weakened their power and strengthened the crown. He also focused on diplomacy, avoiding costly wars and securing peace with France and Scotland.

Henry VII died on 21 April 1509, leaving a stable monarchy and a prosperous treasury. His son, Henry VIII, succeeded him, inheriting a kingdom that had recovered from the turbulence of the Wars of the Roses. Henry VII’s legacy was one of restoration, consolidation, and economic recovery, though his methods sometimes crossed into tyranny, as later revealed by his successors.

title: Ian Khama
text:
Ian Khama, born on 27 February 1953 in Chertsey, Surrey, is a prominent Motswana politician and former military officer who served as President of Botswana from 2008 to 2018. He is the son of Sir Seretse Khama, Botswana's first president and a key independence leader, and comes from a long line of Bamangwato chiefs, including his great-grandfather, Khama III, a revered king. His name, Seretse Khama Ian Khama, reflects his lineage, with "Seretse" symbolizing reconciliation and unity.

Educated at Waterford Kamhlaba in Swaziland and the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, Khama is also a qualified pilot. He joined the Botswana Defence Force (BDF) in 1977 and rose to become its commander in 1989, retiring in 1998. During his military career, he received several honors, including the Founder Officer Medal and the Distinguished Service Medal.

Khama entered politics in 1998 when he was appointed Vice-President under President Festus Mogae, a position he held until 2008. He was elected Chairman of the Botswana Democratic Party (BDP) in 2003, a role that positioned him to succeed Mogae. In 2008, he became acting president and was later elected to full terms in 2009 and 2014.

As president, Khama implemented policies aimed at addressing alcohol abuse, including a proposed 70% alcohol levy, later reduced to 30% after industry consultations. He also established the Directorate of Intelligence and Security Services (DISS), which faced criticism for its potential misuse. His administration banned elephant hunting in 2014, a move aligned with his conservationist stance.

Khama was a vocal critic of authoritarian regimes, including Zimbabwe’s Robert Mugabe and North Korea’s leadership, which he condemned for human rights abuses. He advocated for economic diversification, particularly in agriculture and tourism, to reduce Botswana’s reliance on diamonds.

However, his presidency was not without controversy. He was accused of authoritarian tendencies, particularly after pardoning soldiers involved in the 2009 killing of John Kalifatis, which some believed implicated him in the incident. His successor, Mokgweetsi Masisi, later clashed with Khama, leading to his departure from the BDP and the formation of the Botswana Patriotic Front (BPF).

After retiring, Khama joined Conservation International and went into self-imposed exile in 2021, claiming a plot to poison him. In 2022, he was charged with illegal firearm possession, allegations he maintained were politically motivated. The charges were later dropped in 2024, and he resumed his traditional role as Kgosikgolo (paramount chief) of the Bamangwato people, taking the title Khama IV. In January 2025, he became a member of the Ntlo ya Dikgosi, an advisory body for Parliament.

Khama’s legacy remains a mix of progressive policies and contentious decisions, reflecting his complex role in Botswana’s political and military history.

title: Juan Nepomucino Goetz
text:
Juan Nepomucino Goetz, also known by his German name Johannes Nepomuk Goetz, was an Austrian Catholic priest who became involved in significant controversies after arriving in Cuba. His career in the island began notably during a tumultuous period when Toussaint-Louverture expelled the British from the region. Goetz responded to this event by ringing the church bells and performing celebrations. However, he soon relocated to Santiago de Cuba, where his proficiency in multiple languages earned him the role of the "foreigners' priest," catering to the needs of non-Spanish-speaking communities.

Goetz's most notable conflict arose in Havana, where he became entangled in a dispute over the position of choirmaster at the cathedral. The vacancy occurred after the death of the previous choirmaster, Lazo de la Vega. Four candidates competed for the role: José Francisco Rensoli, a 28-year-old first violinist; Luis Lazo, a singer; Cayetano Solis, a maestro; and Cayetano Pagueras, a Catalan religious composer who also performed as the first contralto. Each candidate was prepared to undergo a competitive examination to determine their suitability for the position. Pagueras, in particular, claimed expertise in four key musical disciplines: plainsong, organ playing, counterpoint, and composition.

The situation took an unexpected turn when a letter from Goetz arrived on July 29, 1803, in which he offered his services for the choirmaster position. After evaluating the candidates, Goetz submitted a detailed report to the Havana town council, offering sharp assessments of the choir's members. His critique was particularly scathing. He described Pagueras as a "second contralto with a terrible voice, no expressiveness, and nearly blind, though a good composer who couldn’t sing his own works." Regarding Luis Lazo, he stated that he was a "third contralto who knew nothing of music and never would, having fraudulently entered the chapel and being totally inept and superfluous." He also criticized Don Juan Alcayado, a third tenor, for having a "terrible voice, rarely attending rehearsals, and when present, constantly speaking and disturbing others," deeming him a "totally useless human being" and recommending the abolition of the third tenor position as redundant.

Goetz’s evaluation extended beyond individual critiques. As a trained musician, he proposed a restructuring of the choir and its accompanying orchestra. His reforms included reducing the number of positions, promoting younger singers, and requiring those demoted in rank to retake both theoretical and practical examinations. By 1806, under his revised system, the choir and orchestra consisted of a choirmaster, four sopranos, two contraltos, two tenors, one baritone, two clarinets, two bassoons, two horns, four violins, a bass viol, and a bass. His reforms aimed to streamline the ensemble, prioritizing skill and dedication over seniority or nepotism.

Goetz’s interventions in Havana were marked by both controversy and reform, reflecting his uncompromising standards for musical and liturgical excellence. His sharp critiques and systematic restructuring of the cathedral choir left a lasting impact on the institution, even as they stirred debate among its members. His career in Cuba highlights his dual role as a religious figure and a rigorous evaluator of artistic talent, shaping the cultural and musical landscape of Havana during his tenure.

title: Sam Michael
text:
Sam Michael is an Australian motorsport engineer and designer who has had a notable career in Formula One and Supercars. Born on 29 April 1971 in Western Australia, he grew up in Canberra. His early interest in motorsport led him to work briefly on Neal Bates' Toyota Celica GT-Four rally car before pursuing a degree in mechanical engineering at the University of New South Wales. His thesis focused on data acquisition systems for racing cars, and during his studies, he worked part-time for Greg Siddle on Mark Larkham's Formula Holden team, allowing him to balance his academic and professional commitments.

Michael’s professional career in motorsport began in 1993 when he was recruited by the UK-based Lotus team. After Lotus went bankrupt in 1994, he joined Jordan Grand Prix, where he played a key role in establishing the team’s research and development department. His work included developing data acquisition systems and installing a seven-post rig for suspension simulation and designing an active differential. In 1997, he became part of Jordan’s test team, and by 1998, he was promoted to race engineer for Ralf Schumacher. When Schumacher left for Williams in 1999, Michael took over as race engineer for Heinz-Harald Frentzen, a partnership that proved successful, culminating in victories at the 1999 French and Italian Grands Prix.

In 2001, Sir Frank Williams recruited Michael to Williams as Senior Operations Engineer, where he managed the team’s engineers during races and tests. His contributions were significant, and in May 2004, he was promoted to Technical Director, a role that allowed him to oversee the team’s engineering strategy. In 2011, Michael moved to McLaren as Sporting Director, where he became part of the senior technical management team. Despite initial challenges, particularly with pitstop failures, he was defended by Martin Whitmarsh, and improvements followed.

Michael returned to Australia in 2014 after resigning from McLaren. In 2016, he joined the Australian Institute for Motor Sport Safety’s board, focusing on motorsport safety. He later took on a part-time mentoring role with Triple Eight Race Engineering, a Supercar team, after Ludo Lacroix’s departure. His involvement in safety expanded further when he became an advisor to the FIA’s Research Working Group, which reviews new safety devices, and he later joined the FIA Single Seater Commission. In 2022, he served as President of the FIA Safety Commission, demonstrating his ongoing commitment to motorsport safety.

Beyond his motorsport career, Michael is the CEO of Ox Mountain, a machine learning company he co-founded in 2015. The company specializes in optimizing maintenance in industries such as mining and rail. Additionally, he serves as a part-time lecturer at the University of Western Australia, sharing his expertise with the next generation of engineers. His career reflects a blend of high-level technical leadership in racing, a dedication to safety advancements, and entrepreneurial ventures in technology.

title: Virginia Christine
text:
Virginia Christine, born Virginia Christine Ricketts on March 5, 1920, in Stanton, Iowa, was a versatile American actress with a career spanning stage, radio, film, television, and voice acting. She began her professional life with aspirations of becoming a concert pianist but later turned to acting, starting her career in radio while attending UCLA. She was of Swedish descent and had changed her last name to "Kraft" after her mother's remarriage before settling on "Christine" as her professional name.

Christine began working in radio during her college years, appearing in multiple episodes of the radio version of *Gunsmoke*. She trained with actor and director Fritz Feld, whom she married in 1940. Her stage debut came in 1942 in the Los Angeles production of *Hedda Gabler*, which led to a film contract with Warner Bros. Her first film, *Edge of Darkness* (1943), featured her as a Norwegian peasant girl, but she was soon dropped by the studio and signed with Universal Pictures in 1944. That year, she appeared in *The Mummy's Curse* and *The Wife of Monte Cristo*, the latter alongside her husband. She also had a supporting role in the 1946 serial *The Scarlet Horseman* and the film noir classic *The Killers* (1946), where she initially auditioned for the lead role but was ultimately cast as Lilly Harmon Lubinsky.

Throughout the 1950s, Christine worked frequently with producer Stanley Kramer, appearing in *Cyrano de Bergerac* (1950), *High Noon* (1952), *Not as a Stranger* (1955), and *Judgment at Nuremberg* (1961). She also appeared in the 1956 science-fiction horror film *Invasion of the Body Snatchers*. In 1967, she played a memorable role as the bigoted co-worker of Katharine Hepburn’s character in *Guess Who’s Coming to Dinner*.

On television, Christine was a prolific guest star, appearing in series such as *The Abbott and Costello Show*, *Dragnet*, *Alfred Hitchcock Presents*, *Gunsmoke*, *Perry Mason*, *The Twilight Zone*, *Rawhide*, *Bonanza*, and *The Fugitive*. Her most famous role, however, was as "Mrs. Olson" in Folgers Coffee commercials, a character she portrayed from 1965 to 1986. The commercials became iconic, and the character was widely parodied in comedy shows. In 1971, her hometown of Stanton, Iowa, honored her by transforming its water tower into a giant Swedish coffee pot.

Christine continued acting until 1979, her final role being in the animated series *Scooby-Doo and Scrappy-Doo*, where she provided additional voices. After retiring, she volunteered at Planned Parenthood and served as a judge at the American College Theatre Festival. She was also appointed honorary mayor of Brentwood, Los Angeles, where she lived with her husband, Fritz Feld, until his death in 1993.

Christine passed away on July 24, 1996, at her Brentwood home due to cardiovascular disease. She was interred at the Jewish Mount Sinai Memorial Park Cemetery in Los Angeles. Her legacy endures through her extensive film and television work, as well as her enduring portrayal of Mrs. Olson in Folgers commercials.

title: A. K. Ramanujan
text:
A. K. Ramanujan (1929–1993) was a distinguished Indian poet, scholar, and linguist, renowned for his contributions to Indian literature, folklore, and cultural studies. Born on 16 March 1929 in Mysore (now in Karnataka), he came from a family with a strong academic background—his father was an astrologer and mathematics professor with a deep interest in languages, including English, Kannada, and Sanskrit. Ramanujan attended Marimallappa's High School and Maharaja College in Mysore, initially studying science before switching to English literature at his father’s urging. He later became a Fellow at Deccan College, Pune, and a Fulbright Scholar at Indiana University, where he earned his PhD in Linguistics.

Ramanujan's career spanned multiple disciplines and institutions. He began as a lecturer in English at universities in Quilon and Belgaum, later teaching at the Maharaja Sayajirao University in Baroda for eight years. In 1962, he joined the University of Chicago as an assistant professor, where he remained for the rest of his career, influencing the South Asian Studies program and teaching across departments such as Linguistics and the Committee on Social Thought. He also held visiting positions at Harvard, Wisconsin, Michigan, and Berkeley. In 1983, he was awarded the prestigious MacArthur Fellowship and became the William E. Colvin Professor at Chicago. His work explored the intersections of Indian and Western cultures, reflected in his poetry and essays, such as "Conventions of Despair."

Ramanujan’s scholarly contributions were vast. He wrote extensively on Indian folklore, literature, and philosophy, emphasizing the diversity of oral and written traditions. His essay "Is There an Indian Way of Thinking?" (1990) analyzed Indian cultural and cognitive frameworks, while his work in folklore, such as *Folktales from India* (1991), highlighted the intertextuality of Indian storytelling. *Speaking Śiva* (1973), a study of Vīraśaiva devotion in Karnataka, became a cornerstone of South Asian religious studies.
