His translations from Old Tamil, Kannada, and Telugu, including *The Interior Landscape* (1967) and *Poems of Love and War* (1985), introduced classical and regional texts to global audiences.

Ramanujan’s poetry was celebrated for its originality and sophistication, earning him the Sahitya Akademi Award posthumously in 1999 for *The Collected Poems*. His literary output included collections like *Relations* (1971) and *Second Sight* (1986), as well as translations of Kannada works, such as U.R. Ananthamurthy’s *Samskara*.

Controversy arose over his 1991 essay "Three Hundred Ramayanas," which discussed alternative versions of the Ramayana, including those depicting Rama and Sita as siblings. In 2006, its inclusion in Delhi University’s curriculum sparked protests from Hindu groups, who deemed it offensive. Though a committee recommended retaining the essay, the university removed it in 2011, drawing criticism from academics who saw the decision as censorial.

Ramanujan died in Chicago on 13 July 1993 due to an adverse reaction to anesthesia before surgery. His legacy endures in his interdisciplinary scholarship, literary translations, and poetry, which bridged Indian and global traditions.

title: Carlos Ghosn
text:
Carlos Ghosn, born on March 9, 1954, in Porto Velho, Brazil, is a businessman and former automotive executive with a distinguished career in the global automotive industry. His grandfather, Bichara Ghosn, emigrated from Lebanon to Brazil, where he became an entrepreneur. Carlos’s father, Jorge Ghosn, was a diamond trader and airline industry worker, who was convicted of murder in Lebanon and later fled to Brazil. Carlos moved to Lebanon with his family at the age of six, where he completed his secondary education at the Jesuit school Collège Notre-Dame de Jamhour. He later studied in Paris, graduating as an engineer from the École Polytechnique in 1974 and the École des Mines de Paris in 1978.

Ghosn began his career in 1978 at Michelin, Europe’s largest tire manufacturer, where he spent 18 years in various leadership roles. In 1985, at age 30, he was appointed chief operating officer (COO) of Michelin’s South American operations, turning around an unprofitable division in Brazil. By 1990, he became CEO of Michelin North America, overseeing the restructuring of the company after its acquisition of Uniroyal Goodrich.

In 1996, Ghosn joined Renault as executive vice president, leading its restructuring and contributing to the company’s profitability. In 1999, Renault acquired a 36.8% stake in Nissan, and Ghosn moved to Japan to oversee its recovery. As CEO, he implemented the "Nissan Revival Plan," which included cutting jobs, closing plants, and reducing debt. Despite skepticism, Nissan returned to profitability within a year, and by 2002, it was one of the most profitable automakers. In 2005, Ghosn also became CEO of Renault, making him the first person to simultaneously lead two Fortune Global 500 companies.

Ghosn expanded the Renault-Nissan Alliance, leading efforts to develop electric vehicles, including the Nissan Leaf, which became the world’s best-selling electric car. In 2016, he became chairman of Mitsubishi Motors after Nissan acquired a controlling stake, forming the world’s fourth-largest automotive group.

In 2018, Ghosn was arrested in Japan on allegations of financial misconduct, including underreporting his salary and misusing company funds. He denied wrongdoing, claiming the payments were legal and approved by auditors. Detained for 108 days under harsh conditions, he criticized Japan’s pre-trial system. Released on bail in March 2019 under strict surveillance, he was rearrested shortly after. In a dramatic escape in December 2019, Ghosn fled Japan, hiding in a musical instrument case and traveling to Lebanon, where he remains.

Ghosn’s career was marked by his ability to turn around struggling companies, his emphasis on cross-cultural management, and his leadership in the global automotive industry. However, his legal troubles and escape have overshadowed his legacy.

title: Ramkumar Mukhopadhyay
text:
Ramkumar Mukhopadhyay, born on 8 March 1956 in Calcutta, is a prominent Bengali writer known for his contributions to literature, including novels, short stories, and works for both adults and children. His father was Ramangamohan Mukhopadhyay, and his mother was Kanaklata Mukhopadhyay. He completed his early education at Ramakrishna Mission Vidyamandir, a residential college in Belur, before pursuing a Masters in English from the University of Calcutta. Later, he earned a Ph.D. from Jadavpur University, solidifying his academic foundation.

Mukhopadhyay began his professional career as the Regional Secretary for East India at Sahitya Akademi, a prestigious literary organization. He also served as the Convener of the Bengali Advisory Board for Sahitya Akademi and later became the President of the Bharatiya Bhasha Parishad. In his later years, he worked as the Director of the Publishing Department at Visva-Bharati, a role he retired from. Throughout his career, he has maintained strong ties with Bengali little magazines, contributing to their literary landscape.

His literary journey began in 1984 with the publication of *Madale Natun Bol* (The New Beats on the Drum), a collection of 14 short stories. This was followed by his first novel, *Charane Prantare* (At the Grazing Ground, at the Horizon), published in 1993. Over the years, he has expanded his repertoire to include travelogues, essays, and juvenile literature, demonstrating his versatility as a writer. Additionally, he has compiled and edited several works, further enriching his literary contributions.

Mukhopadhyay’s work has been widely recognized, earning him numerous prestigious awards. In 2000, he received the Somenchandra Award from the Paschimbanga Bangla Akademi, followed by the Galpamela Puraskar in 2004. His achievements continued with the Katha Award in New Delhi in 2005, the Bankimchandra Smriti Puraskar from the West Bengal government in 2006, and the Saratchandra Smriti Puraskar in Bhagalpur in 2007. He also won the Sis Puraskar in 2008 and the Gajendra Kumar Mitra Birth Centenary Award in 2009. His literary accolades include the Ananda Puraskar from *Ananda Bazar Patrika* and *Desh* in 2013, the D.L. Ray Award in 2014, and the Kusumanjali Award in New Delhi the same year. In 2016, he was honored with the Krititwa Samagra Puraskar from the Bharatiya Bhasha Parishad. Most recently, in 2023, he received the Karmayogi Nanigopal Chakraborty Smriti Sahitya Puraskar, underscoring his enduring impact on Bengali literature.

Through his extensive body of work and his involvement in literary institutions, Ramkumar Mukhopadhyay has established himself as a significant figure in contemporary Bengali literature. His dedication to storytelling, both for adults and younger audiences, along with his scholarly background, has solidified his reputation as a respected and celebrated writer.

title: Anurag Kashyap
text:
Anurag Kashyap is a prominent Indian filmmaker and actor, best known for his contributions to Hindi cinema. Born on 10 September 1972 in Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh, he hails from a middle-class Hindu family, with his father being a retired Chief Engineer. Kashyap received his early education in Dehradun and Gwalior before pursuing zoology at Hansraj College in Delhi. His early interest in science shifted to filmmaking after he attended a film festival and was deeply influenced by Vittorio De Sica’s *Bicycle Thieves*.

Kashyap’s career began in the 1990s when he moved to Mumbai with minimal funds, facing financial struggles before finding work in theater. His breakthrough came as a co-writer for Ram Gopal Varma’s *Satya* (1998), a critically acclaimed crime drama. He made his directorial debut with *Paanch* (1999), a film that faced censorship issues and was never theatrically released. His next major work, *Black Friday* (2004), based on the 1993 Bombay bombings, was delayed due to legal concerns but later received critical acclaim.

Throughout the 2000s, Kashyap experimented with various genres, including the surrealistic thriller *No Smoking* (2007) and the modern retelling of *Devdas*, *Dev.D* (2009), which was both a critical and commercial success. His socio-political drama *Gulaal* (2009) and the thriller *That Girl in Yellow Boots* (2011) further solidified his reputation as an avant-garde filmmaker.

Kashyap gained widespread recognition with *Gangs of Wasseypur* (2012), a two-part crime saga that became a cult film and received international acclaim. He continued to collaborate with other filmmakers, co-producing *The Lunchbox* (2013) and *Shahid* (2012), the latter earning him a BAFTA nomination. His anthology *Bombay Talkies* (2013) and the psychological thriller *Ugly* (2014) were also well-received.

In 2015, he directed *Bombay Velvet*, a period film that despite its artistic merits, underperformed at the box office, leading to personal and professional challenges. However, he rebounded with *Raman Raghav 2.0* (2016), a film inspired by a real-life serial killer, and *Mukkabaaz* (2018), a boxing drama praised for its storytelling.

Kashyap ventured into digital content, co-directing Netflix’s *Sacred Games* (2018), a critically acclaimed crime series, and contributing to anthology films like *Lust Stories* (2018) and *Ghost Stories* (2020). His later works include *Choked* (2020), a dark comedy, and *Dobaaraa* (2022), a sci-fi thriller. He also explored audio storytelling with *Thriller Factory* (2019) for Amazon’s Audible Suno.

Kashyap’s work is marked by its unconventional themes, gritty realism, and bold narrative choices, earning him four Filmfare Awards and the Knight of the Order of Arts and Letters from the French government in 2013. His films often challenge conventional Hindi cinema, making him a pivotal figure in contemporary Indian filmmaking.

title: Mateo Correa Magallanes
text:
Mateo Correa Magallanes, also known as Fr. Correa, was a Mexican priest and a member of the Knights of Columbus, specifically Council 2140. Born in Tepechitlán, Zacatecas, on July 23, 1866, he demonstrated an early calling to the priesthood, attending the seminary in Zacatecas on a scholarship in 1881. After years of study, he was ordained a priest in 1893 at the age of 27. During his early ministry, he had the honor of administering the sacrament of First Holy Communion to Miguel Pro, another future priest who would later be martyred for his faith.

Correa served as a parish priest in several locations, beginning with Concepción del Oro in 1898 and later moving to Colotlán in 1908. His priestly work continued amid growing tensions between the Mexican government and the Catholic Church. By 1910, the government had intensified its persecution of the Church, forcing Correa to go into hiding. Despite the dangers, he resumed his pastoral duties when assigned to Valparaíso in 1926, just a year before his martyrdom.

In 1927, during the height of government persecution, Correa was arrested while performing a sacred duty—bringing Viaticum (the last rites) to a gravely ill woman. Accused of being part of the Cristero rebellion, an armed uprising of Catholic militants resisting government oppression, he was imprisoned in Zacatecas and later transferred to Durango. While in custody, General Eulogio Ortiz, a government official, requested that Correa hear the confessions of imprisoned Cristeros facing execution. Correa agreed to administer the Sacrament of Reconciliation, a sacred act of mercy that ensured the prisoners' spiritual preparation for death. However, after hearing their confessions, Ortiz demanded that Correa reveal the contents of the confessions, a direct violation of the seal of confession, which is inviolable in Catholic teaching. Correa refused, upholding his duty as a priest. Enraged, Ortiz pointed a gun at Correa’s head and threatened him with immediate death if he did not comply. Correa remained steadfast, choosing death over betraying the sacred trust of the confessional. At dawn on February 6, 1927, he was taken to a cemetery on the outskirts of Durango and executed by a gunshot to the head.

Correa’s martyrdom was later recognized by the Catholic Church, and he was canonized as a saint by Pope John Paul II on May 21, 2000. The ceremony, held in St. Peter’s Square at the Vatican, drew thousands of pilgrims from Mexico and beyond. In his homily, Pope John Paul II praised Correa’s heroic witness of faith and love, highlighting his willingness to lay down his life for the Gospel. He urged the faithful to follow Correa’s example, especially in the face of persecution and violence. Correa is remembered as a symbol of courage and unwavering fidelity to Christ, and his canonization remains a significant moment for the Church in Mexico and worldwide.

title: Stephanie Beatriz
text:
Stephanie Beatriz Bischoff Alvizuri, born on February 10, 1981, in Neuquén, Argentina, is an American actress known for her versatile work in television, film, and voice acting. Her parents, a Colombian father and a Bolivian mother, moved the family to the United States when she was two years old, settling in Webster, Texas. She attended Clear Brook High School and developed an interest in acting after participating in speech and debate, which led to her involvement in theater. Beatriz became a U.S. citizen at 18 and later attended Stephens College, an all-women's institution in Missouri, graduating in 2002. She then moved to New York City to pursue acting before relocating to Los Angeles in 2010.

Beatriz's early career included roles in theater, particularly at the Oregon Shakespeare Festival, where she performed in productions like *A View From a Bridge* (2008), *Cat on a Hot Tin Roof* (2010), and *Measure for Measure* (2011). On television, she appeared in episodes of *The Closer* and *Southland* before landing a recurring role as Sonia Ramirez in *Modern Family*. Her breakthrough came in 2013 when she was cast as Detective Rosa Diaz in the comedy series *Brooklyn Nine-Nine*, a role she played for eight seasons. In 2019, she directed an episode of the show, titled "He Said, She Said."

In film, Beatriz starred in *The Light of the Moon* (2017), a critically acclaimed independent drama that premiered at the South by Southwest Film Festival. Her performance earned praise, with critics highlighting her authenticity and emotional depth. She also voiced characters in animated projects, including General Sweet Mayhem in *The Lego Movie 2: The Second Part* (2019) and Gina Cazador in *BoJack Horseman* (2018–2019). In 2021, she starred in the musical film *In the Heights* and voiced the lead character, Mirabel Madrigal, in Disney's *Encanto*, both collaborations with Lin-Manuel Miranda.

Beatriz has also ventured into podcasting, voicing the lead in the crime procedural *Tejana* (2021) and starring in the sci-fi thriller *Solar*. She executive-produced *Tejana* and sought to develop a television series based on it. Additionally, she hosted *Wondery's Twin Flames*, a podcast investigating a dating cult. In 2024, she began voicing Vaggie in *Hazbin Hotel*.

In her personal life, Beatriz has spoken openly about her struggles with severe astigmatism, which complicates her work on camera, and her history with disordered eating. She came out as bisexual in 2016, having realized her identity in her early teens but facing biphobia and erasure. In 2017, she announced her engagement to actor Brad Hoss, and the couple married in 2018. In 2021, she welcomed a daughter.

Throughout her career, Beatriz has been vocal about representation, co-hosting the National Hispanic Media Coalition Impact Awards in 2019 alongside *Brooklyn Nine-Nine* co-star Melissa Fumero. Her work spans multiple mediums, showcasing her talent as an actress, director, producer, and advocate for diversity in entertainment.

title: R. Selvaraj (politician)
text:
R. Selvaraj was a politician from Kerala, India, who served as a Member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) representing the Neyyattinkara constituency in Thiruvananthapuram. Born on 5 March 1949 in Dhanuvachapuram, near Neyyattinkara, he was the son of Shri. Varghese Nadar and Smt. Ruthe Nadar. He had an elder sister, R. Sarojam, and an elder brother, R. Chinnappan. Selvaraj married Smt. Mary Valsala, and the couple had two daughters, Divya M.S. and Deepthi M.S., and resided near Dhanuvachapuram.

Selvaraj began his political career through the student wing of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI(M)), specifically the Students' Federation of India (SFI) and the Kerala Students Youth Federation (KSYF). His early political roles included serving as the CPI(M) Area Secretary for Parassala, Vice-President of Kollayil Panchayat, and District Joint Secretary of the Karshaka Sangham (a farmers' organization) in Thiruvananthapuram. He was also a member of the CPI(M) District Committee in Thiruvananthapuram.

His first electoral victory came in 2006 when he was elected to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from the Parassala constituency. In the 2011 state elections, he won from the Neyyattinkara constituency. However, due to growing factionalism within the CPI(M) and alleged targeting by a section of the party leadership, Selvaraj resigned from both his MLA position and his membership in the CPI(M) District Committee on 9 March 2012. He later joined the Indian National Congress (INC), the ruling party in Kerala at the time.

After joining the Congress, Selvaraj contested a by-election in Neyyattinkara under the party's "Hand" symbol. The election was highly competitive, involving a three-way contest, but Selvaraj emerged victorious with a margin of 6,334 votes. His win strengthened the United Democratic Front (UDF), the ruling coalition in Kerala, increasing its majority in the 140-member assembly to 73 seats.

Selvaraj continued to contest from the Neyyattinkara constituency in the 2016 and 2021 state elections, but he was defeated both times. In 2016, he lost to K. Ansalan of the CPI(M) by a margin of 9,543 votes, and in 2021, the margin of defeat increased to 14,262 votes. Despite these setbacks, his political journey remained significant, particularly due to his shift from the CPI(M) to the Congress and his impact on Kerala's political landscape.

title: Angela Bairstow
text:
Angela Bairstow (1942–2016) was a highly accomplished English badminton player who made a significant impact on the sport during the 1960s. Born in 1942, she grew up on Plough Lane in Purley and attended Dinorben School, a private girls' school in Wallington. Her badminton career began to take shape in her teenage years when she won the English National Junior singles title in 1958, followed by further wins in 1959 and 1960. She also secured four English National Junior doubles titles during this period, establishing herself as a rising star in the sport.

As she transitioned to senior competition, Bairstow reached the final of the prestigious All England Badminton Championships in 1963, where she lost to Judy Hashman. That same year, she was seeded to win in all three disciplines—singles, doubles, and mixed—at the All England Championships, though she did not claim any titles. Despite this, she became a dominant force in international badminton from 1964 to 1968, winning numerous titles, including the Scottish Open, German Open, Dutch Open, Asia Cup, Irish Open, English National Badminton Championships, and the European Badminton Championships. Her dominance was particularly evident in 1965 when she won the Dutch Open in singles, doubles, and mixed in the same year, a feat she later repeated at the second Asian Championships in Lucknow. This remarkable achievement led to the organizers banning non-Asian players from future Asian Championships, a testament to her skill and influence.

Bairstow was known for her deceptive backhand sliced serve and flick, techniques that often caught opponents off guard. She is the only player in history to have won medals in both the Asian and European Championships, a rare accomplishment that highlighted her versatility and adaptability. Her contributions to English badminton were further cemented when she represented her country at the 1966 British Empire and Commonwealth Games in Kingston, Jamaica, where she won two gold medals and one silver medal in women's singles, women's doubles, and mixed doubles, respectively.

In her personal life, Bairstow married her coach, H. Ian Palmer, in 1970. The couple had three children, born in 1969, 1970, and 1972, and later became grandparents to four grandchildren. Her career spanned a decade of excellence, during which she amassed an impressive collection of titles and remains one of the most decorated English badminton players of her era. Though she never won an All England title, her international success and influence on the sport were undeniable, leaving a lasting legacy in badminton history.

title: Mindy Smith
text:
Mindy Smith, born Melinda Leigh Smith on June 1, 1972, is an American singer-songwriter whose career began after she recorded a cover of Dolly Parton’s "Jolene" for a tribute album. Adopted at birth by a Protestant minister and his wife, who was a church choir director, Smith grew up on Long Island, New York. After her mother’s death from cancer in 1991, she attended Cincinnati Bible College for two years. Later, she and her father relocated to Knoxville, Tennessee, where she discovered a passion for folk and bluegrass music, influenced by artists like Alison Krauss and the Cox Family. In 1998, she moved to Nashville to pursue a music career and, in 2000, reached the finals of the Kerrville Folk Festival, which secured her a contract with Big Yellow Dog Music.

Smith gained attention in 2003 when her rendition of "Jolene" appeared on the Dolly Parton tribute album *Just Because I'm a Woman*, leading to a recording contract with Vanguard Records. Her debut album, *One Moment More*, was released in 2004 and showcased her admiration for country and folk legends like Parton, John Prine, and Patty Griffin. The song "Come to Jesus" became her biggest hit, receiving airplay across multiple radio formats, including country, Christian, and adult album alternative stations, and peaking at No. 32 on *Billboard*’s Adult Top 40 chart. That same year, she performed at the prestigious Cambridge Folk Festival in the U.K., which was broadcast nationally on BBC Radio.

In 2006, Smith released "Out Loud," the lead single from her second album, *Long Island Shores*, which was well-received by AAA rock and CMT. The following year, she appeared on *The Tonight Show with Jay Leno*, performing "Please Stay." In October 2007, she released *My Holiday*, a Christmas album featuring six original songs, including "I Know the Reason," co-written with Thad Cockrell. Two years later, she released *Stupid Love*, her fourth studio album, and performed its lead single, "Highs and Lows," on *The Early Show*. During a 2009 interview on *World Cafe*, she publicly disclosed her struggle with obsessive–compulsive disorder.

In 2012, Smith launched her independent label, Giant Leap, and released her self-titled eponymous album. That same year, Vanguard Records compiled her works into *The Essential Mindy Smith*. In 2013, she released *Snowed In*, a holiday EP blending original Christmas songs with covers. Between 2015 and 2018, she contributed as a songwriter to the television series *Nashville*, with her compositions featured on the show’s soundtrack in its final seasons.

Beyond music, Smith has engaged in charitable work. In 2013, she collaborated with the clothing retailer Anthropologie to raise funds and awareness for the Captain Planet Foundation, with a portion of sales from her in-store performance donated to the cause.

Smith’s contributions to music have been recognized with awards, including the Americana Music Association’s Best New/Emerging Artist of the Year in 2004. Her discography includes multiple studio albums, compilations, and collaborations, such as her cover of "Jolene" on the Dolly Parton tribute album and contributions to Beatles and Olivia Newton-John tribute projects. Her work spans country, folk, and Christian music, reflecting a diverse musical influence and a career built on both independent and major-label platforms.

title: Nobuhiro Shimatani
text:
Nobuhiro Shimatani, known professionally as Check Shimatani, is a Japanese professional wrestler born on February 27, 1996. Currently a freelancer, he is most recognized for his time in DDT Pro-Wrestling and his involvement with Gleat, where he is part of the BULK Orchestra stable. His career has spanned multiple promotions, showcasing his versatility in various match types and events.

Shimatani made his professional wrestling debut on March 21, 2016, at DDT’s *Judgement 2016: DDT 19th Anniversary*, teaming with Kouki Iwasaki and Rainbow Kawamura in a losing effort against Shunma Katsumata, Guanchulo, and Mao Inoue. He frequently participated in DDT’s signature events, such as *Judgement*, *Ryōgoku Peter Pan*, *Ultimate Party*, and *Into The Fight*. At *Ryōgoku Peter Pan 2018*, he won a Rumble rules match by lastly eliminating Gorgeous Matsuno. His work in DDT included competing in unusual matches, such as a 28-person battle royal for a one-night general manager position in 2018, where he faced wrestlers like Danshoku Dino, Harashima, and Yuko Miyamoto. He also participated in multi-person tag team matches, including a notable loss at *Judgement 2020* alongside Tetsuya Endo and T-Hawk against Eruption (Kazusada Higuchi, Yukio Sakaguchi, and Saki Akai).

Outside DDT, Shimatani worked for Pro Wrestling Noah, teaming with Kazusada Higuchi and Kota Umeda in a losing effort to Atsushi Kotoge, Kenoh, and Masa Kitamiya in 2018. He also wrestled for Big Japan Pro Wrestling, defeating Alejandro, Kazuki Hashimoto, and Kosuke Sato alongside Takato Nakano and Kota Sekifuda in 2021. In April 2024, he competed for Soft Ground Wrestling (SGW) in Uganda, defeating local wrestler KY Kapeeka in a soft-ground wrestling match, accompanied by Cima.

Throughout his career, Shimatani has held several championships. In DDT, he won the Ironman Heavymetalweight Championship nine times and the King of Dark Championship once. He also captured the BBW Tag Team Championship in Best Body Japan Pro-Wrestling with Yakan Nabe. In Gleat, he won the G-Infinity Championship with Hayato Tamura. His diverse skill set and willingness to participate in unconventional matches have made him a notable figure in Japanese wrestling.

title: George Washington
text:
George Washington was born on February 22, 1732, in Westmoreland County, Virginia, to Augustine and Mary Ball Washington. His father died when he was young, leaving him Ferry Farm and ten slaves, while his older half-brother Lawrence inherited Mount Vernon. Washington received limited formal education but developed skills in mathematics, surveying, and drafting. At 16, he surveyed land in the Shenandoah Valley and later inherited Mount Vernon after Lawrence’s death in 1752.

Washington began his military career during the French and Indian War (1754–1763). In 1753, he was sent by Virginia’s governor, Robert Dinwiddie, to deliver a warning to the French occupying the Ohio Valley. His successful mission brought him recognition. The following year, he led Virginia troops to Fort Necessity, where he was forced to surrender after a brief battle, marking the war’s first major conflict. He later served under General Edward Braddock, who was killed in an ambush. Washington’s leadership in organizing the retreat improved his reputation. Though he resigned from the Virginia Regiment in 1758 after failing to secure a higher British commission, he gained valuable military experience and a dislike for British command structures.

In 1759, Washington married Martha Dandridge Custis, a wealthy widow, which significantly increased his social and financial standing. He expanded Mount Vernon to 6,500 acres and diversified its crops from tobacco to wheat and hemp. As a member of the Virginia House of Burgesses, Washington initially took a passive role but later became a vocal critic of British taxation policies, particularly the Stamp Act of 1765, which he saw as oppressive. He advocated for colonial rights and supported boycotts of British goods.

When the American Revolutionary War began in 1775, Washington was appointed commander-in-chief of the Continental Army. He led the poorly equipped Patriot forces against the disciplined British troops, facing early setbacks like the retreat from New York in 1776. However, victories at Trenton and Princeton boosted morale. Despite criticism over supply shortages and troop discipline, he persisted, ultimately securing a decisive victory at Yorktown in 1781 with French assistance. The war ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783, recognizing American independence.

Washington then presided over the Constitutional Convention in 1787, which drafted the U.S. Constitution. In 1789, he was unanimously elected the first U.S. president, setting key precedents such as the two-term limit and the title "Mr. President." He maintained neutrality during the French Revolution while supporting the Jay Treaty with Britain. His 1796 farewell address emphasized national unity and warned against regionalism and foreign influence.

Washington owned slaves at Mount Vernon but expressed growing opposition to slavery late in his life, freeing them in his will. He died on December 14, 1799. Remembered as the "Father of the Nation," Washington remains one of the most revered figures in American history, with his legacy enshrined in monuments, the nation’s capital, and the state of Washington.

title: Ernestine Eckstein
text:
Ernestine Eckstein (April 23, 1941 – July 15, 1992) was a pioneering African-American activist in the early LGBTQ+ and Black feminist movements. Born Ernestine Delois Eppenger in Indiana, she adopted the surname Eckstein to protect her identity while engaging in activism. After graduating from Indiana University in 1963 with a degree in Magazine Journalism and minors in Psychology and Russian, she moved to New York City, where she embraced her lesbian identity and began her activism. Her early involvement in the Civil Rights Movement, including work with the NAACP and CORE, deeply influenced her approach to political organizing.

Eckstein became a key figure in the Daughters of Bilitis (DOB), the first lesbian civil rights organization in the U.S. She served as Vice President of the New York chapter, pushing for a shift from negotiating with medical professionals—who still classified homosexuality as a mental illness—to more confrontational tactics like public demonstrations. Her leadership was part of a broader movement within the homophile organizations, including the Mattachine Society, to adopt direct action strategies. In 1965, she participated in the first Annual Reminder Day protest in Philadelphia and marched in front of the White House, becoming the only person of color at these early LGBTQ+ demonstrations.

Her correspondence with Frank Kameny, a prominent gay rights activist, revealed her efforts to bring his militant approach to DOB. Though Kameny was initially invited to speak at DOB’s headquarters in 1966, the organization ultimately withdrew the invitation, reflecting internal tensions over activism. Eckstein believed the movement should focus on government discrimination, employment, and military service, as well as religious opposition. She saw parallels between the struggles of Black Americans and LGBTQ+ individuals, advocating for coalition-building across movements. Her perspective was ahead of its time, as the NAACP would not formally acknowledge LGBTQ+ rights as civil rights until 2012.

By the late 1960s, disillusioned with the internal conflicts in DOB, Eckstein moved to Northern California to focus on broader social justice issues. She became involved with Black Women Organized for Action (BWOA), a radical Black feminist group formed in 1973 to address the lack of representation of Black women in political organizing. BWOA rejected traditional hierarchies, emphasizing collective leadership and grassroots activism. The organization’s inclusive approach welcomed Black women regardless of class or appearance, though it notably did not address heterosexism as a systemic issue. Eckstein’s involvement reflected her progressive beliefs, which emphasized coalition-building and intersectional activism.

Her political views were shaped by her experiences in the Civil Rights Movement, where she saw demonstrations as essential to social change. She advocated for inclusive movements that transcended labels, stating that cooperation between different groups was necessary for progress. In a 1966 interview in *The Ladder*, the DOB’s magazine, she became one of the first women of color featured on its cover, challenging stereotypes about lesbian identity. The interview remains the most substantial record of her thoughts and activism.

Eckstein’s later life remains undocumented, though records indicate she died in San Pablo, California, in 1992. Her contributions to both the LGBTQ+ and Black feminist movements were groundbreaking, particularly her advocacy for intersectional organizing and direct action. Her legacy endures in discussions about the historical connections between civil rights, LGBTQ+ rights, and Black feminist activism.

title: Manny Pacquiao
text:
Manny Pacquiao, born on December 17, 1978, in the Philippines, is a celebrated professional boxer, businessman, former politician, and one of the most accomplished athletes in history. Nicknamed "PacMan," he is widely regarded as one of the greatest boxers of all time, having won twelve major world titles across eight weight divisions—a record unmatched in boxing history. He is the only fighter to hold world championships in four decades (1990s, 2000s, 2010s, and 2020s) and became the oldest welterweight champion at age 40 in 2019. His fights have generated over $1.3 billion in pay-per-view revenue, and he was ranked the second-highest-paid athlete in the world in 2012 and 2015. In 2024, ESPN named him the greatest Asian athlete of the 21st century, and he was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2025.

Born into poverty, Pacquiao had a difficult childhood, moving to Manila at 14 and living on the streets before turning to boxing at 12 under the guidance of his uncle. He made his professional debut at 16 and won his first world title, the WBC flyweight championship, at 19. Over his career, he defeated 22 world champions, including legendary fighters like Marco Antonio Barrera, Érik Morales, Oscar De La Hoya, and Floyd Mayweather Jr. (though their controversial 2015 fight was a draw). He retired from boxing in 2021 but returned for an exhibition match in 2024.

Beyond boxing, Pacquiao pursued a political career, serving as a congressman from 2010 to 2016 and then as a senator from 2016 to 2022. He ran for president in 2022 but lost to Bongbong Marcos. He also ventured into basketball, playing as a coach-player in the Philippine Basketball Association (PBA) from 2014 to 2017 and later founding the Maharlika Pilipinas Basketball League.

A devout Evangelical Christian, Pacquiao is also a philanthropist, entrepreneur, and entertainer, having released music, acted in films, and hosted TV shows. His influence extends globally, with Guinness World Records recognizing his achievements, including the most consecutive world title fight victories at different weights and the most titles won in different divisions. Despite never competing in the Olympics, he carried the Philippine flag in the 2008 Opening Ceremony. His legacy as a sports icon, political figure, and cultural ambassador remains unparalleled.

title: Raghav Juyal
text:
Raghav Juyal, born on 10 July 1991, is an Indian actor, dancer, choreographer, and television presenter known for his unique slow-motion dance style, which earned him the nicknames "Crockroaxz" and the "King of Slow Motion." He gained fame as a contestant and finalist on Zee TV's *Dance India Dance 3* (DID 3) in 2012, where he introduced a new dance form despite having no prior professional training. His audition video went viral, and though he wasn't initially selected in the top 18, public demand led to his re-entry as a "trump card" introduced by Grand Master Mithun Chakraborty. He became the most popular contestant, securing the highest number of No. 1 weekly positions and eventually finishing as the 2nd runner-up with 3.48 million votes.

After *DID 3*, Juyal became a skipper in *Dance India Dance Li'l Masters 2* (2014), leading "Raghav Ke Rockstars" and choreographing for Saumya Rai and Rohan Parkale, who both reached the finale. He later captained team "Yahoo" in *Dance Ke Superkids*, winning the competition against team "Wakao" led by Dharmesh Yelande. His influence extended beyond dancing as he ventured into acting, hosting, and choreography.

In 2014, Juyal made his acting debut in *Sonali Cable*, a comedy film co-starring Rhea Chakraborty and Ali Fazal, where critics praised his performance. The following year, he appeared in the dance film *ABCD 2* alongside Varun Dhawan and Shraddha Kapoor. He also hosted multiple dance and reality shows, including *Dance Plus* (seasons 2–5), *Rising Star*, and *Dance Champions*. In 2016, he participated in *Fear Factor: Khatron Ke Khiladi 7* and later co-hosted awards shows like the *Star Parivaar Awards* and *Colors Golden Petal Awards*.

Juyal continued to diversify his roles, appearing in *Street Dancer 3D* (2020) and *Bahut Hua Samman* (2020), the latter earning positive reviews for his performance in a satirical comedy. He also played a negative role for the first time in the Zee5 series *Abhay 2*. Other notable projects include *Wedlock* (2021) and the film *Yudhra* (2022), produced by Farhan Akhtar's Excel Entertainment. In 2024, he gained further recognition for his role in the Hindi-action thriller *Kill*, which won him an award.

His signature dance move, the "Slow Motion Walk," was praised by choreographers like Geeta Kapoor, Remo D'Souza, and Terrence Lewis, who noted its realism. Juyal is also a trained actor, mentored by Saurabh Sachdeva. Born in Dehradun, Uttarakhand, into a Garhwali Brahmin family, he had no formal dance training but learned through online and TV performances. He attended Doon International School and pursued a B.Com at DAV (PG) College. In 2025, he received the IIFA Award for Best Performance in a Negative Role at the 25th IIFA Awards.

title: Ezekiel Elliott
text:
Ezekiel "Zeke" Elliott, born on July 22, 1995, in Alton, Illinois, is an accomplished American football running back. He comes from a family with a strong athletic background. His mother, Dawn Huff, was a state champion in high school and a track athlete at the University of Missouri, while his father, Stacy, played linebacker for Missouri and later became CEO of Fifth Down Enterprises. Elliott’s uncle, Shawn Huff, is a professional basketball player in Finland. Despite this athletic lineage, Elliott attended the academically rigorous John Burroughs School in Ladue, Missouri, where he excelled in football, basketball, and track and field. As a junior in 2012, he was named the St. Louis Post-Dispatch offensive player of the year after rushing for 1,802 yards and 34 touchdowns. In his senior year, he amassed 3,061 all-purpose yards and 50 total touchdowns, including 2,155 rushing yards and 40 rushing touchdowns. He also stood out in track and field, winning four state championships in sprinting and hurdling events, and was named the Gatorade Track Athlete of the Year in Missouri.

Elliott committed to Ohio State University, choosing it over his parents’ alma mater, the University of Missouri. As a true freshman in 2013, he played sparingly as a backup to Carlos Hyde, rushing for 262 yards and two touchdowns. In 2014, with Hyde’s departure to the NFL, Elliott took over as the starting running back. He rushed for over 100 yards six times that season and had a standout performance in the Big Ten Championship Game against Wisconsin, rushing for 220 yards and two touchdowns. He carried that momentum into the 2015 Sugar Bowl, where he ran for 230 yards and an 85-yard touchdown against Alabama, earning Offensive Player of the Game honors. In the College Football Playoff National Championship Game, he rushed for 246 yards and four touchdowns, securing Offensive MVP honors. Over his college career, Elliott set numerous Ohio State records, including second in career rushing yards (3,961) and second in 100-yard rushing games (22). He was named a unanimous first-team All-Big Ten selection in 2015 and finished eighth in Heisman Trophy voting.

Elliott declared for the 2016 NFL draft, where he was selected fourth overall by the Dallas Cowboys. He signed a four-year, $24.9 million contract, making him the first running back drafted that year. In his rookie season, Elliott led the NFL in rushing yards (1,631), the third-most by a rookie in league history, and was named a first-team All-Pro and Pro Bowl selection. He also tied for second in rookie touchdowns (15) and was ranked seventh in the NFL Top 100 Players of 2017. His 2017 season was marred by a six-game suspension due to domestic violence allegations, though he was never criminally charged. Legal battles delayed the suspension, and he ultimately missed only six games, finishing the season with 983 rushing yards and seven touchdowns in 10 games.

In 2018, Elliott bounced back, leading the league in rushing yards again (1,434) and earning his second Pro Bowl and first All-Pro selection. He also set career highs in rushing touchdowns (16) and total touchdowns (19). His performance earned him a spot on the NFL Top 100 Players of 2019, ranked 11th. The Cowboys released Elliott after the 2022 season, and he played the 2023 season with the New England Patriots before re-signing with Dallas in 2024. Over his career, Elliott has established himself as one of the NFL’s most productive and consistent running backs, known for his durability, work ethic, and ability to excel in both the rushing and passing games.

title: Tim Ferguson
text:
Tim Ferguson, born on 16 November 1963, is an Australian comedian, film director, screenwriter, author, and screenwriting teacher. He spent his early years in Singapore and later grew up on a rural property near Perthville, New South Wales. His father, Tony Ferguson, was a notable journalist, including being the first to report the Tet Offensive, and later worked as an executive producer at the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. Tim attended All Saints College in Bathurst before moving to Canberra, where he studied at the School Without Walls and Narrabundah College.

Ferguson began his career as part of the musical comedy trio Doug Anthony All Stars (DAAS) alongside Richard Fidler and Paul McDermott, gaining fame on UK television shows like *Friday Night Live* and *Viva Cabaret*. DAAS later starred in Australian productions such as *The Big Gig* and the sitcom *DAAS Kapital*. Throughout the 1990s, Ferguson appeared in various TV projects, including *Funky Squad* and *Don’t Forget Your Toothbrush*, which won a Logie Award. He also wrote a satirical novel, *Left, Right and Centre*, and contributed a comedic rewrite of the Australian Constitution preamble, which humorously mocked national stereotypes.

In the 2000s, Ferguson transitioned into filmmaking, co-directing the romantic comedy *Spin Out* (2016) with Marc Gracie and co-writing *The BBQ* (2017). He also acted in films like *That’s Not My Dog!* and *Fat Pizza*. His comedy career continued with stand-up shows, including *Carry a Big Stick* (2012) and *Smashing Life* (2021), which addressed his experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS). He reformed DAAS in 2014, performing internationally and winning awards like the Edinburgh Festival’s Spirit of the Fringe. Additionally, he co-hosted the podcast *Bunga Bunga*, which won a Castaway Best Comedy Podcast Award in 2017.

Ferguson has been active in teaching comedy screenwriting at institutions like New York University, RMIT, and AFTRS. He authored *The Cheeky Monkey: Writing Narrative Comedy*, a guide for aspiring writers, and writes a satirical column, *The Ferguson Report*, for *The New Daily*. His autobiography, *Carry a Big Stick* (2013), details his life, career, and battles with MS, which he was diagnosed with at 19 and now lives with using a wheelchair. He has been a vocal advocate for disability rights, serving as an ambassador for organizations like MS Australia and IncludeAbility, and campaigning for better housing and accessibility standards. In 2017, he launched the MS Australia Connections Hub, offering support and advice for those living with MS.

Beyond comedy and advocacy, Ferguson has dabbled in visual art, exhibiting works under the name "Tim Awt," and has a significant collection of Star Wars toys. He has also engaged in political activism, running as an independent candidate for the seat of Kooyong in 1990 and later announcing a satirical Senate candidacy in 2013. Despite controversies, such as apologizing for abusive letters sent to a TV critic in the 1990s, Ferguson remains a prominent figure in Australian entertainment and disability advocacy, continuing to tour, teach, and create work that balances humor with social awareness.

title: Martha Cunz
text:
Martha Cunz (1876–1961) was a Swiss artist who gained recognition as a master of the modernist woodcut, becoming one of the earliest European artists of the 20th century to excel in this medium. Born in St. Gallen, Switzerland, she pursued her art education primarily at the Women's Art School in Munich, where she studied under notable artists such as Christian Landenberger, Ludwig Schmid-Reutte, and Peter Paul Müller. Her artistic training continued in Paris in 1900, where she learned from Luc-Olivier Merson and Lucien Simon. The following year, she returned to Munich and took a lithography course with Ernst Neumann, which sparked her lifelong interest in printmaking. By 1902, she had transitioned to woodcuts, and in 1903, she became a founding member of the German Association of Graphics, signaling her early dedication to the field.

Cunz spent much of her early career in Munich, only returning to Switzerland briefly each year. She also traveled extensively across Europe, visiting Holland in 1904 and 1911 and Italy in 1914. World War I marked a turning point in her life, as she settled permanently in St. Gallen, constructing a studio at her parents' home, where she lived and worked for the rest of her life.

Her artistic output was characterized by a focus on lithographs and woodcuts, particularly color woodcuts, which she executed using a Japanese multi-block technique. This method allowed her to create intricate, layered compositions with subtly contrasting colors that overlapped to produce a luminous effect. By 1905, her work was featured in the prestigious Glass Palace Exhibition in Munich, and some of her earliest woodcuts appeared in the journal *Deutsche Kunst und Dekoration* alongside works by Wassily Kandinsky and other prominent Munich artists. Over the course of her career, she produced 71 woodcuts, the last of which was completed in 1927. Her lithographic work continued until 1931, after which she shifted her focus entirely to painting, primarily landscapes and portraits.

Cunz's influence extended beyond her own work, as she inspired contemporary artists such as Carl Thiemann and taught printmaking to others, including Rosa Paul. Her contributions to the development of modernist woodcut techniques in Europe were significant, and her legacy endures in the fields of printmaking and painting.

Scholarship on Cunz includes works by Dani Studer, who has written extensively on her life and art, as well as exhibition catalogs and biographical entries in broader studies of Swiss and European art. Her work has been featured in publications and museum collections, solidifying her place in the history of 20th-century art.

title: Aaron Burr
text:
ote democracy and challenge the Federalist-controlled financial institutions. By establishing a rival banking institution, Burr sought to provide financial opportunities to a broader segment of society, particularly small businessmen who were excluded from the Federalist-dominated banking system. The company's success allowed it to become a major financial force in New York, eventually evolving into the modern-day JPMorgan Chase.

### Political Rivalry and the Duel with Hamilton
Burr's relationship with Alexander Hamilton, a leading Federalist, deteriorated over time due to political and personal disagreements. Their rivalry culminated in the infamous Burr–Hamilton duel on July 11, 1804. The duel was sparked by increasingly hostile exchanges between the two men, particularly Burr's perception that Hamilton had undermined his political career. During the duel in Weehawken, New Jersey, Burr fatally wounded Hamilton, who died the following day. Burr was indicted for dueling, which was illegal in both New York and New Jersey, but the charges were eventually dropped due to lack of jurisdiction. The incident ruined Burr’s political career, as he was widely condemned for the act.

### The 1800 Election and Vice Presidency
Burr’s political career reached its peak in the 1800 presidential election, which resulted in a tie between Thomas Jefferson and himself in the Electoral College. After a contentious election dispute resolved by the House of Representatives, Jefferson was elected president, and Burr became his vice president. However, Burr’s relationship with Jefferson was strained from the beginning. Jefferson distrusted Burr and marginalized him in the administration. This tension was exacerbated by the passage of the 12th Amendment in 1804, which required electors to cast separate votes for president and vice president, preventing another tie. As a result, Jefferson did not select Burr as his running mate for the 1804 election, effectively ending Burr’s political future.

### The Burr Conspiracy
After leaving office, Burr traveled westward, reportedly seeking new economic and political opportunities. His activities during this period became the subject of intense speculation and suspicion. In 1806, he was arrested on charges of treason for allegedly plotting to create an independent nation in the western territories, an event known as the Burr Conspiracy. Burr was tried in the U.S. Supreme Court before Chief Justice John Marshall, who presided over the case. Despite the prosecution’s efforts, Burr was acquitted due to a lack of sufficient evidence. The trial further damaged his reputation, and he briefly fled to Europe to avoid public scrutiny.

### Later Life and Death
Burr returned to the United States in 1812 and resumed his law practice in New York City. He spent his remaining years in relative obscurity, though he remained a controversial figure. He died on September 14, 1836, at the age of 80. Despite his legal and political achievements, Burr is most remembered for his fatal duel with Hamilton and the cloud of controversy that surrounded his later years. His legacy remains divided, with some viewing him as a brilliant but flawed figure, while others see him as a dangerous and unprincipled man.

title: Prince Carl Philip, Duke of Värmland
text:
Prince Carl Philip of Sweden, Duke of Värmland, was born on 13 May 1979 at Stockholm Palace as the only son and second child of King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Silvia. He was initially heir apparent to the Swedish throne but lost this title in January 1980 when the constitution changed to prioritize natural birth order over male primogeniture, making his older sister, Victoria, the new heir. As of 2022, he is fourth in the line of succession, behind Victoria, her daughter Princess Estelle, and her son Prince Oscar. He resides in Villa Solbacken in Djurgården, Stockholm, with his wife, Princess Sofia, and their four children.

Carl Philip attended various schools in Sweden, including Enskilda Gymnasiet in Stockholm, and was confirmed in 1994. He later studied at Kent School in the United States and completed his upper secondary education at Lundsbergs School in 1999. In 2007–2008, he pursued graphic design at the Rhode Island School of Design and later studied Agricultural and Rural Management at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, graduating in 2011. Like his father and sister, he has dyslexia.

An avid athlete and outdoor enthusiast, Carl Philip enjoys football, swimming, sailing, and skiing. He completed the Vasaloppet, the world’s longest cross-country ski race, in 2003. He is also passionate about car racing, participating in the Porsche Carrera Cup Scandinavia and the Scandinavian Touring Car Championship. He served in the Swedish military, completing his service as a combat boat commander in 2000 and later rising to the rank of major in 2014. Additionally, he has a strong interest in design, founding Bernadotte & Kylberg in 2012, a company that produces design products for various brands.

Carl Philip is involved in several charitable initiatives. In 2013, he founded the Prince Carl Philip Racing Cup to support young karting talents. He and his wife established the Prince Carl Philip and Princess Sofia’s Foundation in 2015, which focuses on combating bullying. He is also a patron of several organizations, including the Swedish National Dyslexia Association and the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

His personal life includes a past relationship with Emma Pernald from 1999 to 2009. In 2010, he began a relationship with Sofia Hellqvist, whom he married in 2015. The couple has four children: Prince Alexander (born 2016), Prince Gabriel (born 2017), Prince Julian (born 2021), and Princess Ines (born 2025). In 2019, King Carl XVI Gustaf stripped Carl Philip’s sons of their royal titles, though they remain princes and retain their places in the line of succession. The couple has expressed that this change allows their sons more personal freedom.

Carl Philip holds numerous national and foreign honors, including the Swedish Royal Order of the Seraphim and the Grand Cross of the Order of the White Rose of Finland. His military career includes promotions from second lieutenant to major, and his coat of arms features elements of the Swedish royal arms and the eagle of Värmland.

Overall, Prince Carl Philip balances his royal duties with his personal interests in sports, design, and military service, while actively supporting charitable causes.

title: Kaká
text:
Ricardo Izecson dos Santos Leite, commonly known as Kaká, is a Brazilian former professional footballer recognized as one of the greatest players of all time. Born on 22 April 1982 in Gama, Brazil, Kaká rose to fame as an attacking midfielder, celebrated for his pace, dribbling, passing, and goal-scoring ability. He is one of only nine players to have won the FIFA World Cup, the UEFA Champions League, and the Ballon d'Or.

Kaká began his professional career at São Paulo FC in 2001, where he quickly made an impact, scoring 12 goals in 27 appearances in his debut season. He led São Paulo to the Torneio Rio-São Paulo title, scoring two crucial goals in the final. His performances attracted attention from European clubs, and in 2003, he joined AC Milan for a reported €8.5 million. In his first season with Milan, he helped the club win the Serie A title and was named Serie A Footballer of the Year. Over the next six years, Kaká became a key figure for Milan, winning the 2006–07 UEFA Champions League as the competition's top scorer with 10 goals. His standout performances earned him the FIFA World Player of the Year, the 2007 Ballon d'Or, and the UEFA Club Footballer of the Year.

In 2009, Kaká joined Real Madrid for a then-record transfer fee of €67 million. However, his time in Madrid was hampered by injuries, which slowed his pace and form. He spent four seasons there, contributing with goals and assists but failing to replicate his Milan success. In 2013, he returned to AC Milan for a season before moving to MLS side Orlando City SC in 2014. He initially went on loan to his former club São Paulo before returning to Orlando, where he retired in 2017.

Kaká’s international career with Brazil was equally distinguished. He made his debut in 2002 and was part of the squad that won the 2002 FIFA World Cup. He also played in the 2006 and 2010 World Cups and was a key player in Brazil’s victories at the 2005 and 2009 FIFA Confederations Cups, winning the Golden Ball as the tournament’s best player in 2009.

Throughout his career, Kaká was recognized as one of the world’s best players, earning multiple nominations for the FIFA World Player of the Year and Ballon d'Or awards. Between 2006 and 2009, he was named in the FIFA World XI and the UEFA Team of the Year three times. In 2010, he was inducted into the AC Milan Hall of Fame. Beyond football, Kaká was a global ambassador for humanitarian causes, including the UN World Food Programme, and was named by *Time* magazine as one of the world’s 100 most influential people in 2008 and 2009.

Kaká’s early life was marked by a strong family background, with his father being a civil engineer and his mother an elementary school teacher. His nickname "Kaká" originated from his younger brother’s childhood struggle to pronounce "Ricardo." A devout Christian, he attributed his recovery from a career-threatening spinal injury at 18 to his faith and donated a portion of his earnings to his church.

Known for his sportsmanship and influence, Kaká was the first athlete to amass 10 million followers on Twitter and remains a revered figure in football history. His legacy is defined by his skill, achievements, and contributions both on and off the pitch.

title: Uee
text:
Uee, born Kim Yu-jin on April 9, 1988, in Daejeon, South Korea, is a singer and actress best known for her time as a member of the girl group After School from 2009 to 2017. Her father, Kim Sung-kap, is a retired professional baseball player and former coach, and she has an older sister. Uee attended Guwol Girls' Middle School and Incheon Physical Education High School, where she was a competitive swimmer, and later graduated from Sungkyunkwan University with a degree in Performing Arts. Before her rise to fame, she gained attention as a teenager when she was photographed at her father's baseball game, earning the nickname "Mok-dong Girl."

Uee's career began in 2007 as a member of the short-lived girl group Five Girls under Good Entertainment. The group disbanded before their official debut due to financial issues. She later joined Pledis Entertainment and debuted with After School in April 2009 with their single "Diva." During this time, she gained popularity for her "honey thighs" and frequently topped online search rankings. In addition to her musical career, Uee quickly transitioned into acting, making her debut in the historical drama *Queen Seondeok* in 2009. She also appeared in the drama *You're Beautiful* and joined the project group 4Tomorrow, releasing the single "Dugeundugeun Tomorrow."

Her acting career flourished in 2011 with lead roles in *Birdie Buddy* and *Ojakgyo Family*, earning her critical acclaim and Best New Actress awards at major ceremonies. She also released her first solo single, "Sok Sok Sok," and co-hosted variety shows like *Night After Night*. In 2012, she became a permanent host on *Music Bank* and starred in the historical drama *Jeon Woo-chi*, where she expressed her desire to be taken seriously as an actress. Throughout the 2010s, she appeared in numerous dramas, including *Golden Rainbow* (2013), *Hogu's Love* (2015), *Marriage Contract* (2016), and *My Only One* (2018). She also participated in variety shows like *Law of the Jungle* and *Barefooted Friends*, showcasing her versatility.

Uee left After School and Pledis Entertainment in 2017 and signed with Yuleum Entertainment. Since then, she has continued to focus on acting, starring in dramas like *Manhole* and *Ghost Doctor*. She has also appeared on variety programs such as *I Live Alone*, *Cabin Crew*, and *Spicy Girls*, where she shared her love for spicy food and became an endorser for Samyang’s "Fire Chicken Sauce" series. Her personal life has included relationships with actors Lee Sang-yoon and Kangnam, though both ended after a short time. Uee has faced significant criticism, particularly regarding her weight, which she revealed caused her to restrict her eating habits for years. In 2018, her agency took legal action against online defamation.

Beyond entertainment, Uee has engaged in philanthropy, donating funds in 2022 to support hygiene products for young women in need. Her career has spanned music, drama, and variety shows, establishing her as a multifaceted figure in Korean entertainment. As of 2023, she remains active in acting and hosting, maintaining a strong presence in the industry.

title: Kiara Advani
text:
Kiara Advani, born Alia Advani on 31 July 1991, is an Indian actress known for her work in Hindi and Telugu films. One of the highest-paid actresses in India, she has received multiple awards, including an IIFA Award and two Zee Cine Awards, along with nominations for two Filmfare Awards. Before pursuing acting, she briefly worked as a teacher. Advani made her film debut in 2014 with *Fugly*, a comedy that underperformed at the box office but earned her a nomination for Best Female Debut at the Screen Awards. Despite the setback, she persisted, and her career took a significant turn with *M.S. Dhoni: The Untold Story* (2016), where she portrayed the wife of the cricket legend. The film was a commercial success, grossing over ₹216 crore worldwide.

In 2018, Advani gained critical praise for her role in the Netflix anthology *Lust Stories*, playing a sexually dissatisfied wife, and also starred in the Telugu political thriller *Bharat Ane Nenu*, which was a box office hit. However, her next Telugu film, *Vinaya Vidheya Rama*, did not fare as well. The following year, she achieved widespread recognition with *Kabir Singh* (2019), a romantic drama that sparked controversy for its portrayal of toxic masculinity but became one of the highest-grossing films of the year. She further solidified her stardom with *Good Newwz*, a comedy-drama that earned her an IIFA Award for Best Supporting Actress.

Advani continued to deliver successful performances in 2021 with *Shershaah*, a war film based on the life of army officer Vikram Batra, for which she received a Filmfare nomination. She also starred in *Bhool Bhulaiyaa 2* (2022), a horror comedy, and *Jugjugg Jeeyo*, a family drama, both of which were commercially successful. In 2023, she earned another Filmfare nomination for *Satyaprem Ki Katha*, a romantic drama about a troubled marriage.

Beyond acting, Advani is a prominent brand endorser, representing companies like Audi, Colgate, and Mango, and has a brand value estimated at $60 million. She is also involved in social causes, including supporting initiatives for children and daily wage workers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Advani made her Met Gala debut in 2025 while pregnant, further cementing her status as a global fashion icon.

In her personal life, Advani married actor Sidharth Malhotra in 2023, and the couple welcomed a daughter in 2025. Their marriage attracted significant media attention, with their wedding photos becoming the most-liked Instagram post in India. Advani has been recognized as one of the most desirable and influential figures in Bollywood, ranking among the top-paid and most-searched celebrities in India.

title: Maurice Jones-Drew
text:
Maurice Christopher Jones-Drew, known as "MJD," was an American professional football player who spent nine seasons in the National Football League (NFL) as a running back. Born on March 23, 1985, in Oakland, California, he was raised in Antioch and attended De La Salle High School in Concord. During his high school career, Jones-Drew was part of the De La Salle football team, which held the longest winning streak in high school history at 151 games. He played a key role in a nationally televised game against Long Beach Poly as a junior, scoring all four of his team's touchdowns, including a spectacular somersault into the end zone. He rushed for nearly 2,000 yards and 26 touchdowns during his junior season, earning recognition as a four-star recruit and the top all-purpose back in the nation. He also excelled in track, running a personal best of 10.80 seconds in the 100 meters.

Jones-Drew attended the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), where he played football for the Bruins from 2003 to 2005 under head coach Karl Dorrell. Despite being undersized, he led the Bruins in rushing all three years and was known for his versatility as a pass-catcher and return specialist. In 2005, he set an NCAA single-season record with a 28.5-yard average on punt returns, breaking a 54-year-old record. He also set UCLA records, including the career all-purpose yardage record (4,688 yards). As a sophomore, he rushed for 322 yards in a single game against Washington, setting a school record for rushing yards and touchdowns in a game. In his junior year, he was a unanimous All-American as an all-purpose back and kick returner, the first Bruin since Jackie Robinson to lead the country in punt returning. He also led the Pac-10 as a first-team All-Pac-10 selection and was second-team All-Pac-10 as a running back.

After his college career, Jones-Drew was selected by the Jacksonville Jaguars in the second round of the 2006 NFL draft, 60th overall. Many teams passed on him due to his height (5 feet 6¾ inches), but he became a key player for the Jaguars. In his rookie season, he set a franchise record with 303 all-purpose yards, including a 93-yard kickoff return for a touchdown, and finished third in the NFL in kickoff returns and touchdowns scored. He was named AFC Special Teams Player of the Week and finished tied for second in Offensive Rookie of the Year voting. Over his first four seasons, he became one of the most versatile running backs in the league, excelling as a rusher, receiver, and return specialist. In 2009, he had a breakout season, rushing for 1,391 yards and 15 touchdowns, earning his first Pro Bowl selection.

In 2010, Jones-Drew played the entire season with a torn meniscus in his left knee, which he kept secret to avoid being targeted. He was named to his second Pro Bowl and was later named Running Back of the Year by the NFL Alumni Association. In 2011, he led the NFL in rushing yards, had 24 total points in a single game, and was selected to his third Pro Bowl. He played eight seasons with the Jaguars before finishing his career with the Oakland Raiders in 2014.

After retiring, Jones-Drew transitioned into broadcasting, working as a football color analyst for NFL Now and other shows on NFL Network. He also hosted a Monday Night studio show for CBS Sports’ UK networks and currently serves as the color analyst for the Los Angeles Rams. His career is marked by his versatility, durability, and ability to overcome expectations due to his height, making him one of the most accomplished running backs of his era.

title: Witold Gombrowicz
text:
Witold Marian Gombrowicz (1904–1969) was a Polish writer and playwright whose works are marked by deep psychological analysis, paradox, absurdity, and an anti-nationalist bent. Born into a wealthy gentry family in Małoszyce, near Opatów, he grew up in Warsaw and studied law at Warsaw University before spending time in Paris. His early literary attempts were unsuccessful, but he gained recognition with his first novel, *Ferdydurke* (1937), which explores themes of immaturity, identity formation, and social roles in Polish society. The novel’s sharp satire and psychological depth divided critics but established his reputation in literary circles.

Just before World War II, Gombrowicz traveled to Argentina on the Polish liner *MS Chrobry* and remained there throughout the war, facing poverty and obscurity. He published *Ferdydurke* in Spanish in 1947, which became a significant event in Argentine literature, though it did not bring him immediate fame. During his exile, he worked as a bank clerk, formed friendships with Argentine intellectuals, and began publishing in the Paris-based journal *Kultura*. His novel *Trans-Atlantyk* (1953) controversially addressed themes of national identity in emigration, while his plays, such as *Ślub* (*The Marriage*), critiqued romantic traditions and power structures.

Despite his growing international recognition in the 1960s, Gombrowicz’s works were banned or heavily censored in Poland until the late 1950s. His diaries, published serially from 1953 and considered his masterpiece, blend autobiography, philosophy, and sharp social commentary. In 1963, he returned to Europe with the help of a Ford Foundation scholarship, settling in France. His later works, including *Pornografia* (1960) and *Kosmos* (1965), further explored themes of human identity, form, and societal constraints. Though his health declined, he received the Prix International in 1967 and married his secretary, Rita Labrosse, the following year. He died in Vence in 1969, leaving behind a legacy of works that challenged Polish romantic traditions and engaged with existentialist and structuralist thought.

Gombrowicz’s style is characterized by psychological depth, irony, and a satirical examination of social roles. His plays, such as *Ivona, Princess of Burgundia* (1938), and novels like *Ferdydurke* and *Kosmos* use neologisms and paradoxical narratives to critique societal expectations. His works have been translated into over 30 languages and adapted into films, including *Ferdydurke* (1991) and *Pornografia* (2003). Despite his late recognition, he remains one of Poland’s most influential literary figures, known for his uncompromising originality and incisive social critique.

title: Geraldo de Barros
text:
Geraldo de Barros (1923–1998) was a pioneering Brazilian artist whose work spanned painting, photography, engraving, graphic arts, and industrial design. Born in Chavantes, São Paulo, he began experimenting with photography at 16, using a homemade camera and manipulating negatives. Initially studying figurative and landscape painting under Clóvis Graciano and others, he later shifted to abstraction, influenced by European constructivism, Piet Mondrian, and the De Stijl movement. In 1946, he joined the Associaçião Paulista de Belas Artes and co-founded Grupo XV in 1948, a collective exploring Post-Impressionism.

De Barros's most famous work, *Fotoformas* (1946–1952), pioneered experimental abstract photography in Brazil, using multiple exposures and rotated images to capture urbanization's impact. His 1950 exhibition at the Museu de Arte de São Paulo marked a turning point in Brazilian photography. He later studied in Paris and Germany, focusing on lithography and concrete art, co-founding Grupo Ruptura in 1952 with other abstract artists. His work in concrete art reflected his interest in form and industrial design, influenced by Gestalt theory and Bauhaus principles.

In the 1950s and 1960s, De Barros founded furniture design companies Unilabor and Hobjeto, and collaborated with Nelson Leirner on pop art experiments. He also co-founded Galeria Rex, an art market experiment. Despite economic challenges leading to bankruptcy, these ventures showcased his innovative approach to design. Later, he returned to geometric art and industrial design, using materials like Formica.

De Barros abandoned photography for decades but resumed it in the 1990s after a series of health issues, creating *Sobras*, a final series of 250 works with assistance from photographer Ana Moraes. His legacy grew posthumously, with retrospectives in Europe and North America, including exhibitions in Switzerland, Germany, and the U.S. A 1999 documentary, *Sobras em Obras*, further cemented his influence.

He received awards at the São Paulo Biennials, including a First Prize for Graphic Design in 1952 and Acquisition Awards in 1953 and 1967. His work is held in major institutions like the Museum of Modern Art (São Paulo) and the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. Despite his contributions, his first U.S. exhibition occurred in 1998, just before his death. De Barros remains a central figure in Brazilian modernism, recognized for his interdisciplinary innovation and lasting impact on art and design.

title: Roman Šebrle
text:
Roman Šebrle, born on 26 November 1974 in Lanškroun, Czechoslovakia, is widely regarded as one of the greatest decathletes in history. Initially a high jumper, he transitioned to combined events and became a dominant force in the sport. In 2001, he set a world record in the decathlon with a score of 9,026 points at the Hypo-Meeting in Götzis, Austria, becoming the first athlete to surpass the 9,000-point barrier. This record stood for over eleven years and surpassed the previous best set by his compatriot, Tomáš Dvořák, in 1999.

Šebrle’s Olympic career was marked by both success and near-misses. He earned a silver medal in the 2000 Sydney Olympics after a controversial decision involving a discus throw by Estonian Erki Nool, which initially disqualified Nool but was later overturned. In 2004, he finally claimed Olympic gold in Athens, scoring 8,893 points and breaking the 20-year-old Olympic record set by Daley Thompson. His victory earned him the unofficial title of "World's Greatest Athlete." A panel of experts convened by the *Wall Street Journal* in 2008 also ranked him as the world's greatest athlete, though he finished sixth in the 2008 Beijing Olympics.

His early career was shaped by a childhood injury. At age six, he fractured his leg in a football match, requiring two months in a cast and a year to recover. He first competed in a decathlon in 1991, scoring 5,187 points, before being coached by Jiří Čechák, who convinced him to move schools and focus on athletics. In 1995, he joined the army sports club TJ Dukla Praha, where he trained under Zdeněk Váňa and later Dalibor Kupka. His military service earned him the rank of major after his 2004 Olympic victory.

Throughout his career, Šebrle achieved numerous accolades. He won gold at the 2007 World Championships in Osaka, silver in 2003 (Paris) and 2005 (Helsinki), and multiple medals in the heptathlon at World Indoor Championships, including gold in 2001 (Lisbon) and 2004 (Budapest). He also secured back-to-back European Championships victories in 2002 (Munich) and 2006 (Gothenburg). His consistency was unmatched, as he completed 40 decathlons with scores over 8,000 points and 20 over 8,500. His combined personal bests in individual disciplines totaled 9,326 points, the third-highest ever at the time.

In 2007, Šebrle suffered a near-fatal training accident when a javelin thrown by South African athlete Sunette Viljoen struck his shoulder, piercing 12 cm deep. Despite the shock, he removed the javelin himself and required only 11 stitches, though his training was briefly disrupted, particularly in the pole vault.

Outside of athletics, Šebrle studied at Gymnázium Františka Martina Pelcla in Rychnov nad Kněžnou and Gymnázium Pardubice before pursuing a degree in Information Science and Computer Technology. He married Eva Kasalová, a former Czech track athlete, in 2000, and they have two children: Štěpán, a professional footballer, and daughter Kateřina.

Šebrle was honored as the Best Czech Athlete of the Year five consecutive times (2002–2006) and received the Czech Sportsman of the Year title in 2004. His world record earned him the Guth-Jarkovský Trophy from the Czech Olympic Committee. His legacy as a decathlon pioneer and role model in Czech athletics remains unmatched.

title: Charles B. McVay III
text:
Charles Butler McVay III (1898–1968) was an American naval officer best known as the commanding officer of the USS *Indianapolis*, which was lost in action during World War II. He is the only U.S. Navy captain in history to be court-martialed for losing a ship sunk by enemy action, despite the fact that his vessel was on a top-secret mission under radio silence. The sinking of the *Indianapolis* on July 30, 1945, resulted in the deaths of 879 of the 1,195 crew members, making it one of the worst U.S. Navy disasters.

Born in Pennsylvania into a Navy family, McVay graduated from the U.S. Naval Academy in 1920. Before taking command of the *Indianapolis* in 1944, he served in key intelligence roles, including as chairman of the Joint Intelligence Committee of the Combined Chiefs of Staff. He had previously been awarded the Silver Star for bravery. During the war, he led the *Indianapolis* through major battles, including the invasions of Iwo Jima and Okinawa, where the ship was struck by a kamikaze but later repaired.

The *Indianapolis* was carrying nuclear materials for the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki when it was torpedoed by the Japanese submarine *I-58* under Commander Mochitsura Hashimoto. The ship sank in just 12 minutes. Survivors faced a harrowing four-day ordeal in the water, suffering from dehydration, shark attacks, and exposure. The delayed rescue was partly due to the Navy’s failure to act on received distress signals, as well as a misunderstanding of the ship’s overdue status.

McVay was wounded but survived the sinking. He was later court-martialed for failing to order the ship to zigzag and for not abandoning ship quickly enough, despite testimony from Hashimoto and American submarine experts that zigzagging would not have prevented the attack. The Navy’s decision to prosecute McVay remains controversial, as he was not informed of confirmed Japanese submarine activity in the area, and other commanders had ignored SOS signals. Admiral Ernest King, who harbored a personal grudge against McVay’s father, played a role in pushing for the trial. Though McVay was convicted, his sentence was later remitted, and he retired as a rear admiral in 1949. However, the stigma of the trial haunted him for the rest of his life, worsened by persistent harassment from the families of the lost sailors.

McVay struggled with depression and loneliness, especially after his wife’s death in 1961. On November 6, 1968, he died by suicide at his home in Connecticut. Years later, survivors of the *Indianapolis* and advocates, including a young student named Hunter Scott, successfully campaigned to clear McVay’s name. In 2000, Congress and President Bill Clinton posthumously exonerated him, acknowledging that he was unjustly blamed for the tragedy. The resolution was later entered into his official Navy records.

McVay’s story has been depicted in films and documentaries, including *Mission of the Shark: The Saga of the U.S.S. Indianapolis* (1991) and *USS Indianapolis: The Final Chapter* (2019). His legacy remains tied to the *Indianapolis* disaster, a tragic chapter in U.S. naval history that highlighted systemic failures and the unwarranted scapegoating of a dedicated officer.

title: Zié Ouattara
text:
Zié Mohamed Ouattara is a professional footballer from Ivory Coast, born on 9 January 2000. He plays primarily as a right-back and currently represents the Polish club Radomiak Radom. His football career began in his home country, where he was part of the youth setup at ASEC Mimosas, a well-known Ivorian football academy.
