In January 2018, he transferred to Portuguese club Vitória S.C., a significant step in his professional development. His professional debut came with Vitória B, the reserve team of Vitória S.C., in a LigaPro match against F.C. Penafiel on 9 December 2018. That game ended in a 3–2 defeat for his team, but it marked the start of his senior career.

Ouattara has also represented his national team at the youth level. He made his debut for the Ivory Coast U23 team in March 2019, participating in two qualification matches for the 2019 Africa U-23 Cup of Nations. His participation in this tournament was notable, as the Ivory Coast U23 team went on to finish as runners-up in the competition. This achievement highlights his involvement in a successful national team campaign, even at a young age.

His career has since seen him move to Poland, where he continues to play at the professional level. While the Wikipedia article does not provide extensive details about his time at Radomiak Radom, his journey from Ivory Coast to Europe reflects a common path for many African footballers seeking to develop their careers in top-tier leagues. His experience with Vitória S.C. and his involvement with the Ivory Coast U23 team demonstrate both his technical abilities and his potential for further growth in the sport.

Overall, Zié Ouattara’s career to date includes key milestones such as his youth development in Ivory Coast, his transition to European football, and his contribution to the national youth team. His role as a right-back suggests he brings defensive solidity and possibly attacking contributions to his teams. While the article does not delve deeply into his playing style or individual statistics, his career trajectory indicates a promising future in professional football.

title: Shakira
text:
Shakira Isabel Mebarak Ripoll, born on February 2, 1977, in Barranquilla, Colombia, is a globally celebrated singer-songwriter known as the "Queen of Latin Music." With a career spanning over three decades, she has significantly influenced Latin music, helping to popularize it on an international scale. Shakira has received numerous accolades, including four Grammy Awards and fifteen Latin Grammy Awards, with three wins in the Song of the Year category. Her music blends diverse cultural influences, particularly Middle Eastern and Western sounds, making her an artistic bridge between different regions.

Shakira's musical journey began at a young age. She signed her first record deal with Sony Music Colombia at 13, debuting with *Magia* (1991) and *Peligro* (1993), both of which underperformed commercially. However, her breakthrough came with *Pies Descalzos* (1995), which became a massive success, selling over 5 million copies. The album, produced in collaboration with Luis Fernando Ochoa, spawned hit singles like "Estoy Aquí" and "¿Dónde Estás Corazón?" and earned her three Billboard Latin Music Awards. This success was followed by *Dónde Están los Ladrones?* (1998), further solidifying her status in Latin music.

Shakira expanded her reach into the English-speaking market with *Laundry Service* (2001), which sold over 13 million copies worldwide, making it the best-selling album by a female Latin artist. The album featured hits like "Whenever, Wherever" and "Underneath Your Clothes." She continued to release successful Spanish-language albums, including *Fijación Oral, Vol. 1* (2005), *Sale el Sol* (2010), *El Dorado* (2017), and *Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran* (2024), all of which topped the *Billboard* Top Latin Albums chart, making her the first woman to achieve number-one albums across four different decades. Her English-language albums, such as *Oral Fixation, Vol. 2* (2005), *She Wolf* (2009), and *Shakira* (2014), also received platinum certifications in multiple countries.

Throughout her career, Shakira has written or co-written most of her music, showcasing her lyrical and melodic talent. Her discography includes iconic hits like "La Tortura," "Hips Don't Lie," "Waka Waka (This Time for Africa)," "Loca," and "Chantaje." She has collaborated with numerous artists and ventured into television, serving as a coach on *The Voice* (2013–2014) and voicing a character in the animated film *Zootopia* (2016). Additionally, she has been recognized for her humanitarian efforts, including founding the Barefoot Foundation, which focuses on children's education, and advocating for underrepresented groups. In 2011, she received the Latin Recording Academy Person of the Year and Harvard Foundation Artist of the Year awards, and in 2012, she was named a Chevalier of the Order of Arts and Letters by the French government.

Shakira's early life was marked by both personal and professional challenges. Her father's bankruptcy when she was eight forced her family to downsize, an experience that deeply influenced her. She began writing poetry at four and composed her first song, "Tus Gafas Oscuras," at eight, inspired by her father's grief. Despite facing rejection in school for her strong vibrato, she persevered, winning a talent show at ten. Her early performances in Barranquilla caught the attention of industry professionals, leading to her signing with Sony Music Colombia at 13.

Her breakthrough came after the success of "¿Dónde Estás Corazón?" in 1994, which led to the recording of *Pies Descalzos*. The album's success launched her international career, followed by extensive touring and further musical experimentation. Shakira's ability to merge different musical styles, combined with her powerful vocals and dynamic stage presence, has made her one of the world's best-selling musicians. Billboard named her the Top Female Latin Artist of the Decade twice (2000s and 2010s), highlighting her enduring impact on the music industry.

Beyond music, Shakira has been a vocal advocate for education, gender equality, and social justice, using her platform to support global causes. Her philanthropic work, combined with her musical achievements, has cemented her legacy as an influential artist and humanitarian. Shakira's journey from a young poet in Colombia to a global superstar reflects her resilience, creativity, and dedication to her craft.

title: Vasily Chuikov
text:
Vasily Ivanovich Chuikov (1900–1982) was a distinguished Soviet military commander and Marshal of the Soviet Union, best known for his leadership during the Battle of Stalingrad and his role in the fall of Berlin. Born into a poor peasant family in the Tula region, Chuikov left home at 12 to work in a factory in Saint Petersburg. After the Russian Revolution of 1917, he joined the Red Guards and later the Red Army, where he rose through the ranks during the Russian Civil War. He earned two Orders of the Red Banner for bravery and was wounded four times, including a severe injury that left a shrapnel fragment in his arm for life.

After the Civil War, Chuikov graduated from the Frunze Military Academy and was assigned to China as a military attaché, where he learned Chinese and studied Chinese politics. He later served in the Far East, supporting Soviet interests in the region. At the outbreak of World War II, he commanded the 4th Army during the Soviet invasion of Poland and the 9th Army in the Winter War against Finland. In 1940, he returned to China as a military advisor to Chiang Kai-shek, ensuring Chinese resistance against Japan to prevent a two-front war for the USSR.

In 1942, Chuikov was recalled to the Soviet Union to defend against the German invasion. He was appointed commander of the 62nd Army in Stalingrad, where he implemented a brutal yet effective strategy of keeping Soviet forces as close to German positions as possible, minimizing the effectiveness of German airpower and armor. His leadership and harsh disciplinary measures, including executing officers for cowardice, prevented the army’s collapse. Despite heavy losses, the 62nd Army held the city, forcing a German retreat and eventual encirclement. After Stalingrad, Chuikov led the 8th Guards Army through Poland and Germany, playing a key role in the liberation of Majdanek concentration camp and the capture of Berlin. On 2 May 1945, he personally accepted the surrender of German forces in Berlin.

After the war, Chuikov held high-ranking positions, including commander of Soviet forces in Germany, head of the Kiev Military District, and Deputy Minister of Defense. He was twice named a Hero of the Soviet Union and received the Distinguished Service Cross from the United States. He died in 1982 and was buried at the Stalingrad memorial on Mamayev Kurgan, a site of intense fighting during the war.

title: Carol Chell
text:
Carol Julia Chell, born in July 1941, is a British children's television presenter and TV executive who began her career as a teacher before transitioning into educational television in the 1960s. She is best remembered for her long tenure as a presenter on two iconic British children's programs: *Play School* (1966–1988) and *Play Away* (1971–1980). Chell's early education took place at Nottingham Girls' High School, a direct grant grammar school, where she grew up on Tudor Road in West Bridgford. She later attended the Royal Central School of Speech and Drama, which equipped her with the skills that would later serve her well in broadcasting.

Before entering television, Chell worked as a teacher at Pierrepont Secondary Modern School for Girls in Nottingham. During her time there, she crossed paths with Brian Clark, a future television writer known for *Telford's Change*. Her move into television came naturally, given her background in education and her training in speech and drama. Early in her career, she contributed to various educational TV shows, laying the groundwork for her later success.

Chell's most enduring work was her role as a presenter on *Play School*, a beloved British children's program that aired on the BBC. She was part of the show for over two decades, from 1966 until 1988, becoming a familiar face to generations of young viewers. Around the same time, she also co-presented *Play Away*, a companion series aimed at slightly older children, which ran from 1971 to 1980. Her warm and engaging presenting style made her a favorite among children, and her contributions helped shape early childhood television in the UK.

Beyond her work on *Play School* and *Play Away*, Chell appeared in other television projects, including a 1981 episode of *The Adventure Game*, a BBC quiz show where she played a "time-traveller" alongside other contestants. She also participated in the ATV schools series *Starting Out* in 1982. Later in her career, she took on an executive role at The Children's Channel, a satellite TV station, where she served as head of pre-school programming until the channel closed in 1998.

In her later years, Chell remained connected to children's television, appearing in a 2014 celebrity edition of *Pointless* on BBC One alongside Johnny Ball, another well-known figure from children's programming. This appearance allowed her to reconnect with audiences and celebrate her legacy in the industry.

Chell's personal life includes her marriage to Ian Price, which took place on October 9, 1965, at St Peter's Church in Tollerton, Nottinghamshire. At the time, she was 23 years old, and her parents resided in Christchurch, Dorset. The couple settled in Blackheath, London. Together, they have two daughters, Emily and Sophie, and six grandchildren. Her family life has been a significant part of her identity, complementing her successful career in television.

Throughout her career, Carol Chell demonstrated a deep commitment to children's programming, using her background in education and her natural charisma to create engaging and meaningful content for young audiences. Her work on *Play School* and *Play Away* left a lasting impact, and her contributions to children's television continue to be remembered fondly by those who grew up watching her.

title: Alen Omić
text:
Alen Omić, born on 6 May 1992, is a Slovenian professional basketball player who currently plays for Budućnost in both the Prva A Liga (Slovenian league) and the Adriatic League. His professional career began with Zlatorog Laško, where he played from 2009 to 2012, honing his skills for three seasons before moving to Union Olimpija. Omić signed a four-year contract with Olimpija in August 2012, marking a significant step in his early career.

In 2014, he participated in the NBA Summer League with the Brooklyn Nets, showcasing his talent on an international stage. The following year, he returned to the Summer League, this time representing the Denver Nuggets. His performances caught the attention of European clubs, leading to a two-year deal with Gran Canaria in August 2015. During his time with Gran Canaria, Omić made a strong impression, earning a spot on the All-EuroCup First Team for the 2015-16 season, a testament to his skill and impact on the court.

After his stint with Gran Canaria, Omić signed with Turkish powerhouse Anadolu Efes in June 2016. However, his time with Efes was short-lived, as he left the club in January 2017 to join Spanish team Unicaja for the remainder of the season. With Unicaja, Omić achieved a major milestone by winning the EuroCup after defeating Valencia Basket in the Finals, adding a championship to his resume.

Omić continued to move between top European teams, signing with Israeli club Hapoel Jerusalem in July 2017. However, he left Hapoel just six months later to join Serbian club Crvena zvezda for the rest of the 2017-18 season. The following year, in January 2019, he signed with Olimpia Milano, further expanding his experience in Europe’s elite leagues.

In June 2019, Omić joined Joventut Badalona in Spain’s Liga ACB, where he averaged 11.1 points and 6.5 rebounds per game. The next season, he moved to JL Bourg Basket in France’s LNB Pro A, improving his statistics with averages of 11.4 points, 9.0 rebounds, and 1.9 assists per game. In November 2021, he returned to Cedevita Olimpija, where he continued to excel, eventually breaking the ABA League’s all-time Offensive Rebounds record in May 2023 with 434 offensive rebounds in a single game.

Later that year, in August 2023, Omić signed with the Guangxi Rhinos in China’s National Basketball League, where he delivered impressive performances, averaging 19.43 points, 14.14 rebounds, and 3.57 assists per game over seven appearances. He later joined French team Metropolitans 92 in November 2023 before returning to Cedevita Olimpija in February 2024. Most recently, in October 2024, he signed with Budućnost, continuing his journey in professional basketball.

On the international stage, Omić made his debut for the Slovenian national team at the 2014 FIBA World Cup. He also represented Slovenia at EuroBasket 2015, where the team was eliminated in the eighth finals by Latvia. Throughout his career, Omić has demonstrated versatility and durability, playing across multiple top-tier European leagues and making significant contributions to each team he has joined. His ability to adapt and perform at a high level has solidified his reputation as a reliable and skilled player in European basketball.

title: Nick Kyrgios
text:
Nicholas Hilmy Kyrgios, born on 27 April 1995 in Canberra, Australia, is a professional tennis player known for his powerful and unpredictable playing style. His father, George, is of Greek origin, while his mother, Norlaila ("Nill"), is a former Malaysian princess who gave up her royal title when she moved to Australia. Kyrgios has two siblings, a sister named Halimah and a brother named Christos. He attended Radford College and Daramalan College in Canberra before focusing on tennis at the Australian Institute of Sport.

Kyrgios began his junior career in 2008, winning his first ITF junior title in Fiji in 2010. By 2012, he rose to junior world No. 3, winning doubles titles at the French Open and Wimbledon. In 2013, he claimed the Australian Open junior singles title and another Wimbledon junior doubles crown. His rapid rise led him to turn professional later that year.

His professional career took off in 2013, where he won his first Challenger title in Sydney and made his Grand Slam debut at the French Open, defeating former world No. 8 Radek Štěpánek. By the end of 2014, Kyrgios had reached the Wimbledon quarterfinals as a wildcard, defeating Rafael Nadal en route—a remarkable achievement for a debutant. This performance propelled him into the top 100 rankings.

In 2015, Kyrgios continued his ascent, reaching the Australian Open quarterfinals as a teenager, becoming the first male teen to achieve this since Roger Federer. He also reached his first ATP final in Estoril, though he lost to Richard Gasquet. Later that year, he upset world No. 2 Roger Federer in Madrid, saving two match points in a dramatic tiebreak.

2016 was a breakthrough year for Kyrgios. He won his first ATP title in Marseille, defeating Richard Gasquet and Marin Čilić. He also won the Hopman Cup with Daria Gavrilova, defeating Andy Murray in straight sets. Kyrgios reached his first Masters 1000 semifinal in Miami and won his second ATP title in Atlanta. By the end of the year, he had climbed to a career-high ranking of No. 13.

Kyrgios is known for his ability to defeat top players early in his career, becoming only the third player to beat all three members of the "Big Three" (Novak Djokovic, Roger Federer, and Rafael Nadal) in their first meetings. His aggressive, unfiltered personality and spectacular shot-making have made him both a fan favorite and a polarizing figure in tennis.

In doubles, Kyrgios has also found success, reaching a career-high ranking of No. 11 and winning the 2022 Australian Open with Thanasi Kokkinakis. His most notable singles achievement came at the 2022 Wimbledon Championships, where he reached his first Grand Slam final, though he lost to Novak Djokovic.

Kyrgios' career has been marked by both brilliance and inconsistency, often drawing attention for his outspoken nature and on-court antics. Despite this, his talent and achievements have cemented his place as one of Australia’s most exciting tennis players.

title: George Eacker
text:
George I. Eacker (c. 1774 – January 4, 1804) was a prominent New York lawyer best remembered for his fatal duel with Philip Hamilton, the eldest son of Alexander Hamilton, in 1801. Born in Palatine, New York, during the colonial era, Eacker was the son of Jacob Eacker, a German immigrant who fought in the American Revolution and later served as a county judge and state assemblyman, and Anna Margaret Finck. He had one younger brother, Jacob, and four sisters. Eacker attended a preparatory school in Schenectady and graduated from Columbia College in 1793, after which he studied law under Henry Brockholst Livingston, a future Supreme Court justice.

Eacker quickly established a successful legal career in New York City, gaining prominence in social and political circles. He lived on Wall Street, employed household staff, and became involved in Freemasonry, the militia, and the local fire brigade. In 1798, he faced legal trouble for an unspecified offense, possibly a duel, and was required to post a bond for good behavior. By 1801, he had been appointed a master in the New York Court of Chancery, the state’s highest court.

Eacker’s political alignment with Aaron Burr and the Democratic-Republicans placed him in opposition to Federalist leader Alexander Hamilton. In 1801, he delivered a Fourth of July oration in New York City, which some Federalists interpreted as criticizing Hamilton, though Eacker’s supporters claimed the speech was merely patriotic. This political tension escalated on November 20, 1801, when Eacker attended a play at the Park Theatre with his fiancée, Harriet Livingston. Philip Hamilton and Stephen Price approached him, loudly mocking him. Eacker responded with a severe insult, calling them "damned rascals," leading to two duels.

The first duel, against Stephen Price on November 22, 1801, ended without injury after four exchanged shots. The second duel, the next day, was with Philip Hamilton. After the men counted paces, Hamilton initially refused to fire, following his father’s advice to avoid firing first. Eacker, however, took aim and shot Hamilton above the hip, the bullet passing through his body and lodging in his arm. Hamilton, possibly in a reflexive action, fired his pistol into the air. Despite the severe wound, Hamilton survived the encounter but died the following day from his injuries.

Eacker continued his legal and civic duties after the duel, but in January 1802, he fought a fire in freezing conditions, becoming soaked and falling ill. This exposure worsened into tuberculosis, which ultimately caused his death on January 4, 1804, at the age of 30. His funeral was attended by military and Masonic groups, and he was buried in the graveyard of St. Paul’s Chapel. His fiancée, Harriet Livingston, later married the inventor Robert Fulton.

Eacker’s role in Philip Hamilton’s death was later dramatized in the 2015 Broadway musical *Hamilton*, where the song "Blow Us All Away" recounts the duel. Despite the tragic circumstances, Eacker never expressed regret for the duel, and his death was commemorated with military honors. His legacy remains tied to the Hamilton family’s history and the culture of dueling in early American politics.

title: Alice Torriani
text:
Alice Torriani is an accomplished Italian actor, author, and screenwriter, born on 25 March 1984. She is best known for her role as Andreina in the popular TV series *Il Paradiso delle Signore* (Ladies' Paradise) and for authoring the novel *L'altra Sete* (A Different Thirst). Torriani graduated from the prestigious Paolo Grassi Drama School in Milan in 2007, where she underwent rigorous training before embarking on a successful career.

After graduating, Torriani quickly gained recognition, landing the lead role in Chekhov’s *Three Sisters* under the direction of Massimo Castri. This performance took her on a year-long tour across Italy’s most renowned theaters. Following this success, she was cast in Gabriele Lavia’s adaptation of Dostoyevsky’s *Memoirs from the House of the Dead*. Shortly after, she starred in the film *Ten Winters* (2010), which earned the David di Donatello prize for Best Debut and the Silver Ribbon for Best First Work at the Venice Film Festival. Additionally, she participated in the European project “Prospero” with Latvian director Alvis Hermanis, performing in *The Young Ladies of Wilko* across multiple European cities, including Milan, Paris, Berlin, and Moscow.

Throughout her career, Torriani has appeared in several films, including *Ten Winters*, *E'nata una star* (based on Nick Hornby’s novel *Not a Star*), *D.A.D.*, and *Them Who?*. To refine her craft, she has attended workshops with prestigious directors such as Luca Ronconi and Antonio Latella, as well as acting studios in Los Angeles and New York. Between 2009 and 2013, she worked on various TV series and, in 2013-2014, starred in *Visita al padre* at Milan’s Piccolo Teatro di Milano. She also appeared in an episode of the popular Italian series *Montalbano*.

In 2014, she worked with acclaimed director Romeo Castellucci in *The Four Seasons Restaurant*, and in 2015, she took on a major role in the TV adaptation of *Il Paradiso delle Signore*, based on Émile Zola’s novel. She later collaborated with legendary comedian Franca Valeri in the play *Il cambio dei cavalli*. In 2016, she played Cristina Fabricetti in the fourth season of the TV series *Un Paso dal Cielo*.

Beyond acting, Torriani has also ventured into writing. Her debut novel, *L'altra Sete*, was published in 2015 and was selected to represent Italy at the Festival Européen du Premier Roman in Germany. In 2018, she published her second novel, *Una Vita a Posto*. Additionally, she co-wrote the screenplay for the 2017 TV series *Cleaning your Shit*, in which she also starred.

Torriani’s career reflects a dedication to both performance and storytelling, spanning theater, film, television, and literature. Her work has been recognized with prestigious awards, and she continues to be a prominent figure in Italian theater and cinema.

title: Albert Outler
text:
Albert Cook Outler (1908–1989) was a prominent American Methodist historian, theologian, and pastor who made significant contributions to Methodism, ecumenism, and theological scholarship in the 20th century. Born and raised in Georgia, he was ordained as a Methodist elder and served in various pastoral roles before pursuing higher education. He earned his Doctor of Philosophy from Yale University and taught at Duke University, Yale, and Southern Methodist University (SMU), where he spent much of his academic career. His teaching focused on Christian history, theology, doctrine, and Wesleyan studies.

Outler was a key figure in the ecumenical movement, serving as a delegate to the Consultation on Church Union and as an official observer representing Methodism at the Second Vatican Council. He also worked on the Faith & Order board of the World Council of Churches, furthering interdenominational dialogue and cooperation. His involvement in these initiatives highlighted his commitment to Christian unity and theological reconciliation.

Theologically, Outler is best known for his work on John Wesley, particularly his role in establishing Wesley as a significant theologian in the Western tradition. His 1964 book *John Wesley* in the *Library of Protestant Thought* series was groundbreaking, and his critical editions of Wesley’s sermons for the *Works of John Wesley* project were foundational for modern Wesleyan scholarship. Outler is credited with identifying Wesley’s theological method, which he termed the "Wesleyan Quadrilateral"—a framework that emphasizes Scripture, church tradition, reason, and personal experience as sources of theological discernment. This model has become central to Methodist doctrine, especially in the United Methodist Church, and Outler played a key role in shaping the denomination’s theological statement after its formation in 1968. Some scholars argue that his most original contribution was introducing the concept of "Tradition" into Wesleyan theology, which influenced later movements like paleo-orthodoxy and contemporary evangelicalism, particularly through the work of theologians like Thomas C. Oden.

Beyond Wesleyan studies, Outler wrote extensively on patrology (early Christian history), psychotherapy, and theology. His works included books like *Psychotherapy and the Christian Message* (1954) and *The Christian Tradition and the Unity We Seek* (1957), reflecting his interdisciplinary approach. Many of his writings were later compiled in the *Albert Outler Library* series, ensuring their continued influence. He also published numerous articles, such as "Pneumatology as an Ecumenical Frontier" (1989), which explored the role of the Holy Spirit in ecumenical dialogue.

Outler’s legacy endures through his scholarly contributions, his role in Methodist ecumenical efforts, and his lasting impact on Wesleyan theology. His work remains a cornerstone of Methodist thought, particularly his articulation of the Wesleyan Quadrilateral, which continues to shape theological education and practice in the United Methodist Church and beyond.

title: Gulshan Kumar
text:
Gulshan Kumar Dua, born on 5 May 1956, was a prominent Indian film and music producer and businessman, best known as the founder of T-Series, one of India's leading record labels in the Bollywood industry. Born into a Punjabi Hindu family in Delhi, his parents had migrated from Jhang in West Punjab after the 1947 partition of India. His father was a fruit juice vendor in Daryaganj, and Kumar began working with him at a young age. A devout Hindu, he was particularly devoted to Shiva and Vaishno Devi, even establishing a free meal service at the Vaishno Devi Temple in 1983, which continues to operate today under his son Bhushan Kumar’s management.

Kumar’s foray into the music business began when his family acquired a shop selling records and cassettes. Recognizing the potential of the industry, he launched "Super Cassettes Industries," which later became T-Series in 1983. Initially based in Noida, he later moved to Mumbai as his business expanded. His first Bollywood film production was *Lal Dupatta Malmal Ka* (1989), but his breakthrough came with *Aashiqui* (1990), a musical hit composed by Nadeem–Shravan. Other notable films he produced include *Bahaar Aane Tak*, *Dil Hai Ke Manta Nahin*, and *Meera Ka Mohan*.

Under Kumar’s leadership, T-Series became a dominant force in the Indian music industry. By 1991, its annual earnings had surged from ₹20 crore ($16 million) in 1985 to ₹200 crore ($88 million). By the time of his death, the company’s revenue had reached ₹500 crore ($140 million). T-Series controlled over 60% of the Indian music market and had a global presence, exporting to 24 countries. The label’s success was instrumental in revitalizing the Indian music industry in the 1990s.

Tragically, Gulshan Kumar was assassinated on 12 August 1997 outside the Jiteshwar Mahadev Mandir in Mumbai. Despite receiving two extortion threats earlier that month, he refused to pay the demanded money. The attack occurred when his usual bodyguard was absent due to illness. Shot 16 times, Kumar sought refuge in nearby huts, but residents refused to help. His driver, Suraj, was also wounded. The Mumbai underworld group D-Company was linked to the murder, with allegations that film composer Nadeem Saifi of Nadeem–Shravan had orchestrated the attack due to a personal dispute. However, in 2001, Abdul Rauf Merchant confessed to being the shooter. He was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2002, though he escaped in 2009 and was later extradited from Bangladesh in 2016.

Kumar’s legacy endures through T-Series, which remains a major player in the music and film industries. His family, including his brother Krishan Kumar, son Bhushan Kumar, and daughters Tulsi Kumar and Khushalii Kumar, continues to manage the business. In 2017, T-Series announced plans for a biographical film about him, titled *Mogul – The Gulshan Kumar Story*, further cementing his influence in Indian entertainment.

title: William M. Brodhead
text:
William M. Brodhead is a former American politician and lawyer who represented Michigan in the U.S. House of Representatives for four terms, serving from 1975 to 1983. Born on September 12, 1941, in Cleveland, Ohio, Brodhead attended elementary and high school in Cleveland before moving to Detroit. He earned a Bachelor of Arts degree from Wayne State University in 1965 and a Juris Doctor from the University of Michigan Law School in 1967. After being admitted to the Michigan Bar in 1968, he began practicing law in Detroit.

Brodhead entered politics in 1970 when he was elected to the Michigan House of Representatives, winning re-election in 1972. In 1974, he successfully ran for the U.S. House of Representatives in Michigan’s 17th District after the incumbent, Martha W. Griffiths, chose not to seek re-nomination. He was elected to the 94th Congress in 1974 and subsequently re-elected three more times, serving until 1983. During his tenure in Congress, Brodhead was a member of the House Ways and Means Committee and the Budget Committee. Additionally, he chaired the Democratic Study Group, a liberal caucus in the House.

Brodhead decided not to run for re-election in 1982 and returned to Detroit, where he joined the law firm Plunkett & Cooney as a partner, practicing law from 1983 to 2003. In 2003, he left the firm to practice independently until 2006, when he fully retired. Beyond his legal career, Brodhead was actively involved in various non-profit organizations in Michigan. He served on the boards of Detroit Public Television, Mt. Carmel Hospital, Michigan’s Children, and the Citizen’s Research Council. He held leadership roles as the board chair of several organizations, including the Skillman Foundation, Covenant House Michigan, Focus:Hope, and the Oakland Mediation Center.

In 1994, Brodhead made another political run, seeking the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senator. However, he lost the primary to Bob Carr, who ultimately lost the general election to Spencer Abraham. In his personal life, Brodhead married Kathleen in 1965, and they have two adult children and a granddaughter. After retiring, he moved to Northern California, where he served on the board of directors for Covenant House, California.

title: Félix María Zuloaga
text:
Félix María Zuloaga Trillo (1813–1895) was a prominent Mexican conservative general and politician who played a pivotal role in the Reform War (1857–1861), a conflict between liberal and conservative factions over Mexico's future. Born on 31 March 1803 in Álamos, Sonora, Zuloaga came from a modest background, the son of Manuel José de Zuloaga and María Anna Gertrudis Trillo. His military career began in 1834 when he was appointed colonel of the national guard, leading campaigns against Indigenous groups until 1837. He later defended the government during the Federalist Revolt of 1840, which sought to restore the 1824 Constitution, and in 1841, he was promoted to captain. He fought in the Caste Wars in Yucatán and later in Tabasco, where he was granted the rank of lieutenant colonel.

During the Mexican-American War (1846–1848), Zuloaga oversaw fortifications in Monterrey and Saltillo and contributed to Mexico City's defenses. After retiring briefly in 1848, he returned to politics as an alderman in Chihuahua before rejoining the military in 1853. He participated in President Santa Anna’s campaigns against liberal revolutionaries, including the Plan of Ayutla, which overthrew Santa Anna’s dictatorship in 1855. After the liberal victory, Zuloaga joined the government of Ignacio Comonfort, a moderate liberal, and was entrusted with suppressing a conservative rebellion in Puebla.

However, tensions escalated when the liberal-dominated Congress approved the 1857 Constitution, which imposed secular reforms, including the Ley Lerdo, which forced the Catholic Church and Indigenous communities to sell communal lands. Conservatives, including Zuloaga, opposed these changes. In December 1857, Zuloaga and other conservatives drafted the Plan of Tacubaya, which sought to suspend the 1857 Constitution and establish a more conservative government. Comonfort initially accepted the plan but later resigned, passing the presidency to Benito Juárez, a liberal. Zuloaga then seized control of Mexico City, dissolved Congress, and arrested Juárez, who later escaped.

On 22 January 1858, a conservative junta declared Zuloaga president. His government was recognized by most foreign powers except the United States. He immediately reversed liberal reforms, nullifying the Ley Lerdo and restoring church properties, while also reinstating civil servants who had refused to swear loyalty to the 1857 Constitution. Despite early military successes, including capturing Guanajuato and San Luis Potosí, the conservatives struggled to secure a decisive victory. The liberals, led by Juárez, remained entrenched in Veracruz, and the conservatives were divided into factions, including the Santanistas (supporters of Santa Anna), the Zuloaguistas, and the Fusionists, who favored compromise.

In December 1858, a moderate conservative faction overthrew Zuloaga, hoping to negotiate with the liberals. Manuel Robles Pezuela briefly became president, but when Juárez rejected compromise, the conservatives elected Miguel Miramón as their leader. Zuloaga initially supported Miramón but later retreated from politics. After the Reform War ended in 1861 with a liberal victory, Zuloaga briefly tried to reclaim power but failed and went into exile in Cuba. He returned during the Second Mexican Empire (1864–1867) but played no significant role. After the empire’s fall, he returned to Mexico, living in obscurity until his death in 1895. Zuloaga’s presidency, though short-lived, marked a critical phase in Mexico’s struggle between liberal reform and conservative resistance.

title: Frank Middlemass
text:
Frank Middlemass (28 May 1919 – 8 September 2006) was an English actor with a long and distinguished career in theatre, television, film, and radio. Born in Eaglescliffe, County Durham, he was raised in Newcastle upon Tyne and educated in Stockton-on-Tees. At 19, he joined the army and was wounded during the Dunkirk retreat. He left the military at 30, having risen to the rank of lieutenant colonel.

Middlemass began his acting career in repertory theatre in Penzance, Cornwall, before joining the Old Vic Company. With them, he toured extensively across North and South America, Australia, New Zealand, Israel, Lebanon, Russia, Poland, and the Far East. Among his notable roles was playing opposite Vivien Leigh in a production of *Twelfth Night*. In the 1960s, he toured with Ian McKellen’s Actors’ Company and performed at the Nottingham Playhouse, appearing alongside Peter O’Toole in *Waiting for Godot*.

His television debut came in 1958 in *Dixon of Dock Green*, followed by appearances in *Z-Cars*, *Softly, Softly*, *The Avengers*, and *Jackanory*. Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, he featured in *Doctor at Large*, *War and Peace* (where he played General Mikhail Kutuzov), *Crown Court*, *Last of the Summer Wine*, *Ripping Yarns*, *Upstairs, Downstairs*, *Poldark*, *The Sweeney*, and *Emmerdale Farm*. He also had a role in Stanley Kubrick’s *Barry Lyndon* (1975) as Sir Charles Lyndon.

Middlemass’s first leading television role was in *To Serve Them All My Days* (1980), where he played Algy Herries. He later appeared in the BBC’s *King Lear* as The Fool and in *The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes* (both the BBC and Granada adaptations). His other notable TV roles included *Yes Minister*, *Only When I Laugh*, *Oliver Twist*, *Miss Marple*, and *Heartbeat*, where he played Dr. Alex Ferrenby in 20 episodes between 1992 and 1993. His most enduring role, however, was as Rocky Hardcastle in *As Time Goes By*, a part he played from 1993 to 2002, including two reunion specials in 2005.

In addition to television, Middlemass was active in radio, most notably as Dan Archer in *The Archers* from 1982 to 1986. He also contributed to radio plays and albums, including *The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy* and *Carol and the Advent Calendar*. His film roles included *Otley* (1968), *Frankenstein Must Be Destroyed* (1969), *Madame Sin* (1972), *Dreamchild* (1985, as the voice of the Caterpillar), and *Mrs Caldicot’s Cabbage War* (2002).

A member of the Royal Shakespeare Company from 1984, he performed in *Romeo and Juliet*, *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*, and *Love’s Labour’s Lost*, among other classic plays. Even in his later years, he continued acting, appearing in *The Importance of Being Earnest* and touring with a one-man show called *Frankly Speaking*. His final television appearances were in *Kavanagh QC*, *Casualty*, and *Midsomer Murders* (2005).

Middlemass never married and lived for 40 years in the home of his close friend, actor Geoffrey Toone, who died in 2005. Despite occasional misunderstandings about their relationship, they were not romantic partners. Middlemass passed away in September 2006 at the age of 87 in Northwood, London.

title: Annie Landouw
text:
Annie Landouw, born in 1913 in Surakarta, Central Java, was a prominent Indonesian keroncong singer and film actress. She lost her sight as a child due to a prolonged illness and was later adopted by her aunt and uncle. Her career began in 1927 when she won a singing competition at a night fair in Surakarta, catching the attention of Beka, a recording company, which signed her shortly after. She then moved to Batavia (now Jakarta), the capital of the Dutch East Indies, where her popularity quickly grew.

By 1938, Landouw had joined the NIROM radio troupe, where she performed keroncong, a traditional Indonesian musical genre. The following year, she became part of Hugo Dumas' troupe Lief Java. Around this time, she also entered the film industry, initially as a vocalist. In 1938, she provided the vocals for *Fatima*, a film by Tan's Film, and repeated this role in 1939 for *Gagak Item* (Black Raven). That same year, she made her onscreen debut in *Siti Akbari*. Her acting career continued with appearances in *Sorga Ka Toedjoe* (Seventh Heaven) in 1940 and *Roekihati* in the same year.

Landouw's talent as a keroncong singer made her widely admired. In 1940, she was scheduled to undergo eye surgery, and her fans organized a fundraising campaign to help cover the costs. However, she ultimately declined the financial assistance. After Indonesia gained independence, she continued her musical career but did not act in any further films. She passed away on 17 August 1982.

Some scholars, such as music expert Peter Keppy, speculate that Landouw's fame as a keroncong singer may have influenced the character of Yah in Armijn Pane's 1940 novel *Belenggu*. In the novel, Yah is a celebrated keroncong singer who performs under the stage name Siti Hayati, suggesting a possible connection to Landouw's real-life success in the genre.

title: Felician of Foligno
text:
Felician of Foligno, also known as San Feliciano di Foligno, was a Christian saint and the patron saint of the city of Foligno in Italy. Born around 160 in Forum Flaminii, a town located on the Via Flaminia (now known as San Giovanni Profiamma), he came from a Christian family. As a young man, he studied under Pope Eleuterus and later became a prominent evangelist, preaching in several cities across Italy, including Foligno, Spello, Bevagna, Assisi, Perugia, Norcia, Plestia, Trevi, and Spoleto. His missionary work was instrumental in spreading Christianity in the region.

Around 204, Felician was consecrated as the first bishop of Foligno by Pope Victor I, a position that granted him significant religious authority. One of his notable accomplishments as a bishop was ordaining Valentine of Terni as a priest. His tenure as bishop lasted over 50 years, making him one of the first and longest-serving Christian bishops in northern Italy. His leadership and dedication to the faith earned him great respect among his followers.

In his old age, Felician was arrested at the age of 94 during the persecutions of the Roman Emperor Decius. His refusal to renounce his Christian faith and participate in pagan sacrifices led to his imprisonment. While in custody, he was visited by one of his disciples, Messalina of Foligno, who provided him with support. Despite his advanced age, Felician endured severe torture and scourging. He ultimately died en route to Rome, where he was to be executed, outside the city of Foligno.

After his death, a church was constructed over his burial site in Foligno, serving as a place of veneration for centuries. However, his relics were later moved multiple times. In 970, some of his relics were transferred to Metz, while in 965, others were taken to Minden in Germany. This relocation led to a historical misconception, as Felician was mistakenly believed to have been a bishop of Minden, resulting in a separate feast day on October 20 being attributed to him in the Roman Martyrology. Some of his relics were eventually returned to Foligno between 1673 and 1674, allowing his followers to honor him in his original diocese. Today, Foligno Cathedral houses a statue of the saint, crafted by the renowned sculptor Giovanni Battista Maini, further solidifying his legacy in the region.

Felician’s life was marked by his unwavering faith, his role as a spiritual leader, and his martyrdom. His contributions to early Christianity in Italy, particularly in central and northern regions, remain significant. His veneration continues through various religious artifacts and institutions, ensuring that his memory endures as a symbol of devotion and perseverance.

title: Jo Koy
text:
Joseph Glenn Herbert, known professionally as Jo Koy, is an American stand-up comedian and actor born on June 2, 1971. His parents were an American father, John C. Herbert, who was stationed in Japan with the U.S. Air Force, and a Filipina mother, Josie Harrison. His stepfather, Fredrick Harrison, also played a significant role in raising him. The family moved from Spanaway, Washington, to Tacoma, Washington, before eventually relocating to Las Vegas to be near his ailing grandmother. Koy attended Spanaway Lake High School and Foss High School before enrolling at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, though he dropped out to pursue a career in stand-up comedy. His stage name, "Koy," originated from a childhood nickname. During a 1989 conversation with his cousin, his aunt called him to dinner, yelling "Jo Ko, eat!"—a phrase meaning "my Jo" in Tagalog, which he misheard as "Koy" and adopted as his professional name.

Koy’s comedy career spans over three decades, beginning with open mic nights and leading to regular gigs, including appearances at the MGM Grand Hotel and Casino’s Catch a Rising Star. He took initiative by renting the Huntridge Theater in Las Vegas and selling tickets door-to-door to promote his shows. His prominence grew through frequent appearances on E!’s *Chelsea Lately*, where he became a regular guest, boosting his visibility in the U.S. He hosts a weekly podcast, *The Koy Pond*, where he discusses various topics with fellow comedians. Koy has released six comedy specials, including *Jo Koy: Comin’ in Hot* (2019) and *Jo Koy: In His Elements* (2020), the latter featuring Filipino American comedians, DJs, and B-boys. His 2020 *Just Kidding World Tour* took him to the United Arab Emirates, Australia, New Zealand, and the Philippines.

In 2024, Koy hosted the 81st Golden Globe Awards, a role that drew significant criticism. His monologue was widely panned, with reviewers calling it awkward and distasteful. Many jokes failed to land, and his decision to blame his writers during the strike’s aftermath was poorly received. Some jokes, particularly those targeting *Barbie*, Taylor Swift, Meryl Streep, and Robert De Niro, were met with groans and boos. The audience’s disapproval was notable, with stars like Selena Gomez and Helen Mirren visibly reacting. Koy later admitted the backlash hurt but defended his performance, stating he enjoyed the experience despite the challenges of hosting. Fellow comedians, including Steve Martin and Whoopi Goldberg, expressed sympathy, acknowledging the difficulty of the role.

Koy has cited Bill Cosby, Eddie Murphy, Robin Williams, Billy Crystal, Whoopi Goldberg, Chris Rock, and Steve Martin as his comedy influences. In 2022, he was named one of the "75 Most Influential Filipino-Americans." His personal life includes a past marriage to Filipino-American singer Angie King, with whom he has a son, Joseph Jr., born in 2003. He was previously in a relationship with Chelsea Handler from 2021 to 2022. As of 2023, he lived in Los Angeles, while his son split time between his and his mother’s homes, which are just one block apart. His stepfather, a retired Army sergeant who received multiple honors, including two Purple Hearts and two Bronze Stars, passed away in 2023. Koy’s mother supports the Republican Party, but he avoids political commentary in his comedy. Additionally, Koy practices Brazilian jiu-jitsu and, in 2023, got a tattoo by a traditional Filipino tattoo artist in Baguio, Philippines.

title: Zhang Yaokun
text:
Zhang Yaokun, born on April 17, 1981, is a retired Chinese professional footballer. His career began in 1998 with Dalian Shide, where he initially struggled to secure a regular position due to an ankle fracture. However, after recovering from his injury, he became a key player in Dalian’s defense, contributing to their dominance in Chinese football. During his time with Dalian, he won multiple league titles in the 2001 and 2002 seasons, as well as the Chinese FA Cup in 2001. The team also secured the Chinese FA Super Cup in 2000 and 2002. After a disappointing 2004 season for Dalian, manager Vladimir Petrović loaned Zhang to Sichuan Guancheng for the 2005 season, where he quickly became a crucial player. He returned to Dalian the following year and eventually became the team’s captain.

In December 2012, Zhang transferred to Guangzhou R&F, another Chinese Super League team. He made his debut for the club on March 9, 2013, in a 4-2 loss against Liaoning Whowin. In February 2017, he moved to League One side Wuhan Zall, where he played until his retirement. After helping Wuhan Zall secure promotion to the Chinese Super League in 2018, Zhang announced his retirement from professional football on November 12, 2018.

On the international stage, Zhang was selected for the Chinese national team for the 2004 AFC Asian Cup, where he appeared as a substitute and played in various defensive positions. He remained a regular in the national squad and was part of the team that qualified for the 2007 AFC Asian Cup. During that tournament, he formed a strong defensive partnership with Li Weifeng, serving as the first-choice center back pairing.

Throughout his career, Zhang accumulated an impressive list of honors. With Dalian Shide, he won the Chinese Jia-A League four times (1998, 2000, 2001, 2002), the Chinese FA Cup in 2001, and the Chinese FA Super Cup twice (2000, 2002). With Wuhan Zall, he won the China League One title in 2018. Additionally, he contributed to China’s victory in the 2005 East Asian Football Championship. Individually, he was recognized as part of the Chinese Super League Team of the Year in 2004.

Zhang Yaokun’s career was marked by resilience, leadership, and success at both the club and international levels, making him a notable figure in Chinese football history.

title: Profit (gamer)
text:
Park Joon-yeong, known professionally as Profit, was a highly accomplished South Korean *Overwatch* player who retired in February 2024. Born on November 19, 1999, in Jinju, South Korea, he began his professional career in April 2017 with the team GC Busan. His breakthrough came during *OGN APEX Season 4*, where he played a crucial role in leading GC Busan to victory in the best-of-seven finals against RunAway. Park was named the APEX Finals most valuable player (MVP) after recording 134 kills and only 55 deaths in the series. He later contributed to GC Busan’s win at the 2017 APAC Premier finals in China, solidifying his reputation as a top-tier player.

In November 2017, Park, along with his entire GC Busan roster, signed with the London Spitfire in the newly formed *Overwatch League* (OWL). The 2018 season marked his most successful year in the league. Early on, he was fined $1,000 for an on-camera gesture, though he claimed it was a response to a joke made by his teammates off-camera. Despite this, his play remained dominant. The Spitfire advanced to the Stage 1 Finals, where Park contributed to 38.2% of his team’s kills in a 3–2 victory over the New York Excelsior. By the end of the regular season, he was the highest-rated damage (DPS) player across all heroes. In the playoffs, he averaged 8,790 damage per 10 minutes in the quarterfinals and semifinals, ranking second overall. The Spitfire reached the 2018 Grand Finals, where Park delivered a standout performance, including securing five final blows as Tracer in the final map to clinch the first game of the series. His exceptional play earned him the Grand Finals MVP award, and the Spitfire won the inaugural OWL championship. In recognition of his contributions, the team retired his number 13 jersey on January 15, 2020.

In October 2019, Park was traded to the Seoul Dynasty, joining teammates Hong "Gesture" and Choi "Bdosin." During the 2020 season, he became the first OWL player to reach 10,000 total eliminations. The Dynasty made a strong playoff run but ultimately lost 4–2 to the San Francisco Shock in the Grand Finals. The 2022 season saw Park win the Kickoff Clash, the league’s first midseason tournament, after defeating the Philadelphia Fusion in the finals. He was also awarded a Role Star commendation and was a finalist for the regular season MVP. However, in the playoffs, the Dynasty faced an early exit after Park was experimented with as the support hero Kiriko—a role outside his usual DPS specialization—in a losing match against the San Francisco Shock.

Following the dissolution of the *Overwatch League*, the Seoul Dynasty released its entire roster in October 2023. Park announced his retirement from esports on February 20, 2024, ending a career marked by championship wins, individual accolades, and a lasting impact on the competitive *Overwatch* scene.

title: Bhāskara I
text:
Bhāskara I was a 7th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer who made significant contributions to both fields. Born around 600 CE, he is best known for his work on the Hindu-Arabic decimal system, where he was the first to write numbers using a circle to represent zero. His writings indicate that he likely received his early education from his father and may have been born in the Saurastra region of Gujarat, later moving to other parts of India, including Aśmaka. Bhāskara was a prominent scholar of Aryabhata's astronomical school, alongside Brahmagupta, and both are celebrated as key figures in Indian mathematics, particularly for their work on fractions.

One of Bhāskara's most notable achievements was his use of a positional numeral system, which was truly innovative compared to earlier methods. Before his time, Indian astronomers represented numbers through words or allegories, such as using "moon" for 1 or "eyes" for 2, arranged in a reverse order of powers of ten (higher powers to the right). Bhāskara, however, introduced a system where numerals were written in descending order from left to right, similar to the modern decimal system. He used the first nine Brahmi numerals, with a small circle for zero, and explicitly stated numerical values in his works, making his system more precise and widely applicable.

Bhāskara's most famous work is his commentary on Aryabhata's *Āryabhaṭīya*, titled *Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya*, completed in 629 CE. This work is one of the oldest known prose texts in Sanskrit on mathematics and astronomy. In it, he provided detailed explanations of the 33 verses from Aryabhata's treatise that dealt with mathematics, emphasizing the importance of proving scientific principles rather than relying on tradition. His other major works include the *Mahābhāskarīya* ("Great Book of Bhāskara") and the *Laghubhāskarīya* ("Small Book of Bhāskara"), both of which focused on mathematical astronomy.

In the *Mahābhāskarīya*, Bhāskara presented a groundbreaking approximation for the sine function, which he attributed to Aryabhata. His formula, \(\sin x \approx \frac{16x(\pi - x)}{5\pi^2 - 4x(\pi - x)}\), for \(0 \leq x \leq \pi\), has a maximum error of only 1.859%, demonstrating remarkable precision for its time. He also explored relationships between sine and cosine and provided methods for calculating trigonometric values for angles beyond 90 degrees. Bhāskara was one of the first to solve equations now recognized as Pell's equations, such as \(8x^2 + 1 = y^2\), and he clearly understood that π was irrational, criticizing approximations like \(\sqrt{10}\) used by Jain mathematicians. Additionally, he was the first to discuss quadrilaterals with four unequal, nonparallel sides.

In astronomy, Bhāskara's *Mahābhāskarīya* covered topics such as planetary longitudes, conjunctions, lunar phases, eclipses, and planetary risings and settings. His work was later translated into Arabic, spreading his ideas beyond India. The Indian Space Research Organisation honored Bhāskara's legacy by naming its first satellite, Bhāskara I, launched in 1979. Despite the limited details of his personal life, Bhāskara's mathematical and astronomical contributions remain influential, marking him as a pioneering figure in the history of science.

title: Damon Herriman
text:
Damon Herriman is an Australian actor born on 31 March 1970 in Adelaide, South Australia. He began his acting career at a young age, appearing in local television commercials at eight and landing a significant role as Frank Errol in *The Sullivans* at ten. His early career included roles in Australian series such as *The Patchwork Hero*, *Sara Dane*, *For the Term of His Natural Life*, and *Taurus Rising*, earning him three Logie Award nominations. He also starred in *The Flying Doctors*, for which he won the Penguin Award for Excellence in a Performance by a Juvenile, and the children's miniseries *Elly & Jools*.

Herriman continued his career with notable roles in Australian productions, including *The Big Steal*, where he played Mark Jorgensen, the best friend of Ben Mendelsohn’s character. He has also worked in film, television, and theatre, as well as writing and directing short films, such as *They* and *The Date*. He won the Best Screenplay award at Flickerfest in 2004 for *Soar*, in which he also performed. Additionally, he contributed to the ABC sketch comedy series *The Elegant Gentleman's Guide to Knife Fighting* as both a performer and writer.

Throughout his career, Herriman has appeared in a variety of Australian projects, including *Love My Way*, *Laid*, *100 Bloody Acres*, *The Outlaw Michael Howe*, *INXS: Never Tear Us Apart*, *The Little Death*, *Down Under*, *Secret City*, *Mr Inbetween*, *The Eleven O'Clock*, *Riot*, *The Nightingale*, and *Lambs of God*. In 2019, he won the AACTA Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role for his performance in *Judy and Punch*.

His American career began in 2004 with a role in the horror film *House of Wax*. Since then, he has appeared in numerous U.S. productions, including *The Unit*, *Redbelt*, *Breaking Bad*, *Wilfred*, *Cold Case*, and *Vegas*, where he played the hitman Mr. Jones. He also appeared in *J. Edgar* (2011) as Bruno Hauptmann, the convicted kidnapper of the Lindbergh baby, and in *The Lone Ranger* (2013) as a member of the Cavendish gang. Other notable roles include Buddy in *Quarry*, Romeo in *Flesh and Bone*, and Charles Manson in both *Mindhunter* (2019) and *Once Upon a Time in Hollywood* (2019). In 2021, he voiced Kabal in *Mortal Kombat*, while stuntman Daniel Nelson portrayed the character in the suit.

Herriman has received critical acclaim for his performances, including an AACTA nomination for Best Supporting Actor for *The Nightingale* (2018) and a win for Best Leading Actor for *Judy and Punch* (2019). In 2018, he was honored with the Orry-Kelly Award, recognizing his contributions to Australia's national identity through his work. Beyond acting, he has also contributed to music, appearing in the 2015 song "Raining Gold" by ARO (Aimee Osbourne). His extensive and varied career has solidified his reputation as a versatile and respected actor in both Australian and international entertainment.

title: Liam Neeson
text:
Liam Neeson, born William John Neeson on 7 June 1952 in Ballymena, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, is a celebrated actor who has earned numerous accolades, including nominations for an Academy Award, a BAFTA, three Golden Globes, and two Tony Awards. In 2020, he was ranked seventh on *The Irish Times*' list of Ireland's 50 Greatest Film Actors. Recognized for his contributions to film and theatre, he was appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in 2000.

Neeson’s early acting career began in the 1970s, performing with the Lyric Players’ Theatre in Belfast. His first film role was in *Pilgrim’s Progress* (1978), followed by notable early performances in *Excalibur* (1981), *The Bounty* (1984), and *The Mission* (1986). His career gained momentum in 1993 when he portrayed Oskar Schindler in Steven Spielberg’s *Schindler’s List*, earning an Academy Award nomination for Best Actor. This role solidified his reputation as a serious dramatic actor, leading to lead roles in films like *Nell* (1994), *Rob Roy* (1995), and *Michael Collins* (1996), the latter earning him a Golden Globe nomination and the Volpi Cup for Best Actor at the Venice Film Festival.

Neeson also starred in major blockbusters, including *Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace* (1999) as Qui-Gon Jinn and *Batman Begins* (2005) as Ra’s al Ghul. He voiced Aslan in *The Chronicles of Narnia* trilogy (2005–2010) and appeared in films like *Gangs of New York* (2002), *Love Actually* (2003), and *Kinsey* (2004). His stage work includes Tony-nominated performances in *Anna Christie* (1992) and *The Crucible* (2002), as well as his portrayal of Oscar Wilde in *The Judas Kiss* (1998).

In the 2000s, Neeson transitioned into action films, becoming an iconic action star with the *Taken* series (2008–2014) and collaborations with director Jaume Collet-Serra, including *Unknown* (2011), *Non-Stop* (2014), *Run All Night* (2015), and *The Commuter* (2018). He also starred in dramas like *Silence* (2016), *A Monster Calls* (2016), and *Ordinary Love* (2019).

Born into a working-class Catholic family in a predominantly Protestant town, Neeson grew up feeling like a "second-class citizen" but avoided political activism until the Troubles influenced his awareness of local history. He trained as a boxer in his youth and briefly pursued football before turning to acting. After studying physics and computer science at Queen’s University Belfast, he left to work at the Guinness Brewery before dedicating himself to acting.

Neeson’s career reflects a balance of prestige drama and commercial success, with a legacy spanning film, theatre, and voice acting. His ability to command both intense dramatic roles and action-packed performances has made him one of Ireland’s most respected actors.

title: Neha Sargam
text:
Neha Dubey, professionally known as Neha Sargam, is an Indian actress and singer who has made a mark in both television and theater. She first gained attention as a contestant on *Indian Idol 4* in 2009, though her journey in the singing competition began earlier. She had initially auditioned for *Indian Idol 2* but was eliminated in the second round after forgetting the lyrics of her song. Despite this setback, she returned to *Indian Idol 4* and performed more successfully, establishing herself in the entertainment industry.

Sargam’s television career includes notable roles in several popular shows. She played the lead role of Sita in *Ramayan* on Zee TV, a modern adaptation of the classic epic. Additionally, she portrayed the character Diya in *Iss Pyaar Ko Kya Naam Doon? Ek Baar Phir*, a romantic drama. She also appeared in *Chand Chupa Badal Mein* on Star Plus, *Doli Armano Ki* on Zee TV, and *Punar Vivaah - Zindagi Milegi Dobara*, where she had a cameo role. In *Paramavatar Shri Krishna*, she took on the role of Lakshmi, further showcasing her versatility as an actress. Other notable appearances include *Yeh Hai Aashiqui*, a series that explores various love stories.

Beyond television, Sargam has also ventured into theater, performing in lead roles in two major musical productions. She starred in *Mughal-E-Azam the Musical*, a celebrated stage adaptation of the classic film, directed by Feroz Abbas Khan and produced by the Shapoorji Pallonji Group. She also participated in *Raunaq and Jassi*, another musical produced by BookMyShow and directed by the same director. These roles allowed her to showcase her talents as both an actor and a singer.

In recent years, Sargam expanded her career into web series, gaining recognition for her role as Saloni Tyagi in *Mirzapur* seasons 2 and 3. The show, known for its intense storytelling and strong performances, further solidified her presence in the digital space.

Throughout her career, Neha Sargam has demonstrated versatility, excelling in singing, acting, and stage performances. From her early days in *Indian Idol* to her roles in television dramas and musical theater, she has carved out a notable place in the Indian entertainment industry. Her work in *Mirzapur* and other projects continues to highlight her growing influence as an artist.

title: Feroze Gandhi
text:
Feroze Jehangir Gandhi, born on 12 September 1912 in Bombay, was an Indian freedom fighter, politician, and journalist who played a significant role in the country's independence movement and post-independence politics. Born into a Parsi family, he was the youngest of five children, with his ancestors originally from Bharuch in South Gujarat. After his father’s death in the early 1920s, Feroze and his mother moved to Allahabad to live with his maternal aunt, a surgeon. He attended Vidya Mandir High School and later Ewing Christian College in Prayagraj before pursuing higher education at the London School of Economics, where he earned a B.Sc. degree.

Feroze Gandhi’s political journey began in the early 1930s when he joined the Indian independence movement. He first met Indira Nehru (later his wife) and her mother Kamala Nehru during a protest outside his college. Impressed by their activism, he abandoned his studies to participate in the movement. He was imprisoned multiple times, including a 19-month detention in Faizabad Jail alongside Lal Bahadur Shastri. He also participated in the agrarian no-rent campaign in the United Provinces (now Uttar Pradesh), leading to further imprisonments in 1932 and 1933.

Feroze developed a close relationship with the Nehru family, particularly Kamala Nehru, whom he supported during her illness, accompanying her to sanatoriums in India and Europe. He later married Indira Nehru in 1942, adopting the surname "Gandhi" as a tribute to Mahatma Gandhi. Both were arrested during the Quit India Movement in 1942, and Feroze spent a year in Allahabad’s Naini Central Prison. After their release, they settled in Allahabad and had two sons, Rajiv and Sanjay, born in 1944 and 1946, respectively.

Post-independence, Feroze became managing director of *The National Herald*, a newspaper founded by Jawaharlal Nehru. He entered politics as a member of the provincial parliament (1950–1952) and later won a seat in the Lok Sabha in 1952 from Rae Bareli, Uttar Pradesh, with Indira Gandhi serving as his campaign organizer. Feroze earned a reputation as a fearless critic of corruption, exposing financial irregularities involving prominent business figures. In 1955, he revealed how Ram Kishan Dalmia misused public funds, and in 1958, he uncovered the Haridas Mundhra scandal, involving the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), which led to the resignation of Finance Minister T. T. Krishnamachari. He also advocated for the nationalization of LIC and other industries, challenging even powerful conglomerates like TATA Engineering.

Despite his political clashes with his father-in-law’s government, Feroze was respected across party lines. However, his health deteriorated after suffering a heart attack in 1958. He died on 8 September 1960 at Willingdon Hospital in Delhi following a second heart attack. His legacy includes his contributions to anti-corruption efforts and his influence on Indian politics. His Rae Bareli constituency was later represented by his wife, Indira Gandhi, and his daughter-in-law, Sonia Gandhi. A higher education institution in Rae Bareli and an NTPC thermal power plant were named in his honor. His life remains an important but often overlooked chapter in India’s political history.

title: Takuma Asano
text:
Takuma Asano is a Japanese professional footballer born on 10 November 1994, who currently plays as a forward for La Liga club Mallorca and the Japan national team. His younger brother, Yuya, is also a professional footballer, playing for Nagoya Grampus in the J1 League. Asano began his professional career at Sanfrecce Hiroshima in 2013, joining the club at the age of 18 after attending Yokkaichi Chuo Kogyo High School. In his debut season, he contributed to the team's J1 League title win, making one appearance. Over the next two seasons, he became a key player, helping Sanfrecce win the 2014 Japanese Super Cup and the 2015 J1 League title, during which he scored nine goals in 34 appearances. His performances earned him the J1 League Rookie of the Year award in 2015.

In July 2016, Asano signed with Arsenal, described by manager Arsène Wenger as a "talented young striker," but he was denied a work permit to play in the Premier League. Instead, he was loaned to VfB Stuttgart, where he made his debut in a 2-1 loss to 1. FC Heidenheim. On 9 April 2017, he scored his first brace for Stuttgart in a 2-0 win over Karlsruher SC. He helped the team win the 2. Bundesliga and gain promotion to the top flight. His loan was extended for another season in June 2017.

In May 2018, Asano was loaned to Bundesliga side Hannover 96 for the 2018-19 season. In August 2019, he joined Serbian club Partizan on a three-year contract, becoming the first Japanese player in the club's history. He made his debut in the Europa League, scoring in the 67th minute of a 3-1 win over Yeni Malatyaspor. Asano played a key role in Partizan's Europa League campaign, scoring in matches against AZ Alkmaar and Astana. In the Serbian SuperLiga, he scored four goals in 23 appearances, helping Partizan finish second. He also contributed in the Serbian Cup, scoring twice in the quarter-finals, though Partizan lost the final on penalties. In the 2020-21 season, Asano scored 18 goals in 33 league matches before terminating his contract in May 2021.

Asano then joined VfL Bochum on a free transfer in June 2021. He made his debut in a 1-0 loss to Wolfsburg and scored his first goal for the club in a 2-2 draw against FC Köln in January 2022. In April 2022, he scored twice in a 2-1 win over Hoffenheim. He continued to be a key player, scoring in the DFB-Pokal and contributing to Bochum's 3-0 victory over Bayer Leverkusen, which secured their safety in the Bundesliga. At the start of the 2023-24 season, Asano scored twice in a 2-2 draw with FC Augsburg and provided two more goals in a win over Darmstadt 98, marking Bochum's first victory of the season. He later scored against Bayern Munich, his first goal in seven meetings with the club. After leaving Bochum at the end of the 2023-24 season, he joined Mallorca in July 2024, making his debut in a 1-1 draw with Real Madrid.

Internationally, Asano has represented Japan at both youth and senior levels. At the under-23 level, he won the 2016 AFC U-23 Championship, scoring a brace in the final against South Korea. He also played in the 2016 Summer Olympics, where he scored two goals as Japan exited in the group stage. Asano made his senior debut in 2015, scoring his first goal in a 7-2 win over Bulgaria at the 2016 Kirin Cup. However, despite being named in Japan's preliminary squad for the 2018 World Cup, he did not make the final cut due to limited club playing time. In the 2022 World Cup, he scored a crucial goal in the 83rd minute to help Japan defeat Germany.

Asano's career has been marked by consistent goal-scoring contributions, adaptability in different leagues, and key international performances. His move to Mallorca in 2024 represents a new chapter in his professional journey, adding to a career that includes league titles, promotions, and memorable international moments.

title: Lemuel W. Joiner
text:
Lemuel Whiting Joiner was an American farmer, politician, and Wisconsin pioneer, born on November 9, 1810, in Royalton, Vermont. He began his life in Vermont but moved to Cincinnati, Ohio, in 1830, seeking new opportunities. Four years later, in 1834, he relocated to Williamsport, Indiana, continuing his westward migration. In 1845, he settled in Wyoming, Iowa County, Wisconsin, a decision that marked the beginning of his lifelong residence in the state. Joiner spent his later years in Wisconsin, where he became an integral part of the community, contributing significantly to its development and politics. He passed away on October 22, 1886, at the age of 75.

Joiner’s political career was marked by his service in the Wisconsin legislature. He began his political journey in 1853 when he was elected to the Wisconsin State Assembly, representing Iowa County. His tenure in the Assembly lasted only one year, but it set the stage for his later achievements in the Senate. Over the following years, Joiner was elected to the Wisconsin State Senate three times. His first term in the Senate was from 1857 to 1858, followed by a second term from 1861 to 1862. After a brief hiatus, he returned to the Senate for a final term from 1869 to 1870. Throughout his political career, Joiner was a member of the Republican Party, which was a dominant force in Wisconsin politics during that era.

Joiner’s influence extended beyond his own political career, as his son, Robert Joiner, also entered public service. Robert Joiner followed in his father’s footsteps by serving in the Wisconsin Legislature, continuing the family’s legacy of civic engagement. This familial connection highlights the Joiner family’s commitment to public service in Wisconsin.

Beyond politics, Lemuel Joiner was primarily a farmer, a profession that was central to his life and the Wisconsin economy in the 19th century. Farming in Wisconsin during this period was challenging, as settlers had to adapt to the state’s climate and soil conditions. Joiner’s success as a farmer likely contributed to his standing in the community and his ability to engage in political leadership.

Joiner’s life reflects the broader story of westward expansion and political development in the United States. His moves from Vermont to Ohio, Indiana, and finally Wisconsin illustrate the migratory patterns of many early American settlers seeking better economic opportunities and fertile land. His political career in Wisconsin aligns with the state’s emergence as a key player in national politics, particularly during the mid-to-late 19th century. As a Republican, Joiner was part of a political movement that shaped Wisconsin’s identity and policies during a transformative period in U.S. history.

In summary, Lemuel Whiting Joiner was a notable figure in 19th-century Wisconsin, known for his contributions as a farmer, legislator, and community leader. His political service in the Wisconsin State Assembly and Senate, along with his family’s continued involvement in public life, underscores his impact on the state’s development. His life story is a testament to the resilience and ambition of early American settlers who helped build the nation’s frontier regions.

title: Joji (musician)
text:
George Kusunoki Miller, known professionally as Joji, is a Japanese-Australian singer-songwriter, rapper, record producer, and former comedian. Born on September 16, 1993, in Osaka, Japan, to an Australian father and a Japanese mother, Miller attended Canadian Academy in Kobe before moving to the United States to study at the New York Institute of Technology, where he earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree in 2016. His musical style blends R&B, lo-fi, and trip-hop, often characterized by melancholic themes and soulful vocals.

Miller initially gained fame on YouTube through his comedic characters, particularly Filthy Frank, which he created in 2011. The Filthy Frank Show, hosted on multiple channels including TVFilthyFrank, DizastaMusic, and TooDamnFilthy, featured shock humor, extreme challenges, and ukulele performances. The channel's popularity soared, with TVFilthyFrank amassing over 7.88 million subscribers and 1 billion views by 2023. One of Miller's most notable contributions to internet culture was the Harlem Shake meme, which he popularized, leading to the commercial success of Baauer's song of the same name. Under the alias Pink Guy, Miller released two comedy albums, *Pink Guy* (2014) and *Pink Season* (2017), as well as an extended play, *Pink Season: The Prophecy* (2017). He performed as Pink Guy at SXSW in 2017 before transitioning to his Joji persona.

In late 2017, Miller shifted his focus to serious music under the name Joji, a variation of his first name. He signed with 88Rising and 12Tone Music Group, releasing his debut EP, *In Tongues*, in 2017. His first full-length album, *Ballads 1* (2018), peaked at number three on the Billboard 200 and included the hit single "Slow Dancing in the Dark," which charted on the Billboard Hot 100. His second album, *Nectar* (2020), also reached number three on the Billboard 200, and its single "Sanctuary" became a commercial success. In 2022, Joji released *Smithereens*, his third album, preceded by the single "Glimpse of Us," which peaked at number eight on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped the ARIA Charts, becoming his highest-charting song.

Before his music career, Miller's YouTube channels were central to his early fame. The *DizastaMusic* channel, created in 2008, gained traction with the Filthy Frank character, while the *TVFilthyFrank* and *TooDamnFilthy* channels expanded his reach. He also published a book, *Francis of the Filth*, in 2017, summarizing his Filthy Frank content. However, in December 2017, he announced his departure from comedy due to health issues, devoting himself entirely to music.

Joji's music is influenced by artists like James Blake, Radiohead, and Shlohmo, with his work often described as down-tempo and melancholic. His albums explore themes of love and introspection, with *Nectar* dissecting cliché romantic tropes. In addition to his music, Joji has embarked on multiple tours, including the *Ballads 1 Tour* (2018–2019), *Nectar: The Finale* (2021–2022), and the *Smithereens Tour* (2022–2023). He has also performed at major festivals like the Laneway Festival in Australia.

In summary, Joji transitioned from a viral YouTube comedian to a successful musician, blending genres and earning critical acclaim. His impact on internet culture, particularly through the Harlem Shake, remains significant, while his music continues to resonate with a global audience.

title: D. B. Nihalsinghe
text:
D. B. Nihalsinghe, born Diongu Badaturuge Nihalsinghe on 27 May 1939, was a highly accomplished Sri Lankan filmmaker, cinematographer, editor, producer, and television pioneer. He was renowned for his versatility, excelling in multiple aspects of film and television production, including directing, cinematography, and administration. Nihalsinghe played a pivotal role in introducing professional television production to Sri Lanka in 1979, beginning with *Dimuthu Muthu*, South Asia’s first color teledrama. His contributions to the industry were extensive, including his work as the founding Chief Executive Officer and General Manager of the Sri Lanka National Film Corporation, where he significantly boosted domestic film production and audience engagement.

Nihalsinghe’s early interest in film was sparked by his father, the journalist D. B. Dhanapala, who gifted him a 16mm Bolex cine camera upon completing his SSC exams. While studying Economics at the University of Ceylon in Peradeniya, he contributed to the first student-made documentary, *Niyanada Rata*, directed by K. K. L. de Silva. His formal career in film began after university when he secured a position as a cameraman for the Australian Broadcasting Corporation in Colombo. In 1965, he was sent to Vietnam to cover war-related news for Hearst Metrotone News, gaining valuable experience in newsreel cinematography. Upon returning to Sri Lanka, he worked on *Sath Samudura*, a film noted for its innovative, fluid camerawork, which diverged from the rigid Indian studio style of the time.

His directorial debut, *Bakhti*, earned him the Most Promising Filmmaker award at the Cardiff Commonwealth Film Festival in 1965.
