In 1971, he directed *Welikathara*, Sri Lanka’s first and South Asia’s second Cinemascope film, which was later recognized as one of the ten best Sri Lankan films and awarded the Sri Lanka Presidential award. Other notable works include *Maldeniye Simiyon* (1986), which won actress Anoja Weerasinghe the Best Actress award at the 11th Delhi International Film Festival, and *Kelimadala* (1992), which garnered the highest number of national awards at the time. *Ridei Nimanaya* (1982), starring Sanath Gunatileke, was another significant contribution to Sri Lankan cinema.

Beyond his creative work, Nihalsinghe was a key figure in Sri Lankan film administration. At just 29, he became the youngest Director of the Ceylon Government Film Unit, succeeding George Wicremasinghe. He revitalized documentary film production and introduced 35mm still film to replace 120 film for the National Identity Card project, a move that modernized Sri Lankan photography. As the founding CEO of the State Film Corporation from 1972 to 1978, he implemented policies that increased domestic film screenings from 20% to 58% by 1979, dramatically boosting local film consumption.

In 1979, Nihalsinghe co-founded Tele-Cine Limited, South Asia’s first professional color television production company. He directed *Dimuthu Muthu*, the region’s first color teledrama, and established production standards that influenced Sri Lankan television for decades. Later, he worked in Malaysia as the General Manager of Film and Television Production for ASTRO, training hundreds of young professionals in film and television techniques. He held a PhD in Public Enterprises from the University of South Australia and was the only Sri Lankan to receive Life Fellowship from the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE) in 2004, recognizing his outstanding contributions to the industry.

Nihalsinghe’s legacy extends beyond his filmography, as he was instrumental in shaping Sri Lanka’s film and television infrastructure. He received the Sri Lankan national honor of Kala Keerthi and was also a Fellow of the British Kinematograph, Sound, and Television Society. His pioneering work in both film and television cemented his status as a foundational figure in South Asian media. He passed away on 21 April 2016, leaving behind a lasting impact on the region’s cinematic and television landscape.

title: Rory Byrne
text:
Rory Byrne, born on 10 January 1944 in South Africa, is a highly successful semi-retired engineer and car designer, renowned for his work in Formula One. His career spans several decades, beginning in South Africa and later moving to Europe, where he became one of the most influential figures in the sport. Byrne’s designs have achieved an impressive 99 Grand Prix victories, along with seven constructors' and seven drivers' championships, placing him as the third most successful Formula One designer in history, behind Adrian Newey and Colin Chapman.

Byrne’s early interest in motor racing was sparked during his time at Witwatersrand University in Johannesburg. Initially a competitor, he soon shifted his focus to the technical aspects of racing. After graduating in 1964, he worked briefly as a chemist but remained deeply involved in motorsport. In the late 1960s, he co-founded a company called Auto Drag and Speed Den, which imported performance car parts. During this period, he began designing racing cars, including a competitive Formula Ford racer that performed well in the 1972 championship. In 1973, Byrne moved to England to pursue a career in racing car design, eventually joining the Royale Formula Ford team after its founder, Bob King, sold the team. Byrne spent four years designing cars for Royale, honing his skills without formal engineering training.

In 1977, Byrne met Ted Toleman, the owner of a Formula 2 team, who hired him as a designer. The team achieved notable success, including first and second place in the 1980 European Formula 2 championship, which paved the way for Byrne’s entry into Formula One. His first F1 car, the Hart-powered TG181, debuted at the 1981 San Marino Grand Prix. The Toleman team, later purchased by the Benetton family, gradually improved, securing points and establishing Byrne’s reputation in the sport. A key moment came in 1985 when Benetton acquired Toleman, providing more resources and a powerful BMW turbo engine. Byrne’s designs eventually led to the team’s first victory in 1986, with Gerhard Berger winning the Mexican Grand Prix.

Byrne’s tenure at Benetton reached its peak in the mid-1990s, particularly with the arrival of Michael Schumacher. The B193 and B194 cars, featuring advanced technologies like semi-automatic gearboxes and active suspension, dominated the 1994 and 1995 seasons, securing both drivers' and constructors' titles. However, after Schumacher’s departure to Ferrari, Byrne retired from Benetton in 1996.

Ferrari recruited Byrne to rebuild their underperforming team, alongside technical director Ross Brawn. His designs helped Ferrari return to dominance, winning six consecutive constructors' and five consecutive drivers' titles between 1999 and 2004. Byrne’s philosophy of "Evolution Not Revolution" emphasized gradual but consistent improvements, a strategy that led to unprecedented success. He retired from his role as chief designer in 2006 but continued working with Ferrari in advisory and mentorship roles, contributing to projects like the LaFerrari hypercar and the 2022 F1-75 car. His influence remained strong, and his contract was extended multiple times.

Beyond Formula One, Byrne has worked as a Special Engineering Advisor for Discovery Insure in South Africa, where he helps improve road safety and driving behavior. His legacy in motorsport is marked by his innovative designs, strategic approach, and unparalleled success, making him one of the most respected figures in the history of Formula One.

title: Shigeru Fukudome
text:
Shigeru Fukudome was a high-ranking admiral in the Imperial Japanese Navy who played a significant role during World War II. Born on 1 February 1891 in Yonago, Tottori Prefecture, he graduated from the Imperial Japanese Naval Academy in 1912, ranking 8th in his class. His early naval career included service on various ships, such as the cruisers *Soya* and *Izumo*, the battleship *Satsuma*, and later the *Hizen* and *Kashima* after his promotion to ensign. He furthered his training at torpedo and naval artillery schools, serving on patrol boats and cruisers before being promoted to lieutenant in 1918. After navigational training, he became chief navigator on the destroyer *Sakura* and the cruiser *Niitaka*. In 1921, he was assigned as chief navigator on the oiler *Kamoi* during its voyage to the United States, returning to Japan in 1922. He then held several staff positions and graduated with honors from the Naval War College in 1924, earning promotion to lieutenant commander.

Throughout the 1930s, Fukudome held various staff roles, including as chief of staff for the 1st Fleet and vice-chief-of-staff of the China Area Fleet. He was promoted to captain in 1933 and later commanded the battleship *Nagato* from 1938 to 1939. By November 1939, he had risen to rear admiral. In 1940, he joined the Combined Fleet, where he participated in aerial torpedo exercises with Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, which contributed to the planning of the attack on Pearl Harbor. Promoted to vice admiral in 1942, he served as Chief of Staff under Admiral Mineichi Koga from 1943 to 1944.

A pivotal moment in Fukudome's career came on 31 March 1944, when his plane crashed in a typhoon near Cebu while en route to deliver the "Z Plan"—Japan's counterattack strategy for the Marianas—to Davao. He became the first Japanese flag officer captured by enemy forces when Filipino guerrillas detained him. Though released to prevent civilian reprisals, the captured battle plans were turned over to the Americans. After Koga's death in the same incident, Fukudome took command of the 1st Combined Base Air Force and the 2nd Air Fleet, overseeing air operations in the Kyūshū-Okinawa-Formosa region. In October 1944, following heavy Japanese losses in the Philippines, his command expanded to include the Philippines, and he relocated his headquarters to Manila. By January 1945, the 2nd Air Fleet was dissolved, and Fukudome was transferred to Singapore to lead the 10th Area Fleet, which included the 13th Air Fleet and the 1st Southern Expeditionary Fleet. However, American dominance in the Pacific rendered his position ineffective, and he remained in Singapore until the war's end.

After Japan's surrender, Fukudome was interrogated by the U.S. Navy in December 1945. He later assisted the British in repatriating Japanese nationals from Singapore. In 1947, he was arrested and tried by a military tribunal for war crimes related to the execution of two American airmen during his command in Singapore. Found guilty of negligence, he was released in 1950. Post-war, he contributed to the organization of the Japanese Self-Defense Force as part of a government advisory commission. Fukudome died on 6 February 1971 and was buried at Tama Cemetery in Fuchu, near Tokyo. He was portrayed in the 1970 film *Tora! Tora! Tora!* by actor Koji Kawamura.

title: Napoleon
text:
Napoleon Bonaparte, born Napoleone di Buonaparte on 15 August 1769 in Corsica, was a French military and political leader who rose to power during the French Revolution. His family, of Italian nobility, had settled in Corsica in the 16th century. Napoleon’s early life was shaped by his education in France, where he attended military schools, excelling in mathematics but struggling with French. His childhood was marked by bullying and a deep sense of Corsican nationalism, which eventually gave way to his loyalty to the French Republic.

Napoleon’s military career began in 1785 when he was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the French Royal Army. He returned to Corsica in 1789, supporting the French Revolution and becoming a key figure in the island’s pro-French faction. His first major military success came in 1793 during the Siege of Toulon, where his strategic artillery tactics recaptured the port from British and royalist forces. This victory earned him national recognition and rapid promotions, including the rank of brigadier general.

In 1795, Napoleon defended the French Directory against royalist rebels in the streets of Paris during the uprising of 13 Vendémiaire. His use of artillery to quell the rebellion solidified his political influence. Shortly after, he married Joséphine de Beauharnais, the former mistress of Paul Barras, a key figure in the Directory.

Napoleon’s first major campaign as a commander was the Italian Campaign of 1796. He led the French Army of Italy against the Austrians and their allies, achieving a series of decisive victories, including the Battle of Montenotte, Castiglione, Bassano, Arcole, and Rivoli. His success in Italy not only secured French dominance in the region but also made him a national hero. The campaign ended with the Treaty of Campo Formio in 1797, which temporarily stabilized France’s position in Europe.

In 1798, Napoleon launched an invasion of Egypt, aiming to challenge British interests and secure French influence in the Mediterranean. Though the campaign was militarily inconclusive—marked by the famous Battle of the Pyramids and the decisive British naval victory at the Battle of the Nile—the expedition had a lasting cultural impact, as Napoleon’s scholars documented Egypt’s ancient heritage. His return to France in 1799, after his departure from Egypt, set the stage for his political rise.

On 9 November 1799 (18 Brumaire in the French Republican calendar), Napoleon staged a coup d’état, overthrowing the Directory and establishing the Consulate. He became First Consul, effectively ruling France as a dictator. In 1804, he crowned himself Emperor of the French, marking the beginning of the Napoleonic Empire.

Napoleon’s reign saw extensive legal and administrative reforms, including the Napoleonic Code, which standardized French laws and influenced legal systems across Europe. He centralized power, suppressed dissent, and expanded France’s territorial ambitions. However, his rule was also marked by authoritarian measures, such as censorship, the suppression of political opposition, and the reinstatement of slavery in French colonies, though Haiti remained independent.

His military campaigns continued across Europe, including victories at Austerlitz (1805), Jena-Auerstedt (1806), and Wagram (1809), which solidified French dominance. However, his invasion of Russia in 1812 ended in disaster, with his Grande Armée devastated by starvation and the harsh Russian winter. The following year, the Sixth Coalition defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig (1813), leading to his first abdication in 1814.

Exiled to Elba, Napoleon escaped in 1815 and briefly regained power during the Hundred Days before being defeated at the Battle of Waterloo by a coalition led by Britain and Prussia. He was then exiled to Saint Helena, where he died on 5 May 1821, likely from stomach cancer.

Napoleon’s legacy remains complex. While he modernized France and spread revolutionary ideals, his wars caused immense destruction, and his authoritarian rule contradicted the principles of liberty and equality. His military genius and reforms continue to be studied, but his historical impact is both celebrated and criticized.

title: Vladimir Lenin
text:
funds for a Marxist newspaper, *Iskra* (The Spark), which aimed to unite Russian Social-Democrats. The newspaper was co-founded with Plekhanov, Axelrod, Vera Zasulich, and others. Lenin's contributions were often written under pseudonyms, and the publication was distributed illegally across Russia, becoming a key tool for mobilizing revolutionary sentiment. The group behind *Iskra* also laid the groundwork for the Second Congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party (RSDLP) in 1903, where Lenin's faction, the Bolsheviks ("Majority"), clashed with the Mensheviks ("Minority") over party structure and strategy. Lenin advocated for a tightly disciplined, professional revolutionary vanguard, while the Mensheviks favored a broader, more democratic organization. This split marked a lasting ideological division within the socialist movement.

Lenin spent much of this period in exile, moving between Munich, London, and Geneva. In 1902, he published *What Is to Be Done?*, a foundational text outlining his vision for a revolutionary party. The pamphlet emphasized the need for a cadre of professional revolutionaries to guide the proletariat, as Lenin believed workers alone could not develop the necessary political consciousness. This theory became central to Leninism and distinguished his approach from other Marxist factions. Lenin also participated in the 1905 Revolution, returning briefly to Russia to help organize strikes and protests. Though the uprising was suppressed, it demonstrated the potential for mass mobilization and influenced Lenin's strategic thinking.

World War I and the February Revolution: 1914–1917
During World War I, Lenin, like many socialists, opposed the conflict, which he saw as a struggle between capitalist powers. In 1915, he attended the Zimmerwald Conference, a gathering of anti-war socialists, where he advocated for transforming the imperialist war into a class war. His position alienated him from some fellow revolutionaries, including the Mensheviks, who supported the war effort. Lenin’s increasingly radical stance was outlined in his 1916 pamphlet *Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism*, which argued that capitalism had entered a phase of imperialist competition, making revolution inevitable.

In 1917, the February Revolution overthrew Tsar Nicholas II, leading to the establishment of a Provisional Government. Lenin, who had been living in Switzerland, saw this as an opportunity to advance the revolution. With German assistance (as part of an effort to destabilize Russia), he and other revolutionaries traveled to Russia in a sealed train. Upon arrival, he delivered his April Theses, calling for the overthrow of the Provisional Government, the transfer of power to the soviets (workers' councils), and the implementation of socialist policies. His message was initially met with skepticism, but the Bolsheviks gained support as the Provisional Government struggled with economic crises and the ongoing war.

The October Revolution and Bolshevik Consolidation: 1917–1922
In October 1917, the Bolsheviks seized power in a coup, establishing a Soviet government with Lenin as its leader. The new regime quickly implemented radical reforms, including the abolition of private land ownership, nationalization of industry, and the withdrawal from World War I through the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (1918). Lenin also founded the Communist International to promote global revolution. However, the Bolsheviks faced fierce opposition, including from the White Army and other anti-communist forces. The ensuing civil war (1918–1921) was marked by violence on both sides, with the Bolsheviks carrying out the Red Terror, a campaign of repression against perceived enemies.

To address economic collapse and popular discontent, Lenin introduced the New Economic Policy (NEP) in 1921, a temporary retreat from communism that allowed limited private enterprise. The Bolsheviks also consolidated power, suppressing rival socialist parties and establishing the Soviet Union in 1922. By this time, Lenin’s health was declining, and he suffered a series of strokes that left him partially paralyzed. Before his death in 1924, he warned against Stalin’s accumulation of power, but his concerns went unheeded. Lenin’s legacy remains deeply contested, with admirers crediting him for creating the first socialist state, while critics blame him for authoritarianism and repression. His ideas, however, continued to shape communist movements worldwide.

title: Kion Smith
text:
Kion Smith, born on October 7, 1998, is an American professional football player who serves as an offensive tackle for the Miami Dolphins in the National Football League (NFL). He began his football journey at Lumberton High School, where he played high school football. However, his senior season was cut short due to an injury, which forced him to miss the entire year. After high school, Smith attended Fayetteville State University, where he played college football for the Fayetteville State Broncos. During his time at Fayetteville State, he participated in a total of 20 games. His senior season in 2020 was entirely canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic, which disrupted college sports nationwide.

Following his college career, Smith went undrafted in the 2021 NFL Draft. Despite not being selected, he received an opportunity to sign a contract with the Atlanta Falcons. However, he did not make the Falcons' final 53-man roster, meaning he was not retained for the regular season. On September 6, 2021, Smith joined the Miami Dolphins as a member of their practice squad, a role that allows players to develop while being part of the team without a guaranteed spot on the active roster. On January 11, 2022, the Dolphins signed him to a reserve/future contract, indicating that the team saw potential in his development and intended to keep him in the organization. However, on August 30, 2022, Smith was waived by the Dolphins, only to be re-signed to the practice squad shortly after. This pattern of being waived and re-signed to the practice squad is not uncommon in the NFL, as teams often make roster decisions based on performance, injuries, and strategic needs.

Smith’s tenure with the Dolphins continued with another reserve/future contract on January 16, 2023, showing that the team remained interested in his development. However, his career faced another setback on August 10, 2024, when he suffered a torn ACL during the preseason. As a result, he was placed on season-ending injured reserve, meaning he would miss the entire 2024 NFL season. Injuries have been a recurring challenge in Smith’s football career, from his high school days to his professional journey. Despite these obstacles, he has persevered, demonstrating resilience and determination in his pursuit of an NFL career.

Throughout his time in the NFL, Smith has navigated the challenges of being an undrafted player, making the most of practice squad opportunities, and dealing with significant injuries. His path highlights the difficulties faced by many players at the NFL level, where competition is fierce and career stability is never guaranteed. The Miami Dolphins’ repeated signings and re-signings reflect their belief in his potential, even if he has not yet secured a full-time role on the active roster. As of his most recent injury, Smith’s future with the team remains uncertain, but his experience serves as an example of the perseverance required in professional sports.

title: F. Gwynplaine MacIntyre
text:
Fergus or Feargus Gwynplaine MacIntyre, born Paul Grant Jeffery on March 9, 1956, was a New York City-based journalist, novelist, poet, and illustrator who became known for his eccentric life and prolific but often obscure literary output. His best-known work is *The Woman Between the Worlds*, a science fiction novel, and *MacIntyre’s Improbable Bestiary*, a collection of humor pieces and verse. He also contributed to the *Tom Swift IV* series, writing *The DNA Disaster* under the pseudonym "Victor Appleton," though his name appears in the acknowledgments.

MacIntyre’s early life was shrouded in mystery and fabrications. Born in New York City to Canadian-born editor Grant Turner Peter Jeffery and Mathilde Barbara Mantano, the daughter of Italian immigrants, he had three brothers and two sisters. Throughout his life, he invented elaborate backstories, claiming to have been orphaned and raised in an Australian orphanage and a child labor camp, though acquaintances recalled him speaking with a plain New York accent in his youth. He legally changed his name and adopted the middle name "Gwynplaine" from the protagonist of Victor Hugo’s *The Man Who Laughs*, with whom he claimed to identify. His brother later confirmed that many of his personal stories were fictional.

MacIntyre worked in the 1970s for a Manhattan publisher of pornographic novels, where he was paid to produce entire books in a week. His most recognized works, however, were in science fiction, fantasy, horror, and mystery. His short stories appeared in prominent magazines like *Weird Tales*, *Analog*, *Asimov’s Science Fiction*, and *The Strand Magazine*, as well as anthologies such as *Best Science Fiction of the Year* and *The Mammoth Book of Best New Horror*. One of his notable contributions, "Death in the Dawntime," is a prehistoric locked-room mystery set 35,000 years ago in Australia, which is considered one of the farthest-reaching historical whodunnits.

MacIntyre was known for his linguistic creativity, coining new words and reviving obscure ones. Language expert William Safire acknowledged his neologism "Clintonym." He also contributed book reviews to *The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction* and illustrated some of his own stories, as well as work by others, in *Analog*. He claimed to have contributed significantly to a 2006 documentary about Theda Bara, though his role was only acknowledged in the credits under "Special Thanks."

In 2000, MacIntyre was arrested after a neighbor accused him of assault, including duct-taping her to a chair and shaving her head. He pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor. His later years were marked by increasing isolation and mental distress. In 2010, he sent mass emails to friends discussing his troubled childhood and referencing suicide. The day before his death, he posted a final film review on IMDb, hinting at his impending end. On June 25, 2010, he set his Brooklyn apartment on fire, and his body was found among the ruins. The fire, fueled by his extensive hoarding, took over an hour to extinguish and destroyed much of the building, though no other fatalities occurred. His brother later confirmed that MacIntyre’s life stories were largely fabricated, though he provided few details about the real Paul Jeffery.

MacIntyre’s works include the novel *The Woman Between the Worlds* and the poetry collection *MacIntyre’s Improbable Bestiary*. His short stories, many of which appeared in genre magazines, showcased his talent for blending humor, science fiction, and the macabre. Despite his reclusive and often controversial life, he left behind a body of work that remains notable in niche literary and film circles.

title: Jonathan Roy
text:
Jonathan Piuze-Roy, known professionally as Jonathan Roy, is a Canadian pop singer, songwriter, and former ice hockey goaltender born on March 15, 1989. He is the son of Hockey Hall of Fame goaltender Patrick Roy, an influence that initially shaped his early life. At the age of six, his family moved from Montreal to Colorado following his father's trade, and he grew up surrounded by his mother's frequent piano playing, which sparked his early interest in music. By the age of 13 or 14, Roy began writing poetry, and around 16, he started setting his poems to music. Although he played hockey for the Quebec Remparts at 17, with his father acting as the team's coach, his true passion lay in music. Inspired by artists like the Backstreet Boys, John Mayer, and Ray LaMontagne, he decided to pursue a music career at 18 after his father advised him to plan for an education outside of hockey. However, in 2009, Roy faced legal trouble when he was charged with assault after attacking an opposing goaltender during a hockey brawl, an incident that further cemented his shift away from the sport.

Roy's music career began with the release of his debut album, *What I've Become*, in 2009, followed by *Found My Way* in 2010. His first French-language album, *La route*, was released in 2011 and featured a duet with Natasha St-Pier on the title track, which gained significant attention. In 2012, he had a critically acclaimed role in the revival of the musical *Don Juan*, showcasing his versatility as a performer. A pivotal moment in his career came when his father introduced him to 1980s pop star Corey Hart, who signed him to his label, Siena Records, after Roy performed a Teddy Thompson song at Hart's home in the Bahamas. The collaboration led to a hit holiday duet with Hart on Chris Rea's *"Driving Home for Christmas"* in 2016.

In 2017, Roy released *Mr. Optimist Blues*, his major-label debut on Siena Records, which included three songs written by Hart. The album, executive-produced by Hart, blended easygoing 21st-century pop with light reggae influences, drawing comparisons to artists like Ed Sheeran, Paolo Nutini, and Bob Marley. Based in Toronto, Roy frequently collaborates with Kim Richardson as a duet or backing vocalist. In 2023, he participated in an all-star recording of Serena Ryder's *"What I Wouldn't Do"* as a charity single supporting Kids Help Phone's youth mental health campaign.

Roy's discography includes *My Lullaby* (2021), *Life Distortions* (2023), and *Symphony of Doubts, Part 1* (2024), in addition to his earlier work. His albums have seen varying degrees of commercial success in Canada, with *Mr. Optimist Blues* peaking at No. 3 and *What I've Become* at No. 18. Roy's career reflects his transition from hockey to music, driven by his passion and the support of his family, particularly his father, and his collaboration with Corey Hart. His work spans multiple genres, showcasing his talent as both a songwriter and a performer.

title: Hiren Gohain
text:
Hiren Gohain, born in 1939, is a prominent Assamese polymath known for his contributions as a scholar, writer, literary critic, and social scientist. His academic journey began at Cotton College, followed by graduation from Presidency College in Calcutta and post-graduation in English literature at Delhi University. He later taught at Kirori Mal College before pursuing doctoral research at Cambridge University on *Paradise Lost and the 17th Century Crisis*, which was later published as *Tradition and Paradise Lost: A Heretical View*, a work praised for its innovative scholarship. Upon returning to India, he became a professor in the Department of English at Gauhati University.

Gohain played a pivotal role in introducing Anglo-American New Criticism to Assamese and Indian literature. Initially influenced by eclectic radical ideologies during his time in Cambridge, he later embraced Marxism, incorporating the ideas of critics like György Lukács and Antonio Gramsci into Assamese literary criticism. His notable works in Assamese include *Sahityar Satya*, *Sahitya Aru Chetana*, and *Biswayatan*, along with four volumes of memoirs that blend personal narratives with social and historical insights. He has also contributed to prominent journals such as *Economic and Political Weekly* and *Frontier*, and writes columns for regional and national newspapers.

Beyond academia, Gohain has been actively involved in socio-political issues. His book *Assam: A Burning Question* (1984) addresses the socio-political crises in Assam during the 1980s, particularly the Assam Movement and extremist influences. He later played a significant role in mediating peace talks between the Indian government and the insurgent group ULFA. As the founder president of the Asomiya Sahitya Sanmilani, he has been a key figure in promoting Assamese literature.

His published works span both English and Assamese, covering literary criticism, history, and political analysis. Notable English works include *Nature and Art in Shakespeare*, *The Magic Plant*, and *Aspects of Early 19th Century Bengalee Culture*. In recognition of his contributions, he received the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1989 for his book on Sankardev.

Politically, Gohain has been a vocal critic of extremism, including Assamese nationalist extremism and Hindutva ideology. He strongly opposed the Citizenship (Amendment) Act (CAA), comparing its exclusion of Muslims to the Nazi persecution of Jews. A vocal critic of Narendra Modi, he participated in an anti-CAA protest organized by the All Assam Journalists Union. His activism reflects his commitment to progressive and inclusive socio-political discourse in Assam.

title: William G. Angel
text:
William Gardner Angel (1790–1858) was an American politician and lawyer who served two non-consecutive terms in the U.S. House of Representatives for New York’s 13th congressional district. Born in New Shoreham, Rhode Island, on July 17, 1790, he was the son of William and Susannah (Gardner) Angel. In 1792, his family moved to a farm in Richfield, New York, which later became the Town of Exeter in 1799. Angel attended local common schools while working on the family farm. In 1807, he began studying at Dr. Buckingham’s Grammar School and briefly pursued medicine.

Angel’s legal career began in 1809 when he worked as a witness in a trial where William Dowse, a Cooperstown lawyer, represented the defense. Impressed, Dowse hired Angel as a handyman, and during this time, Angel read law and worked as a clerk in Dowse’s office. After Dowse’s death, Angel continued his legal studies with Farrand Stranahan and later joined William Welton’s law office in Sherburne, Chenango County. In 1817, he entered a partnership with Luther Elderkin, but Elderkin later absconded with clients’ funds, leaving Angel to repay them. Angel then took over Elderkin’s law practice in Burlington, where he worked until 1833. He also served as Surrogate of Otsego County from 1821 to 1824.

In 1812, Angel married Emily P. English (1790–1822), with whom he had several children, including William P. Angel (1813–1869) and Wilkes Angel (1817–1889). After Emily’s death, he married Clarissa English, and together they had ten children, including James R. Angel (1836–1899) and Texas Angel (1839–1903), who became a lawyer in Idaho and ran as a Populist candidate for U.S. Senator in 1897.

Angel’s political career began when he was elected as a Jacksonian to the 19th, 21st, and 22nd U.S. Congresses, serving from 1825 to 1827 and again from 1829 to 1833. After leaving Congress, he moved to Hammondsport and practiced law with Morris Brown. During this time, Martin Grover studied law under Angel, first in Burlington and later in Hammondsport. Grover became a lawyer in Angelica, New York, and in 1835, Angel joined him in practice. From 1835 to 1843, Angel and Grover worked together, and from 1843 to 1847, Angel practiced law with his son Wilkes. In 1846, he was a delegate to the New York State Constitutional Convention. From 1847 to 1851, he served as First Judge and Surrogate of the Allegany County Court.

William G. Angel died on August 13, 1858, in Angelica, Allegany County, New York, and was buried at Until the Day Dawn Cemetery in the same town. His legacy includes his contributions to law and politics in New York, as well as his influence on his children, several of whom also became lawyers and political figures.

title: Stephen J. Mackwell
text:
Stephen J. Mackwell is a distinguished researcher in geophysics, with a focus on laboratory-based studies of the physical, chemical, and mechanical properties of geological materials. His work also examines the transport of fluid components in mantle and crustal rocks at both microscopic and macroscopic scales, as well as the effects of these components on mechanical properties. He has contributed significantly to the field, authoring or co-authoring over 80 articles in international scientific journals and editing a book on comparative climatology of terrestrial planets, published by the University of Arizona Press.

Mackwell received his initial education at the University of Canterbury in Christchurch, New Zealand, earning a B.Sc. in Physics and Mathematics in 1978 and an M.Sc. in Physics in 1979. His master's thesis explored excitation temperatures for late-type stars. He also obtained a Diploma of Education from Christchurch Teachers College in 1979. Later, he earned his Ph.D. in Geophysics in 1985 from the Australian National University, with a dissertation on the diffusion and weakening effects of water in quartz and olivine.

His early career began as a postdoctoral fellow at Cornell University from 1984 to 1987, followed by a move to Pennsylvania State University, where he became an assistant professor in 1987 and an associate professor of geosciences in 1992. From 1993 to 1994, he served as program director for geophysics in the Earth Sciences Division at the National Science Foundation. In 1996, he was awarded an Alexander von Humboldt Fellowship, which he used to conduct research at the Bayerisches Geoinstitut in Bayreuth, Germany. In 1998, he became a full professor of experimental geophysics at the same institution and later served as its director from 2000 to 2002.

In 2002, Mackwell returned to the United States to lead the Lunar and Planetary Institute (LPI) in Houston, Texas, a role he held until 2016. During his tenure, he also managed USRA’s Houston facility and education programs, including the NASA Internships Program and the Air Force Research Laboratory Intern Program. After his directorship, he became the USRA Corporate Director of Science Programs. Throughout his career, he has contributed to several planetary science journals, serving as editor-in-chief of *Geophysical Research Letters* from 2002 to 2004 and on the advisory board of *Physics and Chemistry of Minerals* from 1996 to 2004. He has also participated in the 2013–2022 Planetary Science Decadal Survey Steering Group and Inner Planets Panel. Since 2018, he has been a member of the Space Studies Board of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine.

Mackwell has held adjunct professorships at Rice University since 2005, the University of Minnesota from 2021 to 2022, and the University of Maryland–College Park since 2022. From 2019 to 2021, he served as Deputy Executive Officer of the American Institute of Physics. More recently, from 2022 to 2025, he held the position of Section Head for Disciplinary Programs and later served as Acting Deputy Division Director in the Division of Earth Sciences at the National Science Foundation.

Mackwell has received numerous honors, including being named a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 2017, a Fellow of the American Geophysical Union in 2010, and a Fellow of the Mineralogical Society of America in 1996. He was also recognized as a Stipendiat der Alexander von Humboldt-Stiftung in 1996 and was honored with the naming of asteroid 5292 Mackwell by the International Astronomical Union in 2016. This asteroid, discovered in 1991, is part of the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

Among his notable publications, Mackwell edited *Comparative Climatology of Terrestrial Planets* (2013) and co-authored influential studies on the deformation of rocks, the strength of the lithosphere, and the mechanisms of hydrogen diffusion in olivine. His work has significantly advanced the understanding of planetary geophysics and Earth sciences.

title: Vujadin Savić
text:
Vujadin Savić, born on 1 July 1990 in Serbia, is a former professional footballer and current coach who played as a center-back. He began his football journey at the age of eight with Red Star Belgrade, progressing through the club's youth ranks before making his senior debut. Between 2007 and 2009, Savić played for Rad, a club in the Serbian SuperLiga, before returning to Red Star. In 2010, he moved to France to join Bordeaux, where he spent two seasons. In January 2012, during his time with Bordeaux, he was loaned to Dynamo Dresden for the remainder of the 2011–12 season. His time in Germany was followed by a short stint with English Championship club Watford in 2015, though he was released without making an appearance.

In 2015, Savić joined Sheriff Tiraspol in Moldova, where he spent two seasons, making 40 appearances and scoring four goals. Notably, he scored a bicycle kick in a league match against Zaria Bălți on 19 September 2015. In 2017, he returned to his home club, Red Star Belgrade, signing a two-year contract. During his first season back, Red Star achieved historic success by reaching the 2018 Europa League knockout phase, marking the first time a team had advanced from the first qualifying round. They also made it past the group stage of a UEFA competition for the first time in 26 years. Savić was part of a strong defensive partnership with Srđan Babić and Damien Le Tallec, helping Red Star concede only two goals in the Europa League group stage, the second-best defensive record in the competition. In May 2018, he was named to the Serbian SuperLiga's Team of the Season. The following season, Savić played a key role as Red Star qualified for the UEFA Champions League for the first time in their history, conceding just three goals in the qualifying rounds. He captained the team in four games, including matches against Napoli and Liverpool, where Red Star kept clean sheets. However, an injury forced him to miss the latter stages of the competition. He extended his contract with Red Star until 2022 in January 2019.

In July 2019, Savić moved to Cypriot club APOEL on a free transfer, signing a three-year contract with a provision that Red Star would receive half of his next transfer fee. However, a groin injury in August 2019 required surgery, and in February 2021, he was loaned to Slovenian club Olimpija Ljubljana for the remainder of the 2020–21 season, where he helped the team win the Slovenian Cup.

At the international level, Savić represented Serbia at the 2009 UEFA European Under-21 Championship. In March 2018, he received his first call-up to the senior Serbia national team under coach Mladen Krstajić for friendly matches against Morocco and Nigeria, but an injury prevented him from making his debut.

In his personal life, Savić is the son of former Serbian footballer Dušan Savić. He has four children with actress Mirka Vasiljević, his common-law spouse. Savić was named after Serbian coach and former player Vujadin Boškov and is also nicknamed "Giška" after his relative Đorđe Božović. Throughout his career, he won several domestic titles, including two Serbian SuperLiga championships, two Moldovan league titles, and the Slovenian Cup. His contributions to Red Star Belgrade during their UEFA campaigns were particularly notable, cementing his reputation as a reliable defender.

title: Marli Renfro
text:
Marli Renfro, born on April 3, 1938, in Los Angeles, California, is an American former showgirl, model, Playboy cover girl, and actress. She is best known for her role as Janet Leigh’s body double in the infamous shower scene of Alfred Hitchcock’s 1960 film *Psycho*. Renfro, described as a free spirit with a lifelong commitment to nudism, appeared in numerous men’s magazines, including *Ace*, *Adam*, *Beau*, *Dude*, *Escapade*, *Follies*, *Gala*, and *Modern Man*. She also graced the cover of the September 1960 issue of *Playboy*. Before her acting career, Renfro worked as a showgirl in Las Vegas and as a Playboy Bunny.

Renfro’s most notable role was as the body double for Janet Leigh in *Psycho*. The shower scene, one of the most famous in cinema history, features over 50 camera cuts in just three minutes and took six days to film. Though the scene suggests nudity through rapid cuts, no explicit nudity is shown. Initially, Hitchcock and Leigh claimed only Leigh appeared in the scene, but Hitchcock later acknowledged that Renfro stood in for Leigh in most shots, except for close-ups of Leigh’s face. Leigh, however, later stated that all the actual shower footage was of her, and Renfro was only used in an overhead shot that was eventually cut due to censorship concerns.

Following *Psycho*, Renfro appeared in Francis Ford Coppola’s 1962 film *Tonight for Sure*. Decades later, she was featured in the 2017 documentary *78/52*, which examines the making of the *Psycho* shower scene in detail.

A significant misconception arose regarding Renfro’s identity and survival. During the filming of *Psycho*, Janet Leigh had a stand-in named Myra Davis (also known as Myra Jones) to assist with lighting. In 1988, Davis was tragically raped and murdered by her neighbor, Kenneth Dean Hunt. Due to the public’s fascination with the *Psycho* shower scene, some media outlets incorrectly reported that Davis was Leigh’s body double. The BBC went further, falsely claiming Davis was the voice of Norman Bates’ mother, though the role was actually performed by Virginia Gregg and Jeanette Nolan. The confusion was compounded in 2002 when author Don Lasseter wrote in *Body Double* that Davis and Renfro were the same person, leading to the mistaken belief that Renfro had died. Robert Graysmith, a longtime admirer of Renfro, investigated and discovered she was alive and living in California. He later wrote *The Girl in Alfred Hitchcock’s Shower* (2010), clarifying her role in *Psycho* and dispelling the myths surrounding Davis’s death.

Renfro married and is known as Marli Renfro Peterson. She has lived in the Mojave Desert since 1970. Her contributions to cinema, particularly in *Psycho*, have cemented her place in film history, despite the surrounding confusion about her identity.

title: Gubby Allen
text:
Sir George Oswald Browning "Gubby" Allen, born on 31 July 1902 in Sydney, Australia, was a prominent cricketer and administrator. His family moved to England when he was six, and he was educated at Eton College, where he excelled at cricket despite frequent injuries. Allen played for Cambridge University from 1922, earning a blue for his fast bowling, though his career was briefly derailed by academic issues. He later joined Middlesex, balancing cricket with a career in finance, which often limited his availability.

Allen’s Test debut for England came in 1930, following a strong season where he took all ten wickets in an innings for Middlesex, a rare feat. Though inconsistently selected due to injuries and work commitments, he was appointed England captain in 1936. During the 1936–37 tour of Australia, he led the team to a 3–2 series loss after winning the first two Tests. Despite his irregular play, Allen performed well in major tours, particularly against Australia. His bowling was often erratic but occasionally devastating, and he was known as a reliable lower-order batsman under pressure.

After retiring from first-class cricket in the 1950s, Allen transitioned into administration. He became a key figure in the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC), serving as chairman of the England selectors from 1955 to 1961, overseeing a successful era. He later became MCC president in 1963 and treasurer in 1964, playing a significant role in the D’Oliveira affair, a controversial selection dispute over Basil D’Oliveira’s potential tour to South Africa. Allen was knighted in 1986 and spent his later years near Lord’s, where he died in 1989 at the age of 87. His legacy includes both his playing career and his influential administrative work in English cricket.

title: Rii Sen
text:
Rii Sen, born Rituparna Sen, is an Indian actress known for her work in Bengali cinema, particularly in alternative and experimental films. She began her career as a freelance model and television actress before transitioning to films. Her debut feature, *Tepantorer Mathe* (2009), was not released due to its controversial content. Prior to her film career, she appeared in television series such as *Tithir Otithi* and *Ekhane Akash Neel*, and also participated as a contestant in *Bigg Boss Bangla* Season 2, where she finished as the second runner-up.

Sen gained attention for her roles in unconventional films, often pushing the boundaries of Bengali cinema. In *Bishh* (2009), directed by Qaushik Mukherjee, she played Anushka, a complex college student, a role she described as emotionally challenging. Her performance in *Gandu* (2010), where she portrayed a character requiring frontal nudity, was praised for its boldness. The director noted that she was the only actress in the Bengali film industry at the time who could have taken on such a role. Critics commended her confidence and maturity in the film.

In 2012, she starred in *Cosmic Sex*, directed by Amitabh Chakraborty, which explores a young man’s sexual journey. Her portrayal earned her the Best Actress award at the Osian’s Cinefan Festival of Asian and Arab Cinema. The film was well-received, particularly for its daring themes. That same year, she appeared in *Koyekti Meyer Golpo*, playing a don’s wife, and in *Tasher Desh* (2013), a surreal adaptation of Rabindranath Tagore’s play. She also acted in *Byanka Prithibi* (2013), directed by Anirban Mukherjee, and was cast in *LUDO* (2014), an experimental film by Qaushik Mukherjee and Nikon, where she played a role not previously seen in Indian cinema.

Sen is recognized as a significant figure in alternative Bengali cinema, known for challenging traditional norms. She has expressed a desire to explore sexuality in film, pushing it to its limits for artistic purposes. Unlike other actresses, she was one of the first in Indian cinema to perform full-frontal nudity, predating Paoli Dam’s similar scenes. She views her body as a tool for meaningful artistic expression, emphasizing that her work should not be dismissed as a gimmick.

In addition to films, she has continued her television career with appearances in *Jai Kali Kalkattawali*, *Durga Durgeshwari*, and *Uron Tubri*, among others. Her filmography includes documentaries such as *Love in India* (2009) and *Many Stories of Love and Hate* (2009), the latter of which was screened at the Mumbai International Film Festival.

Sen’s contributions to Bengali cinema, particularly in avant-garde and boundary-pushing roles, have solidified her reputation as a courageous and talented actress. Her willingness to take on challenging and often controversial roles sets her apart in the industry, making her a notable figure in alternative filmmaking.

title: Fidel Castro
text:
Fidel Castro was a Cuban revolutionary and political leader who governed Cuba for nearly five decades, from 1959 until 2008. Born on 13 August 1926 in Birán, Cuba, to a wealthy Spanish immigrant farmer and his mistress, Castro was raised in a Roman Catholic environment and attended Jesuit schools before studying law at the University of Havana. During his student years, he became involved in anti-imperialist and leftist politics, joining the Partido Ortodoxo and engaging in protests against government corruption and U.S. influence in the Caribbean.

In 1947, Castro participated in an aborted expedition to overthrow the Dominican Republic’s dictator, Rafael Trujillo, and later joined protests in Colombia against government repression. By the late 1940s, he had adopted Marxist ideas, believing that Cuba’s problems stemmed from capitalism and that only a proletarian revolution could bring meaningful change. In 1952, after General Fulgencio Batista seized power in a military coup, Castro organized a failed attack on the Moncada Barracks in 1953, aiming to spark a rebellion. The assault was a disaster, resulting in numerous deaths and Castro’s imprisonment. During his trial, he defended his actions in a speech later published as *History Will Absolve Me*, which argued that Batista’s regime was illegitimate and that revolution was justified.

After a brief release in 1955, Castro was exiled to Mexico, where he formed the 26th of July Movement (MR-26-7) with his brother Raúl and Argentine revolutionary Ernesto "Che" Guevara. Returning to Cuba in 1956, Castro led a guerrilla war from the Sierra Maestra mountains, gradually gaining support among peasants and urban rebels. By 1959, Batista’s regime collapsed, and Castro assumed power as prime minister. His government nationalized industry, implemented socialist reforms, and established a one-party communist state—the first in the Western Hemisphere.

Castro’s rule was marked by confrontation with the United States, which opposed his Marxist policies. The U.S. imposed an economic embargo, supported exiles in the failed Bay of Pigs Invasion (1961), and attempted assassination plots. In response, Castro aligned Cuba with the Soviet Union, leading to the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, a pivotal Cold War event. Domestically, his government expanded healthcare and education but suppressed dissent and controlled the media.

Internationally, Castro supported revolutionary movements in Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East, sending troops to conflicts such as the Angolan Civil War and the Yom Kippur War. He also championed the Non-Aligned Movement and Cuban medical internationalism, sending doctors abroad. Following the Soviet Union’s collapse in 1991, Cuba faced economic hardship during the "Special Period," but Castro maintained power by embracing environmental and anti-globalization policies.

In the 2000s, he strengthened ties with leftist governments in Latin America, forming the Bolivarian Alliance for the Americas. Illness led him to transfer power to his brother Raúl in 2006, who became president in 2008. Castro remained a polarizing figure—admired by supporters as a socialist and anti-imperialist icon but criticized by opponents for authoritarian rule and human rights abuses. He died on 25 November 2016, leaving behind a deeply contested legacy.

title: Avraham Eilam-Amzallag
text:
Avraham (Avi) Eilam-Amzallag is an Israeli musician and composer, born on 28 September 1941 in Casablanca, Morocco. As a child, he immigrated to Israel, where he began his musical education. Initially, he studied the flute, later expanding his training to include composition at the Buchman-Mehta Music Academy in Tel Aviv. This academic background laid the foundation for his career, which blends traditional and contemporary musical styles.

Eilam-Amzallag is known for founding an ensemble dedicated to performing oriental music, reflecting his deep connection to the musical traditions of the Middle East and North Africa. His compositions often merge oriental Jewish musical elements with modern compositional techniques, creating a distinct and innovative sound. This fusion is a defining aspect of his work, appealing to audiences interested in both traditional and experimental music.

Among his notable compositions are *Desolation* (a piece for flute lasting 3 minutes and 33 seconds) and *Mawal* (a 5-minute and 13-second work). Another significant piece is his *Music for flute and percussion*, completed in 1975. This composition showcases his ability to integrate different instrumental textures while maintaining a strong thematic identity. While the article does not provide extensive details about the content or reception of these works, they exemplify his approach to blending cultural influences with contemporary compositional methods.

In addition to his performing and composing activities, Eilam-Amzallag has contributed to the broader discourse on Israeli music. His work is listed in the context of the *Music of Israel*, highlighting his role in shaping the country's diverse musical landscape. Although the article does not delve into his personal life or later career developments, it positions him as a notable figure in the Israeli musical scene, particularly for his contributions to oriental and experimental compositions.

The article’s brevity suggests that more extensive documentation of his career and influences may exist elsewhere, but it provides a clear overview of his early life, education, and artistic contributions. His legacy lies in his ability to bridge traditional and modern musical expressions, leaving a mark on both Israeli and global music scenes.

title: Funke Abimbola
text:
Funke Abimbola MBE is a highly accomplished Nigerian businesswoman and lawyer who has made significant contributions to diversity and inclusion, particularly within the legal profession in the United Kingdom. Born into a family of medical doctors, she initially pursued her education at Burgess Hill Girls but later decided against studying medicine due to her fears of pain and blood (algophobia and hemophobia). Instead, she chose to study law at Newcastle University. After completing her degree, she returned to Nigeria to prepare for and pass the Nigerian Bar examination. While in Nigeria, she worked with the law firm F. O. Akinrele & Co. Before long, she became a mother at the age of 28 while employed at Campbell Hooper, a significant milestone in her personal and professional life. In 2000, she qualified as an in-house solicitor, marking the beginning of her legal career in the UK.

Abimbola’s career has been distinguished by her rise to prominent roles in the corporate legal sector. She became the most senior black solicitor for Roche’s pharmaceutical operations, overseeing the company’s legal affairs in the UK, Ireland, Gibraltar, and Malta. Her journey to this position was not without challenges, particularly when she first sought an entry-level job in the UK. She faced difficulties securing interviews and employment, leading her to proactively reach out to the top 100 corporate law firms and 50 in-house legal teams. Her persistence paid off, and she eventually secured a position that allowed her to qualify as a solicitor. Her experience highlighted the racial barriers she encountered, which later fueled her advocacy for diversity in the legal profession.

Throughout her career, Abimbola has held several key roles at Roche. In 2012, she joined the company as Managing Counsel for the UK and Ireland and later served as the UK Data Protection Officer. In December 2015, she was promoted to General Counsel and Company Secretary, and by January 2017, she became the General Counsel and Head of Financial Compliance. Her leadership in these roles has been instrumental in shaping corporate governance and compliance strategies. Additionally, she has been a vocal advocate for corporate and social diversity, using her platform to promote inclusivity in the legal sector and beyond.

Abimbola’s contributions have been widely recognized through numerous awards and honors. In 2013, she was featured in the Diversity League Table as one of the Black Solicitors. The following year, she was nominated for both the National Diversity Awards and the Law Society Excellence Awards. In 2015, she received a Positive Role Model Award, and in 2016, she was honored with a “Point of Light” award by the UK Prime Minister for her volunteer work in diversity. Her most prestigious recognition came in June 2017 when she was awarded an MBE (Member of the Order of the British Empire) by Queen Elizabeth II for her services to diversity in the legal profession and her work with young people. In September 2019, she was further honored with an honorary doctor of laws from the University of Hertfordshire in recognition of her contributions to social and corporate diversity.

Beyond her professional achievements, Abimbola has been actively involved in community and educational roles. In 2010, she was appointed as a governor of Uxbridge College in London, serving a four-year term. She is also a mother to a 19-year-old son who is currently studying Software Engineering at Newcastle University, the same institution where she earned her law degree. Abimbola’s journey, marked by resilience, determination, and a commitment to diversity, serves as an inspiration to many in the legal profession and beyond. Her advocacy and leadership continue to drive meaningful change, fostering a more inclusive environment in the UK and the global legal community.

title: Bir Hambir
text:
Bir Hambir, also known as Hambir Malla Dev, was the forty-ninth king of Mallabhum, a region primarily located in the present-day Bankura district of West Bengal, India. He ruled from 1565 to 1620 AD, a period marked by his strategic alliances, military prowess, and cultural contributions. His reign coincided with the expansion of the Mughal Empire under Emperor Akbar, with whom he formed a significant alliance. Hambir supported Akbar’s campaigns against the Afghan ruler Qutlu Khan Lohani, particularly in the late 16th century, when Mughal forces intervened in Midnapore and Bishnupur. He provided military assistance to Mughal general Man Singh’s son, Jagat Singh, and played a crucial role in rescuing him from an Afghan ambush. This act of bravery strengthened the relationship between Bishnupur and the Mughals, securing his kingdom’s autonomy while acknowledging Mughal suzerainty.

Hambir was also linked to the Baro-Bhuyans, a group of twelve powerful landlords in Bengal who resisted Mughal dominance. Though not a member of the Baro-Bhuyans himself, his opposition to Mughal centralization aligned with their goals. His military strength and alliances with other regional chiefs helped defend Bishnupur from external threats. Additionally, he played a pivotal role in the Midnapore Raj, aiding in the restoration of Raja Chhotu Roy to the throne after the defeat of Shyam Singh, a puppet ruler installed by Isha Khan of the Lohani Dynasty.

A devout follower of Vaishnavism, Hambir was deeply influenced by the teachings of Srinivasa, a Vaishnava devotee. After hearing Srinivasa recite the Bhagavata, he converted to Vaishnavism, donated land and wealth to the movement, and introduced the worship of Madan Mohan in Bishnupur. His religious devotion was reflected in his reign, during which the title "Dev" was added to the royal title "Malla," symbolizing a period of stability and security for Mallabhum.

One of Hambir’s most notable military achievements was the Battle of Mundamala Ghat in 1575 AD, where he defeated Daud Khan Karrani, the son of the Pathan ruler Sulaiman Khan Karrani. After a fierce battle near the Mundmal fort, Hambir captured Daud Khan and, showing mercy, released him. As a tribute to his victory, he is said to have created a garland of the fallen enemy soldiers' heads, offering it to Maa Mrinmayee, the kuladevi (family deity) of Mallabhum. This act earned him the title "Bir Hambir," meaning "brave Hambir."

Hambir’s cultural legacy includes the construction of the Rashmancha, a historical building in Bishnupur commissioned in 1600 CE. This structure was used to worship Radha-Krishna idols during the Vaishnava Ras festival. Another significant contribution from his reign was the creation of the Dalmadal cannon, one of the largest-bored cannons of its time, crafted by Jagannath Karmakar. The cannon’s name, meaning "destruction of the enemy," reflected its military significance.

Bir Hambir’s influence extended beyond his lifetime, with his story being adapted into a film and his legacy preserved in cultural works. His reign remains a testament to his leadership, military strategy, and religious devotion, leaving a lasting impact on the history of Bankura and Bengal.

title: Sayuri Yamauchi
text:
Sayuri Yamauchi, born on May 28, 1956, and passing away on March 6, 2012, at the age of 55, was a prominent Japanese voice actress known for her extensive work in anime, video games, and dubbing. She was professionally active under the stage name Sayuri and was affiliated with the talent agencies Kyu Production and Aigumi, the latter being her agency at the time of her death. Yamauchi’s career spanned decades, during which she contributed to numerous beloved productions, leaving a lasting impact on the Japanese animation and voice acting industries.

In anime, Yamauchi lent her voice to a variety of memorable characters. One of her notable roles was Vera Ronstadt in *The Big O*, a sci-fi series that combined noir aesthetics with mecha action. She also voiced Hikaru Kosaka in *The Brave Fighter of Legend Da-Garn*, a classic mecha anime, and appeared in *City Hunter* as a dress store clerk and a performer in its film adaptation. In *Crayon Shin-chan*, she played recurring characters like Nanako Ohara and the flamboyant Lulu Lu Lulu, showcasing her versatility in both comedic and dramatic roles. Yamauchi also contributed to *Cyborg 009*, *Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood* (as Satella), and *Mobile Suit Gundam Wing*, where she voiced Lady Une, a key supporting character. Other notable anime roles included Osuzu in *Samurai Champloo*, Maya in *Shaman King*, and Tiara in *Shamanic Princess*.

Yamauchi’s voice work extended to video games, where she brought depth to characters in titles like *Baten Kaitos Origins* (as Gena), *Dragon Force II* (as Bjorn and Medea), and *Xenoblade Chronicles* (as Lorithia). She was also a frequent presence in the *Super Robot Wars* series, voicing characters such as Ai Anami, Primarda, and Ikumi Kaidoh across multiple installments. Her role in *Robot Alchemic Drive* as Tomoe Kawasaki further demonstrated her ability to embody diverse roles.

Her dubbing work included high-profile live-action films and TV shows. In *The Simpsons*, she notably voiced Itchy, the cartoon cat, and Maude Flanders, Ned Flanders’ late wife. She also dubbed roles in Hollywood films, such as Monica Swinton in *A.I. Artificial Intelligence*, Donna Jensen in *Erin Brockovich*, and Trin in *The Long Kiss Goodnight*. Her performance as Audrey Horne in *Twin Peaks* marked another significant contribution to anime fans, as the series gained a cult following in Japan. She also lent her voice to *The Matrix* (as Switch), *Mission: Impossible* (as Claire Phelps), and *The Sea Inside* (as Rosa).

Yamauchi’s career was cut short by cancer, but her legacy endures through her extensive filmography. Her ability to adapt to a wide range of roles, from comedic to dramatic, in both Japanese and Western productions, solidified her as a respected figure in the voice acting industry. Despite her passing, her work continues to be celebrated by fans and colleagues alike.

title: Date Narikuni
text:
Date Narikuni (1817–1841) was a samurai of the late Edo period in Japan, serving as the 12th *daimyō* of Sendai Domain and the 28th hereditary chieftain of the Date clan. Born on November 6, 1817, he was the son of Date Munemitsu, a member of the Tome-Date clan, a subordinate branch of the main Date family, and the grandson of Date Yoshimura, the 5th *daimyō* of Sendai. His childhood names included Kōgorō, Tosaburō, and later Sojirō.

Narikuni’s ascension to leadership came during a critical period for Sendai Domain. In 1828, the death of Date Nariyoshi left the domain in crisis, as Nariyoshi’s heir, Date Yoshikuni, was only two years old. The Tokugawa shogunate, having previously intervened in Sendai’s succession disputes, was growing impatient. Initially, the *rōjū* (elder statesman) Mizuno Tadaakira proposed marrying Nariyoshi’s daughter, Masahime, to a son of Shōgun Tokugawa Ienari. However, this plan did not materialize, and instead, Masahime was married to Narikuni, who belonged to a cadet branch of the Date clan. Narikuni then adopted Yoshikuni as his heir, ensuring the continuation of the Date lineage. As part of this arrangement, Narikuni received court ranks, first as Junior Fourth, Lower Grade with the title of Mutsu-no-kami in 1828, and later as Junior Fourth, Upper Grade and Sakonoe-chūshō in 1831.

Narikuni was known for his scholarly interests and literary knowledge, though his time as *daimyō* was brief. In 1840, while fulfilling his *sankin-kōtai* (alternate attendance) duties in Edo, he fell ill. He died the following year at the age of 25, cutting short his leadership of the Sendai Domain.

His family connections were crucial to his role. His father, Date Munemitsu, lived from 1787 to 1843, and his mother was Tsuneko-hime. His wife, Masahime, was born in 1824 and died in 1861. Narikuni’s death left the domain to his adopted heir, Yoshikuni, whom he had been tasked with protecting. His brief tenure reflects the political maneuvering and succession challenges faced by the Date clan during the Tokugawa shogunate’s later years.

title: Nonzee Nimibutr
text:
Nonzee Nimibutr, born on December 18, 1962, is a prominent Thai film director, producer, and screenwriter, widely recognized as a key figure in the "New Wave" of Thai cinema, alongside directors like Pen-Ek Ratanaruang, Wisit Sasanatieng, and Apichatpong Weerasethakul. His work has significantly revitalized the Thai film industry, blending traditional storytelling with modern cinematic techniques. Nimibutr comes from a notable family, being a relative of Lieutenant General Phachoen Nimitbutr, the founder of Thailand’s first television station, Army TV Channel 5. He studied visual communication design at Silpakorn University, where he met future collaborators Wisit Sasanatieng and production designer Ek Iemchuen. Beginning his career in television commercials and music videos, he transitioned to feature films in the late 1990s.

His directorial debut, *Dang Bireley's and Young Gangsters* (1997), written by Wisit Sasanatieng, was a period drama about young criminals in 1950s Bangkok, influenced by the style of John Woo. The film won the best picture award at the Thailand National Film Awards and was nominated internationally. His next film, *Nang Nak* (1999), a ghost thriller based on a famous Thai folktale, further cemented his reputation. The film, also scripted by Sasanatieng, won multiple awards, including best picture at the Thailand National Film Awards, and was a commercial success, contributing to the revival of Thai cinema.

With *Jan Dara* (2001), Nimibutr expanded his reach by collaborating with Hong Kong actress Christy Chung and securing international funding, marking the beginning of pan-Asian film production in Thailand. The film’s controversial themes of incest, rape, and abortion led to censorship in Thailand, though it was shown uncut at film festivals. Nimibutr also became an influential producer, backing films like *Bangkok Dangerous* (1999) by the Pang Brothers, *Tears of the Black Tiger* (2000) by Wisit Sasanatieng, and *Bang Rajan* (2000) by Thanit Jitnukul. He co-founded the production company Cinemasia with Duangkamol Limcharoen, who tragically passed away in 2003. His next major project was the horror anthology *Three* (2002), in which he directed a segment alongside Hong Kong’s Peter Chan and South Korea’s Kim Ji-Woon.

In 2003, he directed *OK Baytong*, a drama set in southern Thailand, addressing contemporary social issues. He also produced several films, including *Monrak Transistor* (2001) by Pen-Ek Ratanaruang. In 2005, he made *The Ceiling*, an English-language short film for the Asian Film Academy, starring South Korean actors. His next feature, *Queens of Langkasuka* (2008), was an epic fantasy about three princesses defending their kingdom, originally titled *Queens of Pattani* before the name was changed to avoid political sensitivities related to the southern Thai insurgency. The film starred prominent Thai actors like Ananda Everingham and Sorapong Chatree.

Nimibutr has continued producing and directing, including *Distortion* (2012), *Timeline* (2015), *The Gift* (2017), and *Once Upon a Star* (2023), a Netflix film. His producing credits include *Noo Hin: The Movie* (2006), based on a popular Thai comic, and *The Cursed Land* (2024). In 2008, he received the prestigious Silpathorn Award from the Thailand Culture Ministry, recognizing his contributions to cinema. Throughout his career, Nimibutr has remained a pivotal figure in both Thai and pan-Asian cinema, known for his bold storytelling and innovative collaborations.

title: Joseph Jaquet
text:
Joseph Jaquet, a Belgian sculptor born on 30 January 1822 in Antwerp, came from a modest background as the son of a baker. He pursued his artistic education at the Brussels Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts under the guidance of Guillaume Geefs. Jaquet was closely associated with the painter Peter Ludwig Kühnen, a romantic landscape artist from Aachen, and maintained a lifelong friendship with him. His brother Jacques, born in 1830, joined him in Brussels and became an active collaborator, contributing his own works to the Brussels art salons between 1843 and 1873.

Jaquet’s career began to take shape in 1842 when he exhibited several notable works at the Brussels Art Salon, including a marble bust, three plaster busts, and two sculptures—*Moses Saved from the Waters* and *Meditating Saint Paul*. These works brought him early recognition. His participation in subsequent salons, particularly the 1845 exhibition where he presented a model for a bronze statue of Froissart intended for Chimay, further solidified his reputation. However, it was in 1854 with *The Golden Age* that he achieved lasting notoriety.

Throughout his career, Jaquet lived in different parts of Brussels, first on Goffard Street and later on Charles Quint Street. His professional success expanded beyond Belgium when, in 1864, he received his first major commission in Amsterdam—a statue titled *The Victory* for the Paleis voor Volksvlijt. This was followed by a second commission in The Hague for the decoration of the national monument in Willemspark. In 1868, he created the equestrian statue of Baldwin I of Constantinople in Mons, and in 1872, he contributed the pediment and lion sculptures for the Brussels Stock Exchange.

Another significant work was the statue of Louise of Orléans, the first Queen of the Belgians, commissioned in 1879. Initially placed on the Place d'Armes in Philippeville, the statue was later relocated to the old École moyenne on Namur Street.

In addition to his artistic endeavors, Jaquet held an academic position as a professor at the Brussels Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts and mentored the sculptor Charles Samuel. His contributions to the arts were recognized with prestigious honors, including the title of Officer of the Order of Leopold and Officer of the Order of the Oak Crown. He was also elected a member of the Royal Academy of Science, Letters and Fine Arts of Belgium.

Joseph Jaquet died on 9 June 1898 in Schaerbeek, a municipality in the Brussels-Capital Region. His legacy as a skilled sculptor and educator remains an important part of Belgian art history.

title: Ralph Macchio
text:
Ralph George Macchio Jr. was born on November 4, 1961, in Huntington, New York. His parents, Ralph Sr. and Rosalie (née DeSantis), owned laundromats and a wastewater disposal company. His father had Italian and Greek ancestry, while his mother was of Italian descent. Macchio has a younger brother, Steven. He began tap dancing at age three and was discovered by a talent agent at 16. Before landing his breakout role, he had minimal martial arts training, learning karate and jiujitsu in elementary school.

Macchio’s acting career began with a role in the TV series *Eight Is Enough* (1980–1981), followed by his breakout performance as Johnny Cade in Francis Ford Coppola’s *The Outsiders* (1983), where he starred alongside actors like Tom Cruise, Matt Dillon, and Patrick Swayze. His next major role was as Daniel LaRusso in *The Karate Kid* (1984), a part he reprised in *The Karate Kid Part II* (1986) and *The Karate Kid Part III* (1989). The character became iconic, and Macchio later appeared in the 2007 music video for *Sweep the Leg* by No More Kings, mocking his own fame. In 2010, he starred in *Wax On, F*ck Off*, a comedic short that humorously exaggerated his typecasting as Daniel LaRusso. Three decades after the original film, he reprised the role in *Cobra Kai* (2018–2025), a YouTube Premium/Netflix series that reexamined the *Karate Kid* story from Johnny Lawrence’s perspective. Macchio’s performance earned him two Critics’ Choice Award nominations and a Primetime Emmy nomination. In 2022, he published *Waxing On: The Karate Kid and Me*, a memoir reflecting on the franchise’s legacy. He continued the role in *Karate Kid: Legends* (2025), teaming up with Jackie Chan.

Outside the *Karate Kid* franchise, Macchio appeared in *Crossroads* (1986), *Cuba and His Teddy Bear* (Broadway, 1986), and *My Cousin Vinny* (1992), where he played Billy Gambini, a young man wrongly accused of murder. He also starred in the U.S. tour of *How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying* (1996), receiving praise for his performance. On television, he had roles in *Ugly Betty* (2008–2009) and *The Deuce* (2017–2019). In 2011, he competed on *Dancing with the Stars*, placing fourth. He also appeared in music videos for Danko Jones and *Hitchcock* (2012), where he portrayed screenwriter Joseph Stefano.

In 2024, Macchio received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. In his personal life, he married Phyllis Fierro in 1987, whom he met at 15 through his grandmother. They have two children, Julia and Daniel. Julia appeared in *Cobra Kai* as Vanessa LaRusso, a cousin of Daniel LaRusso. Macchio is a fan of the New York Islanders and even earned a bobblehead in their uniform, striking the famous *Karate Kid* crane kick pose. In 2025, he earned his black belt in karate, over 40 years after his first role in the franchise. That same year, he and Jackie Chan received an honorary black belt from the World Karate Federation. Macchio’s enduring career spans film, television, theater, and memoir, solidifying his status as a beloved Hollywood figure.

title: Ariel Behar
text:
Ariel Behar is a Uruguayan professional tennis player born on November 12, 1989, who has established himself as a prominent doubles specialist. His career-high doubles ranking is World No. 34, achieved on May 6, 2024. Behar has won three ATP titles, all with his long-time partner, Ecuadorian player Gonzalo Escobar. His first major breakthrough came in the early 2020s, where he and Escobar formed a successful partnership, winning titles at the 2021 Delray Beach Open and the 2021 Andalucía Open, along with reaching several other ATP finals. They also secured 15 Challenger titles between 2018 and 2022, helping Behar enter the top 50 of the doubles rankings.

Behar began playing tennis at the age of three and started competing seriously at ten. He grew up admiring tennis legends Roger Federer and Andre Agassi. Although he comes from a Jewish family, he has stated that he is not particularly religious. His professional career began in earnest in the mid-2010s, competing on the ATP Challenger Tour, where he won seven doubles titles. A notable early achievement was his semifinal appearance at the 2017 Estoril Open with Aliaksandr Bury, followed by his Grand Slam debut at Wimbledon in the same year.

From 2018 to 2022, Behar and Escobar dominated the Challenger circuit, winning eight titles together and reaching multiple ATP finals. Their success culminated in Behar’s first ATP 250 title at the 2022 Serbia Open, where they defeated top seeds Nikola Mektić and Mate Pavić. By the end of 2021, Behar had achieved a career-high ranking of No. 41, cementing his place among the world’s top doubles players.

In 2023, Behar continued to excel, reaching the quarterfinals at Wimbledon with a new partner, Adam Pavlásek. They upset former champions Mektić and Pavić before losing to eventual winners Wesley Koolhof and Neal Skupski. This result propelled Behar back into the top 50. He also reached two ATP finals that year, including the European Open, where he and Pavlásek were defeated by the Tsitsipas brothers. Later, at the 2023 Córdoba Open and the Argentina Open, he reached the quarterfinals and final, respectively, with Nicolas Barrientos.

The 2024 season saw Behar achieve new milestones. At the Australian Open, he and Pavlásek advanced to the quarterfinals, upsetting fifth-seeded Santiago González and Neal Skupski. His performance in the 2024 Madrid Masters was even more remarkable, as he and Pavlásek reached their first Masters 1000 final, defeating several top teams, including third seeds Joe Salisbury and Neal Skupski, before losing to Sebastian Korda and Jordan Thompson. This success pushed Behar into the top 35 of the rankings. He also reached another final at the Japan Open with Robert Galloway, losing to Julian Cash and Lloyd Glasspool.

Throughout his career, Behar has proven to be a strong competitor in doubles, with a record of 6–12 against top-10-ranked players. He has accumulated 15 ATP finals appearances, winning three titles, and has won 27 Challenger and Futures doubles events. His success in both lower-tier and high-profile tournaments demonstrates his consistency and adaptability. Behar has also represented Uruguay in the Davis Cup since 2009, contributing to his country’s international tennis presence. His journey from a young aspiring player to a top-ranked doubles specialist highlights his dedication and skill in the sport.

title: DeAnna Bennett
text:
DeAnna Danielle Bennett, born on November 18, 1984, is an American mixed martial artist who has competed in the Flyweight division. She began her professional MMA career in 2012 and has fought for major promotions like Bellator, Invicta Fighting Championships, and the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC). Before entering MMA, Bennett wrestled and played water polo at American High School, graduating in 2002. She briefly attended an art college but dropped out. Her motivation to get into martial arts came from her desire to stay in shape, leading her to kickboxing and eventually Muay Thai.

Bennett made her professional MMA debut in 2012 with Showdown Fights, where she won all four of her fights, including notable victories over Sharon Jacobson, Colleen Schneider, and Julianna Peña. She then transitioned to Invicta FC, making her debut in 2014. Her first fight in the promotion was against Michelle Ould, whom she defeated by second-round TKO.
